Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Mahāvaṃsapāḷi

The Pāḷi of the Great Chronicle

Pathamapariccheda

The First Chapter

Mahiyaṅgaṇāgamanaṃ

The Visit to Mahiyangana

1.

1.

Namassitvāna [M 0.0001] sambuddhaṃ, susuddhaṃ suddhavaṃsajaṃ;

Mahāvaṃsaṃ pavakkhāmi, nānānūnādhikārikaṃ.

Having paid homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supremely pure, born of a pure lineage, I shall recite the Mahāvaṃsa, which is free from the various faults of being deficient or excessive.

2.

2.

Porāṇehi kato’peso, ativitthārito kvaci;

Atīva kvaci saṃkhitto, anekapunaruttako.

For this work, composed by the ancients, is in some places too detailed and in others too brief, and it contains many repetitions.

3.

3.

Vajjitaṃ tehi dosehi, sukhaggahaṇadhāraṇaṃ;

Pasādasaṃvegakaraṃ, sutito ca upāgataṃ.

Free from those faults, easy to grasp and remember, arousing serene faith and spiritual urgency, and handed down by tradition,

4.

4.

Pasādajanake ṭhāne, tathā saṃvegakārake;

Janayanto pasādañca, saṃvegañca suṇātha taṃ.

Listen, then, to this work, which arouses serene faith and spiritual urgency in appropriate places.

5.

5.

Dīpaṅkarañhi sambuddhaṃ, passitvā no jino purā;

Lokaṃ dukkhā pamocetuṃ, bodhāya paṇidhiṃ akā.

In the past, our Victor, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One Dīpaṅkara, made the aspiration for enlightenment in order to liberate the world from suffering.

6.

6.

Tato tañceva sambuddhaṃ, koṇḍaññaṃ maṅgalaṃ muniṃ;

Sumanaṃ revataṃ buddhaṃ, sobhitañca mahāmuniṃ.

Then from that same Perfectly Enlightened One, Koṇḍañña, from the sage Maṅgala, from Sumana, from the Buddha Revata, and from the great sage Sobhita;

7.

7.

Anomadassiṃ sambuddhaṃ, padumaṃ nāradaṃ jinaṃ;

Padumuttarasambuddhaṃ, sumedhañca tathāgataṃ.

from the Perfectly Enlightened One Anomadassī, from Paduma, from the Victor Nārada, from the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara, and from the Tathāgata Sumedha;

8.

8.

Sujātaṃ piyadassiñca, atthadassiñca nāyakaṃ;

Dhammadassiñca siddhatthaṃ, tissaṃ phussajinaṃ tathā.

from Sujāta and Piyadassī, from the leader Atthadassī, from Dhammadassī and Siddhattha, and likewise from Tissa and the Victor Phussa;

9.

9.

Vipassiṃ sikhīsambuddhaṃ, sambuddhaṃ vessabhuṃ vibhuṃ;

Kakusandhañca sambuddhaṃ, koṇāgamanameva ca.

from Vipassī, from the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhī, from the Lord, the Perfectly Enlightened One Vessabhū, from the Perfectly Enlightened One Kakusandha, and also from Koṇāgamana;

10.

10.

Kassapaṃ sugatañca’me, sambuddhe catuvīsati;

Ārādhetvā mahāvīro, tehi bodhāya byākato.

and from the Well-farer Kassapa—having won the favor of these twenty-four Perfectly Enlightened Ones, the great hero was by them given the prophecy of his enlightenment.

11.

11.

Puretvā [M 0.0002] pāramī sabbā, patvā sambodhimuttamaṃ;

Uttamo gotamo buddho, satte dukkhā pamocayi.

Having fulfilled all the perfections and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, the supreme Buddha Gotama liberated beings from suffering.

12.

12.

Magadhesu ruvelāyaṃ, bodhimūle mahāmuni;

Visākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ so, patto sambodhimuttamaṃ.

In the land of Magadha, at Uruvelā, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the great sage attained supreme perfect enlightenment on the full-moon day of the month of Visākha.

13.

13.

Sattāhāni tahiṃ satta, so vimuttisukhaṃ paraṃ;

Vindantaṃ madhurattañca, dassayanto vasī vasi.

For seven weeks the Master dwelt there, experiencing the supreme bliss of liberation and showing forth its sweetness.

14.

14.

Tato bārāṇasiṃ gantvā, dhammacakkaṃ pagattayi;

Tattha vassa vasanto’va, saṭṭhiṃ arahataṃ akā.

Then, going to Bārāṇasī, he set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma. While dwelling there for the rains-residence, he made sixty men Arahants.

15.

15.

Te dhammadesanatthāya, vissajjetvāna bhikkhavo;

Vinetvā ca tato tiṃsa-sahā ye bhaddavaggiye.

Having sent forth those bhikkhus for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, he then disciplined the thirty companions of the Bhaddavaggiya group.

16.

16.

Sahassajaṭile nātho, vinetuṃ kassapādike;

Hemante uruvelāyaṃ, vasite paripācayaṃ.

In order to discipline the thousand matted-hair ascetics headed by the Kassapas, the Lord dwelt in Uruvelā during the winter, bringing them to maturity.

17.

17.

Uruvelakassapassa, mahāyaññe upaṭṭhite;

Tassa’ttano nāgamane, icchācāraṃ vijāniya.

When the great sacrifice of Uruvela Kassapa was imminent, knowing his wish that he himself would not come,

18.

18.

Uttarakuruto bhikkhaṃ, āharitvā rimaddano;

Anotattadahe bhutvā, sāyanhasamaye sayaṃ.

the Subduer of Foes brought his alms-food from Uttarakuru, ate it by Lake Anotatta, and in the evening, he himself—

19.

19.

Bodhito navame māse, phussapuṇṇamiyaṃ jino;

Laṅkādīpaṃ visodhetuṃ, laṅkādīpamupāgami.

in the ninth month after his enlightenment, on the full-moon day of Phussa, the Victor went to the island of Laṅkā in order to purify it.

20.

20.

Sāsanujjotanaṃ ṭhānaṃ, laṃkā ñātā jinena hi;

Yakkhapuṇṇāya laṅkāya, yakkhā nibbā siyāti ca.

For it was known to the Victor that Laṅkā was a place where the Dispensation would shine, and that the yakkhas had to be expelled from Laṅkā, which was filled with them.

21.

21.

Ñātova laṅkāmajjhamhi, gaṅgābhīre manorame;

Tiyojanāya te ramme, ekayojanavitthate.

It was also known that in the middle of Laṅkā, on the charming bank of the river, in a pleasant spot three yojanas long and one yojana wide,

22.

22.

Mahānāgavanuyyāne, yakkhasaṅgāmabhūmiyā;

Laṅkādīpaṭṭhayakkhānaṃ, mahāyakkhasamāgamo.

in the Mahānāga garden, the meeting place of the yakkhas, there was a great assembly of the yakkhas dwelling on the island of Laṅkā.

23.

23.

Upāgato taṃ sugato, mahāyakkhasamāgamaṃ;

Samāgamassa majjhamhi, tattha tesaṃ siropari.

The Well-farer went to that great assembly of yakkhas. There, in the midst of that assembly, above their heads,

24.

24.

Mahiyaṅgaṇathūpassa, ṭhāne vehāyasaṃ jino;

Vuṭṭhivātandhakāresi, tesaṃ saṃvejanaṃ akā.

at the place of the Mahiyangana Thūpa, the Victor hovered in the air. He created rain, wind, and darkness, causing them terror.

25.

25.

Te bhayaṭṭhā’bhayaṃ yakkhā, ayācuṃ abhayaṃ jinaṃ;

Jino abhayado āha, yakkhe te’ti bhayaddīte.

Those yakkhas, stricken with terror, begged the Victor for safety. The Victor, the giver of safety, said to those fear-stricken yakkhas:

26.

26.

Yakkhā [M 0.0003] bhayaṃ vo dukkhañca, harissāmi idaṃ ahaṃ;

Tumhe nisajjaṭhānaṃ me, samaggā detha no idha.

“O yakkhas, I will remove this fear and distress of yours. All of you together, give me a place here to sit down.”

27.

27.

Āhu te sugataṃ yakkhā, dema mārisa te idha;

Sabbepi sakalaṃ dīpaṃ, dehi no abhayaṃ tuvaṃ.

Those yakkhas said to the Well-farer: ‘Sir, we give you this entire island. You, grant us safety!’

28.

28.

Bhayaṃ sītaṃ tamaṃ tesaṃ, hantvā taṃ dinnabhūmiyaṃ;

Cammakkhandhaṃ attharitvā, tatthā’ sīno jino tato.

Then the Victor, having dispelled their fear, cold, and darkness, spread out his leather rug on the ground that was given to him and sat down there.

29.

29.

Cammakkhaṇḍaṃ pasāresi, ādittaṃ taṃ samantato;

Ghammābhibhūtā te bhītā, ṭhitā ante samantato.

He caused the leather rug to spread out, blazing all around. Overcome by the heat and terrified, they stood on the border all around.

30.

30.

Giridīpaṃ tato nātho, rammaṃ tesaṃ idhā’nayi;

Tesu tattha paviṭṭhesu, yathāṭhāne ṭhapesi ca.

Then the Lord brought the pleasant island of Giri here for them. When they had entered it, he restored it to its former place.

31.

31.

Nātho taṃ saṃkhipi dhammaṃ, tadā devā samāgamuṃ;

Tasmiṃ samāgame tesaṃ, satthā dhamma madesayi.

When the Lord had folded up his leather rug, the devas assembled. In that assembly, the Teacher taught them the Dhamma.

32.

32.

Nekesaṃ pāṇakoṭīnaṃ, dhammābhisamayo ahu;

Saraṇesu ca sīlesu, ṭhitā āsuṃ asaṃkhiyā.

The penetration of the Dhamma occurred for many crores of living beings, and a countless number were established in the refuges and the precepts.

33.

33.

Sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā, sele sumanakūṭake;

Mahāsumanadevindo, pūjiyaṃ yāci pūjiyaṃ.

The great deva-king Mahāsumana of the Sumanakūṭa mountain, who had attained the fruit of stream-entry, asked the One Worthy of Worship for something to worship.

34.

34.

Siraṃ parāmasitvāna, nīlāmalasiroruho;

Pāṇimatteadā kese, tassa pāṇa hito jino.

The Victor, who is devoted to the welfare of beings, stroked his head with its dark, pure hair and gave him a handful of hairs.

35.

35.

So taṃ suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭa-varenādāya satthuno;

Nisinnaṭṭhānaracite, nānāratanasañcaye.

Having received them from the Teacher, he placed them in a superb golden casket on a heap of various jewels that was piled up on the spot where the Teacher had been seated.

36.

36.

Sabbato sattaratane, te ṭhapetvā siroruhe;

So indanīlathūpena, pidahesi namassi ca.

Having enshrined the hairs on that pile of the seven kinds of gems, he covered them over with a stūpa made of sapphire and paid homage.

37.

37.

Parinibbutamhi sambuddhe, citakato ca iddhiyā;

Ādāya jinagīvaṭṭhiṃ, thero sarabhūnāmako.

When the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained Parinibbāna, the elder named Sarabhū, by his psychic power, took the collar-bone relic of the Victor from the funeral pyre.

38.

38.

Therassa sāriputtassa, sisso ānīya cetiye;

Tasmiṃyeva ṭhapetvāna, bhikkhūhi parivārito.

A pupil of the Elder Sāriputta, he, surrounded by bhikkhus, brought it and enshrined it in that same cetiya.

39.

39.

Chādāpetvā medavaṇṇa-pāsāṇehi mahiddhiko;

Thūpaṃ dvādasahatthuccaṃ, kārāpetvāna pakkami.

The one of great psychic power had it covered over with stones the color of ghee, had a stūpa built twelve cubits high, and then he departed.

40.

40.

Devānaṃpiyatissassa, rañño bhātukudhārako;

Uddhacūḷābhayo nāma, disvā cetiya mabbhutaṃ.

The younger brother of King Devānampiyatissa, named Uddhacūḷābhaya, saw the wonderful cetiya,

41.

41.

Taṃ [M 0.0004] chādayitvā kāresi, tiṃsahatthucca cetiyaṃ;

Maddanto damiḷe rājā, tatraṭṭho dukkhagāmaṇi.

and had it covered over, making it into a cetiya thirty cubits high. Later, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi, while dwelling there subduing the Damiḷas,

42.

42.

Asītihatthaṃ kāresi, tassa kañjukacetiyaṃ;

Mahiyaṅgaṇathūpoya-meso evaṃ patiṭṭhito.

had a mantle-cetiya built over it eighty cubits high. Thus was the Mahiyangana Thūpa established.

43.

43.

Evaṃ dīpamimaṃkatvā, manussārahamissaro;

Uruvelamagā dhīro, uruvīra parakkamoti.

Thus the Lord, the Wise One of great heroic energy, having made this island fit for human habitation, went to Uruvelā.

Mahiyaṅgaṇāgamanaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Visit to Mahiyangana is concluded.

Nāgadīpāgamana

The Visit to Nāgadīpa

44.

44.

Mahākāruṇiko satthā, sabbalokahite rato;

Bodhito pañcame vasse, vasaṃ jetavane jino.

The Teacher, greatly compassionate, delighting in the welfare of all the world, the Conqueror, was dwelling in the Jeta's Grove in the fifth year after his Awakening.

45.

45.

Mahodarassa nāgassa, tathā cūḷodarassa ca;

Mātulabhāgineyyānaṃ, maṇipallaṅkahetukaṃ.

On account of a jeweled throne, a battle was impending between the nāga Mahodara and Cūḷodara, who were uncle and nephew.

46.

46.

Disvā sapārisajjānaṃ, saṅgāmaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ;

Sambuddho cittamāsassa, kāḷapakkhe uposathe.

The Perfectly Enlightened One, seeing the battle at hand for them and their retinues, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight in the month of Citta,

47.

47.

Pātoyeva samādāya, pavaraṃ pattacīvaraṃ;

Anukampāya nāgānaṃ, nāgadīpamupāgami.

taking his excellent bowl and robe early in the morning, out of compassion for the nāgas, went to Nāgadīpa.

48.

48.

Mahādaro’piso nāgo, tadā rājā ahiddhiko;

Samudde nāgabhavane, dasaddhasatayojane.

That nāga Mahodara was then a king of great psychic power in his nāga-abode in the ocean, which was five hundred yojanas in extent.

49.

49.

Kaṇiṭṭhikā tassa kaṇhā, vaḍḍhamānamhi pabbate;

Nāgarājassa dinnā’si, tassa cūḷodaro suto.

His youngest sister, Kaṇhā, had been given to the nāga king of Mount Vaḍḍhamāna; Cūḷodara was their son.

50.

50.

Tassa mātā mahāmātu, maṇipallaṅkamuttamaṃ;

Datvā kālakatā nāgī, mātulena tathā hi so.

His mother's father had given his mother the excellent jeweled throne; after that nāgī passed away, a conflict arose for her son with his uncle.

51.

51.

Ahosi bhāgineyyassa, saṅgāmo paccupaṭṭhito;

Pabbateyyā’pi nāgā te, ahesuñhi mahiddhikā.

A battle was at hand for the nephew. And those nāgas from the mountain were also of great psychic power.

52.

52.

Samiddhisumano nāma, devo jetavane ṭhitaṃ;

Rājāyatanamādāya, attano bhavanaṃ subhaṃ.

A deva named Samiddhisumana, taking the Rājāyatana tree that stood in Jetavana, his own beautiful abode,

53.

53.

Buddhānumatiyāyeva, chattākāraṃ jinopari;

Dhārayanto upāgañchi, ṭhānaṃ taṃ pubbavuṭṭhakaṃ.

with the Buddha's consent, holding it like a canopy over the Conqueror, approached that place of his former dwelling.

54.

54.

Devo [M 0.0005] hi so nāgadīpe, manusso’nantare bhave;

Ahosi rājāyatana-ṭhitaṭhāne sa addasa.

For in his immediately preceding existence, that deva had been a human being in Nāgadīpa. At the place where a rājāyatana tree stood, he saw

55.

55.

Paccekabuddha bhuñjante, disvā cittaṃ pasādiya;

Pattasodhanasākhāyo, tesaṃ pādāsi tena so.

Seeing Paccekabuddhas eating, his mind became serene; therefore, he gave them branches for cleaning their bowls.

56.

56.

Nibbattitasmiṃ rukkhasmiṃ, jetuyyāne manorame;

Dvārakoṭṭhakapassamhi, pacchā bahi ahosi so.

As a result, he was reborn as that tree in the delightful Jeta's Grove, near the gate-tower; later it stood outside.

57.

57.

Devātidevo devassa, tassa vuddhiñca passiya;

Idaṃ ṭhāna hitatthañca, taṃ sarukkhaṃ idhānayi.

The Deva above devas, seeing the spiritual progress of that deva and for the welfare of this place, had him come here together with his tree.

58.

58.

Saṅgāmamajjhe ākāse, nisinno tattha nāyako;

Tamaṃ tamonudo tesaṃ, nāgānaṃ hiṃsanaṃ akā.

Seated there in the sky in the midst of the battlefield, the Leader, the Dispeller of Darkness, created a terrifying darkness for those nāgas.

59.

59.

Assāsento bhayaṭṭe te, ālokaṃ paviddhaṃsayi;

Te disvā sugataṃ tuṭṭhā, pāde vandiṃsu satthuno.

Comforting them who were stricken with fear, he then shed forth light. Seeing the Well-farer, they were pleased and worshipped the Teacher's feet.

60.

60.

Tesaṃ dhammamadesesi, sāmaggikaraṇaṃ jino;

Ubho’pi te patītā taṃ, pallaṅkaṃ munino aduṃ.

The Conqueror taught them the Dhamma that leads to concord; both of them, delighted, offered the throne to the Sage.

61.

61.

Satthā bhūmigato tattha, pasīdisvāna āsane;

Tehi dibbannapānehi, nāgarājehi tappito.

The Teacher, having alighted there, sat upon the throne; and he was satisfied by the nāga kings with divine food and drink.

62.

62.

Te jalaṭṭhe talaṭṭhe ca, bhujage’sītikoṭiyo;

Saraṇesu ca sīlesu, patiṭṭhāpesi nāyako.

The Leader established eighty crores of those serpents, both water-dwelling and land-dwelling, in the Refuges and the Precepts.

63.

63.

Mahodarassa nāgassa, mātulo maṇiakkhiko;

Kalyāṇiyaṃ nāgarājā, yuddhaṃ kātuṃ tahiṃ gato.

The uncle of the nāga Mahodara was Maṇiakkhika, the nāga king of Kalyāṇī, who had gone there to do battle.

64.

64.

Buddhagāmamhi paṭhame, sutvā saddhammadesanaṃ;

Ṭhito saraṇasīlesu, tatthā’yāci tathāgataṃ.

Having heard the exposition of the true Dhamma during the Buddha's first visit, he became established in the refuges and precepts, and there he made a request of the Tathāgata:

65.

65.

Mahatī anukampāno, katā nātha tayā ayaṃ;

Tavānāgamane sabbe, mayaṃ bhasmī bhavāmahe.

"Great compassion has been shown by you to us, O Protector! Had you not come, we all would have been turned to ashes."

66.

66.

Anukampā mahī pite, visuṃ hotu mahodaya;

Punarāgamanenettha, vāsabhūmiṃ mamā mama.

"O Greatly Compassionate One, may your compassion be especially upon me. By coming here again, may you grace this my dwelling place."

67.

67.

Adhivāsayitvā bhagavā, tuṇhibhāve nidhāgamaṃ;

Patiṭṭhāpesi tattheva, rājāyatanacetiyaṃ.

The Blessed One consented to a future visit by his silence. He then established the Rājāyatana Cetiya right there.

68.

68.

Tañcapi [M 0.0006] rājāyatanaṃ, pallañcaṅka mahārahaṃ;

Appesi nāgarājūnaṃ, lokanātho namassituṃ.

And that Rājāyatana shrine and the priceless throne the Lord of the World gave to the nāga kings to worship.

69.

69.

Paribhogacetiyaṃ mayhaṃ, nāgarājā namassatha;

Taṃ bhavissati votātā, hitāya ca sukhāya ca.

"O nāga kings, you should worship this shrine of things I have used. That, my dears, will be for your welfare and happiness."

70.

70.

Iccevamādiṃ sugato, nāgānaṃ anusāsanaṃ;

Katvā jetavanaṃ eva, gato lokānukampakoti.

Having given this and other instructions to the nāgas, the Well-farer, the Compassionate One to the World, went back to Jetavana.

Nāgadīpāgamanaṃ

The Visit to Nāgadīpa

Kalyāṇāgamanaṃ

The Visit to Kalyāṇī

71.

71.

Tato so tatiye vasse,

Nāgindo maṇiakkhiko;

Upasaṅkamma sambuddhaṃ,

Satasaṅghaṃ nimantayi.

Then, in the third year, the Nāga Lord Maṇiakkhika approached the Perfectly Enlightened One and invited him together with the Saṅgha.

72.

72.

Bodhito aṭṭhame vasse, vasaṃ jetavane jino;

Nātho pañcahi bhikkhūnaṃ, satehi parivārito.

In the eighth year after his Awakening, the Conqueror was dwelling in Jetavana. The Protector, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus,

73.

73.

Dutiye divase bhatta-kāle ārocite jino;

Ramme vesākhamāsamhi, puṇṇamāyaṃ munissaro.

When the mealtime was announced on the next day—on the full-moon day of the beautiful month of Vesākha—the Lord of Sages,

74.

74.

Tattheva pārupitvāna, saṅghāṭiṃ pattamādiya;

Āgā kalyāṇidesaṃ taṃ, maṇiakkhinivesanaṃ.

Putting on his outer robe and taking his bowl, he went to that land of Kalyāṇī, the abode of Maṇiakkhika.

75.

75.

Kalyāṇi cetiyaṭhāne, kate ratanamaṇḍape;

Mahārahamhi pallaṅke, sahasaṅghenu’pāvisi.

At the site of the Kalyāṇī Cetiya, in a jeweled pavilion that had been prepared, he sat down with the Saṅgha on a priceless throne.

76.

76.

Dibbehi khajjabhojjehi, sagaṇo sagaṇaṃ jinaṃ;

Nāgarājā dhammarājaṃ, santappesi sumānaso.

With divine hard and soft foods, the nāga king, with a joyful mind, satisfied the King of Dhamma and his retinue.

77.

77.

Tattha dhammaṃ desayitvā, satthā lonukampako;

Uggantvā sumane kūṭe, padaṃ dassesi nāyako.

Having taught the Dhamma there, the Teacher, compassionate to the world, ascended Sumanakūṭa peak, and there the Leader left his footprint.

78.

78.

Tasmiṃ pabbatapādamhi, sahasaṅgho yathāsukhaṃ;

Divā vihāraṃ katvāna, dīghavāpi mupāgami.

At the foot of that mountain, he and the Saṅgha spent the day in comfort. Then he went to Dīghavāpi.

79.

79.

Tattha [M 0.0007] cetiyaṭhānamhi, sasaṅghova nisīdiya;

Samādhiṃ appayī nātho, ṭhānāgāravapattiyā.

There, at the site for the cetiya, the Protector sat down together with the Saṅgha and entered into an attainment of concentration, out of respect for the place.

80.

80.

Tato vuṭṭhāya ṭhānamhā, ṭhānāṭhānesu kovido;

Mahāmeghavanārāma-ṭhānamāga mahāmuni.

Then, rising from that state, the Great Sage, who is skilled in what is a proper place and what is not, went to the site of the Mahāmeghavana Park.

81.

81.

Mahābodhiṭhitaṭhāne, nisīditvā sasāvako;

Samādhiṃ appayī nātho, mahāthūpaṭhite tathā.

He sat down with his disciples at the place of the future Great Bodhi tree and entered into concentration; likewise he did at the place of the future Great Thūpa.

82.

82.

Thūpārāmamhi thūpassa, ṭhitaṭhāne tatheva ca;

Samādhito’tha vuṭṭhāya, silācetiyaṭhānago.

He did the same at the future site of the thūpa in the Thūpārāma. Then, rising from his concentration, he went to the site of the future Silācetiya.

83.

83.

Sahāgate devagaṇo, gaṇī samanusāsiya;

Tato jetavanaṃ buddho, buddhasabbatthako agā.

Having instructed the hosts of devas who had assembled there, the Leader of the Order, the Buddha, benefactor in all matters, then went to Jetavana.

84.

84.

Evaṃ laṅkāya nātho, hitamamitamatī āyatiṃ pekkhamāno;

Tasmiṃ kālamhi laṃkāsurabhujagagaṇādīnamatthañca passaṃ;

Āgā tikkhattumetaṃ ativipuladayo lokadīpo sudīpaṃ;

Dīpo tenāyamāsi sujanabahumano dhammadīpāva bhāsīti.

Thus the Protector of Laṅkā, with a mind of immeasurable benevolence, foreseeing the future, and seeing the welfare of the hosts of asuras, nāgas, and others in Laṅkā, he, the Light of the World, of exceedingly vast compassion, came three times to this excellent island. Through him this island became highly esteemed by the virtuous, shining forth like the very Island of the Dhamma.

Kalyāṇāgamanaṃ

The Visit to Kalyāṇī

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Great Chronicle, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people.

Tathāgatābhigamanaṃ nāma

The Chapter named 'The Visits of the Tathāgata'

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

Dutiyapariccheda

The Second Chapter

Mahāsammatavaṃsa

The Lineage of Mahāsammata

1.

1.

Mahāsammata [M 0.0008] rājassa, vaṃsajo hi mahāmuni;

Kappassādimhi rājā’si, mahāsammatanāmako.

The great sage was a descendant of King Mahāsammata. At the beginning of the aeon, there was a king named Mahāsammata.

2.

2.

Rojo ca vararojo ca, tathā kalyāṇakā duve;

Uposatho ca mandhātā, carako’pacarā duve.

Roja and Vararoja, and likewise the two Kalyāṇakas; Uposatha and Mandhātā, and the two, Caraka and Upacara.

3.

3.

Cetīyo mucalo ceva, mahāmūcalanāmako;

Mucalindo sāgaro ceva, sāgaro deva vanāmako.

Cetiya and Mucala, and the one named Mahāmucala; Mucalinda and Sāgara, and the one named Sāgaradeva.

4.

4.

Bharato bhagīratho ceva, ruci ca suruci pica;

Patāpo mahāpatāpo, panādā ca tathā duve.

Bharata and Bhagīratha, and also Ruci and Suruci; Patāpa and Mahāpatāpa, and likewise the two Panādas.

5.

5.

Sudassano ca neru ca, tathā eva duve duve;

Pacchimā cā’ti rājāno, tassa puttapaputtakā.

Sudassana and Neru, and likewise two of each; and Pacchima—these kings were his sons and grandsons.

6.

6.

Asaṃkhiyāyukā ete, aṭṭhavīsati bhūmipā;

Kusāvatiṃ rājagahaṃ, mithilañcāpi āvasuṃ.

These twenty-eight rulers had immeasurable lifespans; they dwelt in Kusāvatī, Rājagaha, and also in Mithilā.

7.

7.

Tato satañca rājano, chappaññāsa ca saṭṭhi ca;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, chattiṃsā ca tato pare.

Then there were one hundred kings, and fifty-six, and sixty; eighty-four thousand, and thirty-six thereafter.

8.

8.

Dvattiṃsa aṭṭhavīsā ca, dvāvīsati tato pare;

Aṭṭhārasa sattarasa, pañcadasa catuddasa.

Thirty-two and twenty-eight, and twenty-two thereafter; eighteen, seventeen, fifteen, fourteen.

9.

9.

Nava satta dvādasa ca, pañcavīsa tatopare;

Pañcavīsaṃ dvādasa ca, dvādasañca navā pica.

Nine, seven, and twelve, and twenty-five thereafter; twenty-five and twelve, and twelve and nine as well.

10.

10.

Caturāsītisahassāni, makhādevādikāpi ca;

Caturāsītisahassāni, kaḷārājanakādayo.

Eighty-four thousand, beginning with Makhādeva; and eighty-four thousand, beginning with Kaḷārajanaka.

11.

11.

Soḷasa yāva okkātaṃ, paputtā rāsito ime;

Visuṃ visuṃ pure rajjaṃ, kamato anusāsisuṃ.

Sixteen descendants down to Okkāka, this line of kings, each in his own city, ruled the kingdom in succession.

12.

12.

Okkāmukho jeṭṭhaputto, okkākasā’si bhūpati;

Nipuro candīmā candaṃ-mukho ca sivi sañjayo.

Okkāmukha was the eldest son of King Okkāka. Then came Nipura, Candimā, Candamukha, Sivi, and Sañjaya.

13.

13.

Vessantara [M 0.0009] mahārājā, jālī ca sīhavāhano;

Sīhassaro ca iccete, tassa putta pa puttakā.

The great king Vessantara, Jāli, and Sīhavāhana; and Sīhassara—these were his sons and grandsons.

14.

14.

Dveasīti sahassāni, sīhassarassa rājino;

Putta pa putta rājāno, jayaseno tadantimo.

Eighty-two thousand descendants of King Sīhassara were kings, son after grandson; Jayasena was the last of them.

15.

15.

Ete kapilavatthusmiṃ, sakyarājāti vissutā;

Sīhahanu mahārājā, jayasenassa atrajo.

These were renowned as the Sakyan kings in Kapilavatthu. The great king Sīhahanu was the son of Jayasena.

16.

16.

Jayasenassa dhītā ca, nāmenā’si yasodharā;

Devadaye devadaha-sakko nāmā’si bhūpati.

Jayasena also had a daughter named Yasodharā. In Devadaha there was a Sakyan king named Devadaha.

17.

17.

Añjano cā’tha kaccānā, āsuṃ tassa sutā duve;

Mahesīcā’si kaccānā, rañño sīhahanussa sā.

Añjana and Kaccānā were his two children. That Kaccānā was the chief queen of King Sīhahanu.

18.

18.

Āsī añjanasakkassa, mahesī sā yasodharā;

Añjanassa duve dhītā, māyā cātha pajāpati.

That Yasodharā was the chief queen of the Sakyan Añjana. Añjana had two daughters: Māyā and Pajāpati.

19.

19.

Puttā duve daṇḍapāṇī, suppabuddho ca sākiyo;

Pañca puttā duve dhītā, āsuṃ sīhahanussare.

He also had two sons, Daṇḍapāṇi and the Sakyan Suppabuddha. Sīhahanu had five sons and two daughters.

20.

20.

Suddhodano dhotodano, sakkasukkamitodano;

Amitā pamitācā’ti, ime pañca imā duve.

Suddhodana, Dhotodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, and Amitodana; and Amitā and Pamitā. These were the five sons and two daughters.

21.

21.

Suppabuddhassa sakkassa, mahesī amitā ahu;

Tassā’suṃ bhaddakaccānā, devadatto duve sutā.

The chief queen of the Sakyan Suppabuddha was Amitā. Her two children were Bhaddakaccānā and Devadatta.

22.

22.

Māyā mahāpajāpati ceva, suddhodana mahesīyo;

Suddhodana mahārañño, putto māyāya so jino.

Māyā and Mahāpajāpatī were the chief queens of Suddhodana. The Victor was the son of the great king Suddhodana by Māyā.

23.

23.

Mahā sammatavaṃsamhi, asambhinne mahāmuni;

Evaṃ pavatte sañjāto, sabba khatthiya muddhani.

The great sage was born in this unbroken lineage of Mahāsammata, thus established, at the head of all khattiyas.

24.

24.

Siddhatthassa kumārassa, bodhisattassa sā ahu;

Mahesī bhaddakaccānā, putto tassā’si rāhulo.

Bhaddakaccānā was the chief queen of Prince Siddhattha, the Bodhisatta. Her son was Rāhula.

25.

25.

Bimbisāro ca siddhattha-kumāro ca sahāyakā;

Ubhinnaṃ pitaro cāpi, sahāyāeva te ahuṃ.

Bimbisāra and Prince Siddhattha were companions, and their fathers were also companions.

26.

26.

Bodhisatto bimbisārā, pañcavassādhiko ahu;

Ekūnatiṃso vayasā, bodhisatto’bhinikkhami.

The Bodhisatta was five years older than Bimbisāra. At the age of twenty-nine, the Bodhisatta went forth.

27.

27.

Padahitvāna [M 0.0010] chabbassaṃ, bodhiṃ patvā kamena ca;

Pañcatiṃso tha vayasā, bimbisāramupāgami.

Having striven for six years and attained enlightenment in due course, he then, at the age of thirty-five, went to Bimbisāra.

28.

28.

Bimbisāro pannarasa-vasso’tha pītaraṃ sayaṃ;

Abhisitto mahāpañño, patto rajjassa tassa tu.

The very wise Bimbisāra, at fifteen years of age, was anointed by his father himself and attained the kingship.

29.

29.

Patte soḷasame vasse, satthā dhammamadesayi;

Dvāpaññāseva vassāni, rajjaṃ kāresi so pana.

In the sixteenth year of his reign, the Teacher taught him the Dhamma. He, for his part, ruled the kingdom for fifty-two years.

30.

30.

Rajje samā pannarasa, pubbe jinasamāgamā;

Sattatiṃsa samā tassa, dharamāne tathāgate.

Fifteen years of his reign passed before his meeting with the Victor; thirty-seven years passed while the Tathāgata was still living.

31.

31.

Bimbisārasuto’jāta-sattutaṃ ghātīyā’mati;

Rajjaṃ dvattiṃsavassāni, mahāmittaddukārayī.

Bimbisāra's son, the senseless Ajātasattu, killed him and, that great betrayer of his friend, ruled the kingdom for thirty-two years.

32.

32.

Ajātasattuno vasse, aṭṭhame muni nibbuto;

Pacchā so kārayī rajjaṃ, vassāni catuvīsati.

In the eighth year of Ajātasattu's reign, the Sage attained final Nibbāna. Afterwards, he ruled the kingdom for twenty-four years.

33.

33.

Tathāgato sakalalokaggataṃ gato;

Aniccatāva samavaso upāgato;

Iti’dha yo bhayajananiṃ aniccataṃ,

Avekkhate sa bhavati dukkhapāragūti.

The Tathāgata has gone to the summit of the whole world; he has come under the sway of impermanence. Whoever here contemplates impermanence, the producer of fear, becomes one who has gone beyond suffering.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of the virtuous.

Mahāsammatavaṃso nāma

Entitled: The Lineage of the Great Elect

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Chapter.

Tatiya pariccheda

The Third Chapter

Paṭhamadhammasaṃgīti

The First Dhamma Council

1.

1.

Pañcanetto [M 0.0011] jino pañca-cattālīsasamā’samo;

Ṭhatvā sabbāni kiccāni, katvā lokassa sabbathā.

The peerless Victor with the five eyes, having abided for forty-five years and completed all his duties for the world in every way,

2.

2.

Kusinārāyayamaka-sālānamantare vare;

Vesākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ so, dīpo lokassa nibbuto.

in Kusinārā, between the excellent pair of sāla trees, on the full-moon day of Vesākha, he, the lamp of the world, was extinguished.

3.

3.

Saṅkhyāpathamatikkantā, bhikkhū tattha samāgatā;

Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vassā, suddhā devā tatheva ca.

Innumerable bhikkhus gathered there, as did khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, and devas likewise.

4.

4.

Sattasatasahassāni, tesu pāmokkhabhikkhavo;

Thero mahākassapova, saṅghatthero tadā ahu.

Among them were seven hundred thousand principal bhikkhus. The Elder Mahākassapa himself was at that time the Elder of the Saṅgha.

5.

5.

Satthusarīrasārīra-dhātukiccāni kāriya;

Icchanto so mahāthero, satthu dhammaciraṭṭhitiṃ.

That great elder, having caused the rites for the Teacher's bodily relics to be performed, and desiring the long endurance of the Teacher's Dhamma,

6.

6.

Lokanāthe dasabale, sattāhaparinibbute;

Dubbhāsitaṃ subhaddassa, buddhassa vacanaṃ saraṃ.

and recalling the wrongly spoken word of the old Subhadda, seven days after the Lord of the World, the Ten-Powered One, had attained final Nibbāna,

7.

7.

Saraṃ cīvaradānañca, samatte ṭhapanaṃ tathā;

Saddhammaṭhapanatthāya, muninā’nuggahaṃ kataṃ.

and recalling also the favor done by the Sage for the sake of establishing the good Dhamma—the gift of the robe and likewise his appointment to a state of equality—

8.

8.

Kātuṃ saddhammasaṃgītiṃ, sambuddhānamate yati;

Navaṅgasāsanadhare, sabbaṅgasamupāgate.

The ascetic resolved to hold a council of the good Dhamma in accordance with the intention of the Perfectly Enlightened One, with those who were bearers of the nine-factored Teaching and endowed with all its components.

9.

9.

Bhikkhū pañcasateyeva, mahākhīṇāsave vare;

Sammanni ekenūne tu, ānandattherakāraṇā.

He selected five hundred excellent bhikkhus, great ones whose taints were destroyed, but the number was one short on account of the Elder Ānanda.

10.

10.

Puna ānandattherā’pi, bhikkhūhi abhiyācito;

Sammanni kātuṃ saṃgītiṃ, sā na sakkā hi taṃ vinā.

Then, at the request of the bhikkhus, he also selected the Elder Ānanda, for indeed the council could not be held without him.

11.

11.

Sādhukīḷanasattāhaṃ, sattāhaṃ dhātubhājanaṃ;

Iccaddhamāsaṃ khepetvā, sabbalokānukampakā.

Those elders, compassionate to the whole world, having spent a week in festive homage and a week in distributing the relics, thus passing half a month,

12.

12.

Vassaṃ vasaṃ rājagahe, kassāma dhammasaṅgahaṃ;

Nāññehi tatta vatthabba-miti katvāna nicchayaṃ.

made the decision: 'We shall spend the rains residence in Rājagaha and make a compilation of the Dhamma. No others should reside there.'

13.

13.

Sokāturaṃ [M 0.0012] tattha tattha, assāsento mahājanaṃ;

Jambudīpamhi te therā, vicaritvāna cārikaṃ.

Those elders, consoling the great populace here and there who were afflicted with grief, wandered on tour throughout Jambudīpa.

14.

14.

Āsaḷhisukkapakkhamhi, sukkapakkhaṭhitatthikā;

Upāgamuṃ rājagahaṃ, sampannacatupaccayaṃ.

In the bright fortnight of Āsāḷha, they went to Rājagaha, a place well-provided with the four requisites.

15.

15.

Tattheva vassūpagatā, te mahākassapādayo;

Therā thiraguṇūpetā, sambuddhamatakovidā.

There those elders headed by Mahākassapa, endowed with steadfast virtues and skilled in the doctrine of the Sambuddha, entered upon the rains residence.

16.

16.

Vassānaṃ paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ, sabbasenāsanesu’pi;

Kāresuṃ paṭisaṅkhāraṃ, vatvānā’jātasattuno.

Having informed King Ajātasattu, they spent the first month of the rains residence having repairs made to all the lodgings.

17.

17.

Vihārapaṭisaṅkhāre, niṭṭhite ahu bhūpati;

Idāni dhammasaṃgītiṃ, karissāmi mayaṃ iti.

When the repairs to the monastery were finished, they informed the king: 'Now we shall hold the Dhamma council.'

18.

18.

Kattabbaṃ kintipuṭṭhassa, nisajjaṭhānamādisuṃ;

Rājā katthāti pucchitvā, vuttaṭhānamhi tehi so.

When the king asked, 'What should be done?' they indicated a place for the assembly. The king asked, 'Where?' and at the place they indicated,

19.

19.

Sīghaṃ vebhāraselassa, passe kāresi maṇḍapaṃ;

Sattapaṇṇiguhādvāre, rammaṃ devasabhopamaṃ.

he swiftly had a pavilion built on the side of Mount Vebhāra, at the entrance to the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, a delightful structure like an assembly hall of the devas.

20.

20.

Sabbathā maṇḍayitvā taṃ, attharāpesi tattha so;

Bhikkhūnaṃ gaṇanāyeva, anagghattharaṇāni ca.

Having decorated it in every way, he had priceless floor coverings spread there, according to the number of the bhikkhus.

21.

21.

Nissāya dakkhiṇaṃ bhāgaṃ, uttarāmukhamuttamaṃ;

Therāsanaṃ supaññattaṃ, āsi tattha mahārahaṃ.

On the southern side, a most excellent and valuable Elder's seat was well-prepared, facing north.

22.

22.

Tasmiṃ maṇḍapamajjhasmiṃ, puratthamukhamuttamaṃ;

Dhammāsanaṃ supaññattaṃ, ahosi sugatārahaṃ.

In the middle of that pavilion, a most excellent Dhamma-seat was well-prepared, facing east, one worthy of the Sugata.

23.

23.

Rājā’rocayi therānaṃ, kammaṃ no niṭṭhitaṃ iti;

Te therā theramānanda-mānandakaramabravuṃ.

The king informed the elders, 'Our work is finished.' Those elders then spoke to the Elder Ānanda, the bringer of joy:

24.

24.

Sve sannipāto ānanda, sekhena gamanaṃ tahiṃ;

Na yuttante sadatthe tvaṃ, appamatto tato bhava.

'Ānanda, tomorrow the assembly convenes. It is not fitting for you to go there while still a learner. Therefore, be diligent for your own good.'

25.

25.

Iccevaṃ codito thero, katvāna vīriyaṃ samaṃ;

Iriyāpathato muttaṃ, arahattamapāpuṇi.

Thus admonished, the elder made a balanced effort and, while free from the four postures, attained arahantship.

26.

26.

Vassānaṃ dutiye māse, dutiye divase pana;

Rucire maṇḍape tasmiṃ, therā sannipatiṃsu te.

Then, on the second day of the second month of the rains residence, those elders assembled in that beautiful pavilion.

27.

27.

Ṭhapetvā’nandattherassa, anucchavikamāsanaṃ;

Āsanesu nisīdiṃsu, arahanto yathārahaṃ.

Having prepared a suitable seat for the Elder Ānanda, the arahants sat down on their own seats according to their seniority.

28.

28.

Thero’rahattapattiṃ [M 0.0013] so, ñāpetuṃ tehi nāgamā;

Kuhiṃ ānandatthero’ti, vuccamāne tu kehici.

To make known his attainment of arahantship, that elder did not come with the others. But when some asked, 'Where is the Elder Ānanda?'

29.

29.

Nimmujjitvā pathaviyā, gantvā jotipathena vā;

Nisīdi thero ānando, attano ṭhapitāsane.

the Elder Ānanda, having dived through the earth or traveled through the air, sat down on the seat that had been prepared for him.

30.

30.

Upālithero vinaye, sesadhamme asesake;

Ānandattheramakaruṃ, sabbe therā dhurandhare.

All the elders made the Elder Upāli the authority on the Vinaya, and the Elder Ānanda the authority on the rest of the Dhamma in its entirety.

31.

31.

Mahāthero sakattānaṃ, vinayaṃ pucchituṃ sayaṃ;

Sammannu’pālithero ca, vissajjetuṃ tameva tu.

The Great Elder appointed himself to ask about the Vinaya, and he appointed the Elder Upāli to answer.

32.

32.

Therāsane nisīditvā, vinayaṃ tamapucchi so;

Dhammāsane nisīditvā, vissajjesi tameva so.

Seated on the Elder's seat, he (Mahākassapa) questioned him on the Vinaya. Seated on the Dhamma-seat, he (Upāli) answered it.

33.

33.

Vinayaññūnamaggena, vissajjitakamena te;

Sabbe sajjhāyamakaruṃ, vinayaṃ nayakovidā.

In the sequence that the chief of those who know the Vinaya answered, all those elders, skilled in the method, recited the Vinaya.

34.

34.

Aggaṃ bahussutādīnaṃ, kosārakkhaṃ mahesino;

Sammannitvāna attānaṃ, thero dhammamapucchi so.

Then that elder (Mahākassapa), having appointed himself, questioned the chief of the very learned, the treasurer of the Great Sage (Ānanda), about the Dhamma.

35.

35.

Tathā sammanniya’ttānaṃ, dhammāsanāgato sayaṃ;

Vissajjesi tamānanda-tthero dhammamasesato.

Having been thus authorized, the Elder Ānanda himself ascended the Dhamma-seat and answered concerning the Dhamma in its entirety.

36.

36.

Vedehamuninā tena, vissajjitakamena te;

Sabbe sajjhāyamakaruṃ, dhammaṃ dhammatthakovidā.

In the sequence that it was expounded by that Sage of the Videhans, all of them, being experts in the Dhamma and its meaning, recited the Dhamma together.

37.

37.

Evaṃ sattahi māsehi, dhammasaṃgīti niṭṭhitā;

Sabbalokahitatthāya, sabbalokahi tehi sā.

Thus in seven months that council of the Dhamma was concluded by them for the welfare of the entire world.

38.

38.

Mahākassapatherena, idaṃ sugatasāsanaṃ;

Pañcavassasahassāni, samatthaṃ vattane kataṃ.

By the Elder Mahākassapa, this Dispensation of the Well-farer was made capable of enduring for five thousand years.

39.

39.

Atīva jātapāmojjā, sandhārakajalantikā;

Saṃgītipariyosāne, chaddhākampi mahāmahī.

At the conclusion of the council, the great earth, with exceeding joy arisen, shook in six ways to its ocean boundaries.

40.

40.

Acchariyāni cā’hesuṃ, lokenekāninekadhā;

Thereheva katattā ca, theriyāyaṃ paramparā.

And many and various wonders occurred in the world. Because this was held by the Elders, this tradition is called the Theravāda.

41.

41.

Paṭhamaṃ saṅgahaṃ katvā, sabbalokahitaṃ bahuṃ;

Te yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā, therā sabbepi nibbutā.

Having held the first council, which was of great benefit to the whole world, all those elders, having remained for their lifespan's duration, attained final Nibbāna.

42.

42.

Therā’pi [M 0.0014] te matipadīpahatandhakārā,

Lokandhakārahananamhi mahāpadīpā;

Nibbāpitā maraṇaghoramahānilena,

Tenāpi jīvitamadaṃ matimā jaheyyāti.

Even those elders, who had destroyed darkness with the lamp of wisdom, great lamps for the destruction of the world's darkness, were extinguished by the terrible, great wind of death. Therefore a wise person should abandon the intoxication of life.

Sujanappasādaṃsaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Great Chronicle, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people.

Paṭhamadhammasaṃgītināma

The Chapter named 'The First Dhamma Council'

Tatiyo paricchedo.

The Third Chapter.

Catuttha pariccheda

The Fourth Chapter.

Dutiya saṃgīti

The Second Council.

1.

1.

Ajātasattu putto taṃ, ghātetvā’dāyi bhaddako;

Rajjaṃ soḷasavassāni, kāresi mittadūbhiko.

His son Ajātasattu, a traitor to friends, slew him and ruled the kingdom for sixteen years.

2.

2.

Udayabhadda putto taṃ, ghātetvā anuruddhako;

Anuruddhassa putto taṃ, ghātetvā muṇḍanāmako.

His son Anuruddha slew Udayabhadda; in turn, Anuruddha's son, named Muṇḍa, slew him.

3.

3.

Mittadduno dummatino, te’pi rajjamakārayuṃ;

Tesaṃ ubhinnaṃ rajjesu, aṭṭhavassāna’tikkamuṃ.

Those traitors of evil mind also ruled the kingdom; during the reigns of both of them, eight years passed by.

4.

4.

Muṇḍassa putto pitaraṃ, ghātetvā nāgadāsako;

Catuvīsativassāni, rajjaṃ kāresi pāpako.

Muṇḍa's son, the wicked Nāgadāsaka, slew his father and ruled the kingdom for twenty-four years.

5.

5.

Pitughātakavaṃso’ya, mītikuddhā’tha nāgarā;

Nāgadāsaka rājānaṃ, apanetvā samāgatā.

Angered by this dynasty of patricides, the citizens assembled and deposed King Nāgadāsaka.

6.

6.

Susunāgoti paññātaṃ, amaccaṃ sādhusammataṃ;

Rajje samabhisiñjiṃsu, sabbesaṃ hitamānasā.

They consecrated the well-esteemed minister known as Susunāga to the kingship, their minds set on the welfare of all.

7.

7.

So [M 0.0015] aṭṭhārasavassāni, rājā rajjamakārayi;

Kāḷāso ko tassa putto, aṭṭhavīsati kārayi.

That king ruled the kingdom for eighteen years; his son Kālāsoka ruled for twenty-eight.

8.

8.

Atīte dasame vasse, kāḷāsokassa rājino;

Sambuddhaparinibbānā, evaṃ vassasataṃ ahu.

When the tenth year of King Kālāsoka's reign had passed, one hundred years had thus elapsed since the Parinibbāna of the Self-Enlightened One.

9.

9.

Tadā vesāliyā bhikkhū, anekā vajjiputtakā;

Siṅgīloṇaṃ dvaṅgulañca, tathā gāmantarammi ca.

At that time in Vesālī, many bhikkhus, sons of the Vajjians, upheld the points of 'salt-in-a-horn,' 'two-fingers,' and also 'another-village,'

10.

10.

Āvāsā’numatā’ciṇṇaṃ, amathitaṃ jalogi ca;

Nisīdanaṃ adasakaṃ, jātarūpādikaṃ iti.

'residence,' 'consent,' 'customary practice,' 'un-churned,' 'toddy,' a seat-cloth without a border, and gold and silver.

11.

11.

Dasavatthūni dīpesuṃ, kappantīti alajjīno;

Taṃ sutvāna yasatthero, evaṃ vajjīsu cārikaṃ.

Those shameless ones declared the ten points, saying, 'These are permissible.' Having heard this, the Elder Yasa went wandering among the Vajjians.

12.

12.

Chaḷabhiñño balappatto, yaso kākaṇḍakatrajo;

Taṃ sametuṃ saussāho, tatthāgami’mahāvanaṃ.

Yasa, the son of Kākaṇḍaka, endowed with the six higher knowledges and possessed of great power, eager to settle the matter, went there to the Great Forest.

13.

13.

Ṭhapetvā’posathagge te, kaṃsapātiṃ sahodhakaṃ;

Kahāpaṇādiṃ saṅghassa, detha’nā’hu upāsake.

In the Uposatha hall they placed a bronze bowl filled with water and said to the lay followers: 'Give kahāpaṇas and other coins to the Sangha.'

14.

14.

Na kappate taṃ mā detha, iti thero savārayi;

Paṭisāraṇīyaṃ kammaṃ, yasattherassa te karuṃ.

'This is not permissible, do not give it!' Thus the Elder restrained them. They then performed the act requiring reconciliation against the Elder Yasa.

15.

15.

Yācitvā anudūtaṃ so, saha tena puraṃ gato;

Attano dhammavādittaṃ, saññāpetvā’ga sāgare.

Having requested an attendant, he went with him to the city; having declared his own orthodoxy, he went to Ahogaṅga.

16.

16.

Anudūtavaco sutvā, tamukkhipitumāgatā;

Parikkhipiya aṭṭhaṃsu, saraṃ therassa bhikkhavo.

Hearing the attendant's words, the bhikkhus came to suspend the Elder. They surrounded his lodging and stood there.

17.

17.

Thero uggamma nabhasā, gantvā kosambiyaṃ tato;

Pāveyyakā vantikānaṃ, bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ lahuṃ.

The Elder rose into the sky and went to Kosambī; from there he went swiftly to the bhikkhus of Pāvā and Avantī.

18.

18.

Vesesi dūtetu sayaṃ, gantvā’ho gaṅgapabbataṃ;

Āha sambhūtattherassa, taṃ sabbaṃ sāṇavāsino.

He sent messengers, and he himself went to the Ahogaṅga mountain. There he told the Elder Sambhūta Sāṇavāsī the entire matter.

19.

19.

Pāveyyakā saṭṭhitherā, asitā’vantikāpi ca;

Mahākhīṇāsavā sabbe, ahogaṅgamhi otaruṃ.

Sixty elders from Pāvā and eighty from Avantī, all of them great Arahants, assembled at Ahogaṅga.

20.

20.

Bhikkhavo sannipatitā, sabbe tattha tato tato;

Āsuṃ navutisahassāni, mantetvā akhilā’pi te.

Bhikkhus assembled there from here and there; there were ninety thousand in all, and they all consulted together.

21.

21.

Soreyya [M 0.0016] revatattheraṃ, bahussuta manāsavaṃ;

Taṃ kālapamukhaṃ ñatvā, passituṃ nikkhamiṃsu taṃ.

Knowing that the Elder Revata of Soreyya—who was very learned and taintless—was the foremost person of that time, they set out to see him.

22.

22.

Thero tammantanaṃ sutvā, vesāliṃ gantumeva so;

Icchanto phāsugamanaṃ, tato nikkhami taṅkhaṇaṃ.

Hearing of their consultation, and himself wishing to go to Vesālī, the Elder, desiring a convenient journey, departed from there at that very moment.

23.

23.

Pāto pātova nikkhanta-ṭṭhānaṃ tena mahattanā;

Sāyaṃ sāyamupentānaṃ, sahajotiyamaddasuṃ.

Arriving in the evening at the place from which that great one had departed in the morning, they saw him at Sahajāti.

24.

24.

Tattha sambhūtattherena, yasatthero niyojito;

Saddhammasavanante taṃ, revatathera muttamaṃ.

There, the Elder Yasa was instructed by the Elder Sambhūta to approach the supreme Elder Revata at the conclusion of the Dhamma talk.

25.

25.

Upecca dasavatthūni, pucchi thero paṭikkhipi;

Sutvā’dhikaraṇaṃ tañca, nisedhemāti abravi.

Having approached, the Elder Yasa questioned him about the ten points, and the Elder Revata rejected them. Hearing of the dispute, Revata declared: 'We will put a stop to this!'

26.

26.

Pāpāpi pakkhaṃ pekkhantā, revatatthera muttamaṃ;

Sāmaṇakaṃ parikkhāraṃ, paṭiyādiya te bahuṃ.

The wicked bhikkhus, seeking to win the supreme Elder Revata to their side, prepared many monastic requisites.

27.

27.

Sīghaṃ nāvāya gantvāna, sahajātisamīpagā;

Karonti bhattavissaggaṃ, bhattakāle upaṭṭhite.

Going quickly by boat, they approached Sahajāti. When the mealtime arrived, they made a distribution of food.

28.

28.

Sahajātiṃ āvasanto, sāḷathero vicintiyā;

Pāveyyakā dhammavādī, iti passi anāsavo.

The taintless Elder Sāḷha, while dwelling in Sahajāti, reflected and saw: 'The bhikkhus from Pāvā are speakers of the Dhamma.'

29.

29.

Upecca taṃ mahābrahmā, dhamme niṭṭhāti abravi;

Niccaṃ dhamme ṭhitattaṃ so, attano tassa abravi.

A Mahābrahmā approached him and said: 'Be steadfast in the Dhamma!' The Elder then told him of his own constant steadfastness in the Dhamma.

30.

30.

Te parikkhāramādāya, revatattheramaddasuṃ;

Thero na gaṇhi tappakkha-gāhī sissaṃ paṇāmayī.

Taking the requisites, they approached the Elder Revata. The Elder did not accept them and dismissed the pupil who had taken their side.

31.

31.

Vesāliṃ te tato gantvā, tato pupphapuraṃ gatā;

Vadiṃsu kāḷāsokassa, narindassa alajjīno.

Then those shameless ones went to Vesālī, and from there to Pupphapura. They spoke to the lord of men, King Kālāsoka.

32.

32.

Satthussa no gandhakuṭiṃ, gopayanto mayaṃ tahiṃ;

Mahāvanavihārasmiṃ, vasāma vajjībhūmiyaṃ.

'We dwell in the Mahāvana Monastery in the Vajjian country, guarding our Teacher's Perfumed Chamber.'

33.

33.

Gaṇhissāma vihāra’nti, gāmavāsikasikkhavo;

Āgacchanti mahārāja, maṭisedhaya te iti.

'The bhikkhus from the outlying regions are coming to take the monastery! O great king, you must prevent them!'

34.

34.

Rājānaṃ duggahitaṃ te, katvā vesālimāgamuṃ;

Revatatthera mūlamhi, sahajātiyamettha tu.

Having misled the king, they returned to Vesālī. Meanwhile, at Sahajāti, in the presence of the Elder Revata...

35.

35.

Bhikkhū [M 0.0017] satasahassāni, ekādasa samāgatā;

Navutiñca sahassāni, ahu taṃ vatthu santiyā.

For the pacification of that issue, there assembled eleven hundred-thousand and ninety thousand bhikkhus.

36.

36.

Mūlaṭṭhehi vinā vatthu-samanaṃ neva rocayi;

Thero sabbepi bhikkhū te, vesālimāgamuṃ tato.

The Elder did not approve of settling the issue without the original parties; therefore, he and all those bhikkhus went to Vesālī.

37.

37.

Duggahitova so rājā, tatthāmacce apesayi;

Mūḷā devānubhāvena, aññattha agamiṃsu te.

The king, having been wrongly influenced, sent his ministers there; but they, bewildered by the power of the devas, went elsewhere.

38.

38.

Pesetvā te mahīpālo, taṃ rattiṃ supinenaso;

Apassi sakamattānaṃ, pakkhittaṃ lohakumbhiyaṃ.

Having sent them, that night the king saw in a dream that he himself was being thrown into an iron cauldron.

39.

39.

Atibhīto ahu rājā, tamassā setu māgamā;

Bhaginī nandatherī tu, ākāsena anāsavā.

The king was terrified. To comfort him, his sister, the taintless Elderī Nandā, came to him through the sky.

40.

40.

Bhāriyaṃ te kataṃ kammaṃ, dhammike’yye khamāpaya;

Pakkho tesaṃ bhavitvā tvaṃ, kuru sāsanapaggahaṃ.

'You have done a grievous deed! Ask forgiveness from the righteous elders. Take their side and give your support to the Dispensation.'

41.

41.

Evaṃ kate sotthi tuyhaṃ, hessatīti apakkami;

Pasāteyeva vesāliṃ, gantuṃ nikkhami bhūpati.

Saying, 'If this is done, it will be well with you,' she departed. At dawn, the king set out to go to Vesālī.

42.

42.

Gantvā mahāvanaṃ bhikkhū-saṅghaṃ so sannipātiya;

Sutvā ubhinnaṃ vādañca, dhammapakkhañca rociya.

Going to the Mahāvana, he assembled the Sangha of bhikkhus; having heard the arguments of both sides, he approved of the side of the Dhamma.

43.

43.

Khamāpetvā dhammike te, bhikkhū sabbe mahīpati;

Attano dhammapakkhattaṃ, vatvā tumhe yathāruci.

The king asked for forgiveness from all those righteous bhikkhus. Declaring his own allegiance to the Dhamma party, he said: 'Act according to your pleasure.'

44.

44.

Sampaggahaṃ sāsanassa, karothāti ca bhāsiya;

Datvā ca tesaṃ ārakkhaṃ, agamāsi sakaṃ puraṃ.

'Give your full support to the Dispensation,' he said. Then, having given them protection, he returned to his own city.

45.

45.

Nicchetuṃ tāni vatthūni, saṅgho sannipatī tadā;

Anaggāni tattha bhassāni, saṅghamajjhe ajāyisuṃ.

The Sangha then assembled to decide upon those points, but much worthless chatter arose in their midst.

46.

46.

Tato so revatatthero, sāvetvā saṅghamajjhago;

Ubbhāhikāya taṃ vatthuṃ, sametuṃ nicchayaṃ akā.

Then the Elder Revata, standing in the midst of the Sangha, made an announcement and decided to settle the matter by means of a committee.

47.

47.

Pācinakeca caturo, caturo pāveyyakepi ca;

Ubbhāhikāya sammanni, bhikkhū taṃ vatthu santiyā.

For the pacification of the issue, a committee was appointed with four bhikkhus from the East and four from Pāvā.

48.

48.

Sabbakāmī ca sāḷho ca, khujjasobhitanāmako;

Vāsabhagāmiko cāti, thero pācinakā ime.

The Elders from the East were these: Sabbakāmī, Sāḷha, the one named Khujjasobhita, and Vāsabhagāmika.

49.

49.

Revato [M 0.0018] sāṇasambhūto,

Yaso kākoṇḍakatrajo;

Sumano cāti cattāro,

Therā pāveyyakā ime.

The Elders from Pāvā were these four: Revata, Sambhūta Sāṇavāsī, Yasa son of Kākaṇḍaka, and Sumana.

50.

50.

Sametuṃ tāni vatthūni, appasaddaṃ anākulaṃ;

Agamuṃ vālukārāmaṃ, aṭṭhattherā anāsavā.

To settle those points quietly and without disturbance, the eight taintless Elders went to the Vālukārāma.

51.

51.

Daharenā’ji te nettha, paññatte āsane subhe;

Nisīdiṃsu mahātherā, mahāmuni mataññuno.

There, on fine, prepared seats, the great Elders, who knew the mind of the Great Sage, sat down.

52.

52.

Tesu vatthūsu ekekaṃ, kamato revato mahā;

Thero theraṃ sabbakāmiṃ, pucchi pucchāsu kovido.

The great Elder Revata, skilled in questioning, asked the Elder Sabbakāmī about each of those points in order.

53.

53.

Sabbakāmī mahāthero, tena puṭṭho’tha byākari;

Sabbāni tāni vatthūni, na kappantīti suttato.

Then the great Elder Sabbakāmī, on being questioned by him, replied that, according to the Suttas, all those points were impermissible.

54.

54.

Nihanitvā’dhikaraṇaṃ, taṃ te tattha yathākkamaṃ;

Tatheva saṅghamajjhepi, pucchāvissajjanaṃ karuṃ.

Having settled that dispute there in due order, they conducted the questions and answers in the very same way in the midst of the Sangha.

55.

55.

Niggahaṃ pāpabhikkhūnaṃ, dasavatthukadīpanaṃ;

Tesaṃ dasasahassānaṃ, mahāthero akaṃsu te.

Those great Elders carried out the refutation of the ten thousand wicked bhikkhus by clarifying the ten points.

56.

56.

Sabbakāmī puthaviyā, saṅghatthero tadā ahu;

So vīsaṃ vassasatiko, tadā’si upasampadā.

Sabbakāmī was at that time the Elder of the Sangha on earth; he was then one hundred and twenty years in the higher ordination.

57.

57.

Sabbakāmī ca sāḷho ca,

Revato khujjasobhito;

Yaso kākoṇḍakasuto,

Sambhūto sāṇavāsiko.

Sabbakāmī and Sāḷha, Revata and Khujjasobhita, Yasa son of Kākaṇḍaka, and Sambhūta Sāṇavāsī:

58.

58.

Therā ānandattherassa, ete saddhivihārino;

Vāsabhagāmiko ceva, sumano ca duve pana.

These six elders were pupils of the Elder Ānanda; but the two, Vāsabhagāmika and Sumana, were pupils of the Elder Anuruddha.

59.

59.

Therā’nuruddhattherassa, ete saddhivihārino;

Aṭṭha therā’pi dhaññā te, diṭṭhapubbā tathāgataṃ.

These elders were pupils of the Elder Anuruddha; all eight were fortunate elders who had previously seen the Tathāgata.

60.

60.

Bhikkhū satasahassāni, dvādasāsuṃ samāgatā;

Sabbesaṃ revatatthero, bhikkhūnaṃpamukhotadā.

Twelve hundred thousand bhikkhus had assembled there. At that time, the Elder Revata was the foremost among all the bhikkhus.

61.

61.

Tato [M 0.0019] so revatatthero, saddhammaṭṭhitiyā ciraṃ;

Kāretuṃ dhammasaṃgītiṃ, sabbabhikkhusamūhato.

Then that Elder Revata, for the sake of the long-term stability of the true Dhamma, initiated a recital of the Dhamma, selecting from the entire assembly of bhikkhus.

62.

62.

Pabhinnatthādiñāṇānaṃ, piṭakattayadhārinaṃ;

Satāni sattabhikkhūnaṃ, arahantānamuccini.

He selected seven hundred bhikkhus who were arahants, masters of the three Piṭakas, and possessors of the analytical knowledges.

63.

63.

Te sabbe vālukārāme, kāḷāsokena rakkhitā;

Revatattherapāmokkhā, akaruṃ dhammasaṅgahaṃ.

All of them, led by the Elder Revata and protected by King Kālāsoka, compiled the Dhamma in the Vālukārāma.

64.

64.

Pubbe kataṃ tathā eva, dhammaṃ pacchā ca bhāsitaṃ;

Ādāya niṭṭhapesuṃ taṃ, etaṃ māsehi aṭṭhahi.

They completed this compilation of the Dhamma in eight months, conducting it in the same manner as was done before.

65.

65.

Evaṃ dutiyasaṃgītiṃ, katvā tepi mahāyasā;

Therā dosakkhayaṃ pattā, pattākālena nibbutiṃ.

Thus, having held the Second Recital, those illustrious elders, who had attained the destruction of the taints, in due time attained final Nibbāna.

66.

66.

Iti paramamatīnaṃ pattipattabbakānaṃ,

Tibhavahitakarānaṃ lokanātherasānaṃ;

Sumariyamaraṇaṃ taṃ saṅkhatā sārakattaṃ,

Parigaṇiyamasesaṃ appamatto bhaveyyāti.

Therefore, let the diligent person fully reflect upon the auspicious passing of those great elders—leaders of the world, workers for the welfare of the three realms, possessors of supreme wisdom who had attained the goal—and upon the essential nature of all conditioned things.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate

Composed for the purpose of inspiring serene joy and a sense of spiritual urgency in good people.

Mahāvaṃse dutiyasaṃgīti nāma

In the Mahāvaṃsa, the chapter named 'The Second Recital'.

Catuttho paricchedo.

The Fourth Chapter.

Pañcama pariccheda

The Fifth Chapter.

Tatiyadhammasaṃgīti

The Third Recital of the Dhamma.

1.

1.

Yā mahākassapādīhi[M 0.0020], mahātherehi ādito;

Katā saddhamma saṃgīti, theriyā’ti pavuccati.

That recital of the true Dhamma which was held in the beginning by the great elders headed by Mahākassapa is called the Theriyā, the Doctrine of the Elders.

2.

2.

Eko’va theravādo so, ādivassasate ahu;

Aññācariyavādātu, tato oraṃ ajāyisuṃ.

For the first hundred years, there was only the single Theravāda. The doctrines of other teachers arose after that.

3.

3.

Tehi saṃgītikārehi, therehi dutiyehi te;

Niggahitā pāpabhikkhū, sabbe dasasahassakā.

Those unvirtuous bhikkhus, ten thousand in all, were censured by the elders who held the Second Recital.

4.

4.

Akaṃsā’cariyavādaṃ te, mahāsaṃgītināmakā;

Tato gokulikā jātā, ekabbohārikāpi ca.

They, named the Mahāsaṅgītikas, established their own doctrine. From them arose the Gokulikas and also the Ekabbohārikas.

5.

5.

Gokulikehi paṇṇatti-vādā bāhulikāpi ca;

Cetiyavādā tesveva, samatāsaṅghikā cha te.

From the Gokulikas arose the Paṇṇattivādins and the Bāhulikas. The Cetiyavādins also arose from them. These six schools together are the Mahāsaṅghikas.

6.

6.

Punāpi theravādehi, mahiṃsāsakabhikkhavo;

Vajjīputtakabhikkhū ca, duve jātā ime khalu.

Again, from the Theravādins, two schools indeed arose: the Mahiṃsāsaka bhikkhus and the Vajjīputtaka bhikkhus.

7.

7.

Jātā’tha dhammuttariyā, bhadrayānikabhikkhavo;

Channāgārā sammitiyā, vajjīputtiyabhikkhūti.

From the Vajjīputtaka bhikkhus, in turn, arose the Dhammuttariyas, the Bhadrayānikas, the Channāgārikas, and the Sammitīyas.

8.

8.

Mahiṃsāsakabhikkhūhi, bhikkhū sabbattha vādino;

Dhammaguttiyabhikkhū ca, jātā khalu ime duve.

From the Mahiṃsāsaka bhikkhus, indeed, two schools arose: the Sabbatthavādin bhikkhus and the Dhammaguttika bhikkhus.

9.

9.

Jātā sabbatthivādīhi, kassapiyā tato pana;

Jātā saṅkantikā bhikkhū, suttavādā tato pana.

From the Sabbatthavādins arose the Kassapiyas; from them, in turn, arose the Saṅkantikas, and from them the Suttavādins.

10.

10.

Theravādena saha te, honti dvādasi’mepi ca;

Pubbe vuttachavādā ca, iti aṭṭhārasā khilā.

These schools, together with the Theravāda, are twelve. Adding the six schools mentioned previously, there are thus eighteen factions in all.

11.

11.

Sattarasāpi dutiye, jātā vasassate iti;

Aññācariyavādā tu, tato oramajāyisuṃ.

Thus, the seventeen schismatic schools arose in the second century. Other doctrines of teachers arose even after that.

12.

12.

Hematā [M 0.0021] rājagiriyā, tathā siddhatthikāpi ca;

Pubbaseliyabhikkhū ca, tathā aparaseliyā.

The Hemavatas, the Rājagiriyas, and also the Siddhatthikas; the Pubbaseliya bhikkhus and also the Aparaseliyas.

13.

13.

Vājiriyā cha etehi, jambudīpamhi bhinnakā;

Dhammaruci ca sāgaliyā, laṃkādīpamhi bhinnakā.

These six schools, including the Vājiriyas, broke away in Jambudīpa. The Dhammarucikas and the Sāgaliyas broke away on the island of Laṅkā.

Ācariyakulavādakathā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the account of the doctrines of the schools of teachers.

Dhammāsokābhiseka

The Consecration of Dhammāsoka.

14.

14.

Kāḷāsokassa puttā tu, ahesuṃ dasabhātikā;

Bāvīsatiṃ te vassāni, rajjaṃ samanusāsisuṃ.

The sons of Kālāsoka were ten brothers. They ruled the kingdom together for twenty-two years.

15.

15.

Nava nandā tato āsuṃ, kameneva narādhipā;

Te’pi bāvīsavassāni, rajjaṃ samanusāsisuṃ.

After them came the nine Nandas, who were kings in succession. They too ruled the kingdom for twenty-two years.

16.

16.

Moriyānaṃ khattiyānaṃ, vaṃse jātaṃ siridharaṃ;

Candaguttoti paññātaṃ, cāṇakko brāhmaṇo tato.

Then the brahmin Cāṇakka came upon a glorious youth born in the lineage of the Moriya khattiyas, who was known as Candagutta.

17.

17.

Navamaṃ dhananandaṃ taṃ, ghātetvā caṇḍakodhasā;

Sakale jambudīpasmiṃ, rajje samabhisiñcī so.

Having slain that ninth king, Dhanananda, he, with fierce anger, consecrated Candagutta in sovereignty over all of Jambudīpa.

18.

18.

So catuvīsavassāniṃ, rājā rajjamakārayi;

Tassa putto bindusāro, aṭṭhavīsati kārayi.

That king reigned for twenty-four years. His son, Bindusāra, reigned for twenty-eight.

19.

19.

Bindusārasutā āsuṃ, sataṃ eko ca vissutā;

Asoko āsi tesaṃ tu, puññatejobaliddhiko.

Bindusāra had one hundred and one well-known sons. Among them, Asoka was endowed with merit, glory, strength, and power.

20.

20.

Vemātike bhātaro so, hantvā ekūnakaṃ sataṃ;

Sakale jambudīpasmiṃ, ekarajjamapāpuṇi.

He slew his ninety-nine brothers born of different mothers and attained sole sovereignty over all of Jambudīpa.

21.

21.

Jinanibbānato pacchā, pure tassābhisekato;

Sāṭṭhārasaṃ vassasata-dvayamevaṃ vijāniya.

It should be known that thus two hundred and eighteen years had passed from the Parinibbāna of the Conqueror until his consecration.

22.

22.

Patvā catūhi vassehi, ekarajjaṃ mahāyaso;

Pure pāṭaliputtasmiṃ, attānamabhisecayi.

Four years after attaining sole sovereignty, that illustrious one consecrated himself in the city of Pāṭaliputta.

23.

23.

Tassā’bhisekena [M 0.0022] samaṃ, ākāse bhūmiyaṃ tathā;

Yojane yojane āṇā, niccaṃ pavattitā ahu.

Simultaneously with his consecration, his authority was continuously established, extending for a yojana into the sky above and for a yojana into the earth below.

24.

24.

Anotatto dakākāje, aṭṭhanesuṃ dine dine;

Devā devo akā tehi, saṃvibhāgaṃ janassaca.

Daily, the gods brought eight pole-loads of water from Lake Anotatta. With this, the king made a distribution to the people.

25.

25.

Nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ, ānesuṃ himavantato;

Anekesaṃ sahassānaṃ, devā eva pahonakaṃ.

The gods themselves brought tooth-sticks of Nāgalatā wood from the Himālaya, sufficient for many thousands of people.

26.

26.

Agadā’malakañceva, tathāgada haritakaṃ;

Tato’va amapakkañca, vaṇṇagandharasuttamaṃ.

From there too they brought medicinal myrobalan and yellow myrobalan, as well as ripe mangoes that were supreme in color, fragrance, and taste.

27.

27.

Pañcavaṇṇāni vatthāni, tatthapuñjanapaṭṭakaṃ;

Pītañca dibbapānañca, chaddantadahato maru.

From Lake Chaddanta the gods brought cloths of five colors, yellow cloths, towels for wiping the hands, and a divine beverage.

28.

28.

Marantā nagare tasmiṃ, migasūkarapakkhino;

Āgantvāna mahānasaṃ, sayameva maranti ca.

Deer, boars, and birds that were to be used for food in that city would come to the great kitchen and die there of their own accord.

29.

29.

Gāvo tattha carāpetvā, vajamānenti dīpino;

Khetta vatthutaḷākādiṃ, pālenti migasūkarā.

When cattle were driven out to graze, leopards would drive them back. Deer and boars would guard the fields, grounds, and ponds.

30.

30.

Sumanaṃ pupphapaṭakaṃ, abhuttaṃ dibbamuppalaṃ;

Vilepanaṃ añjanañca, nāgānāgāvimānato.

The Nāgas brought from their palaces baskets of Sumana flowers, divine lotuses that no one else had enjoyed, unguents, and collyrium.

31.

31.

Sālivāhasahassāni, navutiṃ tu suvā pana;

Chaddantadahatoyeva, āhariṃsu dine dine.

Daily, parrots brought ninety thousand cartloads of rice from Lake Chaddanta.

32.

32.

Te sālinitthusakaṇe, akhaṇḍetvāna taṇḍule;

Akaṃsu mūsikā tehi, bhattaṃ rājakule ahu.

Mice would remove the husk and bran from that rice without breaking the grains. With this rice, meals were prepared for the royal household.

33.

33.

Akaṃsu sassataṃ tassa, madhūni madhumakkhikā;

Tathā kammārasālāsu, acchākūṭāni pātayuṃ.

Honeybees constantly made honey for him. Likewise, in the forges, bears would swing the hammers.

34.

34.

Karavikā sakuṇikā, manuññamadhurassarā;

Akaṃsu tassā’gantvāna, rañño madhuravassitaṃ.

Karavīka birds, with charming and sweet voices, would come and sing sweetly for the king.

35.

35.

Rājā’bhisitto so’soko,

Kumāraṃ tissasavhayaṃ;

Kaṇiṭṭhaṃ saṃsodariyaṃ, uparajje’bhisecayi.

Having been consecrated, King Asoka appointed his younger full brother, the prince named Tissa, to the office of viceroy.

Dhammāsokābhiseko niṭṭhito

The Consecration of Dhammāsoka is concluded.

Nigrodhasāmaṇera dassana

The Sight of the Novice Nigrodha

36.

36.

Pitā [M 0.0023] saṭṭhisahassāni, brāhmaṇe brahmapakkhike;

Bhojesi sopi teyeva, tīṇi vassāni bhojayi.

His father had fed sixty thousand Brahmins who were adherents of Brahmā; he too fed them for three years.

37.

37.

Disvā’nupasamaṃ tesaṃ, asoko parivesane;

Viceyya dānaṃ dassanti, amacce sanniyojiya.

Seeing their lack of calm during the distribution, Asoka appointed ministers, instructing them to give the alms with discernment.

38.

38.

Āṇāpayitvā matimā, nānāpāsaṇḍike visuṃ;

Vīmaṃsitvā nisajjāya, bhojāpetvā visajjayi.

Having given the command, the wise one examined the various sectarians separately, had them seated and fed, and then dismissed them.

39.

39.

Kāle vātāyanagato, santaṃ racchāgataṃ yatiṃ;

Nigrodhasāmaṇeraṃ so, disvā cittaṃ pasādayi.

At the proper time, while at a window, he saw the serene ascetic, the novice Nigrodha, walking on the street, and his mind was gladdened.

40.

40.

Bindusārassa puttānaṃ, sabbesaṃ jeṭṭhabhātuno;

Sumanassa kumārassa, putto so hi kumārako.

For that boy was the son of Prince Sumana, the eldest brother of all the sons of Bindusāra.

41.

41.

Asoko pitarā dinnaṃ, rajjamujjeniyañhi so;

Hitvā’gato pupphapuraṃ, bindusāre gilānake.

For Asoka, having left the kingdom of Ujjeni given to him by his father, came to Pupphapura when Bindusāra was ill.

42.

42.

Katvā puraṃ sakāyattaṃ, mate pitari bhātaraṃ;

Ghātetvā jeṭṭhakaṃ rajjaṃ, aggahesi pure vare.

Having brought the city under his control, after his father had died, he slew his eldest brother and seized the kingdom in that excellent city.

43.

43.

Sumanassa kumārassa, devī tannāmikā tato;

Gabbhinī nikkhamitvāna, pācinadvārato bahi.

Then the queen, named after Prince Sumana, being pregnant, went out through the eastern gate.

44.

44.

Caṇḍālagāma magamā, tattha nigrodhadevatā;

Tamālapiyanāmena, mā patvā gharakaṃ adā.

She went to a Caṇḍāla village, where a nigrodha deity named Tamālapiya, having approached her, gave her a small house.

45.

45.

Tadahe’va varaṃ puttaṃ, vijāyitvā sutassa sā;

Nigrodhoti akā nāmaṃ, devatā nuggahānugā.

That very day, having given birth to an excellent son, she named him Nigrodha, in accordance with the deity's favor.

46.

46.

Disvā taṃ jeṭṭhacaṇḍālo, attano sāminiṃ viya;

Maññanto taṃ upaṭṭhāsi, sattavassāni sādhukaṃ.

Seeing him, the chief Caṇḍāla, thinking him to be his master, attended to him well for seven years.

47.

47.

Taṃ mahāvaruṇo thero, tadā disvā kumārakaṃ;

Upanissaya sampannaṃ, arahā pucchi mātaraṃ.

Then the great Elder Varuṇa, an Arahant, seeing the boy who was endowed with the supporting conditions, asked his mother:

48.

48.

Pabbājesi khuragge so, arahattamapāpuṇi;

Dassanāyo’pa gacchanto, so tato mātudeviyā.

He ordained him, and at the razor's edge, he attained arahantship. Then, going to see his mother, the queen, he departed from there.

49.

49.

Dakkhiṇena ca dvārena, pavisitvā puruttamaṃ;

Taṃ gāmagāmimaggena, yāti rājaṅgaṇe tadā.

Entering the excellent city through the southern gate, he then went by the main road to the royal courtyard.

50.

50.

Santāya [M 0.0024] iriyā yasmiṃ, pasīdi samahīpati;

Pubbe’va sannivāsena, pemaṃ tasmiṃ ajāyatha.

The great king was pleased by his serene demeanor; love for him arose as if from a past association.

51.

51.

Pubbe kira tayo āsuṃ, bhātaro madhu vāṇijā;

Eko madhuṃ vikkiṇāti, āharanti madhuṃ duve.

Long ago, it is said, there were three brothers, honey merchants; one sold honey, while the other two gathered honey.

52.

52.

Eko paccekasambuddho, vaṇarogāturo ahu;

Añño paccekasambuddho, tadatthaṃ madhuvatthiko.

One Paccekabuddha was afflicted with a skin disease; another Paccekabuddha, for his sake, was in need of honey.

53.

53.

Piṇḍacārikavattena, nagaraṃ pāvisī tadā;

Titthaṃ jalatthaṃ gacchanti, ekā ceṭī tamaddasa.

As he then entered the city on his alms-round, a certain maidservant, who was going to the ford for water, saw him.

54.

54.

Pucchitvā madhukāmattaṃ, ñatvā hatthena ādisi;

Eso madhvāpaṇo bhante, tattha gacchā’ti abravi.

Having asked about his need for honey and understood it, she pointed with her hand, saying: "That is the honey shop, venerable sir, go there."

55.

55.

Tattha pattassa buddhassa, vāṇijo so pasādavā;

Vissandayanto mukhato, pattapuraṃ madhuṃ adā.

When the Buddha arrived there, that devout merchant, his face radiant with faith, gave honey, filling the bowl.

56.

56.

Puṇṇañca uppatantañca, patitañca mahītale;

Disvā madhuṃ pasanno so, evaṃ paṇidahī tadā.

Seeing the honey filling the bowl, rising up, and falling upon the ground, he was delighted and then made this aspiration:

57.

57.

Jambudīpe ekarajjaṃ, dānenā’nena hotu me;

Ākāse yojane āṇā, bhūmiyaṃ yojaneti ca.

“Through this gift, may I have sole sovereignty in Jambudīpa; and may my command extend a yojana in the sky and a yojana on the earth.”

58.

58.

Bhātare āgate āha, edisassa madhuṃ adaṃ;

Anumodatha tumhe taṃ, tumhākañca yato madhu.

When his brothers arrived, he said, "I gave honey to such a one as this; rejoice in it, for the honey was also yours."

59.

59.

Jeṭṭho āha atuṭṭho so,

Caṇḍālo nūna sosiyaṃ;

Nivāsentīti caṇḍālā,

Kāsāyāni sadā iti.

The eldest, displeased, said: "Surely he must be a Caṇḍāla, for Caṇḍālas always wear ochre robes."

60.

60.

Majjho paccekabuddhaṃ taṃ, khipapāraṇṇave iti;

Pattidānavaco tassa, sutvā te cānumodisuṃ.

The middle one said of that Paccekabuddha, "May he cross to the far shore of the ocean!" Hearing the words of the merit-sharer, they too rejoiced.

61.

61.

Āpaṇā desikaṃ yātu, devittaṃ tassa patthayi;

Ādissamānasandhi ca, rūpaṃ atimanoramaṃ.

The maidservant who pointed out the shop aspired to divinity, and to have an exceedingly delightful form with invisible joints.

62.

62.

Asoko madhudo’sandhi-mittādevī tu ceṭikā;

Caṇḍālavādī nigrodho, tisso so pāravādiko.

Asoka was the honey-giver, and Queen Asandhimittā was the maidservant; Nigrodha was the one who spoke the word 'Caṇḍāla', and Tissa was the one who spoke of the further shore.

63.

63.

Caṇḍālavādī caṇḍāla-gāme āsi yato tu so;

Patthesi mokkhaṃ mokkhañca, satta vassova pāpuṇi.

Because he was the one who spoke the word 'Caṇḍāla', he was reborn in a Caṇḍāla village. He aspired to liberation and attained it when he was just seven years old.

64.

64.

Niviṭṭhapemo [M 0.0025] tasmiṃ so, rājā’ti turito tato;

Pakkosāpesi taṃ so tu, santavuttī upāgami.

The king, his affection for him established, then swiftly had him summoned; and he, of peaceful conduct, approached.

65.

65.

Nisida tātā’nurūpe, āsane tā’ha bhūpati;

Adisvā bhikkhumaññaṃ so, sīhāsanamupāgami.

“Sit down, dear one, on a suitable seat,” said the king. Seeing no other bhikkhu, he approached the lion throne.

66.

66.

Tasmiṃ pallaṅkamāyāte, rājāiti vicintayi;

Ajjā’yaṃ sāmaṇero me, ghare hessati sāmiko.

When he came to the royal couch, the king thought: "Today this novice will be the master of my house."

67.

67.

Ālambitvā karaṃ rañño, so pallaṅke samāruhi;

Nisīdi rājapallaṅke, setacchattassa heṭṭhato.

Taking the king's hand, he ascended the couch; he sat upon the royal couch, beneath the white parasol.

68.

68.

Disvā tathā nisinnaṃ taṃ, asoko so mahīpati;

Sambhāvetvāna guṇato, tuṭṭho’tīva tadā ahu.

Seeing him seated thus, that great king Asoka, esteeming him for his virtue, was then exceedingly delighted.

69.

69.

Attano paṭiyattena, khajjabhojjena tappiya;

Sambuddhadesitaṃ dhammaṃ, sāmaṇeramapucchitaṃ.

Having satisfied him with fine food prepared by himself, he asked the novice about the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

70.

70.

Tassa’ppamādavaggaṃ so, sāmaṇero abhāsatha;

Taṃ sutvā bhūmipālo so, pasanno jinasāsane.

The novice recited to him the chapter on heedfulness. Hearing it, that ruler of the earth became devoted to the Conqueror's dispensation.

71.

71.

Aṭṭha te niccabhattāni, dammi tātā’ti āha taṃ;

Upajjhāyassa me rāja, tāni dammīti āha so.

“I give you eight regular food allowances, dear one,” he said to him. “O king, I give them to my preceptor,” he replied.

72.

72.

Puna aṭṭhasu dinnesu, tāna’dā cariyassa so;

Puna aṭṭhasu dinnesu, bhikkhusaṅghassa tāna’dā.

Again, when eight were given, he gave them to his teacher; again, when eight were given, he gave them to the community of bhikkhus.

73.

73.

Puna aṭṭhasu dinnesu, adhivāsesi buddhimā;

Dvattiṃsabhikkhū ādāya, dutiyadivase gato.

Again, when eight meals were given, the wise one consented; taking thirty-two monks, he departed on the second day.

74.

74.

Sahatthā tappito raññā, dhammaṃ desiya bhūpatiṃ;

Saraṇesu ca sīlesu, ṭhapesi samahājanaṃ.

Having been gratified by the king with his own hand, he taught the Dhamma to the lord of the earth and established the great multitude in the refuges and precepts.

Nigrodhasāmaṇeradassanaṃ

The Sighting of the Novice Nigrodha

Sāsanappavesa

Entry into the Dispensation

75.

75.

Tato rājā pasanno so, diguṇena dine dine;

Bhikkhū saṭṭhisahassāni, anupubbenu’paṭhahi.

Then that pleased king, doubling the provisions day by day, successively attended upon sixty thousand bhikkhus.

76.

76.

Tatthiyānaṃ sahassāni, nikaḍḍhitvāna saṭṭhiso;

Saṭṭhibhikkhusahassāni, ghare niccamabhojayi.

Having expelled sixty thousand sectarians, he constantly fed sixty thousand bhikkhus in his palace.

77.

77.

Saṭṭhibhikkhusahassāni[M 0.0026], bhojetuṃ turito hi so;

Paṭiyādāpayitvāna, khajjabhojjaṃ mahārahaṃ.

Eager to feed the sixty thousand bhikkhus, he had costly hard and soft foods prepared.

78.

78.

Bhūsāpetvāna nagaraṃ, gantvā saṅghaṃ nimantiya;

Gharaṃ netvāna bhojetvā, datvā sāmaṇakaṃ bahuṃ.

Having had the city adorned, he went and invited the Sangha; leading them to his palace, he fed them and gave them abundant requisites.

79.

79.

Satthārā desito dhammo, kittakoti apucchatha;

Byākāsi moggaliputto, tissatthero tadassataṃ.

He asked, “How vast is the Dhamma taught by the Teacher?” The Elder Moggalliputta Tissa then explained its extent.

80.

80.

Sutvāna caturāsīti, dhammakkhandhā’ti so’bravi;

Pūjemi te’haṃ paccekaṃ, vihārenā’ti bhūpati.

Having heard, “There are eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma,” the king declared, “I will honor each one of them with a monastery.”

81.

81.

Datvā tadā channavuti-dhanakoṭiṃ mahīpati;

Puresu caturāsīti-sahassesu mahītale.

Then the lord of the earth gave ninety-six crores of wealth for the eighty-four thousand cities on the earth's surface.

82.

82.

Tattha tatthe’va rājūhi, vihāre ārabhāpayi;

Sayaṃ asokārāmaṃ tu, kārāpetuṃ samārabhi.

In each of those places, he had the local rulers commence the building of monasteries; he himself, however, began to have the Asokārāma constructed.

83.

83.

Ratanattayanigrodha-gilānānanti sāsane;

Paccekaṃ satasahassaṃ, so dāpesi dine dine.

For the oppressed and for the sick within the Dispensation of the Triple Gem, he had a hundred thousand given for each, day by day.

84.

84.

Dhanena buddhadinnena, thūpapūjā anekadhā;

Anekesu vihāresu, aneke akaruṃ sadā.

With the wealth given for the Buddha, many people constantly performed various kinds of offerings to stūpas in many monasteries.

85.

85.

Dhanena dhammadinnena, paccaye caturo vare;

Dhammadharānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, upanetuṃ sadā narā.

With the wealth given for the Dhamma, people always brought the four excellent requisites to the bhikkhus who uphold the Dhamma.

86.

86.

Anotattodakājesu, saṅghassa caturo adā;

Te piṭakānaṃ therānaṃ, saṭṭhiye’kaṃ dine dine.

He gave to the Sangha four portions of water from Lake Anotatta; of these, one was given daily to the sixty elders versed in the Piṭakas.

87.

87.

Ekaṃ asandhimittāya, deviyā tu adāpayi;

Sayaṃ pana duveyeva, paribhuñji mahīpati.

He had one portion given to Queen Asandhimittā, while the lord of the earth himself used the other two.

88.

88.

Saṭṭhibhikkhusahassānaṃ, dantakaṭṭhaṃ dine dine;

Soḷasitthisahassānaṃ, adā nāgalatāvhayaṃ.

Daily he gave tooth-sticks to sixty thousand bhikkhus, and to sixteen thousand women he gave the kind called nāgalatā.

89.

89.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā, catusambuddhadassinaṃ;

Kappāyukaṃ mahākāḷaṃ, nāgarājaṃ mahiddhikaṃ.

Then one day the king heard of the long-lived Mahākāḷa, a nāga king of great psychic power who had seen four Sambuddhas.

90.

90.

Suṇitvā tamānetuṃ, soṇḍasaṅkhalibandhanaṃ;

Pesayitvā tamānetvā, setacchattassa heṭṭhato.

Having heard of him, he sent for him with strong chains; and having brought him, he placed him under the white parasol.

91.

91.

Pallaṅkamhi nisīdetvā, nānāpupphehi pūjiya;

Soḷasitthisahassehi, parivāriya abravi.

Having seated him on a throne and honored him with various flowers, the king, surrounded by his sixteen thousand women, spoke.

92.

92.

Saddhammacakkavattissa[M 0.0027], sambuddhassa mahesino;

Rūpaṃ anantañāṇassa, dassehi mama bho iti.

“O sir, show me the form of the great sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the wheel-turner of the good Dhamma, the one of infinite knowledge!”

93.

93.

Dvattiṃsalakkhaṇūpetaṃ, asītibyañjanujjalaṃ;

Byāmappabhāparikkhittaṃ, ketumālāhi sobhitaṃ.

Endowed with the thirty-two marks, radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, and beautiful with a garland of rays.

94.

94.

Nimmāsi nāgarājā so, buddharūpaṃ manoharaṃ;

Taṃ disvā’ti pasādassa, vimhayassa ca pūrito.

That nāga king created a captivating Buddha-form. Seeing it, the king was filled with extreme faith and wonder.

95.

95.

Etena nimmitaṃ rūpaṃ, īdisaṃ kīdisaṃ nukho;

Tathāgatassa rūpanti, āsi pitunnatunnato.

“If the form created by this one is so magnificent, what must the form of the Tathāgata have been like!” he thought, and he became exceedingly uplifted with joy.

96.

96.

Akkhipūjanti saññātaṃ, taṃ sattāhaṃ nirantaraṃ;

Mahāmahaṃ mahārāja, kārāpesi mahiddhiko.

The mighty great king had a great festival held, known as the “Festival of the Eyes,” which lasted continuously for seven days.

97.

97.

Evaṃ mahānubhāvo ca, saddho cāpi mahīpati;

Thero ca moggaliputto, diṭṭhā pubbe vasīhi te.

Thus the lord of the earth was of great power and also full of faith; he and the Elder Moggalliputta had been foreseen previously by those with mastery.

Sāsanappaveso niṭṭhito.

The Entry into the Dispensation is concluded.

Moggaliputtatissatherādayo

The Elder Moggalliputta Tissa and Others

98.

98.

Dutiye saṅgahe therā, pekkhantā’nāgatehi te;

Sāsanopaddavaṃ tassa, rañño kālamhi addasuṃ.

At the Second Council, those elders, looking into the future, foresaw a calamity for the Dispensation in the time of that king.

99.

99.

Pekkhāntā sakale loke, tadupaddavaghātakaṃ;

Tissabrahmānamaddakkhuṃ, aciraṭṭhāyi jīvitaṃ.

Looking throughout the entire world for a destroyer of that calamity, they saw the Brahmā Tissa, whose life was not to last for long.

100.

100.

Tesaṃ samupasaṅkamma, āyāciṃsu mahāpatiṃ;

Manussesu’papajjitvā, tadupaddavaghātanaṃ.

Approaching that great lord, they entreated him: “Take birth among humans and destroy that calamity!”

101.

101.

Adā paṭiññaṃ tesaṃ so, sāsanujjotanatthiko;

Siggavaṃ caṇḍavajjiñca avocuṃ dahare yati.

Desiring to illuminate the Dispensation, he gave them his promise. Then the elders spoke to the young ascetics, Siggava and Caṇḍavajji.

102.

102.

Aṭṭhārasādikā vassa-satā upari hessati;

Upaddavo sāsanassa, na sambhossāma taṃ mayaṃ.

“In one hundred and eighteen years from now, a calamity will befall the Dispensation. We will not be here to deal with it.”

103.

103.

Imaṃ tumhā’dhikaraṇaṃ, nopagañchittha bhikkhavo;

Daṇḍakammārahā tasmā, daṇḍakammapadañhi vo.

“O bhikkhus, you did not attend to this matter that concerned you. Therefore you are deserving of a disciplinary action, for this is a basis for such an action for you.”

104.

104.

Sāsanujjotanatthāya, tissabrahmā mahāpati;

Moggalibrāhmaṇaghare, paṭisandhiṃ gahessati.

“For the sake of illuminating the Dispensation, the great lord, Brahmā Tissa, will take rebirth in the house of the brahmin Moggali.”

105.

105.

Kāle [M 0.0028] tumhesu eko taṃ, pabbājetu kumārakaṃ;

Eko taṃ buddhavacanaṃ, uggaṇhāpetu sādhukaṃ.

“When the time comes, one of you is to give the going-forth to that boy, and the other is to have him thoroughly learn the word of the Buddha.”

106.

106.

Ahu upālitherassa,

Thero saddhivihāriko;

Dāsako soṇako tassa,

Dve therā soṇakassime.

The Elder Upāli had a pupil who lived with him, the Elder Dāsaka. Dāsaka's pupil was Soṇaka, and these two, Siggava and Caṇḍavajji, were the pupils of the Elder Soṇaka.

107.

107.

Ahu vesāliyaṃ pubbe-dāsako nāma sotthiyo;

Tisissasatajeṭṭho so, vasaṃ ācariyantike.

Formerly in Vesālī there was a brahmin named Dāsaka. He was the chief of three hundred pupils and lived near his teacher.

108.

108.

Dvādasavassikoyeva, vedapāragato caraṃ;

Sasisso vālikārāme, vasantaṃ katasaṅgahaṃ.

When he was only twelve years old, having mastered the Vedas, he was wandering about and saw the Elder Upāli, who had taken part in the council, dwelling with his pupils in the Vālikārāma.

109.

109.

Upālitheraṃ passitvā, nisīditvā tadantike;

Vedesu gaṇṭhiṭhānāni, pucchi so tāni byākari.

Having seen the Elder Upāli and sat down near him, he asked about difficult passages in the Vedas, and the elder explained them.

110.

110.

Sabbadhammānupatito, ekadhammo hi māṇava;

Sabbe dhammā osaranti, ekadhammo hi ko nu so.

“Young man, all dhammas are included in one dhamma; all dhammas converge upon one dhamma. Now what is that one dhamma?”

111.

111.

Iccāha nāmaṃ sandhāya, thero māṇavako tu so;

Nā’ññāsi pucchito manto, buddhamantoti bhāsito.
