Thus the elder spoke, referring to mind. But the young man, when questioned, did not know. He asked, “What is this teaching?” and was told, “It is the teaching of the Buddha.”

112.

112.

Dehīti āha so āha, dema no vesadhārino;

Guruṃ āpucchi mantatthaṃ, mātaraṃ pitaraṃ tathā.

The youth said, “Give it to me.” The elder replied, “We do not give it to one who wears the guise of a layman.” He then asked leave of his teacher, and also of his mother and father, for the sake of this teaching.

113.

113.

Māṇavānaṃ satehe’sa, tīhi therassa santike;

Pabbajitvāna kālena, upasampajji māṇavo.

Then that young man, together with his three hundred pupils, went forth in the presence of the elder; and in due course, he received the higher ordination.

114.

114.

Khīṇāsavasahassaṃ so, dāsakattherajeṭṭhakaṃ;

Upālithero vācesi, sakalaṃ piṭakattayaṃ.

The Elder Upāli taught the entire Tipiṭaka to a thousand arahants who had the Elder Dāsaka as their chief.

115.

115.

Gaṇanā vītivattā te, sesā’riya puthujjanā;

Piṭakānuggahitāni, yehi therassa santike.

Those who learned the Piṭakas in the elder's presence—the remaining noble ones and worldlings—were beyond counting.

116.

116.

Kāsīsu kosalo nāma, satthavāhasuto ahu;

Giribbajaṃ vaṇijjāya, gato mātāpitūhi so.

In the Kāsī country there was the son of a caravan leader named Kosala. He went to Giribbaja with his parents for the sake of trade.

117.

117.

Agā veḷuvanaṃ pañca-dasavaso kumārako;

Māṇavaṃ pañcapaññāsa, parivāriya taṃ gatā.

The boy, who was fifteen years old, went to the Veḷuvana, followed by a retinue of fifty-five young men.

118.

118.

Sagaṇaṃ dāsakaṃ theraṃ, tattha disvā pasīdiya;

Pabbajjaṃ yāci so āha, tavā’puccha guruṃ iti.

There he saw the Elder Dāsaka with his assembly of pupils and was inspired. He requested the going-forth, and the elder told him: “First ask your parents.”

119.

119.

Bhattattayamabhuñjitvā[M 0.0029], soṇako so kumārako;

Mātāpitūhi kāretvā, pabbajjānuññamāgato.

That boy, Soṇaka, after fasting for three meals, obtained permission from his parents for the going-forth and came back.

120.

120.

Saddhiṃ tehi kumārehi, dāsakattherasantike;

Pabbajjaṃ upasampajja, uggaṇhi piṭakattayaṃ.

Together with those boys, he received the going-forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Elder Dāsaka and learned the Tipiṭaka.

121.

121.

Khīṇāsavasahassassa, therasissa gaṇassa so;

Ahosi piṭakaññussa, jeṭṭhako soṇako yati.

That ascetic Soṇaka became the chief among the elder's pupils, a thousand arahants who were learned in the Piṭakas.

122.

122.

Ahosi siggavo nāma, pure pāṭalināmako;

Paññavā’maccatanayo, aṭṭhārasasamo tu so.

In the city of Pāṭaliputta there was a wise minister's son named Siggava, who was eighteen years old.

123.

123.

Pāsādesu vasaṃ tīsu, chaḷaḍḍhautusādhusu;

Amaccaputtaṃ ādāya, caṇḍavajjiṃ sahāyakaṃ.

Living in three mansions suitable for the six seasons, he took with him his companion Caṇḍavajji, who was also a minister's son.

124.

124.

Purisānaṃ dasaddhehi, satehi parivārito;

Gantvāna kukkuṭārāmaṃ, soṇakattheramaddasa.

Surrounded by a thousand and fifty men, he went to the Kukkuṭārāma and saw the Elder Soṇaka.

125.

125.

Samāpattisamāpannaṃ, nisinnaṃ saṃvutindriyaṃ;

Vandi tenālapantaṃ taṃ, ñatvā saṅghamapucchitaṃ.

He saw him seated, having entered a meditative attainment, with his sense faculties restrained. He paid homage, but the elder did not speak, knowing he had not been summoned by the Sangha.

126.

126.

Samāpattisamāpannā, nālapantī’ti āhu te;

Kathannu vuṭṭhahantīti, vuttā āhaṃsu bhikkhavo.

The bhikkhus told him: “Those who have entered a meditative attainment do not speak.” When asked, “Then how do they emerge?” the bhikkhus replied:

127.

127.

Pakkosanāya satthussa, saṅghapakkosanāya ca;

Yathā kālaparicchedā, āyukkhayavasena ca.

“They emerge at a summons from the Teacher, at a summons from the Sangha, at a pre-determined time, or at the exhaustion of their life-span.”

128.

128.

Vuṭṭhahantīti vatvāna, tesaṃ disvo’panissayaṃ;

Pāhesuṃ saṅghavacanaṃ, vuṭṭhāya sa tahiṃ agā.

Having said this and seeing their spiritual potential, they sent the Sangha's summons. The elder emerged from his attainment and went there.

129.

129.

Kumāro pucchi kiṃ bhante, nālapitthāti āha so;

Bhuñjimha bhuñjitabbanti, āha bhojetha no api.

The young man asked: “Venerable sir, why did you not speak?” He replied: “We were eating.” The young man said: “Since you are eating, then please feed us also.”

130.

130.

Āha amhādise jāhe, sakkā bhojayituṃ iti;

Mātāpitu anuññāya, so kumārotha siggavo.

He replied: “It is possible to feed those who have gone forth like us.” Then that young Siggava, with his parents' permission,

131.

131.

Caṇḍavajjī ca tepañca-satāni purisāpi ca;

Pabbajjitvo’pasampajjuṃ, soṇattherassa santike.

along with Caṇḍavajji and those five hundred men, went forth and received the higher ordination in the presence of the Elder Soṇa.

132.

132.

Upajjhāyantikeyeva, te duve piṭakattayaṃ;

Uggahesuñca kālena, chaḷabhiññaṃ labhiṃsu ca.

In the presence of their preceptor, those two learned the Tipiṭaka, and in due course, they attained the six supernormal knowledges.

133.

133.

Ñatvā [M 0.0030] tissa paṭisandhiṃ, tato pabhuti siggavo;

Thero so sattavassāni, taṃ gharaṃ upasaṅkami.

From the time he learned of Tissa's rebirth, the Elder Siggava went to that house for seven years.

134.

134.

Gacchāti vācāmattampi, sattavassāni nālabhi;

Alattha aṭṭhame vasse, gacchāti vacanaṃ tahiṃ.

For seven years he did not receive so much as the words “Go.” Only in the eighth year did he receive the words “Go” there.

135.

135.

Taṃ nikkhamantaṃ pavisanto, disvā moggalibrāhmaṇo;

Kiñci laddhaṃ ghare noti, pucchi āmāti so’bravi.

As the elder was leaving, the brahmin Moggali, who was entering, saw him and asked: “Did you receive anything in the house?” The elder replied: “Yes.”

136.

136.

Gharaṃ gantvāna pucchitvā, dutiye divase tato;

Musāvādena niggaṇhi, theraṃ gharamupāgataṃ.

Having gone home and inquired, on the next day he reproached the elder with an accusation of falsehood when he came to the house.

137.

137.

Therassa vacanaṃ sutvā, so pasannamano dvijo;

Attano pakatena’ssa, niccaṃ bhikkhaṃ pavattayi.

Having heard the elder's words, the brahmin, with a confident mind, regularly offered him alms from his own provisions.

138.

138.

Kamena’ssa pasīdiṃsu, sabbe’pi gharamānusā;

Bhojāpesi dijo niccaṃ, nisīdāpiya taṃ ghare.

Gradually, all the people in the household gained confidence in him. The brahmin had him seated in the house and regularly fed him.

139.

139.

Evaṃ kamena gacchanto, kāle soḷasavassiko;

Ahu tissakumāro so, tivedodadhipārago.

As time went on, the boy Tissa reached the age of sixteen and became one who had crossed the ocean of the three Vedas.

140.

140.

Thero kathāsamuṭṭhānaṃ, hessate’va ghare iti;

Āsanāni na dassesi, ṭhapetvā māṇavāsanaṃ.

Thinking, “A discussion will surely arise in the house,” the elder did not show any seats, except for the young man's seat.

141.

141.

Brahmalokagatattāva, sucikāmo ahosi so;

Tasmā so tassa pallaṅko, vāsayitvā lagīyati.

Having come from the Brahma-world, he was fond of purity; therefore, he was attached to his couch, which he had perfumed.

142.

142.

Aññāsanaṃ apassanto, ṭhite there sasambhamo;

Tassa taṃ āsanaṃ tassa, paññapesi ghare jano.

Seeing no other seat while the elder stood there, the people of the house, at the young man's consternation, prepared that very seat for him.

143.

143.

Disvā tattha nisinnaṃ taṃ, āgammā’cariyantikā;

Kujjhitvā māṇavo vācaṃ, amanāpaṃ udīrayi.

Seeing him seated there upon returning from his teacher, the youth, having become angry, spoke unpleasant words.

144.

144.

Thero māṇava kiṃ mantaṃ, jānāsīti tamabravi;

Tameva pucchaṃ therassa, pacchā rocesi māṇavo.

The elder said to him: “Young man, what mantra do you know?” The young man then questioned the elder about that very thing and was afterwards pleased.

145.

145.

Jānāmīti paṭiññāya, there theraṃ apucchiso;

Gaṇṭhiṭhānāni vedesu, tassa thero’tha byākari.

Having declared, “I know,” he questioned the elder there; the elder then explained to him the difficult points in the Vedas.

146.

146.

Gahaṭṭhoyeva [M 0.0031] thero so,

Vedapāragato ahu;

Na byākareyya kiṃ tassa,

Pabhinnapaṭisambhido.

That elder had reached the further shore of the Vedas even as a householder; being possessed of the analytical knowledges, why would he not explain it to him?

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhati,

Tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissati; Na uppajjissati,

Yassa vā pana cittaṃ nirujjhisati na uppajjissati;

Tassa cittaṃ uppajjati, na nirujjhatīti.

“For whom consciousness arises and does not cease, for them will consciousness cease and not arise? Or for whom will consciousness cease and not arise, for them does consciousness arise and not cease?”

147.

147.

Taṃ cittayamake pañhaṃ, pucchi thero visārado;

Andhakāro viya ahu, tassa so tamavoca so.

The expert elder asked him that question from the Citta Yamaka. It was like darkness to him, and he said as much to the elder.

148.

148.

Bhikkhuko nāma mantoti, buddha mantoti so bravi;

Dehīti vutte novesa-dhārino dammi taṃ iti.

“What is this mantra, monk?” he asked. The elder replied, “It is the Buddha's mantra.” When told, “Give it to me,” the elder said, “I give it only to one who wears this garb.”

149.

149.

Mātāpitūhi’nuññāto, mantatthāya sa pabbajji;

Kammaṭṭhānamadā thero, pabbājetvā yathārahaṃ.

Permitted by his parents, he went forth for the sake of the mantra; the elder, having ordained him as was fitting, gave him a meditation subject.

150.

150.

Bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto, acirena mahāmatī;

Sotāphattiphalaṃ patto, thero ñatvāna taṃ tathā.

The one of great wisdom, devoted to meditation, soon attained the fruit of stream-entry. The elder, knowing this to be so,

151.

151.

Pesesi caṇḍavajjissa, therassantikamuggahaṃ;

Kātuṃ suttābhidhammānaṃ, sotatthā’kātaduggahaṃ.

sent him to the Elder Caṇḍavajji to master the Suttas and Abhidhamma, ensuring a correct understanding for the benefit of future listeners.

152.

152.

Tato so tissadaharo, ārabhitvā vipassanaṃ;

Chaḷabhiñño ahu kāle, therabhāvañca pāpuṇi.

Then that young Tissa, having undertaken insight meditation, in due time became possessed of the six supernormal knowledges and attained the state of an elder.

153.

153.

Atīva pākaṭo āsi, cando’va sūriyo’vaso;

Loko tassa vaco’maññī, sambuddhassa vacopiya.

He was exceedingly renowned, like the moon and the sun; the world esteemed his word as dearly as the word of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Moggaliputtatissatherodayo niṭṭhīto.

The Rise of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa is concluded.

154.

154.

Ekāhaṃ [M 0.0032] uparājā so, adakkhi migavaṃ gato;

Kīḷamāne mige’raññe, disvā etaṃ vicintayi.

One day, that viceroy, having gone hunting, saw deer playing in the forest and reflected thus:

155.

155.

Migāpi evaṃ kiḷanti, araññe tiṇagocarā;

Na kiḷissanti kiṃ bhikkhū, sukhāhāravihārino.

“Even deer that graze on grass in the forest play like this; why should not monks play, who have pleasant food and dwellings?”

156.

156.

Attano cintitaṃ rañño, ārocesi gharaṃ gato;

Saññāpetuṃ tu sattāhaṃ, rajjaṃ tassa adāsi so.

Having gone home, he informed the king of his thought; to make him understand, the king gave him the kingdom for seven days.

157.

157.

Anubhohi ime rajjaṃ, sattāhaṃ tvaṃ kumāraka;

Tato taṃ ghātayissāmi, icca’voca mahīpati.

“Enjoy this kingdom, O prince, for seven days; then I shall have you slain,” thus spoke the lord of the earth.

158.

158.

Āhā’ti tamhi sattāhe,

Tvaṃ kenā’si kiso iti;

Maraṇassa bhayenāti,

Vutte rājā’ha taṃ puna.

“Ah!” he said, “in these seven days, why are you so thin?” When he replied, “From fear of death,” the king then spoke to him again.

159.

159.

Sattāhā’haṃ marissaṃti, tvaṃ na kīḷi ime kathaṃ;

Kīḷissanti yati tāta, sadā maraṇasaññino.

“Thinking, ‘I shall die in seven days,’ you do not play. How is this? Dear one, ascetics who are ever mindful of death will play.”

160.

160.

Iccevaṃ bhākarā vutto, sāsanasmiṃ pasīdi so;

Kālena migavaṃ gantvā, theramadakkhi saññataṃ.

Thus spoken to by his brother, he gained faith in the Dispensation; in due time, going hunting, he saw the self-controlled Elder.

161.

161.

Nisinnaṃ rukkhamūlasmiṃ, so mahādhammarakkhitaṃ;

Sālasākhāya nāgena, bījayanta manāsavaṃ.

The great Dhammarakkhita, seated at the foot of a tree, free from taints, being fanned by a nāga with a Sāla branch.

162.

162.

Ayaṃ thero viyā’hampi, pabbajja jina sāsane;

Viharissaṃ kadā raññe, iti cintayi paññavā.

“When shall I, like this elder, go forth into the Victor’s Dispensation and dwell in the forest?” thus thought the wise one.

163.

163.

Thero tassa pasādatthaṃ,

Upatitvā vihāyasā;

Gantvā asokārāmassa,

Pokkharañño jale ṭhito.

The elder, to inspire faith in him, rising into the sky, went and stood in the water of the pond in Asoka's Park.

164.

164.

Ākāse ṭhapayitvāna, cīvarāni varāni so;

Ogāhitvā pokkharaṇī, gattāni parisiñcatha.

Having placed his excellent robes in the air, he entered the pond and sprinkled water on his limbs.

165.

165.

Taṃ [M 0.0033] iddhiṃ uparājā so, disvā’tīva pasīdiya;

Ajjeva pabbajissaṃti, buddhiṃcā’kāsi buddhimā.

Seeing that psychic power, that viceroy, exceedingly pleased, the wise one resolved: “Today I shall go forth!”

166.

166.

Upasaṅkamma rājānaṃ, pabbajjaṃ yāci sādaro;

Nivāretumasakkonto, tamādāya mahīpati.

Approaching the king, he earnestly requested ordination. The great ruler, unable to prevent him, took him along.

167.

167.

Mahatā parivārena, vihāramagamā sayaṃ;

Pabbaji so mahādhamma-rakkhitattherasantike.

With a great retinue, he himself went to the monastery; he was ordained in the presence of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita.

168.

168.

Saddhiṃ tena catusata-sahassāni narāpi ca;

Anupabbajitānantu, gaṇanā ca na vajjati.

Along with him, four hundred thousand men also went forth; and of those who went forth in their wake, there is no counting.

169.

169.

Bhāgineyyo narindassa, aggi brahmāti vissuto;

Ahosi rañño dhītāya, saṅghamittāya sāmiko.

The king's nephew, well-known as Aggibrahmā, was the husband of the king's daughter, Saṅghamittā.

170.

170.

Tassā tassa suto cāpi,

Sumano nāma nāmaso;

Yācitvā so’pi rājānaṃ,

Uparājena pabbaji.

Their son, Sumana by name, also requested the king and went forth with the viceroy.

171.

171.

Uparājassa pabbajjā, tassā’sokassa rājino;

Catutthe āsivassesā, mahājanahitodayā.

The viceroy's going forth occurred in the fourth year of King Asoka's reign, for the arising of the welfare of the great populace.

172.

172.

Tattheva upasampanno, sampannaupanissayo;

Ghaṭento uparājā so, chaḷa’bhiñño’rahā ahu.

Having received higher ordination right there, endowed with the right conditions, that viceroy, striving, became an arahant possessing the six higher knowledges.

173.

173.

Vihāre tesamāraddhe, sabbe sabbapuresupi;

Sādhukaṃ tīhi vassehi, niṭṭhāpesuṃ manorame.

Having begun to build monasteries in all their respective towns, they splendidly completed the delightful ones within three years.

174.

174.

Therassa indaguttassa, kammādiṭṭhāyakassa tu;

Iddhiyā cā’su niṭṭhāsi, asokārāmasavhayo.

Through the psychic power of the elder Indagutta, the supervisor of the work, the monastery called Asokārāma was quickly completed.

175.

175.

Janena paribhuttesu, ṭhānesu ca tahiṃ tahiṃ;

Cetiyāni akāresi, ramaṇīyāni bhūpati.

The king had delightful shrines built in various places frequented by the people.

176.

176.

Purehi caturāsīti-sahassehi samantato;

Lekhe ekāhamānesuṃ, vihārā niṭṭhitā iti.

From eighty-four thousand cities all around, they brought letters in a single day, announcing: “The monasteries are completed.”

177.

177.

Lekhe sutvā mahārājā, mahātejiddhi vikkamo;

Kātukāmo sakiṃyeva, sabbārāma mahāmahaṃ.

Hearing the letters, the great king, mighty in majesty, psychic power, and valor, desired to hold at once a great festival for all the monasteries.

178.

178.

Pure bheriṃ carāpesi, sattame divase ito;

Sabbārāmamaho hotu, sabbadesesu ekadā.

He had a drum beaten in the city, proclaiming: “Seven days from now, let there be a great festival for all monasteries, in all regions, at one time!”

179.

179.

Yojane [M 0.0034] yojane dentu, mahādānaṃ mahītale;

Karontu gāmārāmānaṃ, maggānañca vibhūsanaṃ.

“Let them give great alms on the earth, league by league; and let them make adornments for villages, monasteries, and roads.”

180.

180.

Vihāresu ca sabbesu, bhikkhusaṅghassa sabbathā;

Mahādānāni vattentu, yathākālaṃ yathābalaṃ.

“And in all monasteries, let them provide great gifts to the Sangha of bhikkhus in every way, according to the proper time and their ability.”

181.

181.

Dīpamālā pumphamālā-laṅkārehi tahiṃ tahiṃ;

Tūriyehi ca sabbehi, upahāraṃ anekadhā.

“With garlands of lamps, garlands of flowers, and ornaments here and there, and with all kinds of musical instruments, let them make manifold offerings.”

182.

182.

Uposathaṅgānā’dāya, sabbe dhammaṃ suṇantu ca;

Pūjāvisesena’neke ca, karontu tadahepi ca.

“Having undertaken the Uposatha observances, let all listen to the Dhamma; and let many perform special acts of devotion on that day as well.”

183.

183.

Sabbe sabbattha sabbathā, yathāṇattādhikāpi ca;

Pūjā sampaṭiyādesuṃ, devalokamanoramā.

All people, everywhere, in every way, and even exceeding what was commanded, prepared offerings delightful to the celestial world.

184.

184.

Tasmiṃ dine mahārājā, sabbālaṅkāra bhūsito;

Sahorodho sahāmacco, balogha parivārito.

On that day, the great king, adorned with all ornaments, together with his women of the court, his ministers, and surrounded by a flood of troops,

185.

185.

Agamāsi sakārāmaṃ, bhindanto viya mediniṃ;

Saṅghamajjhamhi aṭṭhāsi, vanditvā saṅghamuttamaṃ.

went to his own monastery, as if splitting the earth. He stood in the midst of the Sangha, having paid homage to the supreme Sangha.

186.

186.

Tasmiṃ samāgame āsuṃ, asīti bhikkhukoṭi yo;

Ahesuṃ satasahassaṃ, tesu khīṇāsavā yati.

At that gathering there were eighty crores of bhikkhus; among them, a hundred thousand were ascetics who had destroyed the taints.

187.

187.

Navuti bhikkhusahassāni, ahū bhikkhuniyo tahiṃ;

Khiṇāsavā bhikkhuniyo, sahassaṃ āsu tāsu tu.

There were ninety thousand bhikkhus, and bhikkhunis also; among them, a thousand bhikkhunis were those who had destroyed the taints.

188.

188.

Lokavivaraṇaṃ nāma, pāṭihīraṃ akaṃsu te;

Khīṇāsavā pasādatthaṃ, dhammāsokassa rājino.

The arahants performed the miracle called "Opening of the World" for the sake of inspiring faith in King Dhammāsoka.

189.

189.

Caṇḍāsokoti ñāyittha, pubbe pāpena kammunā;

Dhammāsokoti ñāyittha, pacchā puññena kammunā.

He was known as "Asoka the Fierce" before, due to his evil kamma; later, he was known as "Asoka the Righteous," due to his meritorious kamma.

190.

190.

Samuddapariyantaṃ so, jambudīpaṃ samantato;

Passi sabbe vihāre ca, nānāpūjā vibhūsite.

He saw Jambudīpa, surrounded by the ocean on all sides, and all the monasteries adorned with various offerings.

191.

191.

Atīva tuṭṭho te disvā, saṅghaṃ pucchi nisīdiya;

Kassa bhante pariccāgo, mahāsugata sāsane.

Extremely pleased upon seeing them, he sat down and asked the Sangha: "Venerable Sirs, whose sacrifice is the greatest in the dispensation of the Great Sugata?"

192.

192.

Thero so moggaliputto, rañño pañhaṃ viyākari;

Dharamāne’pi sugate, natthi cāgī tayāsamo.

That elder Moggaliputta answered the king's question: "Even while the Sugata was living, there was no giver like you."

193.

193.

Taṃ sutvā vacanaṃ bhiyyo, tuṭṭho rājā apucchi taṃ;

Buddhasāsana dāyādo, hoti kho mādiso iti.

Hearing these words, the king, greatly delighted, asked him further, "Can someone like me become an heir to the Buddha’s dispensation?"

194.

194.

Thero [M 0.0035] tu rājaputtassa, mahindassū’panissayaṃ;

Tatheva rājadhītāya, saṅghamittāya pekkhiya.

But the elder, having observed the decisive condition of Prince Mahinda, and likewise that of Princess Saṅghamittā,

195.

195.

Sāsanassā’bhi vuddhiñca, taṃ hetukama vekkhiya;

Paccābhāsatha rājānaṃ, so sāsanadhurandharo.

and having seen that as the cause for the growth of the Dispensation, that upholder of the Teaching addressed the king:

196.

196.

Tādiso’pi mahācāgī, dāyādo sāsanassa na;

Paccayadāyako’cceva, vuccate manujādhīpa.

Even one so greatly generous is not an heir to the Dispensation; he is merely called a provider of requisites, O lord of men.

197.

197.

Yo tu puttaṃ dhītaraṃ vā,

Pabbajjāpeti sāsane;

So sāsanassa dāyādo,

Hoti no dāyako api.

But whoever causes a son or daughter to go forth in the Dispensation, that one is an heir of the Dispensation, and not merely a donor.

198.

198.

Atha sāsana dāyāda-bhāvamicchaṃ mahīpati;

Mahindaṃ saṅghamittañca, ṭhite tatra apucchatha.

Then the king, desiring the state of being an heir to the Dispensation, asked Mahinda and Saṅghamittā, who were staying there:

199.

199.

Pabbajissatha kiṃ tātā, pabbajjā mahatī matā;

Pituno vacanaṃ sutvā, pitaraṃ te abhāsisuṃ.

"Will you go forth, dear children? Going forth is considered great." Hearing their father's words, they spoke to their father:

200.

200.

Ajjeva pabbajissāma, sace tvaṃ deva icchasi;

Amhañca lābho tumhañca, pabbajjāya bhavissati.

"We will go forth this very day, if you, O king, desire it. It will be a gain for us and for you, by means of this going forth."

201.

201.

Uparājassa pabbajja-kālabho pabhutīhi so;

Sā cāpi aggibrahmassa, pabbajjā katanicchayā.

The time of the viceroy's going forth was for the benefit of the powerful; and she too, wife of Aggibrahma, was resolute in going forth.

202.

202.

Uparajjaṃ mahīndassa, dātukāmo’pi bhūpati;

Tato’pi adhikāsā’ti, pabbajjaṃyeva rocayi.

Though the king wished to bestow the viceroyalty on Mahinda, yet, because of his greater longing, he preferred the going forth itself.

203.

203.

Piyaṃ puttaṃ mahindañca, buddhirūpabaloditaṃ;

Pabbajjā pesi samahaṃ, saṅgha mittañca dhītaraṃ.

He sent forth to the going forth his beloved son Mahinda, endowed with intelligence, beauty, and strength, and his daughter Saṅghamittā.

204.

204.

Tadā vīsativasso so, mahindo rājanandano;

Saṅghamittā rājadhītā, aṭṭhārasasamā tadā.

Then that Mahinda, the king's son, was twenty years old, and Princess Saṅghamittā was eighteen years old then.

205.

205.

Tadaheva ahu tassa, pabbajjā upasampadā;

Pabbajjā sikkhādānañca, tassā ca tadahu ahu.

On that very day, his going forth and higher ordination occurred; and her going forth and the giving of training also occurred on that day.

206.

206.

Upajjhāyo kumārassa, ahu moggalisavhayo;

Pabbājesi mahādeva-tthero majjhantiko pana.

The preceptor of the prince was the one called Moggaliputta; and the elders Mahādeva and Majjhantika ordained him.

207.

207.

Kammavācaṃ akā tasmiṃ, so’pasampadamaṇḍale;

Arahattaṃ mahindo so, patto sapaṭisambhidaṃ.

He performed the formal act in that ordination assembly; and that Mahinda attained arahantship with the analytical knowledges.

208.

208.

Saṅghamittā’hu’pajjhāyā[M 0.0036], dhammapālāti vissutā;

Ācariyā āyupāli, kāle sā’si anāsavā.

Saṅghamittā's preceptor was the renowned Dhammapālā; her teacher was Āyupāli, and in time she became taintless.

209.

209.

Ubho sāsanapajjotā, laṃkādīpopakārino;

Chaṭṭhe vasse pabbajiṃsu, dhammāsokassa rājino.

Both were luminaries of the Dispensation, benefactors of the Isle of Lanka; they went forth in the sixth year of King Dhammāsoka.

210.

210.

Mahāmahindo vassehi, tīhi dīpappasādako;

Piṭakattayaṃ muggaṇhi, upajjhāyassa santike.

Within three years, the great Mahinda, who brought serenity to the island, mastered the Three Baskets in the presence of his preceptor.

211.

211.

Sā bhikkhunī candalekhā, mahindo bhikkhū sūriyo;

Sambuddha sāsanākāsaṃ, te sadā sobhayuṃ tadā.

That bhikkhunī was like a streak of the moon, and the bhikkhu Mahinda was like the sun; they always illuminated the sky of the Sambuddha’s Dispensation at that time.

212.

212.

Vane pāṭaliputtamhā, vane vanacaro caraṃ;

Kuntakinnariyā saddhiṃ, saṃvāsaṃ kappayī kira.

In the forest near Pāṭaliputta, a forest-dweller, wandering in the woods, is said to have lived together with a Kinnarī named Kuntā.

213.

213.

Tena saṃvāsamanvāya,

Sā putte janayī duve;

Tisso jeṭṭho kaṇiṭṭho tu,

Sumitto nāma nāmato.

Through that association, she bore two sons: the elder was Tissa, and the younger was named Sumitta.

214.

214.

Mahāvaruṇattherassa, kāle pabbajja santike;

Arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, chaḷabhiññaṃ guṇaṃ ubho.

Having gone forth in time under the great elder Mahāvaruṇa, both attained arahantship with the quality of the six supernormal powers.

215.

215.

Pāde kīṭavisenā’si, phuṭṭho jeṭṭho savedano;

Āha puṭṭho kaṇiṭṭhena, bhesajjaṃ pasataṃ ghaṭaṃ.

Once, the elder, stung on the foot by an insect’s venom and feeling pain, when asked by the younger, spoke of a remedy: a handful of ghee.

216.

216.

Rañño nivedanaṃ thero, gilānavattato’pi so;

Sappisatthañca caraṇaṃ, pacchābhattaṃ paṭikkhipi.

The elder informed the king on account of his illness; he declined the treatment of his foot with ghee and the afternoon meal.

217.

217.

Piṇḍāya ce caraṃ sappiṃ, labhase tvaṃ tamāhara;

Icchāha tissathero so, sumittaṃ theramuttamaṃ.

“If, while going for alms-food, you obtain ghee, then bring it.” Thus spoke the elder Tissa to the excellent elder Sumitta.

218.

218.

Piṇḍāya caratā tena, na laddhaṃ pasataṃ ghataṃ;

Sappikumbhasatenāpi, byādhijāto asādhiyo.

Though he went about for alms, he did not obtain even a handful of ghee; the disease that arose was incurable even with a hundred pots of ghee.

219.

219.

Teneva byādhinā thero, patto āyukkhayantikaṃ;

Ovaditvāppamādena, nibbātuṃ mānasaṃ akā.

By that same illness, the Elder reached the end of his life-span; having exhorted them with heedfulness, he set his mind on attaining Nibbāna.

220.

220.

Ākāsamhi nisīditvā, tejodhātuvasena so;

Yathāruci adhiṭṭhāya, sarīraṃ parinibbuto.

Sitting in the sky, by means of the fire element, having made a resolution concerning his body according to his wish, he attained final Nibbāna.

221.

221.

Jālāsarīrā nikkhamma, nimmaṃsachārikaṃ ḍahi;

Therassa sakalaṃ kāyaṃ, aṭṭhikānituno ḍahi.

Flames, emerging from his body, burned away the flesh and skin; it burned the elder's entire body, leaving only the bones.

222.

222.

Sutvā [M 0.0037] nibbūtimetassa, tissatherassa bhūpati;

Agamāsi sakārāmaṃ, janogha parivārito.

Hearing of the passing away of this elder Tissa, the king, surrounded by a flood of people, went to his monastery.

223.

223.

Hattikkhandhagato rājā, tānaṭṭhina’varopiya;

Kāretvā dhātusakkāraṃ, saṅghaṃ byādhimapucchitaṃ.

The king, mounted on the back of an elephant, had those relics brought down, and having paid them honor, he inquired of the Saṅgha about the illness.

224.

224.

Taṃ sutvā jātasaṃvego, puradvāresu kāriya;

Sudhācitā pokkharaṇī, bhesajjānañca pūriya.

Hearing this, filled with spiritual urgency, he had a lime-plastered lotus pond constructed at the city gates and had it filled with medicines.

225.

225.

Pāpesi bhikkhusaṅghassa, bhesajjāni dine dine;

Mā hotu bhikkhusaṅghassa, bhesajjaṃ dullabhaṃ iti.

He had medicines sent to the community of monks day by day, thinking: “May medicine not be difficult for the community of monks to obtain.”

226.

226.

Sumittathero nibbāyi, caṅkamanto’va caṅkame;

Pasīdi sāsane’tīva, tenāpi ca mahājano.

The elder Sumitta passed away while walking on the cloister walk; because of him, the great multitude was exceedingly pleased with the Dispensation.

227.

227.

Kuntiputtā duve therā,

Te lokahitakārino;

Nibbāyiṃsu asokassa,

Rañño vassamhi aṭṭhame.

The two elders, sons of Kunti, who worked for the welfare of the world, passed away in the eighth year of King Asoka’s reign.

228.

228.

Tato pabhuti saṅghassa, lābho’tīva mahā ahu;

Pacchā pasannā ca janā, yasmā lābhaṃ pavattayuṃ.

From then on, there was exceedingly great gain for the Saṅgha; for later, people became devout and caused the gain to increase.

229.

229.

Pahīnalābhasakkārā, titthiyā lābhakāraṇā;

Sayaṃ kāsāyamādāya, vasiṃsu saha bhikkhūhi.

Their gain and honor having declined, the sectarians, for the sake of gain, themselves took up the ochre robe and dwelt together with the monks.

230.

230.

Yathāsakañca te vādaṃ, buddhavādo’ti dīpayuṃ;

Yathāsakañca kiriyā, akariṃsu yathāruci.

And they proclaimed their own doctrine as the Buddha's doctrine; and they performed their own practices as they pleased.

231.

231.

Tato moggaliputto so,

Thero thira guṇodayo;

Sāsanabbudamuppannaṃ,

Disvā tamatikakkhalaṃ.

Then that elder Moggaliputta, firm in the arising of virtues, seeing that a very coarse flaw had arisen in the Dispensation,

232.

232.

Tasso’pasamane kālaṃ, dīghadassī avekkhiya;

Datvā mahindatherassa, mahābhikkhugaṇaṃ sakaṃ.

the far-seeing one, reflecting on the time for its pacification, and having entrusted his own great community of monks to the Elder Mahinda,

233.

233.

Uddhaṃ gaṅgāya eko’va, ahogaṅgamhi pabbate;

Vihāsi sattavassāni, viveka manubrūhayaṃ.

alone, he dwelt on Mount Ahogaṅga, upstream from the Ganges, for seven years, cultivating seclusion.

234.

234.

Titthiyānaṃ bahucattā ca, dubbaccattā ca bhikkhavo;

Tesaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhiṃsu, dhammena paṭisedhanaṃ.

Because the sectarians were numerous and unruly, the monks were not able to restrain them in accordance with the Dhamma.

235.

235.

Teneva [M 0.0038] jambudīpamhi, sabbārāmesu bhikkhavo;

Sattavassāni nākaṃsu, uposatha pavāraṇaṃ.

For that very reason, throughout Jambudīpa, in all the monasteries, the monks did not perform the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā for seven years.

236.

236.

Taṃ sutvā mahārājā, dhammāsoko mahāyaso;

Ekaṃ amaccaṃ pesesi, asokārāma muttamaṃ.

Hearing this, the great king Dhammāsoka, of great fame, sent a minister to the excellent Asokārāma.

237.

237.

Gantvā’dhikaraṇaṃ etaṃ, vupasamma uposathaṃ;

Kārehi bhikkhusaṅghena, pamā’rāme tuvaṃ iti.

“Go, settle this dispute, and have the Uposatha performed by the community of monks in my monastery.”

238.

238.

Gantvāna sannipātetvā, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sadummati;

Uposathaṃ karothāti, sāvesi rājasāsanaṃ.

That foolish one, having gone and assembled the community of monks, announced the king's command: “Perform the Uposatha.”

239.

239.

Uposathaṃ tittiyehi, na karoma mayaṃ iti;

Avo ca bhikkhusaṅgho taṃ, amaccaṃ mūḷhamānasaṃ.

“We will not perform the Uposatha with the sectarians,” said the community of monks to that minister of deluded mind.

240.

240.

So’macco katipayānaṃ, therānaṃ paṭipāṭiyā;

Acchindi asinā sīsaṃ, kāremīti uposathaṃ.

That minister, in succession, cut off the heads of several elders with a sword, thinking, “I will have the Uposatha performed.”

241.

241.

Rājabhātā tissatthero, taṃ disvā kiriyaṃ lahuṃ;

Gantvāna tassa āsanne, sāsanamhi nisidi so.

The elder Tissa, the king's brother, seeing that swift action, went and sat down on a seat near him.

242.

242.

Theraṃ disvā amacco so, gantvā rañño nivedayi;

Sabbaṃ pavattiṃ taṃ sutvā, jātadāho mahīpati.

Seeing the Elder, that minister went and informed the king. Having heard the entire account, the monarch was consumed with remorse.

243.

243.

Sīghaṃ gantvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ, pucchi ubbiggamānaso;

Evaṃ katena kammena, kassa pāpaṃ siyā iti.

Going quickly to the community of monks, with an agitated mind, he asked: “By this deed thus done, whose demerit would it be?”

244.

244.

Tesaṃ apaṇḍitā keci, pāpaṃ tuyhanti keci tu;

Ubhinnaṃcā’ti āhaṃsu, natthi tuyhanti paṇḍitā.

Among them, some foolish ones said, “The demerit is yours.” But others said, “It is for both.” The wise ones said, “It is not yours.”

245.

245.

Taṃ sutvā’ha mahārājā, samattho atthi bhikkhuna;

Vimatiṃ me vinodetvā, kātuṃ sāsanapaggahaṃ.

Hearing this, the great king said: “Is there a monk capable of dispelling my doubt and of promoting the Dispensation?”

246.

246.

Atthi moggaliputto so,

Tissatthero rathesabha;

Icchāha saṅgho rājānaṃ,

Rāja tatthā’si sādaro.

“There is that elder Moggalliputta Tissa, a leader,” the Saṅgha said to the king. The king was very attentive to this matter.

247.

247.

Visuṃ bhikkhusahassena, caturo parivārite;

Thero narasahassena, amacce caturo tathā.

Four were surrounded, each by a thousand monks; the elder with a thousand men, and four ministers likewise.

248.

248.

Tadaheyeva pesesi, attano vacanena so;

Theraṃ ānetu me tehi, tathā vutte sanāgami.

On that very day, he sent forth his own command: “Bring the Elder to me with them.” Thus addressed, the messenger departed.

249.

249.

Taṃ [M 0.0039] sutvā puna aṭṭha’ttha, there’macce ca pesayi;

Visuṃ sahassapurise, pubbe viya sanāgami.

Hearing that, he again sent eight elders and eight ministers, each with a thousand men, and they departed as before.

250.

250.

Rājā pucchi kathaṃ thero, āgaccheyya nu kho iti;

Bhikkhū āhaṃsu therassa, tassa’gamanakāraṇaṃ.

The king asked, “How then might the Elder come?” The monks told him the reason for the Elder’s not coming.

251.

251.

Hoti bhante upatthambho, kātuṃ sāsanapaggahaṃ;

Iti vutte mahārāja, thero essati so iti.

“O great king, if this is said: ‘Venerable sir, there is support for upholding the Teaching,’ that Elder will come.”

252.

252.

Punāpi thero’macce ca, rājā soḷasa soḷasa;

Visuṃ sahassa purise, tathā vatvāna pesayi.

Again the king sent sixteen elders and sixteen ministers, each with a thousand men, having spoken thus.

253.

253.

Thero mahallatte’pi, nārohissati yānakaṃ;

Theraṃ gaṅgāya nāvāya, ānethā’ti ca abravi.

“Though the Elder is old, he will not mount a vehicle. Bring the Elder by boat on the Ganges,” he declared.

254.

254.

Gantvā te taṃ tathā’vocuṃ,

So taṃ sutvā’va uṭṭhahi;

Nāvāya theraṃ ānesuṃ,

Rājā paccuggamī tahiṃ.

Going, they spoke thus to him. Hearing this, he arose at once. By boat they brought the Elder. The king went forth to meet him there.

255.

255.

Jāṇumattaṃ jalaṃ rājo’gahetvā dakkhiṇaṃ karaṃ;

Nāvāya otarantassa, therassā’dāsi gāravo.

Wading into the knee-deep water, the reverent king gave his right hand to the Elder as he descended from the boat.

256.

256.

Dakkhiṇaṃ dakkhiṇeyyo so, karaṃ rañño’nukampako;

Ālambitvā’nukampāya, thero nāvāya otari.

The Elder, worthy of offerings, out of compassion took hold of the compassionate king's right hand and descended from the boat.

257.

257.

Rājā theraṃ nayitvāna, uyyānaṃ rativaḍḍhanaṃ;

Therassa pāde dhovitvā, makkhetvā ca nisīdiya.

The king, having led the Elder to the delight-increasing grove, washed the Elder’s feet, anointed them, and sat down.

258.

258.

Samatthabhāvaṃ therassa, vīmaṃsanto mahīpati;

Daṭṭhukāmo ahaṃ bhante, pāṭihīranti abravi.

Wishing to investigate the Elder's ability, the lord of the earth said, “Venerable sir, I wish to see a miracle.”

259.

259.

Kanti vutte mahīkampaṃ, āha taṃ puna rāhaso;

Sakalāye’ka desāya, kataraṃ daṭṭhumicchasi.

When the Elder asked, “Which one?” the king replied, “An earthquake.” The Elder then asked him in private: “Of the whole earth or of a single region, which do you wish to see?”

260.

260.

Ko dukkaroti pucchitvā, eka desāya kampanaṃ;

Dukkaranti suṇitvāna, taṃ duṭṭhukāmataṃ bravī.

Having asked, “Which is more difficult?” and hearing the reply, “To shake a single region is more difficult,” he declared his wish to see that.

261.

261.

Rathaṃ assaṃ manussañca, pātiñcodaka pūritaṃ;

Thero yojana sīmāya, antaramhi catuddise.

The Elder had a chariot, a horse, a man, and a pot filled with water placed in the four directions within the boundary of a yojana.

262.

262.

Ṭhapāpetvā [M 0.0040] tadaḍḍhehi, saha taṃ yojanaṃ mahiṃ;

Cālesi iddhiyā tatra, nisinnassa ca dassayi.

Having had them placed at the boundary and halfway within it, he shook that yojana of earth by his psychic power and showed it to the one seated there.

263.

263.

Tenā’maccena bhikkhūnaṃ, maraṇena’ttanopi ca;

Pāpassa’tthitta natthittaṃ, theraṃ pucchi mahīpati.

The lord of the earth asked the Elder about the existence or non-existence of demerit concerning the death of the monks caused by that minister, and concerning his own self.

264.

264.

Paṭicca kammaṃ natthīti, kiliṭṭhaṃ cetanaṃ vinā;

Thero bodhesi rājānaṃ, vatvā tittirajātakaṃ.

“Without a defiled intention, there is no evil kamma in this matter,” the Elder enlightened the king, reciting the Tittira Jātaka.

265.

265.

Vasanto tattha sattāhaṃ, rājuyyāne manorame;

Sikkhāpesi mahīpālaṃ, sambuddhasamayaṃ subhaṃ.

Residing there for seven days in the king's delightful park, he instructed the great ruler in the auspicious teaching of the Fully Enlightened One.

266.

266.

Tasmiṃyeva ca sattā he, duve yakkhe mahīpati;

Pesetvā mahiyaṃ bhikkhū, asese sannipātayi.

And within that very week, the lord of the earth, having sent forth two yakkhas, assembled all the monks on the earth without exception.

267.

267.

Sattame divase gantvā, sakārāmaṃ manoramaṃ;

Kāresi bhikkhusaṅghassa, sannipātamasesato.

On the seventh day, going to his own delightful monastery, he arranged for a complete assembly of the community of monks.

268.

268.

Therena saha ekante, nisinno sāṇiantare;

Ekekaladdhike bhikkhu, pakkositvāna santikaṃ.

Seated with the Elder in seclusion behind a curtain, he summoned the monks into his presence, group by group according to their views.

269.

269.

Kiṃvādī sugato bhante, iti pucchi mahīpati;

Te sassatādikaṃ diṭṭhiṃ, byākariṃsu yathāsakaṃ.

“Venerable sir, what is the doctrine of the Sugata?” thus asked the lord of the earth. They each declared their own view, such as eternalism.

270.

270.

Te micchādiṭṭhike sabbe, rājā uppabbājāpayī;

Sabbe saṭṭhisahassāni, āsuṃ uppabbajāpitā.

The king had all those of wrong view expelled from the Order; in all, sixty thousand were thus expelled.

271.

271.

Apucchi dhammike bhikkhū, kiṃvādī sugato iti;

Vibhajjavādī tāhaṃsu, taṃ theraṃ pucchi bhūpati.

He asked the righteous monks, “What is the doctrine of the Sugata?” They replied, “He is a teacher of analysis.” The ruler then asked the Elder about this.

272.

272.

Vibhajjavādī sambuddho,

Hoti bhante’ti āha so;

Thero’ āmā’ti taṃ sutvā,

Rājā tuṭṭhamano tadā.

“Venerable sir, is the Fully Enlightened One a teacher of analysis?” he asked. The Elder replied, “Yes.” Hearing that, the king was then pleased in mind.

273.

273.

Saṅgho pisodhito yasmā,

Tasmā saṅgho uposathaṃ;

Karotu bhante iccevaṃ,

Vatvā therassa bhūpati.

“Venerable sir, since the Saṅgha is now purified, therefore let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha.” Thus spoke the ruler to the Elder.

274.

274.

Saṅghassa rakkhaṃ datvāna, nagaraṃ pāvisī subhaṃ;

Saṅgho samaggo hutvāna, tadā’kāsi uposathaṃ.

Having given protection to the Saṅgha, he entered the beautiful city; the Saṅgha, being united, then performed the Uposatha.

275.

275.

Thero [M 0.0041] aneka saṅkhamhā, bhikkhusaṅghā visārade;

Chaḷabhiññe tepiṭake, pabhinnapaṭisambhide.

From the countless Saṅgha of monks, the Elder selected those who were expert, endowed with the six higher knowledges, masters of the Tipiṭaka, and possessed of the analytical knowledges.

276.

276.

Bhikkhusahassaṃ uccini, kātuṃ saddhammaṃ saṅgahaṃ;

Tehi asokārāmamhi, akā saddhamma saṅgahaṃ.

He selected a thousand monks to make a compilation of the true Dhamma; with them, in the Asokārāma, he made the compilation of the true Dhamma.

277.

277.

Mahākassapatthero ca, yasatthero ca kārayuṃ;

Yathā te dhamma saṃgītiṃ, tissattheropi taṃ tathā.

The Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa caused it to be done; just as they conducted that Dhamma recitation, so too did the Elder Tissa.

278.

278.

Tathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ, paravādappamaddanaṃ;

Abhāsi tissatthero ca, tasmiṃ saṃgīti maṇḍale.

Thus, the Elder Tissa also expounded the Kathāvatthu, which crushes opposing views, in that recitation assembly.

279.

279.

Evaṃ bhikkhusahassena, rakkhāya’soka rājino;

Ayaṃ navahi māsehi, dhamma saṃgīti niṭṭhitā.

Thus, with a thousand monks, under the protection of King Asoka, this Dhamma council was completed in nine months.

280.

280.

Rañño sattarase vasse, dvāsattatisamo isi;

Mahāpavāraṇāya’so, saṃgīti taṃ samāpayi.

In the seventeenth year of the king, that sage, who was seventy-two years old, concluded that recitation at the Great Pavāraṇā.

281.

281.

Sādhukāraṃ dadantīva, sāsanaṭṭhiti kāraṇaṃ;

Saṃgīti pariyosāne, akammittha mahāmahī.

As if giving its approval for the sake of the Teaching's stability, at the conclusion of the recitation, the great earth trembled.

282.

282.

Hitvā seṭṭhaṃ brahmavimānampi manuññaṃ;

Jegucchaṃ so sāsanahetunaralokaṃ;

Āgammā’kā sāsanakiccaṃ katakicco;

Konāma’ñño sāsanakiccamhi pamajjeti.

Having left even the excellent and delightful Brahma-abode, he came to this repulsive human world for the sake of the Teaching. Having come and accomplished the work of the Teaching, his task done, who else would be heedless in the work of the Teaching?

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the faith and spiritual emotion of the virtuous.

Tatiyadhammasaṃgīti nāma

The Third Dhamma Council

Pañcamo paricchedo.

The Fifth Chapter.

Chaṭṭhapariccheda

The Sixth Chapter

Vijayāgamanaṃ

The Arrival of Vijaya

1.

1.

Vaṅgesu [M 0.0042] vaṅganagare, vaṅgarājā ahu pure;

Kāliṅgarañño dhītā’si, mahesī tassa rājino.

In the land of the Vaṅgas, in the city of Vaṅga, there was once a king of Vaṅga. The daughter of the Kāliṅga king was the chief queen of that king.

2.

2.

So rājā deviyā tassā, ekaṃ alabhi dhītaraṃ;

Nemittābyākaruṃ tassā, saṃvāsaṃ magarājinā.

That king, by that queen of his, obtained a single daughter. Soothsayers foretold for her a union with the king of beasts.

3.

3.

Atīva rūpiniṃ āsi, atīva kāmagiddhinī;

Devena deviyā’cāpi, lajjāyā’si jagucchitā.

She was exceedingly beautiful and exceedingly lustful; she was despised by god and goddess alike for her shamelessness.

4.

4.

Ekākinī sā nikkhamma, serīcārasukhatthinī;

Satthena saha aññātā, agā magadhagāminā.

Alone she departed, seeking pleasure in independent wandering; unknown, she went with a caravan bound for Magadha.

5.

5.

Lāḷaraṭṭhe aṭaviyā, sīho satthamabhiddhavi;

Aññattha sesā dhāviṃsu, sīhagatadisantusā.

In the forest of the Lāḷa country, a lion attacked the caravan. The others fled elsewhere, terrified by the lion's approach.

6.

6.

Gaṇhitvā gocaraṃ sīho, gacchaṃ disvā tamā’rato;

Ratto upāgalālento, laṅgulaṃ pattakaṇṇako.

Having seized his prey, the lion, while going, saw her from afar. Enamored, he approached, drooling, wagging his tail with ears pricked up.

7.

7.

Sā taṃ disvā saritvāna, nemittavacanaṃ sutaṃ;

Abhītā tassa aṅgāni, rañjayanti parāmasi.

Seeing him and recalling the soothsayers' words she had heard, fearless, she caressingly touched his limbs.

8.

8.

Tassā phassenā’ti ratto, piṭṭhiṃ āropiyā’sutaṃ;

Sīho sakaṃ guhaṃ netvā, tāya saṃvāsamācari.

Greatly enraptured by her touch, the lion quickly placed her upon his back, took her to his own cave, and lived in union with her.

9.

9.

Tena saṃvāsamanvāya, kālena yamake duve;

Puttañca dhītarañcāti, rājadhītā janesi sā.

Following that union, in time, that royal princess bore two twins: a son and a daughter.

10.

10.

Puttassa hatthapādā’suṃ, sīhākārā tato akā;

Nāmena sīhabāhuṃ taṃ, dhītaraṃ sīhasīvaliṃ.

The son's hands and feet were lion-shaped; therefore, he was named Sīhabāhu, and the daughter, Sīhasīvalī.

11.

11.

Putto soḷasavasso so, mātaraṃ pucchi saṃsayaṃ;

Tuvaṃ pitā ca no amma, kasmā visadisā iti.

When that son was sixteen years old, he asked his mother doubtfully, "Mother, why are you and our father so different?"

12.

12.

Sā sabbamabravī tassa, kiṃnayāmā’ti so’bravi;

Guhaṃ thaketitāto te, pāsāṇenāti sā’bravi.

She told him everything. "How then shall we proceed?" he asked. "Your father blocks the cave with a stone," she replied.

13.

13.

Mahāguhāya [M 0.0043] thakanaṃ, khandhenā’dāya so akā;

Ekāhene’va paññāsa-yojanāni gatāgataṃ.

Taking the stone that sealed the great cave upon his shoulder, in a single day he made a journey of fifty yojanas, going and coming.

14.

14.

Gocarāya gahe sīhe, dakkhiṇasmiñhi mātaraṃ;

Vāme kaṇiṭṭhiṃ katvāna, tayo sīghaṃ apakkamī.

When the lion had gone for prey, he placed his mother on his right and his younger sister on his left, and the three of them quickly departed.

15.

15.

Nivāsetvāna sākhaṃ te, paccantaṃ gāmamāgamuṃ;

Tatthāsi rājidhītāya, mātulassa suto tadā.

Having clothed themselves in leaves, they came to a border village. At that time, the son of the royal princess's maternal uncle was there.

16.

16.

Senāpati vaṅgarañño, ṭhito paccanta gāmako;

Nisinnovaṭamūlaleso, kammantaṃ saṃvidhāyakaṃ.

A general of the Vaṅga king was stationed in that border village; he was seated at the foot of a banyan tree, supervising the work.

17.

17.

Disvā te pucchite’vocuṃ, aṭavī vāsino mayaṃ;

Iti so dāpayī tesaṃ, vatthāni dhajinī pati.

Seeing them, he questioned them, and they replied, "We are forest-dwellers." Then that commander of the army had clothes given to them.

18.

18.

Tānā’hesuṃ uḷārāni, bhattaṃ paṇṇesu dāpayi;

Sovaṇṇabhājananā’suṃ, tesaṃ puññena tāni ca.

Those garments became splendid. He had food served in leaves, and these became golden vessels, all due to their merit.

19.

19.

Tena so vimhito pucchi, ke tumheti camūpati;

Tassa sā jātigottāni, rājadhītā nivedayi.

Astonished by this, the army commander asked, "Who are you?" The royal princess then revealed her lineage and clan to him.

20.

20.

Pitucchā dhītaraṃ taṃ so, ādāya dhajinī pati;

Gantvāna vaṅganagaraṃ, saṃvāsaṃ tāya kappayi.

That general, taking his paternal aunt's daughter, went to the city of Vaṅga and lived together with her.

21.

21.

Sīho sīghaṃ guhaṃ gantvā, te adisvā tayo jane;

Aṭṭito puttasokena, na ca khādi na cā’pivi.

The lion, going swiftly to the cave and not seeing those three people, afflicted by grief for his son, neither ate nor drank.

22.

22.

Dārake te gavesanto, agā paccantagāmake;

Ubbāsīyati so so’va, yaṃyaṃ gāmamupeti so.

Searching for those children, he went to the border villages; and whichever village he approached, that very one was laid waste.

23.

23.

Paccantavāsino gantvā, rañño taṃ paṭivedayuṃ;

Sīho piḷeti te raṭṭhaṃ, taṃ deva paṭisedhaya.

The border dwellers went and informed the king: "A lion is oppressing your country, O lord; restrain it."

24.

24.

Alakaṃ nisedhakaṃ tassa, hatthikkhandhagataṃ pure;

Ādetu sīhadāyīti, sahassaṃ so pacārayi.

Finding no one to restrain it, he had a reward of a thousand proclaimed from an elephant's back in the city for the one who could take the lion.

25.

25.

Tatheva dvesahassāni, tīṇicā’pi narissaro;

Dvīsu vāresu vāresi, mātā sīhabhujaṃ hitaṃ.

Likewise, the lord of men proclaimed two thousand, and then three thousand. On two occasions, the mother, for his welfare, restrained Sīhabāhu.

26.

26.

Aggahi tatiye vāre, sīhabāhu apucchiya;

Mātaraṃ tisahassaṃ taṃ, ghātetuṃ pitaraṃ sakaṃ.

On the third occasion, Sīhabāhu, without asking his mother, accepted the three thousand to slay his own father.

27.

27.

Rañño kumāraṃ dassesuṃ, taṃ rājā idha mabravi;

Gahito yadi sīho te, dammi raṭṭhaṃ tadeva te.

They showed the prince to the king, and the king said this to him: "If the lion is taken by you, I will give that very kingdom to you."

28.

28.

So [M 0.0044] taṃ gantvā guhādvāraṃ, sīhaṃ disvāva ārakā;

Entaṃ puttasinehena, vijjhituṃ taṃ saraṃ khipi.

He went to the cave's entrance, and seeing the lion approaching from afar with love for his son, he shot an arrow to pierce it.

29.

29.

Saro naḷātamāhacca, mettacittena thassa tu;

Kumārapādamūle’va, nivatto pati bhūmiyaṃ.

The arrow, having struck his forehead, turned back due to his mind of loving-kindness and fell to the ground at the prince's feet.

30.

30.

Tathā’si yāva tatiyaṃ, tato kujjhimigāmipo;

Tato khitto sarotassa, kāyaṃ nibbijja nikkhami.

Thus it was until the third time; then the lord of beasts became enraged. Then the arrow shot by him pierced its body and went out.

31.

31.

Sakesaraṃ sīhasīsaṃ, ādāya sapuraṃ agā;

Matassa vaṅgarājassa, sattāhāni tadā ahu.

Taking the lion's head with its mane, he went to his city. At that time, seven days had passed since the king of Vaṅga had died.

32.

32.

Rañño aputtakattā ca, patītā cassa kammunā;

Sutvā ca rañño nattuttaṃ, sañjānitvā ca mātaraṃ.

Because the king was without a son, and because they were pleased with his deed, and having heard that he was the king's grandson, and having recognized his mother,

33.

33.

Amaccā sannipatitā, akhilā ekamānasā;

Sīhabāhu kumārassa, rājā hohīti abravuṃ.

all the ministers assembled with one mind and said to Prince Sīhabāhu, "Be king!"

34.

34.

So rajjaṃ sampaṭicchitvā, datvā mātu patissa taṃ;

Sīhasīvalimādāya, jātabhūmiṃ gato sayaṃ.

He accepted the kingdom, gave it to his mother's husband, and taking Sīhasīvalī, he himself went to his birthplace.

35.

35.

Nagaraṃ tattha māpesi, ahu sīhapuranti taṃ;

Araññe yojanasate, gāme cāpi nivesayi.

There he had a city built, and it was called Sīhapura. In that wilderness of a hundred yojanas, he also established villages.

36.

36.

Lāḷaraṭṭhe pure tasmiṃ, sīhabāhunarādhipo;

Rajjaṃ kāresi katvāna, mahesiṃ sīhasīvaliṃ.

In that city in the country of Lāḷa, King Sīhabāhu, having made Sīhasīvalī his chief queen, ruled the kingdom.

37.

37.

Mahesī soḷasakkhattuṃ, yamake ca duve duve;

Putte janayi kālesā, vijayo nāma jeṭṭhako.

The chief queen sixteen times bore twin sons, two by two; in time she bore these sons, of whom the eldest was named Vijaya.

38.

38.

Sumitto nāma dutiyo, sabbe dvattiṃsa puttakā;

Kālena vijayaṃ rājā, uparajje’bhi secayi.

The second was named Sumitta; in all there were thirty-two sons. In time, the king consecrated Vijaya as viceroy.

39.

39.

Vijayo visamācāro, āsi tamparisāpi ca;

Sāhasāni anekāni, dussahāni kariṃsute.

Vijaya was of evil conduct, and so was his retinue. They committed many violent and intolerable acts.

40.

40.

Kuddho mahājano rañño, tamatthaṃ paṭivedayi;

Rājā te saññapetvāna, puttaṃ ovadi sādhukaṃ.

The great populace, angered, reported the matter to the king. The king, having pacified them, advised his son well.

41.

41.

Sabbaṃ tatheva dutiyaṃ, ahosi tatiyaṃ pana;

Kuddho mahājano āha, puttaṃ ghātehi te iti.

Everything happened thus a second time, and then a third. The great populace, enraged, said, "Kill your son!"

42.

42.

Rājā’thavijayaṃ tañca, parivārañca tassa taṃ;

Sattasatāni purise, kāretvā addhamuṇṇake.

Then the king had Vijaya and his retinue of seven hundred men's heads half-shaven.

43.

43.

Nāvāya [M 0.0045] pakkhipāpetvā, vissajjāpesi sāgare;

Tathā tesaṃ bhariyāyo, tatheva ca kumārake.

Having had them put on a ship, he sent them forth upon the ocean. Likewise their wives, and likewise their children.

44.

44.

Visuṃ visuṃ te vissaṭṭhā, purisitthikumārakā;

Visuṃ visuṃ dīpakasmiṃ, okkamiṃsu vasiṃsu ca.

The men, women, and children were sent forth separately; they landed on separate islands and dwelt there.

45.

45.

Naggadīpoti ñāyittha, kumārokkantadīpako;

Bhariyokkantadīpo tu, mahindadīpako iti.

The island where the children landed was known as Naggadīpa; but the island where the wives landed was known as Mahindadīpa.

46.

46.

Suppārake paṭṭanamhi, vijayo pana okkami;

Parisā sāhasene’ttha, bhīto nāvaṃ punā’ruhi.

Vijaya, however, landed at the port of Suppāraka; but frightened by the violence of his retinue, he boarded the ship again.

47.

47.

Laṃkāyaṃ vijayasanāmako kumāro;

Otiṇṇo thiramati tambapaṇṇidīpe;

Sālānaṃ yamakaguṇānamantarasmiṃ;

Nibbātuṃ sayitadine tathāgatassa.

The prince named Vijaya, firm of mind, landed in Laṅkā, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, on the very day the Tathāgata lay down between the twin Sāla trees to enter Nibbāna.

Sujanapasādasaṃve gatthāyakate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and emotion of the virtuous.

Vijayāgamanaṃnāma

The Coming of Vijaya

Chaṭṭhāparicchedo.

The Sixth Chapter.

Sattama pariccheda

The Seventh Chapter.

Vijayābhiseko

The Consecration of Vijaya.

1.

1.

Sabbalokahītaṃ [M 0.0046] katvā, patvā santikaraṃ padaṃ;

Parinibbānamañcamhi, nipanno lokanāyako.

Having accomplished the welfare of all the world, having attained the state that brings peace, the Leader of the World lay down on the bed of final Nibbāna.

2.

2.

Devatāsannipātamhi, mahantamhi mahāmuni;

Sakka tatrasamīpaṭṭhaṃ, avoca vadataṃ varo.

In that great assembly of deities, the Great Sage, the foremost of speakers, addressed Sakka, who was standing nearby.

3.

3.

Vijayo lāḷāvisayā, sīhabāhunarindajo;

Esalaṅkādhanupatto, sattabhaccasatānugo.

Vijaya, son of King Sīhabāhu from the country of Lāḷa, arrived in Laṅkā, followed by seven hundred attendants.

4.

4.

Patiṭṭhahissati devindaṃ, laṃkāyaṃ mama sāsanaṃ;

Tasmā saparivāraṃ taṃ, rakkhalaṃkañca sādhukaṃ.

My Dispensation, O king of devas, will be established in Laṅkā. Therefore, carefully protect him with his retinue, and Laṅkā as well.

5.

5.

Tathāgatassa devindo, vaco sutvāva sādaro;

Devassuppalavaṇṇassa, laṃkārakkhaṃ samappayi.

The king of devas, having heard the Tathāgata’s words with reverence, entrusted the protection of Laṅkā to the deva Uppalavaṇṇa.

6.

6.

Sakkena vuttamattoso, laṅkāmāgammasajjukaṃ;

Paribbājaka vesena, rukkhamūla mūpavisiṃ.

As soon as he was instructed by Sakka, he came swiftly to Laṅkā and, in the guise of a wandering ascetic, sat down at the foot of a tree.

7.

7.

Vijayasammukhā sabbe,

Taṃ upacca apucchisuṃ;

Ayaṃ bho konu dīpotī,

Laṃkādīpoti so bravi.

All of them approached him and asked, “Good sir, what island is this?” He replied, “This is the island of Laṅkā.”

8.

8.

Na santi manujā hettha, na ca hessati vo bhayaṃ;

Iti vatvā kuṇḍīkāya, te jalena nisiñciya.

“There are no humans here, and there will be no fear for you.” Having said this, he sprinkled them with water from his water pot.

9.

9.

Suttañca tesaṃ hatthesu, lagetvānabhasā’gamā;

Dassesi soṇirūpena, parivārikayakkhinī.

Having tied a thread on their hands, he departed through the sky. A yakkha woman with her retinue appeared in the form of a female dog.

10.

10.

Eko taṃ vāriyantopi, rājaputtena anvagā;

Gāmamhi vijjamānamhi, bhavanti sunakhā iti.

One man, though forbidden by the prince, followed her, thinking: “Where there is a village, there are dogs.”

11.

11.

Tassā ca sāmīnī tattha, kuveṇīnāma yakkhinī;

Nisīdi rukkhamūlamhi, kantanti tāpasī viya.

And there her mistress, a yakkha woman named Kuveṇī, sat at the foot of a tree, spinning like a female ascetic.

12.

12.

Disvāna [M 0.0047] so pokkharaṇī, nisinnaṃ tañca tāpasiṃ;

Tattha nhātvā pivitvā ca, ādāya ca mulāliyo.

Seeing the lotus pond and that female ascetic seated there, he bathed and drank, and took lotus stalks.

13.

13.

Vāriñca pokkhareheva, vuṭṭhāsi sātamabravi;

Bhakkho’si mama tiṭṭhāti, aṭṭhā baddho vaso naro.

As he was rising from the water, she said to him, “You are my food! Stop!” The man stood, bound and under her power.

14.

14.

Parittasutta tejena, bhakkhituṃ sā na sakkuṇī;

Yāciyantopi taṃ suttaṃ, nā’dāyakkhiniyā naro.

By the power of the protection-thread, she could not devour him. Though she begged for that thread, the man did not give it to the yakkha woman.

15.

15.

Taṃ gahetvā suruṅgāyaṃ, rudantaṃ yakkhinī khipi;

Evaṃ ekekaso tattha, khipī sattasatānipi.

Seizing the weeping man, the yakkha woman threw him into a cavern. Thus, one by one, she threw all seven hundred there.

16.

16.

Anāyantesu sabbesu, vijayo bhayasaṃkito;

Nantapañcāyudho gantvā, disvā pokkharaṇiṃ subhaṃ.

When none of them returned, Vijaya, filled with fear, went forth armed with the five weapons and saw the beautiful lotus pond.

17.

17.

Apassa muttiṇṇapadaṃ, passaṃ tañceva tāpasiṃ;

“Imāya khalu bhaccā me, gahitānu”ti cintiya.

He saw no footprints of anyone who had come out, but seeing that same female ascetic, he thought: “Surely my servants have been seized by this woman.”

18.

18.

Kiṃ na passasi bhacce me,

Hoti tvaṃ iti āhataṃ;

“Kiṃ rājaputta bhaccehi,

Piva nahāyā”ti āhasā.

“Good lady, have you not seen my servants?” he said to her. She replied, “O prince, what need is there for servants? Drink and bathe!”

19.

19.

Yakkhinī tāva jānāti, mama jātinti nicchito;

Saṅghaṃ sanāmaṃ sāvetvā, dhanuṃ sandhāyu’ pāgato.

Knowing her to be a yakkha woman, and confident in his lineage, Vijaya announced his name and clan, strung his bow, and approached.

20.

20.

Yakkhiṃ ādāya gīvāya, nārā ca valayena so;

Vāmahatthena kesesu, gahetvā dakkhiṇe na tu.

He seized the yakkha woman by the neck with a strong loop, and grasping her hair with his left hand, he raised his sword with his right.

21.

21.

Ukkhipitvā asiṃāha, “bhacce me dehi dāsitaṃ;

Māremī”ti bhayaṭṭāsā, jīvitaṃ yāci yakkhinī.

Raising his sword, he said, “Slave, give me my servants! I will kill you!” Stricken with fear, the yakkha woman begged for her life.

22.

22.

Jīvitaṃ dehi me sāmi, rajjaṃ dajjāmi te ahaṃ;

Karissami’tti kiccañca, kiccaṃ aññaṃ yathicchitaṃ.

“Spare my life, lord! I will give you a kingdom, and I will perform a woman's service for you, and any other task you may desire.”

23.

23.

Adubbhātthāya sapathaṃ, so taṃ yakkhiṃ akārayi;

“Ānehi bhacce sīgha”nti, vuttamattāva sā’nayi.

To ensure she would not betray him, he made that yakkha woman swear an oath. “Bring my servants quickly!” As soon as this was said, she brought them.

24.

24.

“Ime jātā”ti vuttāsā,

Taṇḍulādiṃ viniddisi;

Bhakkhitānaṃ vāṇijānaṃ,

Nāvaṭṭhaṃ vivikhaṃ bahuṃ.

“These are provisions,” she said, and pointed out much rice and other goods scattered about from the ships of merchants who had been devoured.

25.

25.

Bhaccā [M 0.0048] te sādhayitvāna, bhattāni byañjanānica;

Rājā puttaṃ bhojayitvā, sabbecāpi abhuñjisuṃ.

His servants, having prepared rice and curries, fed the prince, and then they all ate as well.

26.

26.

Dāpitaṃ vijayena’ggaṃ, yakkhī bhuñjiya pīṇitā;

Soḷasavassikaṃ rūpaṃ, māpayitvā manoharaṃ.

The yakkha woman, having been given the best portion by Vijaya, ate and was satisfied. She then created an enchanting form for herself, like that of a sixteen-year-old girl.

27.

27.

Rājaputta mupagañchi, sabbābharaṇabhūsitā;

Māpesi rukkhamūlasmiṃ, sayanañca mahārahaṃ.

Adorned with all her ornaments, she approached the prince. At the foot of a tree, she had a splendid bed prepared.

28.

28.

Sāṇiyā suparikkhittaṃ, vitānasamalaṅkataṃ;

Taṃ disvā rājatanayo, pekkhaṃ atthamanāgataṃ.

Well-enclosed by a curtain and adorned with a canopy; seeing that, the prince foresaw his future benefit.

29.

29.

Katvāna tāyanāvāyaṃ, nipajja sayane sukhaṃ;

Sāṇī parikkhipitvāna, sabbe bhaccā nipajjisuṃ.

Having made a protective enclosure, he lay down comfortably on the bed. Having drawn the curtain around, all his servants also lay down.

30.

30.

Rattiṃ tūriyasaddañca, sutvā gītaravañca so;

Apucchi sahasemānaṃ, kiṃ saddo iti yakkhiniṃ.

Hearing the sound of musical instruments and song at night, he asked the yakkha woman in haste, “What sound is that?”

31.

31.

Rajjañca sāmino deyyaṃ, sabbe yakkhe ca ghātiya;

Manussā vāsakaraṇā, yakkhā maṃ ghātayantihi.

The kingdom should be given to my lord, and all the yakkhas slain; humans are making a settlement, and the yakkhas will surely kill me.

32.

32.

Iti cintiya yakkhī sā, abravi rājanandanaṃ;

Sīrīsavatthunā metaṃ, sāmi yakkhapuraṃ idha.

Thus reflecting, that yakkha woman spoke to the prince: “My lord, this yakkha city here is named Sīrīsavatthu.”

33.

33.

Tattha jeṭṭhassa yakkhassa, laṃkānagaravāsinī;

Kumārikā idhā’nītā, tassā mātā ca āgatā.

A maiden from the city of Laṅkā has been brought here for the eldest yakkha, and her mother has also come.

34.

34.

Āvāha maṅgale tattha, idhāpi ussave mahā;

Vattate tattha saddoyaṃ, mahāhesa samāgamo.

A wedding festival is taking place there, and here also is a great celebration. That sound is from there; it is a great gathering.

35.

35.

Ajjeva yakkhe ghātehi,

Na hi sakkhā ito paraṃ;

So āhā’dissa mānete,

Ghātessāmi kathaṃ ahaṃ.

“Slay the yakkhas this very day, for it will not be possible hereafter.” He replied: “How shall I slay them, who are unseen?”

36.

36.

Yattha saddaṃ karissāma, tena saddena ghātaya;

Āyudhaṃ me’nubhāvena, tesaṃ kāye patissati.

“Where we shall make a sound, strike at that sound. By my power, the weapon will fall upon their bodies.”

37.

37.

Tassā sutvā tathā katvā, sabbe yakkhe aghātayi;

Sayampi laddhavijayo, yakkharāja pasādhanaṃ.

Having heard her and acted thus, he slew all the yakkhas. He himself, having gained the victory, took the adornments of the yakkha king.

38.

38.

Pasādhanehi sesehi, taṃtaṃ bhaccaṃ pasādhayi;

Katipahaṃ vasitve’ttha, tambapaṇṇimupāgami.

With the remaining adornments, he adorned each of his servants. After dwelling there for some days, he went to Tambapaṇṇi.

39.

39.

Māpayitvā [M 0.0049] tampapaṇṇi-nagaraṃ vijayo tahiṃ;

Vasī yakkhiniyā saddhiṃ, amacca parivārito.

Having caused the city of Tambapaṇṇi to be built there, Vijaya dwelt with the yakkha woman, surrounded by his ministers.

40.

40.

Nāvāya bhūmimotiṇṇā, vijayapamukhā tadā;

Kilantā pāṇinābhūmiṃ, ālambiya nisīdisuṃ.

Having disembarked from the ship onto the land, Vijaya and his followers, being weary, supported themselves on the ground with their hands and sat down.

41.

41.

Tambabhūmirajophuṭṭho, tambopāṇi yato ahuṃ;

So desoceva dīpo ca, tena tannāmako ahu.

Because their hands became copper-colored, being touched by the dust of the copper-colored earth, that region and the island came to have that name.

42.

42.

Sīhabāhu narindo so, sīhamādinnavā iti;

Sīhaḷo tena sambandhā, ete sabbepi sīhaḷā.

That king was Sīhabāhu, because he had captured a lion. From that connection, all these are Sīhaḷas.

43.

43.

Tattha tattha ca gāme te, tassā’maccā nivesayuṃ;

Anurādhagāmaṃ tannāmo, kadamba nadīyantike.

His ministers founded villages here and there. The village named Anurādhagāma was near the Kadamba river.

44.

44.

Gambhīranadīyā tīre, upatisso purohito;

Upatissagāmaṃ māpesi, anurādhassa uttare.

On the bank of the Gambhīra river, the chaplain Upatissa had Upatissagāma built, to the north of Anurādhagāma.

45.

45.

Aññe tayo amaccā te, māpayiṃsu visuṃ visuṃ;

Ujjeniṃ uruvelañca, vijitaṃ nagaraṃ tathā.

The other three ministers each had a city built separately: Ujjeni, Uruvela, and the city of Vijita.

46.

46.

Nivāsetvā janapadaṃ, sabbe’maccā samaccataṃ;

Avocuṃ rājatanayā, sāmi rajjebhisecaya.

Having settled the country, all the ministers assembled and spoke to the king’s son: “Lord, consecrate yourself for the kingship.”

47.

47.

Iti vutto rājaputto, na icchi abhisecanaṃ;

Vinā khattiyakaññāya, abhisekaṃ mahesiyā.

Thus addressed, the prince did not desire the consecration without a Khattiya maiden for the consecration of his chief queen.

48.

48.

Athāmaccā sāmino he, abhiseka katā darā;

Dukkaresupi kiccesu, tadatthabhirutā tigā.

Then the ministers, eager for their lord’s consecration and devoted to his welfare, were resolute even in difficult tasks.

49.

49.

Paṇṇākāre mahāsāre, maṇimuttādike bahū;

Gāhāpayitvā pāhesuṃ, dakkhiṇaṃ madhuraṃ puraṃ.

Having had many gifts of great value taken, such as jewels and pearls, they sent them to the southern city of Madhurā.

50.

50.

Paṇḍurājassa dhītatthaṃ, sāmino sāmibhattino;

Aññesaṃ cāpi dhītatthaṃ, amaccānaṃ janassa ca.

For the daughter of King Paṇḍu for their lord, from his devoted followers; and also for the daughters of the other ministers and the people.

51.

51.

Sīghaṃ nāvāya gantvāna, dūtā te madhuraṃ puraṃ;

Paṇṇākāre ca lekhañca, tassa rañño adassayuṃ.

Going swiftly by ship, those envoys went to the city of Madhurā and presented the gifts and the letter to that king.

52.

52.

Tato rājāamaccehi, mantayitvā sadhītaraṃ;

Pāhetukāmo’maccānaṃ, aññesaṃ cāpi dhītaro.

Then the king, having consulted with his ministers, desired to send his own daughter and also the daughters of his ministers.

53.

53.

Laddhā ūnasataṃ kaññā, athabheriṃ carāpayi;

Laṃkāya dhītugamanaṃ, icchamānā narā idha.

Having obtained nearly a hundred maidens, he then had the drum beaten: “Let those men here who desire their daughters to go to Laṅkā…”

54.

54.

Nivāsayitvā [M 0.0050] diguṇaṃ, gharadvāresu dhītaro;

Ṭhapentu tena liṅgena, ādīyissāmitā iti.

“...dress their daughters with a double provision and place them at the doors of their houses. By that sign I will take them.”

55.

55.

Evaṃ laddhā bahūkaññā, tappayitvāna taṃ kulaṃ;

Sampannasabbālaṅkāraṃ, dhītaraṃ sampaṭicchadaṃ.

Thus obtaining many maidens and satisfying their families, he sent his own daughter, endowed with all ornaments.

56.

56.

Sabbā tā laddhasakkārā, kaññāyo ca yathārahaṃ;

Rājārahe ca hatthassa-rathapessiya kārake.

All those maidens received honor as was fitting, and also artisans worthy of a king: elephant-keepers, horse-trainers, charioteers, and servants.

57.

57.

Aṭṭhārasannaṃ seṇīnaṃ, sahassañca kulāni so;

Lekhaṃ datvāna pesesi, vijayassa jitā’rino.

He sent a thousand families of the eighteen guilds to Vijaya, conqueror of his foes, giving them a letter.

58.

58.

Sabboso’tarī nāvāhi, mahātitthe mahājano;

Teneva paṭṭanaṃ tañhi, mahātitthaṃti vuccati.

All that great multitude disembarked from the ships at the great ford. Therefore, that very port is called Mahātittha.

59.

59.

Vijayassa sutodhītā, tassā yakkhiniyā ahu;

Rājakaññāgamaṃ sutvā, vijayo āha yakkhiniṃ.

A son and a daughter were born to Vijaya by that yakkhiṇī. Hearing of the arrival of the king’s daughter, Vijaya spoke to the yakkhiṇī.

60.

60.

“Gaccha dāni tuvaṃ bhoti, ṭhapetvā puttake duve;

Manussā amanussehi, bhāyintīhi sadā” iti.

“Go now, good lady, leaving behind the two children. Humans are always afraid of non-humans,” thus he said.

61.

61.

Sutvā taṃ yakkhabhayato, bhītaṃ taṃ āha yakkhiniṃ;

Mā cintayi sāhassena, dāpayissāmi te baliṃ.

He spoke to that yakkhiṇī, who, having heard that, was terrified with fear of the yakkhas: 'Do not worry; I will give you a thousand and also offerings.'

62.

62.

Punappunaṃ taṃ yācitvā, ubho ādāya puttake;

Bhītāpi sā agatiyā, laṃkāpuramupāgami.

Again and again she begged him, and taking both her children, though filled with fear and without refuge, she went to the city of Laṅkāpura.

63.

63.

Putte bihi nisīdetvā, sayaṃ pāvisi taṃ puraṃ;

Sañjānitvāna taṃ yakkhiṃ, bhītā corīti saññito.

Having seated her children outside, she herself entered that city. Recognizing that yakkhiṇī, they were terrified, thinking she was a thief.

64.

64.

Saṃkhubhiṃsu pure yakkhā, eko sāhasiko pana;

Ekapāṇippahārena, vilayaṃ nayi yakkhiniṃ.

The yakkhas in the city were agitated, but one reckless one, with a single blow of his hand, brought the yakkhiṇī to destruction.

65.

65.

Tassātu mātulo yakkho, nikkhamma nagarā bahi;

Disvā te dārake pucchi, tumhe kassa sutā iti.

Her maternal uncle, a yakkha, having gone out from the city and seeing those children, asked, “Whose children are you?”

66.

66.

Kuveṇiyā’ti sutvā’ha, mātā vo māritā idha;

Tumhepi disvā māreyyuṃ, palāyatha lahuṃ iti.

Hearing, “Kuveṇī’s,” he said, “Your mother was killed here. If they see you too, they might kill you. Flee quickly!”

67.

67.

Āguṃ sumanakūṭaṃ te, palāyitvā tato lahuṃ;

Vāsaṃ kappesi jeṭṭho so, vuddho tāya kaṇiṭṭhiyā.

Having fled swiftly from there, they went to Sumanakūṭa. The elder, when he was grown, cohabited there with that younger sister.

68.

68.

Puttadhītāhi [M 0.0051] vaḍḍhitvā, rājānuññāya te vasuṃ;

Tattheva malaye eso, pulindānañhi sambhavo.

Increasing with sons and daughters, they dwelt there in Malaya with the king’s permission. This, indeed, was the origin of the Pulindas.

69.

69.

Paṇḍurājassa dūtā te, paṇṇākāraṃ samappayuṃ;

Vijayassa kumārassa, rājādhikārikā ca tā.

Those envoys of King Paṇḍu presented tribute to Prince Vijaya and to the royal officials.

70.

70.

Katvā sakkārasammānaṃ, dūtānaṃ vijayo pana;

Adā yāthārahaṃ kaññā, amaccānaṃ janassa ca.

Having shown honor and respect to the envoys, Vijaya then gave suitable maidens to the ministers and to the people.

71.

71.

Yathā vidhi ca vijayaṃ, sabbe maccāsamāgatā;

Rajjesamabhisiñciṃsu, kariṃsuca mahāchaṇaṃ.

And according to the rite, all the assembled ministers anointed Vijaya in the kingship and held a great festival.

72.

72.

Tato so vijayo rājā, paṇḍurājassa dhītaraṃ;

Mahatā parihārena, mahesitte’bhisecayi.

Then that King Vijaya, with great ceremony, consecrated the daughter of King Paṇḍu in the office of chief queen.

73.

73.

Dhanāna’dā amaccānaṃ, adāsi sasurassatu;

Anuvassaṃ saṅkhamuttaṃ, satasahassa dvayārahaṃ.

He gave wealth to the ministers, and to his father-in-law he gave annually a conch-pearl worth two hundred thousand.

74.

74.

Hitvā pubbācaritaṃ visamaṃ samena;

Dhammena laṃkamakhilaṃ anusāsamāno;

So tamapaṇṇinagare vijayo narindo;

Rajjaṃ akārayi samā khalu aṭṭhatiṃsā’ti.

Having abandoned his former unjust conduct for what is just, ruling the whole of Laṅkā righteously, that King Vijaya reigned in the city of Tambapaṇṇi for thirty-eight years indeed.

Sujanapasādasaṃve gatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people,

Vijayābhiseko nāma

The chapter named the Anointing of Vijaya.

Sattamo paricchedo.

The Seventh Chapter.

Aṭṭhama pariccheda

The Eighth Chapter

Paṇḍuvāsudevābhiseko

The Anointing of Paṇḍuvāsudeva

1.

1.

Vijayo [M 0.0052] so mahārājā, vasse antimake ṭhito;

Iti cintayi “vuddho’haṃ, na ca vijjati me suto.

That great king Vijaya, being in his last year, thought thus: “I am old, and there is no son of mine.”

2.

2.

Kicchena vāsitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ, nasseyya mama accaye;

Āṇāpeyyaṃ rajjahetu-sumittaṃ bhātaraṃ mama.

The kingdom, established with difficulty, might perish after my passing. I should send for my brother Sumitta for the sake of the kingdom.

3.

3.

Athā’maccehi mantetvā, lekhaṃ tattha visajjayi;

Lekhaṃ datvāna vijayo, na cirena divaṅgato.

Then, having consulted with his ministers, he dispatched a letter there. Having sent the letter, Vijaya not long after passed away.

4.

4.

Tasmiṃ mate amaccā te, pekkhantā khattiyāgamaṃ;

Upatissagāme ṭhatvāna, raṭṭhaṃ samunusāsisuṃ.

When he died, those ministers, awaiting the arrival of a khattiya, stayed in Upatissagāma and governed the kingdom.

5.

5.

Mate vijayarājamhi, khattiyāgamanā purā;

Ekaṃ vassaṃ ayaṃ laṃkā-dīpo āsi arājako.

When King Vijaya died, before the arrival of a khattiya, this island of Laṅkā was without a king for one year.

6.

6.

Tasmiṃ sīhapure tassa, sīhabāhussa rājino;

Accayena sumitto so, rājā tassa suto ahu.

In that Sīhapura, after the passing of that King Sīhabāhu, his son Sumitta became king.

7.

7.

Tassa puttā tayo āsuṃ, maddarājassa dhītuyā;

Dūtā sīhapuraṃ gantvā, rañño lekhaṃ adaṃsu te.

He had three sons by the daughter of the Madda king. Those messengers went to Sīhapura and gave the letter to the king.

8.

8.

Lekhaṃ sutvāna so rājā, putte āmantayī tayo;

Ahaṃ mahallako tātā, eko tumhesu gacchatu.

That king, having heard the letter, addressed his three sons: “I am old, my dears, let one of you go.”

9.

9.

Laṃkaṃ nekaguṇaṃ kantaṃ, mama bhātussa santakaṃ;

Tassa’cca yena tattheva, rajjaṃ kāretu sobhanaṃ.

Laṅkā, lovely and possessing many virtues, belongs to my brother. After his demise, therefore, let him establish a glorious kingdom there.

10.

10.

Kaṇiṭṭhako paṇḍuvāsu-devo rājakumārako;

“Gamissāmīti cintetvā, ñatvā sotthi gatampi ca.

The youngest Prince Paṇḍuvāsudeva, thinking, “I will go,” and also knowing that his going would be safe,

11.

11.

Pitarā samanuññāto, dvattiṃsāmacca dārake;

Ādāya āruhī nāvaṃ, paribbājakaliṅgavā.

Permitted by his father, taking with him thirty-two sons of ministers, he boarded a ship in the guise of wanderers.

12.

12.

Mahākandaranajjā te, mukhadvāramhi otaraṃ;

Te paribbājake disvā, jano sakkari sādhukaṃ.

They disembarked at the mouth of the Mahākandara River. Seeing those wanderers, the people honored them well.

13.

13.

Pucchitvā [M 0.0053] nagaraṃ ettha, upayantaṃ kamena te;

Upatissa gāmaṃ sampattā, devatā paripālitā.

Having inquired about the city there, they, proceeding gradually, reached Upatissagāma, protected by deities.

14.

14.

Amaccā’numato’macco, pucchi nemittakā tahiṃ;

Khattiyā’gamanaṃ tassa, so byākāsi paraṃpi ca.

The minister, with the approval of the other ministers, questioned the soothsayers there. One of them predicted the arrival of a noble and also spoke further.

15.

15.

Sattame dīvaseyeva, āgamissati khattiyo;

Buddhasāsana metassa, vaṃsajo’va ṭhapessati.

“On the seventh day itself, a noble will arrive; a descendant of his will indeed establish the Buddha’s Dispensation.”

16.

16.

Sattame divaseyeva, te paribbājake tahiṃ;

Patte disvāna pucchitvā, amaccā te vijāniya.

On the seventh day itself, having seen and questioned those wanderers who had arrived there, those ministers recognized them.

17.

17.

Taṃ paṇṇuvāsudevaṃ te, laṃkārajjena appayuṃ;

Mahesiyā abhāvāso, na tāva abhisecayi.

They entrusted that Paṇḍuvāsudeva with the kingship of Laṅkā; but due to the absence of a chief queen, they did not yet consecrate him.

18.

18.

Amitodanasakkassa, paṇḍusakko suto ahu;

Ñatvā vināsaṃ sakyānaṃ, so ādāya sakaṃ janaṃ.

Paṇḍu the Sakyan was the son of Amitodana the Sakyan. Knowing of the destruction of the Sakyans, he took his own people,

19.

19.

Gantvā aññāpadesena, gaṅgāpāraṃ tahiṃ puraṃ;

Māpetvā tattha kāresi, rajjaṃ tassa sute labhi.

Having gone to another region, to the far bank of the Gaṅgā, he had a city built there and established a kingdom, which his son obtained.

20.

20.

Dhītā kaṇiṭṭhitā āsi, bhaddakaccāna nāmikā;

Sabbalakkhaṇasampannā, surūpā abhipatthitā.

His youngest daughter was named Bhaddakaccānā; she was endowed with all auspicious marks, beautiful in form, and much sought after.

21.

21.

Tadatthaṃ sattarājāno, paṇṇākāre mahārahe;

Pesesuṃ rājino tassa, bhīto rājūhi so pana.

For her sake, seven kings sent precious gifts to that king. But he, fearing those kings,

22.

22.

Ñatvāna sotthigamanaṃ, abhisekaphalampi ca;

Sahadvattiṃsa itthīhi, nāvaṃ āropiyā’sutaṃ.

Knowing of her safe journey and also of the fruit of her consecration, he secretly placed her on a ship with thirty-two other women.

23.

23.

Gaṅgāya khipi gaṇhātu, pahu me dhītaraṃ iti;

Gahetuṃ te na sakkhiṃsu, nāvāsāpana sīghagā.

He launched her onto the Gaṅgā, thinking, “Let whoever is able take my daughter.” They were not able to seize her, for the ship was indeed swift-going.

24.

24.

Dutiye divaseyeva, goṇāgāmaka paṭṭanaṃ;

Pattāpabbajitā kārā, sabbā tā tattha otaruṃ.

On the second day itself, they arrived at the port of Goṇāgāmaka, and all of them, in the guise of female ascetics, disembarked there.

25.

25.

Pucchitvā nagaraṃ ettha, tā kamenopayantiyo;

Upatissagāmaṃ sampattā, devatā paripālitā.

Having inquired about the city there, they, proceeding gradually, reached Upatissagāma, protected by deities.

26.

26.

Nemittakassa vacanaṃ, sutvā tatthā’gatā tu tā;

Disvā amacco pucchitvā, ñatvā rañño samappayi.

The minister, who had heard the soothsayer's prophecy, saw them who had arrived there. Having questioned and understood their identity, he presented them to the king.

27.

27.

Taṃ paṇḍuvāsudevaṃ te, amaccā suddhabuddhino;

Rajje samabhisiñciṃsu, puṇṇasabbamanorathaṃ.

Those ministers of pure wisdom then consecrated that Paṇḍuvāsudeva in the kingship, he whose every wish was fulfilled.

28.

28.

Subhaddakaccāna [M 0.0054] manomarūpiniṃ;

Mahesībhāve abhisiñciya’ttano;

Sahagatā tāya padāsi attanā;

Sahāgatānaṃ vasi bhūmipo sukhantī.

Having consecrated Bhaddakaccānā of enchanting form as his own chief queen, the king gave her companions to his own companions. The lord of the land dwelt happily.

Sujanappasāda saṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of the virtuous,

Paṇḍuvāsudevābhiseko nāma

Entitled, ‘The Consecration of Paṇḍuvāsudeva’.

Aṭṭhamo paricchedo.

The Eighth Chapter.

Navama pariccheda

The Ninth Chapter

Abhayābhiseko

The Consecration of Abhaya

1.

1.

Mahesī janayī putte, dasa ekañca dhītaraṃ;

Sabbajeṭṭho’bhayo nāma, cittānāma kaniṭṭhikā.

The chief queen gave birth to ten sons and one daughter; the eldest was named Abhaya, and the youngest was named Cittā.

2.

2.

Passitvā taṃ viyākaṃsu, brāhmaṇā mantapāragā;

“Rajjahetu suto assā, ghātayissati mātule”.

Having seen her, the brahmins, who were masters of the sacred texts, declared: “For the sake of the kingdom, a son of hers will slay his maternal uncles.”

3.

3.

Ghātessāmi kaniṭṭhinti, nicchite bhātarā’bhayo;

Vāresi kāle vāsesuṃ, gehaṃ taṃ ekathuṇike.

When his brothers had decided, “We shall kill our youngest sister,” Abhaya restrained them. They then had her dwell in a single-pillared house.

4.

4.

Rañño ca sirigabbhena, tassa dvāramakārayuṃ;

Anto ṭhapesuṃ ekañca, dāsiṃ narasataṃ bahi.

They made the entrance to her chamber through the king’s sleeping chamber. Inside they placed a single female servant, and outside, a hundred men as guards.

5.

5.

Rūpenu’mmādayī nare, diṭṭhamattāva sāyato;

Tato ummādacittā’ti, nāmaṃ sopapadaṃ labhi.

Since she drove men mad with her beauty merely by being seen, she therefore received the descriptive name Ummādacittā.

6.

6.

Sutvāna laṃkāgamanaṃ, bhaddakaccānadeviyā;

Mātarā coditā puttā, ṭhapetve’kañca āgamuṃ.

Having heard of the coming to Laṅkā of Princess Bhaddakaccānā, the sons, urged by their mother, came, having left one behind.

7.

7.

Disvāna te paṇḍuvāsu-devaṃ laṅkindamāgatā;

Disvāna taṃ kaniṭṭhiñca, roditvā saha tāya ca.

Having seen Paṇḍuvāsudeva, who had come as lord of Laṅkā, and having seen that youngest sister, they wept together with her.

8.

8.

Raññā sukatasakkārā, rañño’nuññāya cārikaṃ;

Cariṃsu laṃkādīpamhi, nivasuñca yathāruciṃ.

Having been well honored by the king, and with the king's permission, they wandered throughout the island of Laṅkā and dwelt as they pleased.

9.

9.

Rāmena [M 0.0055] vusitaṭhānaṃ, rāmagoṇanti vuccati;

Uruvelā’nurādhānaṃ, nivāsā ca tathā tathā.

The place where Rāma dwelt is called Rāmagoṇa; and likewise, the dwellings of Uruvela and Anurādha are so called.

10.

10.

Tathā vijitadīghāyu-rohaṇānaṃ nivāsakā;

Vijitagāmo dīghāyu-rohaṇanti ca vuccati.

Likewise, the settlements of Vijita, Dīghāyu, and Rohaṇa are called Vijitagāma, Dīghāyu, and Rohaṇa.

11.

11.

Kāresi anurādho so, vāpiṃ dakkhiṇato tato;

Kārāpetvā rājagehaṃ, tattha vāsamakappayī.

That Anurādha caused a tank to be made to the south of that place; and having had a royal residence built, he took up his dwelling there.

12.

12.

Mahārājā paṇḍuvāsu-devo jaṭṭhasutaṃ sakaṃ;

Abhayaṃ uparajjamhi, kāle samabhisecayi.

The great king Paṇḍuvāsudeva in due time consecrated his own eldest son, Abhaya, in the office of viceroy.

13.

13.

Dīghāyussa kumārassa, tanayo dīghagāmaṇi;

Sutvā ummādacittaṃ taṃ, tassaṃ jātakutūhalo.

Dīghagāmaṇi, the son of Prince Dīghāyu, hearing of Ummādacittā, became curious about her.

14.

14.

Gahetvā’patissa gāmaṃ, taṃ apassi manujādhipaṃ;

Adā sahoparājena, rājupaṭṭhānamassaso.

Having gone to Upatissagāma, he visited that lord of men; he entered the king's service, together with the viceroy.

15.

15.

Gavakkhābhimukhaṭṭhāne, taṃ upecca ṭhitaṃ tusā;

Disvāna gāmiṇiṃ cittā, rattacittā’ha dāsikaṃ.

Seeing the Gāmaṇi standing in a place facing the window, Cittā, her heart impassioned, spoke to the slave girl Tusā, who had approached him.

16.

16.

“Ko eso”ti tato sutvā,

Mātulassa sutoiti;

Dāsiṃ tattha niyojesi,

Saddhiṃkatvāna so tato.

When she asked, 'Who is that?' and heard, 'He is the son of your maternal uncle,' she sent the slave girl to him, with whom he then made an arrangement.

17.

17.
