Purimāya hatthikkhandhañca, gokaṇṇagirimeva ca.

He built the Nagaraṅgaṇa vihāra in the southern direction of the city, and in the eastern direction, the Hatthikkhandha and the Gokaṇṇa.

5.

5.

Vaṅguttare pabbatamhi, pācina pabbatavhayaṃ;

Raheṇakasamīpamhi, tathā koḷambakāḷakaṃ.

He also built the vihāra named Pācīnapabbata on Mount Vaṅguttara, and the Koḷambakāḷaka vihāra near Raheṇaka.

6.

6.

Ariṭṭhapāde maṃ gulakaṃ, purimāya’ccha gallakaṃ;

Girinelapanāyakaṇḍaṃ, nagarassuttharāya tu.

He built the Maṅgulaka vihāra at the foot of Mount Ariṭṭha, the Acchagallaka vihāra to the east, and the Girinīlavāhanakaṇḍa vihāra to the north of the city.

7.

7.

Pañcasatā [M 0.0121] neva mādi-vihāre puthavī pati;

Gaṅgāya orapārañhi, laṃkādīpe tahiṃ tahiṃ.

The lord of the earth built these and other such vihāras, five hundred in all, here and there on the island of Laṅkā, on both sides of the river.

8.

8.

Pure rajjā ca rajje ca, saṭṭhīvassāni sādhukaṃ;

Kāresi ramme dhammena, ratanattaya gāravo.

Reverent towards the Triple Gem, for sixty years, both before and during his reign, he righteously performed many delightful deeds.

9.

9.

Suvaṇṇapiṇḍatissoti, nāmaṃ rajjā tassā ahu;

Suratissoti nāmantu, tassā’purajjapattiyā.

His name was Sūratissa before he attained the kingship; as king, however, his name was Suvaṇṇapiṇḍatissa.

10.

10.

Assanāvikaputtā dve, damiḷā senaguttikā;

Suratissamahīpālaṃ, taṃ gahetvā mahabbalā.

Two Tamils, Sena and Guttika, sons of a horse-trader and men of great power, seized King Sūratissa.

11.

11.

Duve vīsativassāni, rajjaṃ dhammena kārayuṃ;

Te gahetvā aselo tu, muṭasivassa atrajo.

They ruled the kingdom righteously for twenty-two years. Then Asela, a son of Muṭasiva, seized them.

12.

12.

Sodariyānaṃ bhātūnaṃ, navamo bhatuko tato;

Anurādhapure rajjaṃ, dasavassāni kārayi.

He was the ninth of the uterine brothers. This brother then ruled the kingdom in Anurādhapura for ten years.

13.

13.

Coḷaraṭṭhā idha gamma, rajjatthaṃ ujujātiko;

Eḷāro nāma damiḷo, gahetvā’selabhūpatiṃ.

A Tamil named Eḷāra, a man of noble birth, came here from the Coḷa country for the sake of the kingdom and seized King Asela.

14.

14.

Vassāni cattārīsañca, cattāri ca akārayi;

Rajjaṃ vohārasamaye, majjhatto mittasattusu.

He ruled for forty-four years, and in dispensing justice he was impartial towards friend and foe.

15.

15.

Sayanassa siropasse, ghaṇṭaṃ sudīghayottakaṃ;

Lambāpesi vīrāvetuṃ, icchantehi vinicchayaṃ.

At the head of his bed he had a bell with a long rope hung, so that it could be rung by those who desired a legal decision.

16.

16.

Eko putto ca dhītā ca, ahesuṃ tassa rājino;

Rathena tissavāpiṃ so, gacchanto bhūmipālajo.

That king had one son and one daughter. As the prince was going by chariot to the Tissavāpi,

17.

17.

Taruṇaṃ vacchakaṃ magge, nipannaṃ sahadhenukaṃ;

Gīvaṃ akkammacakkena, asañcicca aghātayi.

he unintentionally killed a young calf that was lying on the road with its mother, crushing its neck with the wheel of his chariot.

18.

18.

Gantvāna dhenughaṇṭaṃ taṃ, ghaṭṭesi ghaṭṭitāsayā;

Rājā teneva cakkena, sīsaṃ puttassa chedayi.

The mother cow went and rang the bell. The king had his son's head cut off with that very same wheel.

19.

19.

Dijapotaṃ tālarukkhe, eko sappo abhakkhayi;

Tampotamātā sakuṇī, gantvā ghaṇṭamaghaṭṭayi.

A snake on a palm tree devoured a young bird. The mother bird went and struck the bell.

20.

20.

Āṇāpetvāna taṃ rājā, kucchiṃ tassa vidāḷiya;

Potaṃ taṃ nīharāpetvā, tāle sappamasappayi.

The king had the snake brought, its belly slit open, and the young bird taken out. Then he had the snake impaled on the palm tree.

21.

21.

Ratanaggassa [M 0.0122] ratana-ttayassa guṇasārataṃ;

Ajānantopi so rājā, cārittamanupālayaṃ.

Although that king did not know the supreme essence of the qualities of the Triple Gem, he followed the traditional rules of conduct.

22.

22.

Cetiyadabbataṃ gantvā, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pavāriya;

Āgacchanto rathagato, rathassa yugakoṭiyā.

Once, having gone to Cetiyapabbata and invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, as he was returning in his chariot, the end of the chariot's yoke

23.

23.

Akāsi jinathūpassa,

Ekadesassa bhañjanaṃ;

Amaccā “deva thūpono,

Tayā bhinno’ti āhu taṃ.

struck and damaged a part of the Jina's stūpa. His ministers said to him: 'Your Majesty, the stūpa has been damaged by you!'

24.

24.

Asañcicca kate‘pe’sa, rājā oruyha sandanā;

“Cakkena mama sīsampi, chindathā’ti pathesayi.

Although it was done unintentionally, the king descended from his chariot, lay down on the road, and said: 'Cut off my head too with this same wheel!'

25.

25.

“Parahiṃsaṃ mahārāja, satthā no neva icchati;

Thūpaṃ pākatikaṃ katvā, khamāpehī”ti āhu taṃ.

'Great King, our Teacher does not approve of harming others,' they said to him. 'Restore the stūpa to its original condition and ask for forgiveness.'

26.

26.

Te ṭhapetuṃ pañcadasa, pāsāṇe patite tahiṃ;

Kahāpaṇa sahassāni, adā pañcadase vaso.

To repair the fifteen stones that had fallen there, the ruler gave fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas.

27.

27.

Akā mahallikā vīhiṃ, so setuṃ ātape khipi;

Devo akāle vassitvā, tassā vihiṃ atemayi.

An old woman was drying rice in the sun when a deva rained out of season and soaked it.

28.

28.

Vīhiṃ gahetvā gantvā sā, ghaṇṭaṃ taṃ samaghaṭṭayi;

Akālavassaṃ sutvā taṃ, vissajjetvā tamattikaṃ.

Taking the soaked rice, she went and struck the bell. When the king heard her complaint about the untimely rain, he sent away his own meal.

29.

29.

Rājā dhammamhi vattanto, “kāle vassaṃ labhe”iti;

Tassā vinicchayatthāya, upavāsaṃ nipajji so.

And in order to obtain a just decision for her, he undertook a fast, reflecting: 'A king who abides in righteousness should obtain rain in the proper season.'

30.

30.

Baliggāhī devaputto, rañño tejena otthaṭo;

Gantvā cātumahārāja-santikaṃ taṃ nivedayi.

The guardian deity who receives offerings, oppressed by the power of the king's virtue, went to the Four Great Kings and reported the matter.

31.

31.

Te tamādāya gantvāna, sakkassa paṭivedayuṃ;

Sakko pajjunnamāhuya, kāle vassaṃ upādiyi.

They took the deity with them and went and reported it to Sakka. Sakka summoned Pajjunna and charged him with sending rain in the proper season.

32.

32.

Baliggāhī devaputto, rājino taṃ nivedayi;

Tatoppabhuti taṃ rajje, divā devo na vassatha.

The tribute-receiving deity reported this to the king. From that time onwards in that kingdom, the deva did not send rain by day.

33.

33.

Rattiṃ devo’nu sattāhaṃ, vassiyāmamhi majjhime;

Puṇṇāna’hesuṃ sabbattha, khuddakā vāṭakānipi.

The deva would rain only in the middle watch of the night, every seven days; and everywhere even the small cisterns would be filled.

34.

34.

Agatigamanadoso [M 0.0123] muttamattena eso,

Anupahata kudiṭṭhipīdisiṃ pāpuṇī’ddhiṃ;

Agatigamanadosaṃ suddhadiṭṭhisamāno,

Kathamidhahi manusso buddhimā no jaheyyāti.

Since even one who held wrong view, by being free from the fault of wrong courses of action, attained such majesty, how then could a wise person here, endowed with pure view, not abandon the fault of wrong courses of action?

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, compiled for the serene joy and emotion of the virtuous,

Pañcarājako nāma

named The Five Kings,

Ekavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-First Chapter.

Bāvīsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-Second Chapter.

Gāmaṇikumāra suti

The Birth of Prince Gāmaṇi.

1.

1.

Eḷāraṃ ghātayitvāna, rājā’hu duṭṭhagāmaṇi;

Tadattha dīpanatthāya, anupubbakathā ayaṃ.

Having slain Eḷāra, Duṭṭhagāmaṇi became king. This is the sequential narrative to illuminate that matter.

2.

2.

Devānaṃ piyatissassa, rañño dutiyabhātiko;

Uparājā mahānāgo, nāmānu bhātuno piyo.

King Devānampiyatissa’s younger brother was the viceroy named Mahānāga, who was dear to his brother.

3.

3.

Rañño devī saputtassa, bālā rajjābhikāmini;

Uparājavadhatthāya, jātacittā nirantaraṃ.

The king’s foolish queen, desiring the kingdom for her son, was constantly intent on the viceroy’s death.

4.

4.

Vāpiṃ taracchanāmaṃ sā, kārāpentassa pāhiṇi;

Ambaṃ visena yojetvā, ṭhapetvā ambamatthake.

While he was having the Taraccha tank constructed, she sent him mangoes, having placed on top one that she had mixed with poison.

5.

5.

Tassā putto sahagato, uparājena bālako;

Bhājane vivaṭeyeva, taṃ ambaṃ khādiyā’mari.

Her young son, who had gone with the viceroy, ate that mango as soon as the container was opened, and died.

6.

6.

Uparājā tatoyeva, sadāra bala vāhano;

Rakkhihuṃ sakamattānaṃ, rohaṇā’bhimukho agā.

Therefore, to protect himself, the viceroy set out for Rohaṇa with his wife, forces, and transport.

7.

7.

Yaṭṭhālaya vihārasmiṃ, mahesī tassa gabbhinī;

Puttaṃ janesi so tassa, bhātu nāma makārayi.

In the Yaṭṭhālaya monastery, his pregnant queen gave birth to a son, and he had him named after his brother.

8.

8.

Tato [M 0.0124] gantvā rohaṇaṃ so,

Issaro rohaṇe’khilo;

Mahā bhāgo mahā gāme,

Rajjaṃ kāresi khattiyo.

Then, having gone to Rohaṇa, that fortunate khattiya, as lord of all Rohaṇa, ruled the kingdom from Mahāgāma.

9.

9.

Kāresi so nāgamahā-vihāraṃ sakanāmakaṃ;

Uddhakandarakādī ca, pihāre kārayī bahū.

He had the Nāgamahā-vihāra built, named after himself, and he also had many other vihāras built, such as the Uddhakandaraka.

10.

10.

Yaṭṭhālaya katisso so, tassa putto tadaccaye;

Hattheva rajjaṃ kāresi, tassa putto’bhayo tathā.

After his death, his son, Yaṭālatissa, ruled the kingdom there. Likewise, his son, Goṭhābhaya, also ruled.

11.

11.

Goṭṭhābhayasuto kāka-vaṇṇatissoti vissuho;

Tadaccaye tattha rajjaṃ, so akāresi khattiyo.

The son of Goṭhābhaya, renowned as Kākavaṇṇatissa, that khattiya ruled the kingdom there after his father’s death.

12.

12.

Vihāradevi nāmā’si, mahesī tassa rājino;

Saddhassa saddhāsampannā, dhītā kalyāṇi rājino.

The chief queen of that faithful king was named Vihāradevī; endowed with faith, she was the daughter of the king of Kalyāṇī.

13.

13.

Kalyāṇiyaṃ narindo hi, tisso nāmāsi khattiyo;

Devisaññogajanita-ko potassa kaniṭṭhako.

Indeed, in Kalyāṇī there was a khattiya king named Tissa. A younger brother of his aroused his anger by having an illicit union with the queen.

14.

14.

Bhīto tato palāyitvā, ayyauttiya nāmako;

Aññattha vasi so deso, tena taṃ nāmako ahu.

Frightened by him, the one named Ayya-Uttiya fled and dwelt elsewhere. Therefore, that region became named after him.

15.

15.

Datvā rahassalekhaṃ so, bhikkhuvesadharaṃ naraṃ;

Pāhesi deviyā gantvā, rājadvāre ṭhito tuso.

He gave a secret letter to a man disguised as a monk and sent him to the queen. Having gone there, the man stood at the king’s gate.

16.

16.

Rāja gehe arahatā, bhuñjamānena sabbadā;

Aññāyamāno therena, rañño gharamupāgami.

He entered the king’s house along with an Arahant who always took his meal there, but he was not recognized by the elder.

17.

17.

Therena saddhiṃ bhuñjitvā, rañño saha viniggame;

Pātesi bhūmiyaṃ lekhaṃ, pekkhamānāya deviyā.

Having taken his meal with the elder, as he was leaving with the king, he dropped the letter on the ground while the queen was watching.

18.

18.

Saddena tena rājānaṃ, nivattitvā vilokayaṃ;

Ñatvāna lekhasandesaṃ, kuddho therassa dummati.

At that sound, the king turned back and looked. Having understood the message in the letter, the foolish one became angry with the elder.

19.

19.

Theraṃ taṃ purisaṃ tañca, mārāpetvāna kodhasā;

Samuddasmiṃ khipāpesi, kujjhitvā tena devatā.

Out of anger, he had that elder and that man killed and thrown into the sea. Because of this, the deities became angry.

20.

20.

Samuddeno’ttharā pesuṃ, taṃ desaṃ sotubhūpati;

Attano dhītaraṃ yuddhaṃ, deviṃ nāma surupiniṃ.

They caused the sea to flood that country. Then that king placed his own daughter, the beautiful maiden named Devī,

21.

21.

Likhitvā rājadhītāti, sovaṇṇakkhaliyā lahuṃ;

Nisīdāpiya tattheva, samuddasmiṃ vissajjayi.

Having written ‘King’s Daughter’ on a golden vessel, he quickly had her seated in it and launched her upon the sea.

22.

22.

Okkantaṃ [M 0.0125] taṃ tato laṃke-kākavaṇṇo mahīpati;

Abhisecayi tenā’si, vihāropapadavhayā.

When she landed in Laṅkā, King Kākavaṇṇa consecrated her as his queen. Thus she came to be called Vihāradevī.

23.

23.

Tissa mahāvihārañca, tathā cittalapabbataṃ;

Gamitthavāliṃ kuṭāliṃ, vihāre evamādike.

He had built the Tissa Mahāvihāra and the Cittalapabbata, the Gamitthavāli and Kuṭāli vihāras, and other such monasteries.

24.

24.

Kāretvā supasannena, manasāratanattaye;

Upaṭṭhahi tadā saṅghaṃ, paccayehi catūhi so.

Having had these built, with a mind deeply devoted to the Triple Gem, he then supported the Sangha with the four requisites.

25.

25.

Koṭipabbata nāmamhi, vihāre sīlavattimā;

Tadā ahu sāmaṇero, nānāpuññakaro sadā.

At that time, in the monastery named Koṭipabbata, there was a virtuous novice who was always performing various meritorious deeds.

26.

26.

Sukhenārohaṇatthāya, akāsa cetiyaṅgaṇe;

Ṭhapesi tīṇi pāsāṇe, pāsāṇa phalakāni so.

For ease of ascent to the cetiya terrace, he placed three stone slabs there.

27.

27.

Adā pānīya dānañca, vattaṃ saṅghassa cā’kari;

Sadā kilantakāyassa, tassā’bodho mahā ahu.

He gave the gift of drinking water and performed his duties to the Sangha. His body was always weary, and he contracted a great illness.

28.

28.

Sivikāya kamānetvā, bhikkhavo katavedino;

Silāpassaya pariveṇe, tissārāme upaṭṭhahuṃ.

The grateful monks brought him by palanquin and attended to him in the Silāpassaya Pariveṇa at the Tissārāma.

29.

29.

Sadā vihāradevīsā, rājagehe susaṅkhate;

Purebhattaṃ mahādānaṃ, datvā saṅghassa saññatā.

The self-controlled Queen Vihāradevī would always give a great pre-meal offering to the Sangha in the well-adorned royal palace.

30.

30.

Pacchābhattaṃ gandhamālaṃ, bhesajjavasanāni ca;

Gāhayitvā gatā’rāmaṃ, sakkaroti yathārahaṃ.

After the meal, taking perfumes, garlands, medicines, and robes, she would go to the monastery and pay due honor.

31.

31.

Tadā tatheva katvā sā, saṅghattherassa santike;

Nisīdi dhammaṃ desento, thero taṃ idha mabravi.

Having done so on that occasion, she sat down near the Elder of the Sangha. While teaching the Dhamma, the elder said this to her:

32.

32.

“Mahāsampatti tumhehi, laddhā’yaṃ puññakammunā;

Appamādo’va kātabbo, puññakamme idānipi”.

“This great fortune has been obtained by you through your meritorious deeds. Even now you should be diligent in performing meritorious deeds.”

33.

33.

Evaṃ vutte tu sā āha, “kiṃ sampatti ayaṃ idha;

Yesaṃ no dārakā natthi, vañjhāsampatti tena no”.

When this was said, she replied: “What prosperity is this to us who have no children? Our prosperity is barren.”

34.

34.

Chaḷabhiñño mahāthero, puttalābhamavekkhiya;

“Gilānaṃ sāmaṇeraṃ taṃ, passadevī”ti abravi.

The great elder, who possessed the six supernormal powers, perceiving her prospect of gaining a son, said: “Go, queen, and see that sick novice.”

35.

35.

Sā gantvā’sanna maraṇaṃ, sāmaṇeramavoca taṃ;

“Patthehi mama puttattaṃ, sampattī mahatī hi no”.

She went to the novice, who was near death, and said to him: “Please aspire to become my son, for our good fortune will be great.”

36.

36.

Na [M 0.0126] icchatīti ñatvāna, tadatthaṃ mahatiṃ subhaṃ;

Pupphapūjaṃ kārayitvā, puna yāci sumedhasā.

Knowing that he did not wish it, the wise queen had a great and beautiful flower offering made for that purpose and asked him again.

37.

37.

Evampa’nicchamānassa, atthāyu’pāyakovidā;

Nānā bhesajja vatthāni, saṅghe datvā’tha yācitaṃ.

Although he was still unwilling, she, being skilled in means for his welfare, gave various medicines and robes to the Sangha and then made her request.

38.

38.

Patthesi so rājakulaṃ, sā taṃ ṭhānaṃ anekadhā;

Alaṅkaritvā vanditvā, yānamāruyha pakkami.

He then aspired to be reborn in the royal family. She, having decorated that place in many ways and paid homage, mounted her vehicle and departed.

39.

39.

Tato cuto sāmaṇero, gacchamānāya deviyā;

Tassā kucchimhi nibbatti, taṃ jāniya nivattisā.

Then the novice passed away and was conceived in the queen’s womb as she was departing. Knowing this, she turned back.

40.

40.

Rañño taṃ sāsanaṃ datvā, raññā saha punā’gamā;

Sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā, sāmaṇerassu’bhopite.

Having given the news to the king, she returned with him. They had the funeral rites for the novice performed, and both were filled with joy.

41.

41.

Tasmiṃyeva pariveṇe, vasantā santamānasā;

Mahādānaṃ pavattesuṃ, bhikkhusaṅghassa sabbadā.

Dwelling in that same pariveṇa with peaceful minds, they continually gave great offerings to the Sangha of monks.

42.

42.

Tasse’vaṃ dohaḷo āhi, mahā puññāya mātuyā;

“Usabhamattaṃ madhugaṇḍaṃ, katvā ussīsake sayaṃ.

Then a pregnancy craving arose in the mother of great merit: a desire to make a honeycomb the size of a bull, place it at the head of her bed, and,

43.

43.

Vāmetarena passena, nipannāsayane subhe;

Dvādasannaṃ sahassānaṃ, bhikkhūnaṃ dinnasesakaṃ.

while lying on her left side on a beautiful couch, to eat the leftovers of that honey after it had been given to twelve thousand monks.

44.

44.

Madhuṃ bhuñjitukāmā’si, atha eḷāra rājino;

Yodhāna maggayodhassa, sīsacchinnāsidevanaṃ.

She was desirous of eating the honey. Then, she craved the water used to wash the sword that had cut off the head of the chief warrior among King Eḷāra’s champions,

45.

45.

Tasseva sīse ṭhatvāna, pātuñceva akāmayi;

Anurādha purasseva, uppalakkhettato pana.

and she desired to drink it while standing on that very head. Furthermore, from the lotus fields of Anurādhapura itself,

46.

46.

Ānītuppalamālañca, amilā taṃ pilandhituṃ;

Taṃ devī rājino āha, nemitte pucchi bhūpati.

to wear an unfaded garland of lotuses brought from there. The queen told the king of these cravings, and the ruler questioned the soothsayers.

47.

47.

Taṃ sutvā āhu nemittā, “deviputto nighātiya;

Damiḷe katve’karajjaṃ, sāsanaṃ jotayissati”.

Having heard this, the soothsayers said: “The queen’s son will subdue the Tamils and, making the land a single kingdom, he will make the Buddha’s Dispensation shine brightly.”

48.

48.

Edisaṃ madhugaṇḍaṃ so, dasseti tassa īdisiṃ;

Sampattiṃ deti rājā”ti, ghosāpesi mahīpati.

The ruler had it proclaimed: “The king will give a great reward to whoever can show him such a honeycomb.”

49.

49.

Goṭṭhasamuddavelante, madhupuṇṇaṃ nikujjitaṃ;

Nāvaṃ ñatvāna ācikkhi, rañño janapade naro.

A man from the country, having seen an overturned boat full of honey on the shore of the Goṭṭha sea, informed the king.

50.

50.

Rājā [M 0.0127] deviṃ tahiṃ netvā, maṇḍapamhi susaṅkhate;

Yathicchithaṃ tāya madhuṃ, paribhogamakārayi.

The king took the queen there and, in a well-adorned pavilion, had her consume the honey according to her desire.

51.

51.

Itare dohaḷe tassā, sampādetuṃ mahīpati;

Veḷusumana nāmaṃ taṃ, yodhaṃ tattha niyojayi.

To fulfill her other cravings, the ruler appointed to that task the warrior named Veḷusumana.

52.

52.

So’nurādhapuraṃ gantvā, rañño maṅgalavājino;

Gopakena akā mettiṃ, tassa kiccañca sabbadā.

He went to Anurādhapura and befriended the groom of the king’s state horse, always attending to his duties.

53.

53.

Tassa vissattha taṃ ñatvā, pātova uppalāna’siṃ;

Kadambanadiyā tīre, ṭhapetvāna asaṅkito.

Knowing he was trusted by the groom, he, fearless, at dawn placed a sword and lotuses on the bank of the Kadamba river.

54.

54.

Assaṃ netvā tamāruyha, gaṇhitvāna uppalāna’siṃ;

Nivedayitvāna attānaṃ, assavegena pakkami.

He led out the horse, mounted it, took the sword and the lotuses, and, announcing his name, departed with the speed of the horse.

55.

55.

Sutvā rājā gahetuṃ taṃ, mahā yodhānapesayi;

Dutiyaṃ sammathaṃ assaṃ, āruyha sonudhāpitaṃ.

Hearing this, the king sent a great warrior to capture him. Mounting a second horse of equal speed, the warrior gave chase.

56.

56.

So gumbanissito assa-piṭṭheyeva nisīdiya;

Entassa piṭṭhito tassa, ubbayhā’siṃ pasārayi.

Taking cover by a thicket, while still seated on his horse, he stretched out his sword behind him as the pursuer came from behind.

57.

57.

Assavegenayantassa, sīsaṃ chijja ubhohaye;

Sīsañcā’dāya sāyaṃ so, mahāgāmamupāgami.

As the pursuer came on at the horse’s full speed, his head was cut off. Taking the head, Veḷusumana reached Mahāgāma that evening.

58.

58.

Dohaḷe te ca sā devī, paribhuñji yathāruci;

Rājā yodhassa sakkāraṃ, kārāpesi yathārahaṃ.

And so the queen fulfilled her pregnancy cravings as she desired, and the king had fitting honors bestowed upon the warrior.

59.

59.

Sā devī samaye dhaññaṃ, janayī puttamuttamaṃ;

Mahārājakule tasmiṃ, ānando ca mahā ahu.

In due time, the queen gave birth to a noble son, and there was great joy in that great royal family.

60.

60.

Tassa puññānubhāvena, tadaheva upāgamuṃ;

Nānāratanasampuṇṇā, sattanāvā tato tato.

By the power of his merit, on that very day seven ships filled with various jewels arrived from here and there.

61.

61.

Tasseva puññatejena, chaddantakulato karī;

Hatthicchāpaṃ āharitvā, ṭhapetvā idha pakkami.

By the power of his merit, an elephant from the Chaddanta clan brought a young elephant, left it here, and departed.

62.

62.

Taṃ titthasaratīramhi, disvā gumbantare ṭhitaṃ;

Kaṇḍulavho bālisiko, rañño ācikkhi tāvade.

A fisherman named Kaṇḍula saw it standing among the bushes on the bank of the ford and immediately reported it to the king.

63.

63.

Pesetvā’cariye rājā, tamāṇāpiya posayi;

Kaṇḍulo iti ñāyittha, diṭṭhattā kaṇḍulena so.

The king sent trainers, had the elephant brought, and raised it. It became known as Kaṇḍula because it was seen by Kaṇḍula.

64.

64.

“Suvaṇṇabhājanādīnaṃ[M 0.0128], puṇṇā nāvā idhāgatā”;

Iti rañño nivedasuṃ, rājā tānā’harāpayi.

“Ships laden with golden vessels and the like have arrived here.” So they reported to the king, who had them brought.

65.

65.

Puttassa nāmakaraṇe, maṅgalamhi mahīpati;

Dvādasa sahassasaṅkhaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantiya.

At the great festival for his son’s naming ceremony, the ruler of the land invited twelve thousand monks from the Sangha.

66.

66.

Evaṃ cintesi “yadime, putto laṃkātale’khile;

Rajjaṃ gahetvā sambuddha-sāsanaṃ jotayissati.

He thought thus: “If this son of mine, having taken the kingship over the entire island of Laṅkā, will illuminate the Buddha’s Dispensation,

67.

67.

Aṭṭhuttarasahassañca, bhikkhavo pavisantu ca;

Sabbe te uddhapattañca, cīvaraṃ pārapantu ca.

may one thousand and eight monks enter, and may they all wear their robes with their bowls held upright.

68.

68.

Paṭhamaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ pādaṃ, ummāranto ṭhapentu ca;

Ekacchattayutaṃ dhamma-karaṇaṃ nīharantu ca.

May they place their right foot first as they step over the threshold, and may they bring out the Dhamma-casket under a single parasol.”

69.

69.

Gotamo nāma thero ca, patiggaṇhātu puttakaṃ;

So ca saraṇasikkhā yo, detu” sabbaṃ tathā ahu.

“Let the elder named Gotama receive this son, and let him give the Refuges and the Precepts.” And it all happened thus.

70.

70.

Sabbaṃ nimittaṃ disvāna, tuṭṭhacitto mahīpati;

Datvā saṅghassa pāyāsaṃ, nāmaṃ puttassa kārayi.

Having seen all the omens, the lord of the land, with a pleased mind, gave milk-rice to the Saṅgha and then conferred a name upon his son.

71.

71.

Mahāgāme nāyakattaṃ, pitunāmañca ekato;

Ubho katvāna ekajjhaṃ, gāmaṇiabhayo iti.

Combining the leadership of the great village with his father's name, making both into one, he was called Gāmaṇī Abhaya.

72.

72.

Mahāgāmaṃ pavisitvā, navame divase tato;

Saṅgamaṃ deviyā kāsi, tena gabbhamagaṇhi sā.

Having entered the great village, on the ninth day thereafter he had intercourse with the queen, whereby she conceived.

73.

73.

Kāle jātaṃ sutaṃ rājā, tissanāmaṃ akārayi;

Mahatā parihārena, ubhato vaḍḍhiṃsu dārakā.

When the son was born in due time, the king had him named Tissa. With great care, both boys grew up.

74.

74.

Sitthappavesamaṅgala-kāle dvinnampi sādaro;

Bhikkhusatānaṃ pañcanaṃ, dāpayitvāna pāyasaṃ.

At the auspicious ceremony of the first feeding of rice for both boys, the king, full of respect, had milk-rice offered to five hundred monks.

75.

75.

Tehi upaḍḍhe bhuttamhi, gahetvā thokathokakaṃ;

Sovaṇṇasarakene’saṃ, deviyā saha bhūpati.

When the monks had eaten half of it, the king, together with the queen, taking a little at a time with a golden spoon,

76.

76.

“Sambuddhasāsanaṃ tumhe, yadi chaḍḍetha puttakā;

Mā jīratu kucchigataṃ, idaṃ vo”ti apāpayi.

made them eat, saying: “My sons, if you should ever abandon the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, may this in your bellies not be digested!”

77.

77.

Viññāya bhāsitatthaṃ te, ubho rājakumārakā;

Pāyāsaṃ taṃ abhuñjiṃsu, tuṭṭhacittā’mataṃ viya.

Having understood the meaning of what was said, both royal princes partook of that milk-rice with pleased minds, as if it were ambrosia.

78.

78.

Dasa dvādasavassesu, tesu vīmaṃsanatthiko;

Tatheva bhikkhū bhojetvā, tesaṃ ucchiṭṭhamodanaṃ.

When they were ten and twelve years of age, wishing to test them, he fed the monks in the same way, and their leftover rice

79.

79.

Gāhayitvā [M 0.0129] taṭṭakena, ṭhapāpetvā tadantike;

Tibhāgaṃ kārayitvāna, idha māha mahīpati.

he had taken on a plate and placed near them. Having had it divided into three portions, the lord of the earth said this:

80.

80.

“Kuladevatānaṃ no tātā, bhikkhūnaṃ vimukhā mayaṃ;

Na hessāmā”ti cintetvā, bhāgaṃ bhuñjathi’manti ca.

“Dears, thinking, ‘We will never turn away from the monks, our family deities,’ you should eat this portion.”

81.

81.

“Dve bhātaro mayaṃ niccaṃ, aññamaññamadūbhakā;

Bhavissāmā”ti cintetvā, bhāgaṃ bhuñjithi’manti ca.

“Thinking, ‘We two brothers will always be loyal to one another,’ you should eat this portion.”

82.

82.

Amataṃ viya bhuñjiṃsu, te dve bhāge ubhopi ca;

“Na yujjhissāma damiḷehi”, iti bhuñjathi’maṃ iti.

Both of them ate those two portions as if they were ambrosia. Of the third portion, he said: “Eat this, thinking, ‘We will not fight with the Damiḷas.’”

83.

83.

Evaṃ vuttetu tisso so, pāṇinā khipi bhojanaṃ;

Gāmaṇibhattapiṇḍaṃ tu, khipitvā sayanaṃ gato.

When this was said, Tissa threw the food away with his hand. Gāmaṇī, for his part, threw away his lump of rice and went to his bed.

84.

84.

Saṃkucitvā hatthapādaṃ, nipajji sayena sayaṃ;

Devī gantvā tosayantī, gāmaṇiṃ etadabravi.

Drawing in his hands and feet, he lay down on his bed. The queen went to console him and said this to Gāmaṇī:

85.

85.

Pasāritaṅgo sayane, kiṃ nasesi sukhaṃ suta;

“Gaṅgāpāramhi damīḷā, ito goṭṭhamahodadhi.

“My son, why do you not lie comfortably with limbs outstretched? On the far side of the Gaṅgā are the Damiḷas, and on this side is the Gotha ocean.”

86.

86.

Kathaṃ pasāritaṅgo’haṃ, nipajjāmī’ti so bravi;

Sutvāna tassādhippāyaṃ, tuṇhī āsi mahīpati.

“How can I lie with limbs outstretched?” he said. Having heard his intention, the king became silent.

87.

87.

So kamenā’bhivaḍḍhanto, ahu soḷasavassiko;

Puññavā yasavā dhīmā, tejo balaparakkamo.

Gradually growing up, he reached sixteen years of age, meritorious, famous, wise, and endowed with majesty, strength, and valor.

88.

88.

Calācalāyaṃ gatiyañhi pāṇino,

Upenti puññena yathāruciṃ gatiṃ;

Itīti mantetvā satataṃ mahādaro,

Bhaveyya puññapacayamhi buddhimāti.

Since beings in this fickle round of existence attain a destination through merit as they wish, reflecting thus, the wise, with great reverence, should always be intent on accumulating merit.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Great Chronicle, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of the good,

Gāmaṇikumārasūti nāma

named The Birth of Prince Gāmaṇī,

Bāvīsatimo paricchedo.

the Twenty-Second Chapter.

Tevīsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-Third Chapter

Yodhalābho

The Gaining of the Warriors

1.

1.

Balalakkhaṇarūpeti[M 0.0130],

Tejojavaguṇehi ca;

Aggo hutvā mahākāyo,

So ca kaṇḍūlavāraṇo.

Endowed with the form and signs of strength, and with the qualities of majesty and speed, foremost and with a great body, was the elephant Kaṇḍula.

2.

2.

Nandīmitto suranimilo, mahāsoṇo goṭṭhayimbaro;

Theraputtābhayo bharaṇo, veḷusumano tatheva ca.

Nandimitta, Suranimila, Mahāsoṇa, Goṭṭhayimbara, Theraputtābhaya, Bharaṇa, and Veḷusumana as well,

3.

3.

Khañjadevo phussadevo, labhiyya vasabhopi ca;

Ete dasa mahāyodhā, tassā’hesuṃ mahabbalā.

Khañjadeva, Phussadeva, and Labhiyavasabha—these ten great warriors of mighty strength were his.

4.

4.

Ahu eḷārarājassa, mitto nāma camūpati;

Tassa kammantagāmamhi, pācīnakhaṇḍarājiyā.

There was a general of King Eḷāra named Mitta. In his work-village, in the eastern district,

5.

5.

Cittapabbatasāmantā, ahu bhaginiyā suto;

Kosohitavatthaguyho, mātulasseva nāmato.

near Cittapabbata, a son was born to his sister. He was named after his maternal uncle, and his male organ was retracted as if in a sheath.

6.

6.

Dūrampi parisappantaṃ, daharaṃ taṃ kumārakaṃ;

Ābajjha nandiyā kaṭyaṃ, nisadamhi abandhisu.

When that young boy was crawling far, they tied a strap to his waist and fastened him to a large grinding stone.

7.

7.

Nisadaṃ kaḍḍhato tassa, bhūmiyaṃ parisappato;

Ummārātikkame nandi, sā chajjati yato tato.

As he crawled on the ground dragging the grinding stone, that strap broke when he crossed the threshold.

8.

8.

Nandimittoti ñāyittha, dasanāgabalo ahu;

Vuddho nagaramāgamma, so upaṭṭhāsi mātulaṃ.

He became known as Nandimitta and had the strength of ten elephants. When he grew up, he went to the city and entered the service of his maternal uncle.

9.

9.

Thūpādīsu asakkāraṃ, karonto damiḷe tadā;

Ūruṃ akkammapādena, hatthena itaraṃ tuso.

At that time, seeing Damiḷas showing disrespect at the stūpas and other shrines, he would step on one of their thighs with his foot and seize the other with his hand,

10.

10.

Gahetvā sampadāletvā, bahikkhapatiṃ thāmavā;

Devā antaradhāpenti, tena khittaṃ kaḷevaraṃ.

and, being a man of great strength, would tear them asunder and throw the body outside. The devas would then make the corpse he had thrown disappear.

11.

11.

Damiḷānaṃ khayaṃ disvā, rañño ārocayiṃ sutaṃ;

“Sahoṭṭaṃ gaṇhathetaṃ”ti, vuttaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhisuṃ.

Seeing the decimation of the Damiḷas, people reported the matter to the king. When he ordered, “Seize him in the act!” they were unable to do so.

12.

12.

Cintesi [M 0.0131] nandimitto so, “evampi karato mama;

Janakkhayo kevalañhi, natthi sāsanajotanaṃ.

Then Nandimitta thought: “Even if I act in this way, it only leads to the destruction of people; there is no illumination of the Dispensation.

13.

13.

Rohaṇe khattiyā santi, pasannaṃ ratanattaye;

Tattha katvā rājasevaṃ, gaṇhitvā damiḷe’khile.

In Rohaṇa there are khattiyas who are devoted to the Triple Gem. There I will perform royal service, and after conquering all the Damiḷas,

14.

14.

Rajjaṃ datvā khattiyānaṃ, jotessaṃ buddhasāsanaṃ”;

Iti gantvā gāmaṇissa, taṃ kumārassa sāvayi.

I will give the kingdom to the khattiyas and illuminate the Buddha’s Dispensation.” So thinking, he went to Prince Gāmaṇī and informed him.

15.

15.

Mātuyā mantayitvā so, sakkāraṃ tassa kārayi;

Sakkato nandimitto so, yodho vasi tadantike.

After consulting with his mother, the prince had honors bestowed upon him. Thus honored, the warrior Nandimitta dwelt in his presence.

16.

16.

Kākavaṇṇo tissarājā, vāretuṃ damiḷisadā;

Mahāgaṅgāya titthesu, rakkhaṃ sabbesu kārayi.

King Kākavaṇṇatissa, to hold back the Damiḷas, always had guards stationed at all the fords of the Mahāgaṅgā.

17.

17.

Ahu dīghābhayo nāma, rañño’ñña bhariyā suto;

Kacchakatitthe gaṅgāya, tena rakkhamakārayi.

The king had another son, named Dīghābhaya, by another wife. He had him establish a guard post at the Kacchaka ford on the Gaṅgā.

18.

18.

So rakkhākaraṇatthāya, samantā yojanadvaye;

Mahākulamhā ekekaṃ, puttaṃ āṇāpayi tahiṃ.

23.
