Thus, having heard of these wonders born of good conduct, a wise person who seeks his own welfare should turn away from the path of the unwholesome and always delight in the path of the wholesome.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Great Chronicle, made for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people.

Yodhalābho nāma

The Gaining of the Warriors

Tevīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Third Chapter.

Catuvīsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-fourth Chapter

Dvebhātikayuddhaṃ

The Battle of the Two Brothers

1.

1.

Hatthassa [M 0.0138] tharukammassa, kusalo katupāsano;

So gāmaṇirājasuto, mahāgāme vasī tadā.

Skilled in the work of the elephant-goad and well-practiced, that Prince Gāmaṇi then dwelt in Mahāgāma.

2.

2.

Rājā rājasutaṃ tissaṃ, dīghavāpimhi vāsayi;

Ārakkhituṃ janapadaṃ, sampanna balavāhanaṃ.

The king settled his son Tissa, who was endowed with a strong army and vehicles, at Dīghavāpi to protect the country.

3.

3.

Kumāro gāmaṇikāle, sampassanto balaṃ sakaṃ;

“Yujjhissaṃ damiḷehī”ti, piturañño kathāpayī.

Prince Gāmaṇī, seeing his own strength, sent word to his father the king: 'I shall fight with the Damiḷas.'

4.

4.

Rājā taṃ anurakkhanto, “oragaṅgaṃ alaṃ” iti;

Vāresi yāvatatiyaṃ, so tatheva kathāpayī.

The king, seeking to protect him, forbade him up to the third time, saying, 'This side of the river is enough.' But the prince sent word in just the same way.

5.

5.

Pitā me puriso honto, ne’vaṃ vakkhati teni’daṃ;

Pilandhatūti pesesi, itthālaṅkāramassa so.

'If my father were a man, he would not speak thus.' Therefore, he sent women's ornaments to him, saying: 'Let him wear these!'

6.

6.

Rājā’ha tassa kujjhitvā, “karotha hemasaṅkhaliṃ;

Tāya taṃ bandhayissāmi, nā’ññathā rakkhiyo hi so.

The king, angered with him, said: 'Make a golden chain. With it I will bind him, for he cannot be protected otherwise.'

7.

7.

Palāyitvāna malayaṃ, kujjhitvā pituno agā;

Duṭṭhattāyeva pitari, āhu taṃ duṭṭhagāmaṇi.

Having fled, he went to Malaya, angry with his father. Because of his anger towards his father, they called him Duṭṭhagāmaṇī.

8.

8.

Rājā’tha ārabhī kātuṃ, mahāmaṅgalacetiyaṃ;

Niṭṭhite cetiye saṅghaṃ, sannipātayi bhūpati.

Then the king began to build the Mahāmaṅgala Cetiya. When the cetiya was completed, the lord of the earth assembled the Saṅgha.

9.

9.

Dvādasā’suṃ sahassāni, bhikkhū cittalapabbatā;

Tato tato dvādaseva, sahassāni samāgamuṃ.

There were twelve thousand bhikkhus from Cittalapabbata; and from various other places, twelve thousand more assembled.

10.

10.

Katvāna cetiyamahaṃ, rājā saṅghassa sammukhā;

Sabbe yodhe samānetvā, kāresi sapathaṃ tadā.

Having held a festival for the cetiya, the king, in the presence of the Saṅgha, assembled all the warriors and then had them take an oath.

11.

11.

“Puttānaṃ kalahaṭṭhānaṃ, na gacchissāma no”iti;

Akaṃsu sapathaṃ sabbe, taṃ yuddhaṃ tena nāgamuṃ.

'We will not go to the place of our sons' quarrel.' Thus all took an oath, and for that reason they did not go to that battle.

12.

12.

Catusaṭṭhi vihāre so, kārāpetvā mahīpati;

Tattakāneva vassāni, ṭhatvā maritahiṃ tadā.

That lord of the earth, having caused sixty-four vihāras to be built, lived for just that many years, and then he died there.

13.

13.

Rañño [M 0.0139] sarīraṃ gāhetvā, channayānena rājini;

Netvā tissa mahārāmaṃ, taṃ saṅghassa nivedayi.

The queen, having taken the king's body, conveyed it in a covered vehicle to Tissa Mahārāma and informed the Saṅgha.

14.

14.

Sutvā tissakumāro taṃ, āgantvā dīghavāpito;

Sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā, sakkaccaṃ pituno sayaṃ.

Having heard that, Prince Tissa came from Dīghavāpi and himself respectfully had the funeral rites for his father performed.

15.

15.

Mātaraṃ kaṇḍulaṃ hatthiṃ, ādiyitvā mahabbalo;

Bhātubhayā dīghavāpiṃ, agamāsi lahuṃ tato.

The one of great strength, having taken his mother and the elephant Kaṇḍula, out of fear of his brother, swiftly went from there to Dīghavāpi.

16.

16.

Taṃ pavattiṃ nivedetuṃ, duṭṭhagāmaṇi santikaṃ;

Lekhaṃ datvā visajjesuṃ, saccemaccā samāgatā.

The loyal ministers, having assembled, sent a messenger with a letter to report that news to Duṭṭhagāmaṇī.

17.

17.

So guttahālamāgantvā, tattha cāre visajjiya;

Mahāgāmamupagantvā, sayaṃ rajje’bhisecayi.

Having come to Guttahāla and having sent out spies there, he went to Mahāgāma and had himself consecrated in the kingdom.

18.

18.

Mātatthaṃ kaṇḍūlatthañca, bhātulekhaṃ visajjayi;

Aladdhā yāvatatiyaṃ, yuddhāya samupāgami.

He sent a letter to his brother for his mother and for Kaṇḍula. Not receiving them even up to the third time, he approached for battle.

19.

19.

Ahu dvinnaṃ mahāyuddhaṃ, cūḷaṅgaṇiyapiṭṭhiyaṃ;

Tattha nekasahassāni, patiṃsu rājino narā.

There was a great battle between the two at Cūḷaṅgaṇiyapiṭṭhi. There, many thousands of the king's men fell.

20.

20.

Rājā ca tissāmacco ca, vaḷavādīghutunikā;

Tayoyeva palāyiṃsu, kumāro anubandhite.

The king, the minister Tissa, and the mare Dīghathūnikā, only these three fled, while the prince pursued them.

21.

21.

Ubhinnamantare bhikkhū, mantayiṃsu mahīdharaṃ;

Taṃ disvā “bhikkhusaṅghassa, kammaṃ” iti nivatti so.

Between the two, the bhikkhus created a mountain by their power. Seeing that, he turned back, thinking: 'This is an act of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.'

22.

22.

Kappakandaranajjāso, javamālititthamāgato;

Rājā’ha tissamaccaṃ taṃ, “chātajjhattā mayaṃ”iti.

Having come to the Javamāli ford near the Kappakandara river, the king said to the minister Tissa: 'We are afflicted with hunger.'

23.

23.

Suvaṇṇasarake khitta-bhattaṃ nīharitassa so;

Saṅghe datvā bhuñjanato, kāretvā catubhāgakaṃ.

He (Tissa) brought out for him the food placed in a golden vessel. The king had it divided into four parts and, having given one part to the Saṅgha, prepared to eat.

24.

24.

“Ghosehi kāla”miccā’ha,

Tisso kālamaghosayi;

Suṇitvā dibbasotena,

Rañño sakkhāya dāyako.

'Announce the time,' he said, and Tissa announced the time. A donor who was a friend of the king heard this with his divine ear.

25.

25.

Thero piyaṅgu dīpaṭṭho, theraṃ tattha niyojayi;

Tissaṃ kuṭumbikasutaṃ, so tattha nabhasā’gamā.

The Thera residing on Piyangudīpa appointed for this task the Thera Tissa, son of a householder. He came there through the sky.

26.

26.

Tassa tisso karāpatta-ādāyā’dāsi rājino;

Saṅghassa bhāgaṃ sambhāgaṃ, rājā patte khipāpayi.

Tissa the minister took the bowl from the Thera's hand and gave it to the king. The king had the Saṅgha's share and his own share placed in the bowl.

27.

27.

Sambhāgaṃ [M 0.0140] khipi tisso ca, sambhāgaṃ vaḷavāpi ca;

Na icchitassābhāgañca, tisso pattamhi pakkhipi.

Tissa the minister also put in his share and the mare's share. The Thera Tissa, not desiring his own share, also put it in the bowl.

28.

28.

Bhattassa puṇṇapattaṃ taṃ, adātherassa bhūpati;

Adā gotamatherassa, so gantvā nabhasā lahuṃ.

The lord of the earth gave that bowl full of food to the Thera Gotama. The Thera then went swiftly through the sky.

29.

29.

Bhikkhūnaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ, datvā ālopabhāgaso;

Pañcasatānaṃ so thero, laddhehi tu tadantikā.

That Thera, giving it morsel by morsel to five hundred bhikkhus who were eating, provided for them, and they received it from him.

30.

30.

Bhāgehi pattaṃ pūretvā, ākāse khipi rājino;

Disvā’ gataṃ gahetvā taṃ, tisso bhojisi bhūpatiṃ.

Having filled the bowl with portions, he threw it through the air to the king. Seeing it arrive and taking it, Tissa the minister fed the lord of the earth.

31.

31.

Bhuñjitvāna sayañjāpi, vaḷavañca abhojayi;

Sattāhaṃ cumbaṭaṃ katvā, rājā pattaṃ visajjayi.

After Tissa the minister had eaten, he also fed the mare. The king honored the bowl by placing it on a head-pad for seven days, and then sent it back.

32.

32.

Gantvāna so mahāgāmaṃ, samādāya balaṃ puna;

Saṭṭhisahassaṃ yuddhāya, gantvā yujjhi sabhātarā.

Having gone to Mahāgāma and gathered his forces again, he went to battle with sixty thousand men and fought against his brother.

33.

33.

Rājā vaḷavamāruyha, tisso kaṇḍūla hatthinaṃ;

Dve bhātaro samāgañchuṃ, yujjhamānā raṇe tadā.

The king mounted the mare, Tissa the elephant Kaṇḍula; the two brothers then met, fighting in battle.

34.

34.

Rājā kariṃ karitva’nto, vaḷavāmaṇḍalaṃ akā;

Tathāpi chiddaṃ no disvā, laṅghā petuṃ matiṃakā.

The king, causing the elephant to turn, made a circle with the mare. Yet, seeing no opening, he resolved to leap over.

35.

35.

Vaḷavaṃ laṅghayitvāna, hatthinaṃ bhātiko’pari;

Tomaraṃ khipi cammaṃva, yathā chijjati piṭṭhiyaṃ.

Having caused the mare to leap over his brother on the elephant, he hurled a spear, which cut the armor on his back as if it were leather.

36.

36.

Anekāni sahassāni, kumārassa narātahiṃ;

Patiṃsu yuddhe yujjhantā, bhijja ceva mahabbalaṃ.

Many thousands of the prince's men fell there in battle while fighting, and the great army was shattered.

37.

37.

“Ārohakassa vekallā, itthī maṃ laṅghayī”iti;

Kuddhokarī taṃ cālento, rukkhameka mupāgami.

‘Due to the incompetence of my rider, a female leaped over me’; thus the enraged elephant, shaking him, approached a certain tree.

38.

38.

Kumāro āruhī rukkhaṃ, hatthī sāmimupāgami;

Tamāruyha palāyantaṃ, kumāro manubandhi so.

The prince (Tissa) climbed the tree; the elephant approached its master. That prince (Duṭṭhagāmaṇi), having mounted it, pursued the fleeing one.

39.

39.

Pavisitvā vihāraṃ so, mahāthera gharaṃgato;

Nipajjaheṭṭhā mañcassa, kumāro bhātunobhayā.

Having entered the monastery, he went to the great elder's dwelling. The prince lay down beneath the bed out of fear of his brother.

40.

40.

Pasārayi mahāthero, cīvaraṃ tattha mañcake;

Rājā anupadaṃ gantvā, “kuhiṃ tisso”ti pucchatha.

The great elder spread a robe there upon the bed. The king, following in his tracks, asked, “Where is Tissa?”

41.

41.

“Mañce [M 0.0141] tattha mahārāja”, iti thero avoca taṃ;

Heṭṭhā mañceti jānitvā, tato nikkhamma bhūpati.

“He is not on the bed, great king,” the elder said to him. The king, knowing he was beneath the bed, then departed from there.

42.

42.

Samantato vihārassa, rakkhaṃ kārayi taṃ pana;

Pañcakamhi nipajjetvā, datvā upari cīvaraṃ.

He, however, had guards placed all around the monastery. The monks, having laid the prince upon a bier, placed a robe over him.

43.

43.

Mañcapādesu gaṇhitvā, cattāro daharā yatī;

Matabhikkhuniyāmena, kumāraṃ bahi nīharuṃ.

Grasping the legs of the bed, four young monks carried the prince outside, in the manner of carrying a deceased nun.

44.

44.

Nīyamānantu taṃ ñatvā, idha māha mahīpati;

“Tissa tvaṃ kuladevatānaṃ, sīse hutvāna niyyāsi.

Knowing that he was being carried out, the king said this: “Tissa, you are being carried out on the heads of the tutelary deities of our clan.”

45.

45.

Balakkārena gahaṇaṃ, kuladevehi natthi me;

Guṇaṃ tvaṃ kuladevānaṃ, sareyyāsi kadācipi”.

I cannot seize you by force from the tutelary deities of our clan. May you one day remember the virtue of these tutelary deities of our clan!”

46.

46.

Tatoyeva mahāgāmaṃ, agamāsi mahīpati;

Āṇāpesi ca tattheva, mātaraṃ mātugāravo.

From there the king went to Mahāgāma. And being respectful of his mother, he sent for her there.

47.

47.

[Vassāni aṭṭhasaṭṭhiṃso, aṭṭhā dhammaṭṭhamānaso;

Aṭṭhasaṭṭhivihāre ca, kārāpesi mahīpati.]

For sixty-eight years he reigned, his mind established in the Dhamma; and the king caused sixty-eight monasteries to be built.

48.

48.

Nikkhāmito so bhikkhūhi, tissorāja suto pana;

Dīghavāpiṃ tatoyeva, agama’ññataro viya.

Having been escorted out by the monks, Tissa, the king's son, then went from there to Dīghavāpi, as if he were an ordinary man.

49.

49.

Kumāro godhagattassa, tissatherassa āha so;

“Sāparādho ahaṃ bhante, khamāpessāmi bhātaraṃ.

That prince said to the Elder Tissa, who was called Godhagatta: “Venerable sir, I am at fault; I shall ask forgiveness of my brother.”

50.

50.

Veyyāvaccakarā kāraṃ, tissaṃ pañcasatāni ca;

Bhikkhunamādiyitvā so, thero rāja mupāgami.

That elder, having made Tissa his attendant, and taking with him five hundred monks, approached the king.

51.

51.

Rājaputtaṃ ṭhapetvāna, thero sopāna matthake;

Sasaṅgho pāvisi saddho, nisīdāviya bhūmipo.

Having placed the prince at the head of the stairs, the elder, full of faith, entered with the Sangha; the king invited them to be seated.

52.

52.

Upānayī yāguādiṃ, thero pattaṃ vidhesiso;

“Kinti vutto’bravi tissaṃ, ādāya agatā”iti.

The king had rice-gruel and other foods brought. The elder covered his bowl. When asked, “Why is this?” he replied, “I have come bringing Tissa.”

53.

53.

“Kuhiṃ coro”ti vutto ca, ṭhitaṭhānaṃ nivedayi;

Vihāradevī gantvāna, chādiyaṭhāsi puttaka.

And when asked, “Where is the thief?” he indicated the place where he stood. Vihāradevī went and stood there, covering her son.

54.

54.

Rājā’ha [M 0.0142] theraṃ “ñāto vo,

Dāsabhāvo idāni no;

Sāmaṇeraṃ pesayetha,

Tumhe me sattavassikaṃ.

The king said to the elder: “Our servitude to you is now known. Had you sent even a seven-year-old novice to us, we would not have refused you.”

55.

55.

Janakkhayaṃ vināyeva, kalaho na bhaveyya no;

Rājā saṅghassa doseso, bhaṃghe daṇḍaṃ karissati.

“Without the destruction of men, this quarrel would not have ceased. This is a fault on the part of the Sangha, and creating a schism in the Sangha is a grave offense.”

56.

56.

Hessatā’gatakiccā vo,

Yāgādiṃ gaṇhāthāti so;

Datvā taṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa,

Pakkositvāna bhātaraṃ.

He said, “The purpose of your coming shall be fulfilled; now take the rice-gruel and other foods.” Having given these to the community of monks, he had his brother summoned.

57.

57.

Tattheva saṅghamajjhamhi, nisinno bhātarā saha;

Bhuñjitvā ekatoyeva, bhikkhu saṅghaṃ visajjayi.

Right there in the midst of the Sangha, seated with his brother, and having eaten together with him, he then dismissed the community of monks.

58.

58.

Sassakammāni kāretuṃ, tissaṃ tattheva pāhiṇi;

Sayampi bheriṃ cāretvā, sassakammāni kārayi.

To have the work of the harvest carried out, he sent Tissa to that very place. He himself, having had the drum beaten, also had the harvest work carried out.

59.

59.

Iti veramanekavikappacitaṃ,

Samayanti bahuṃ api sappurisaṃ;

Iti cintiya kohi naro matimā,

Na bhaveyya paresu susanta manoti.

Thus do good people pacify even great enmity built up by manifold imaginings. Reflecting upon this, what wise man would not be of a peaceful mind toward others?

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, made for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in good people.

Dvebhātikayuddhaṃ nāma

Entitled: The War of the Two Brothers.

Catuvīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Fourth Chapter.

Pañcavīsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-Fifth Chapter.

Duṭṭhagāmaṇi vijayo

The Victory of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi.

1.

1.

Duṭṭhagāmaṇirājā’tha[M 0.0143], katvāna janasaṅgahaṃ;

Kunte dhātuṃ nidhāpetvā, sayoggabalavāhano.

Then King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi, having won the support of the people and having placed the relic in his spear, set forth with his chariots, forces, and vehicles.

2.

2.

Gantvā tissamahārāmaṃ, vanditvā saṅghamabravi;

“Pāragaṅgaṃ gamissāmi, jotetuṃ sāsanaṃ ahaṃ.

Having gone to the great monastery of Tissa, he paid homage to the Sangha and said: 'I will go to the far side of the river to illuminate the Dispensation.'

3.

3.

Sakkātuṃ bhikkhavo detha, amhehi sahagāmino;

Maṅgalañceva rakkhā ca, bhikkhūnaṃ dassanaṃ hino.

O monks, grant us monks to go with us, whom we may honor; for the sight of monks is indeed a blessing and a protection for us.

4.

4.

Adāsi daṇḍakammatthaṃ, saṅgho pañcasataṃ yatī;

Bhikkhusaṅghatamādāya, tato nikkhamma bhūpati.

The Sangha granted five hundred ascetics by means of a formal act. Taking that community of monks, the king then departed.

5.

5.

Sodhāpetvāna malaye, idhāgamanamañjasaṃ;

Kaṇḍulaṃ hatthimāruyha, yodhehi parivārito.

Having caused the path of approach to be cleared in the Malaya region, he mounted the elephant Kaṇḍula, surrounded by his warriors.

6.

6.

Mahatā balakāyena, yuddhāya abhinikkhami;

Mahāgāmena sambaddhā, senāgā’guttahālakaṃ.

With a great host of forces, he marched forth to battle. The army, connected with Mahāgāma, came to Guttahālaka.

7.

7.

Mahiyaṅgaṇamāgamma, chattaṃ damiḷamaggahī;

Ghātetvā damiḷe tattha, āgantvā ambatitthakaṃ.

Having come to Mahiyangana, he seized the Tamil Chatta. Having slain the Tamils there, he came to Ambatitthaka.

8.

8.

Gaṅgā parikhāsampannaṃ, titthambadamiḷaṃ pana;

Yujjhaṃ catūhi mā sehi, katahatthaṃ mahabbalaṃ.

Then he fought for four months with the Tamil Titthamba, a skilled and mighty warrior, whose fortress was endowed with the river as a moat.

9.

9.

Mātaraṃ dassayitvāna, tena lesena aggahi;

Tatooruyha damiḷe, sattarāje mahabbale.

He seized him by a stratagem after the commander had shown his mother. Then, descending upon the Tamils, he captured the seven mighty kings.

10.

10.

Ekāheneva gaṇhitvā, khemaṃ katvā mahabbalo;

Balassā’dā dhanaṃ tena, khemārāmoti vuccati.

Having seized them in a single day, the mighty one made the area safe. He gave wealth to his army, and therefore it is called Khemārāma.

11.

11.

Mahākoṭṭhantare sobbhe, doṇo gavaramaggahī;

Hālakole issariyaṃ, nāḷisobbhamhi nāḷikaṃ.

In the chasm of Mahākoṭṭha, he seized Doṇagavara; at Hālakola, Issariya; and at Nāḷisobbha, Nāḷika.

12.

12.

Dīghābhayagallakamhi, gaṇhi dīghābhayampi ca;

Kacchipiṭṭhe kapisīsaṃ, catumāsena aggahi.

At Dīghābhaya-gallaka, he seized Dīghābhaya also. At Kacchapiṭṭha, he seized Kapisīsa in four months.

13.

13.

Koṭanagare [M 0.0144] koṭañca, tato hālavahāṇakaṃ;

Vahiṭṭhe vahiṭṭhadamiḷaṃ, gāmaṇimhi ca gāmaṇiṃ.

In Koṭanagara, he seized Koṭa, and then Hālavahāṇaka; at Vahiṭṭha, the Tamil Vahiṭṭha; and at Gāmaṇi, Gāmaṇi.

14.

14.

Kumbhagāmamhi kumbhañca, nandigāmamhi nandikaṃ;

Gaṇhi khāṇuṃ khāṇugāme, dve tu tambuṇṇame pana.

In Kumbhagāma, he seized Kumbha, and in Nandigāma, Nandika; he seized Khāṇu in Khāṇugāma, and two chieftains in Tambuṇṇama.

15.

15.

Mātulaṃ bhāgineyyañca, tambauṇṇamanāmake;

Jambucaggahī soso ca, gāmo’hu taṃ tadavhayo.

The uncle and the nephew he seized in the place named Tambuṇṇama. And the warrior Soso seized Jambuca, and that village was named after him.

16.

16.

“Ajānitvā sakaṃsenaṃ, ghātenti sajanā” iti;

Sutvāna saccakiriyaṃ, akarī tattha bhūpati.

Having heard, 'Not knowing their own army, people kill their own kinsmen,' the king performed an act of truth there.

17.

17.

Rajjasukhāya vāyāmo, nāyaṃ mama kadācipi;

Sambuddha sāsanasseva, ṭhapanāya ayaṃ mama.

This endeavor of mine is not for the delight of sovereignty, but is always for the establishment of the Dispensation of the Sambuddha.

18.

18.

Tena saccena mesenā-kāyopagatabhaṇḍikaṃ;

Jālavaṇṇaṃva hotūti, taṃ tathevatadā ahu.

By this truth, may the equipment on the bodies of my soldiers become the color of fire!' And so it was at that moment.

19.

19.

Gaṅgātīramhi damiḷā, sabbe ghātitasesakā;

Vijitaṃ nagaraṃ nāma, saraṇatthāya pāvisuṃ.

All the Tamils who survived the slaughter on the riverbank entered the city named Vijita for refuge.

20.

20.

Phāsuke aṅgaṇaṭhāne, khandhāvāraṃ nivesayi;

Taṃ khandhāvāra… ṭhīti, nāmenā’hosi pākaṭaṃ.

In a pleasant, open place, he established a camp. It became known by the name Khandhāvārapiṭṭhi.

21.

21.

Vijitanagaragāhatthaṃ, vīmaṃsanto narādhipo;

Disvā’yantaṃ nandimittaṃ, visajjāpesi kaṇḍulaṃ.

The king, while reconnoitering for the capture of Vijitanagara, saw Nandimitta approaching and sent the elephant Kaṇḍula against him.

22.

22.

Gaṇhituṃ āgataṃ hatthiṃ, nandīmitto karehitaṃ;

Ubho dante pīḷayitvā, ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdayi.

When the elephant came to seize him, Nandimitta, pressing its two tusks with his hands, forced it to sit down on its haunches.

23.

23.

Hatthinā nandimitto tu, yasmā yattha ayujjhi so;

Tasmā tattha tato gāmo, hatthiporoti vuccati.

Because Nandimitta fought there with the elephant, that village is therefore called Hatthipora.

24.

24.

Vīmaṃsitvā ubho rājā, vijitaṃ nagaraṃ agā;

Yodhānaṃ dakkhiṇadvāre, saṅgāmo āsi bhiṃsano.

Having tested them both, the king went to the city of Vijita. At the southern gate, a fierce battle of the warriors took place.

25.

25.

Puratthimamhi dvāramhi, so veḷusumano pana;

Aneka saṅkhe damiḷe, assāruḷhe aghātayi.

At the eastern gate, that Veḷusumana slew countless Tamils mounted on horses.

26.

26.

Dvāraṃ thakesuṃ damiḷā, rājā yodhe visajjayi;

Kaṇṇulo nandimitto ca, suranimilo ca dakkhiṇe.

The Tamils blocked the gate; the king sent forth his warriors. Kaṇḍula, Nandimitta, and Sūranimila were at the southern gate.

27.

27.

Mahāsoṇo [M 0.0145] ca goṭṭho ca,

Thera putto ca te tayo;

Dvāresu tīsu kammāni,

Itaresu tadā karuṃ.

Mahāsoṇa, Goṭhāimbara, and Theraputta, those three then performed their duties at the other three gates.

28.

28.

Nagaraṃ taṃ tiparikhaṃ, uccapākāra gopitaṃ;

Ayokammakatadvāraṃ, arīhi duppadhaṃsiyaṃ.

That city, with its triple moat, protected by a high rampart, and with iron-wrought gates, was difficult for enemies to assault.

29.

29.

Jāṇūhi ṭhatvā dāṭhāhi, bhinditvāna silāyudhā;

Iṭṭhakā ceva hatthi so, ayodvāramupāgami.

Standing on its knees and with its tusks, having broken the stone defenses and also bricks, that elephant approached the iron gate.

30.

30.

Gopuraṭṭhā tu damiḷā, khipiṃsu vividhā’yudhe;

Pakkaṃ ayoguḷañceva, kathikañca silesikaṃ.

From the gate-towers, the Damiḷas hurled various weapons: molten iron balls, boiling pitch, and resinous substances.

31.

31.

Piṭṭhiṃ khitte silesamhi, dhūpāyante’tha kaṇḍulo;

Vedanaṭṭo’dakaṭhānaṃ, gantvāna tattha ogahī.

When resinous substances were thrown on his back, Kaṇḍula smarted as if smoking; afflicted by the pain, he went to a water-place and plunged into it.

32.

32.

Na idaṃ surāpāṇaṃ te, ayodvāra vighāṭanaṃ;

Gaccha dvāraṃ vighāṭehi, iccāhagoṭṭhayimbaro.

“This breaking of the iron gate is not liquor-drinking for you! Go, break open the gate!” thus spoke Goṭṭhayimbara.

33.

33.

So mānaṃ janayitvāna, koñcaṃ katvā gajuttamo;

Udakā uṭṭhahitvāna, thale aṭṭhāsi dappavā.

Aroused to pride, the noble elephant, having trumpeted, rose from the water and stood upon the land, full of spirit.

34.

34.

Hatthivajje viyojetvā, silesaṃ osadhaṃ akā;

Rājā āruyha hatthiṃ taṃ, kumbhe phusiyapāṇinā.

The elephant-doctor removed the resin and applied medicine. The king then mounted that elephant and stroked its forehead with his hand.

35.

35.

“Laṃkādīpamhi sakale, rajjaṃ te tāta kaṇḍula;

Dammī”ti taṃ tosayitvā, bhojetvā varabhojanaṃ.

“Dear Kaṇḍula, I give to you the kingship over the entire island of Laṅkā.” Thus having pleased him, he fed him with the choicest food.

36.

36.

Veṭhayitvā sāṭakena, kārayitvā suvammitaṃ;

Sattaguṇaṃ māhisacammaṃ, bandhetvā cammapiṭṭhiyaṃ.

Having wrapped him in a robe, and having had him well-armored, he bound a seven-fold buffalo hide upon his leather-covered back.

37.

37.

Tasso’ paritelacammaṃ, dāpetvā taṃ visajjayi;

Asanīviya gajjanto, so gahetvā’paddave saha.

Having had a hide soaked in oil placed over that, he sent him forth. Roaring like a thunderbolt, he rushed into the fray.

38.

38.

Padaraṃ vijjhi dāṭhāhi, ummāraṃ padasā’hani;

Saddhārabāhaṃ taṃ dvāraṃ, bhūmiyaṃ saravaṃ pati.

He pierced the door-panels with his tusks and struck the lintel with his foot; that gate with its posts and bars fell to the ground with a crash.

39.

39.

Gopure dabbasambhāraṃ, patantaṃ hattipiṭṭhiyaṃ;

Bāhāhi pariharitvāna, nandīmitto pavaṭṭayi.

As the debris from the gate-tower fell upon the elephant's back, Nandimitta warded it off with his arms and pressed forward.

40.

40.

Disvāna [M 0.0146] tassa kiriyaṃ, kaṇḍulo tuṭṭhamānaso;

Dāṭhāpīṭhanaveraṃ taṃ, chaḍḍhesi paṭhamaṃ kataṃ.

Seeing his action, Kaṇḍula, with a pleased mind, discarded the grudge he had formerly held against him for the pressing of his tusks.

41.

41.

Atthano piṭṭhitoyeva, pavesatthāya kaṇḍulo;

Nivattitvāna oloki, yodhaṃ tattha gajuttamo.

The noble elephant, Kaṇḍula, turned back and looked at the warrior, as if to show him the way to enter from upon his back.

42.

42.

“Hatthinākatamaggena, nappavekkhāmahaṃ”iti;

Nandīmitto vicintetvā, pākāraṃ hani bāhunā.

Nandimitta, thinking, “I shall not enter by the path made by the elephant,” struck the rampart with his arm.

43.

43.

So aṭṭhārasahatthucco, patiaṭṭhusabho kira;

Oloki suranimalaṃ, anicchaṃ sopi taṃ pathaṃ.

He was eighteen cubits high, it is said, and with the might of a bull. He looked at Sūranimala, and he too was unwilling to take that path.

44.

44.

Laṅghayitvāna pākāraṃ,

Nagarabbhantare pati;

Bhinditvā dvāramekekaṃ,

Goṭṭho soṇova pāvisi.

Having leaped over the rampart, he fell within the city. Breaking open gate after gate, Goṭṭha and Soṇa also entered.

45.

45.

Hattī gahetvā rathacakkaṃ, mitto sakaṭapañjaraṃ;

Nāḷikerataruṃ goṭṭho, nimmalo khaggamuttamaṃ.

The elephant seized a chariot wheel, Mitta a cart's framework, Goṭṭha a coconut palm, and Nimmala an excellent sword.

46.

46.

Tālarukkhaṃ mahāsoṇo, theraputto mahāgadaṃ;

Visuṃ visuṃ vīthigatā, damiḷe tattha cuṇṇayuṃ.

Mahāsoṇa took a palmyra palm, the Elder's son a great mace; going separately through the streets, they there crushed the Damiḷas.

47.

47.

Vijitaṃ nagaraṃ bhetvā, catumāsena khattiyo;

Tatho girilakaṃ gantvā, giriyaṃ damiḷaṃ hani.

Having breached the city of Vijitanagara in four months, the king then went to Girilaka and slew the Damiḷa named Giriya.

48.

48.

Gantvā mahelanagaraṃ, timahāparikhaṃ tato;

Kadamba pupphavallīhi, samantā parivāritaṃ.

Then he went to the city of Mahela, which was surrounded on all sides by three great moats and enclosed by flowering Kadamba creepers.

49.

49.

Ekadvāraṃ duppavesaṃ, catumāse vasaṃ tahiṃ;

Gaṇhi mahelarājānaṃ, mantayuddhena bhūmipo.

It had a single gate and was difficult to enter. The lord of the land, remaining there for four months, captured the king of Mahela by means of strategic warfare.

50.

50.

Tato’nurādhanagaraṃ, āgacchanto mahīpati;

Khandhāvāraṃ nivesesi, paritokāsapabbataṃ.

Then the great king, advancing towards the city of Anurādhapura, established his camp near the Kāsa mountain.

51.

51.

Māsamhi jeṭṭhamūlamhi, taḷākaṃ tattha kāriya;

Jalaṃ kīḷi tahiṃ gāmo, posonanagaravhayo.

In the month of Jeṭṭha, under the Mūla constellation, he had a tank constructed there and held water festivities. The village there was named Posonanagara.

52.

52.

Taṃ [M 0.0147] yuddhāyāgataṃ sutvā, rājānaṃ duṭṭhagāmaṇiṃ;

Amacce sannipātetvā, eḷāro āha bhūmipo.

Hearing that King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi had come for battle, the ruler Eḷāra assembled his ministers and spoke.

53.

53.

“So rājā ca sayaṃyodho,

Yodhā cassa mahūkira;

Amacco kinnu kātabbaṃ,

Kinti maññanti no ime.

“That king is himself a warrior, and his warriors, it seems, are mighty. O ministers, what is to be done? What do you all think?”

54.

54.

Dīghajattuppabhutayo, yodhā eḷārarājino;

“Suve yuddhaṃ karissāmi”, iti te nicchayaṃ karuṃ.

The warriors of King Eḷāra, led by Dīghajantu, made a resolution, saying: “Tomorrow we shall do battle.”

55.

55.

Duṭṭhagāmaṇirājāpi, mantetvā mātuyā saha;

Tassā matena kāresi, dvattiṃsa balakoṭṭhake.

King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi also, after consulting with his mother, acted on her advice and had thirty-two strongholds built.

56.

56.

Rājacchattadhare tattha, ṭhapesi rājarūpake;

Abbhantare koṭṭhake tu, sayaṃ aṭṭhāsi bhūpati.

There he placed royal figures holding royal parasols; but the king himself stood within the innermost stronghold.

57.

57.

Eḷārarājā sannaddho, mahāpabbata hatthinaṃ;

Āruyha agamā tattha, sayogga balavāhano.

King Eḷāra, clad in armor, mounted his elephant Mahāpabbata and went there with his well-equipped army and transport.

58.

58.

Saṅgāme vattamānamhi, dīghajattu mahabbalo;

Ādāya khaggaphalakaṃ, yujjhamāno bhayānako.

As the battle was underway, the mighty Dīghajantu, taking up his sword and shield, fought, inspiring terror.

59.

59.

Hatthe aṭṭharasu’ggantvā, nabhaṃ taṃ rājarūpakaṃ;

Chinditvā asinā bhindi, paṭhamaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ.

Having leaped eighteen cubits into the sky, he cut that royal effigy with his sword and destroyed the first stronghold.

60.

60.

Evaṃ sesepi bhinditvā, malakoṭṭhe mahabbalo;

Ṭhitaṃ gāmaṇirājena, balakoṭṭhamupāgami.

Thus, having destroyed the remaining strongholds, the mighty one approached the stronghold where King Gāmaṇi was stationed.

61.

61.

Yodho so suranimalo, gacchantaṃ rājino’pari;

Sāvetvā attano nāmaṃ, tamakkosi mahabbalo.

That mighty warrior Suranimala, announcing his own name, reviled the king who was passing above.

62.

62.

Itaro “taṃ vadhissa”nti, kuddho ākāsamuggami;

Itaro otarantassa, phalakaṃ upanāmayi.

The other, enraged, thinking, “I will slay him,” rose into the sky; the other, as he descended, held up his shield.

63.

63.

“Chindā metaṃ saphalakaṃ”, iti cintiya so pana;

Phalakaṃ hani khaggena, taṃ muñciyi’ tarosayi.

Thinking, “I will cut him down along with his shield,” he struck the shield with his sword; but the other released it.

64.

64.

Kappento muttaphalakaṃ, dīghajattu tahiṃ pati;

Uṭṭhāya sūranimilo, patitaṃ sattiyā’hani.

While cutting at the released shield, Dīghajantu fell there; having risen, Suranimala struck the fallen one with a spear.

65.

65.

Saṅkhaṃ [M 0.0148] dhami phussadevo, senā bhijjittha dāmiḷi;

Eḷaropi nivattittha, ghātesuṃ damiḷe bahū.

Phussadeva blew the conch, and the Damiḷa army was broken; Eḷāra too turned back, and they slew many Damiḷas.

66.

66.

Tattha vāpi jalaṃ āsi, hatānaṃ lohitā vilaṃ;

Tasmā kulatthavā pīti, nāmato vissutaṃ ahu.

The water of the tank there was turbid with the blood of the slain; therefore, it became famous by the name Kulatthavāpī.

67.

67.

Carāpetvā tahiṃ bheriṃ, duṭṭhagāmaṇi bhūpati;

“Na hanissatu eḷāraṃ, maṃmuñciya paro”iti.

Having had the drum beaten there, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi proclaimed, “Let no one but me slay Eḷāra.”

68.

68.

Sannaddho sayamāruyha, sannaddhaṃ kaṇḍulaṃ kariṃ;

Eḷāraṃ anubandhanto, dakkhiṇadvāramāgami.

Clad in armor, he himself mounted his armored elephant Kaṇḍula, and pursuing Eḷāra, he came to the southern gate.

69.

69.

Puradakkhiṇadvāramhi, ubho yujjhiṃsu bhūmipā;

Tomaraṃ khipi eḷāro, gāmaṇi tamavañcayi.

At the southern gate of the city, the two kings fought; Eḷāra hurled a spear, and Gāmaṇi evaded it.

70.

70.

Vijjhāpesi ca dantehi, taṃ hatthiṃ sakahatthinā;

Tomaraṃ khipi eḷāraṃ, sahatthi tattha so pati.

And he had his own elephant pierce that elephant with its tusks; he hurled a spear at Eḷāra, and he fell there together with his elephant.

71.

71.

Tato vijitasaṅgāmo, sayoggabalavāhano;

Laṃkaṃ ekātapattaṃ so, katvāna pāvisi puraṃ.

Then, victorious in battle, with his forces and vehicles, he brought Laṅkā under a single parasol and entered the city.

72.

72.

Puramhi bheriṃ cāretvā, samantā yojane jane;

Sannipātiya kāresi, pūjaṃ eḷārarājino.

Having had the drum beaten in the city, he gathered the people from a yojana all around and performed funeral honors for King Eḷāra.

73.

73.

Taṃ dehapatitaṭhāne, kūṭāgārena jhāpayi;

Cetiyaṃ tattha kāresi, parihāramadāsi ca.

At the place where his body had fallen, he had him cremated in a gabled chamber; he built a cetiya there and bestowed honors upon it.

74.

74.

Ajjāpi laṃkāpatino, taṃ padesasamīpagā;

Teneva parihārena, na vādāpenti tūriyaṃ.

Even to this day, the rulers of Laṅkā, when they come near that place, do not have musical instruments played, because of that honor.

75.

75.

Evaṃ dvattiṃsa damiḷa, rājāno duṭṭhagāmaṇi;

Gaṇhitvā ekacchattena, laṃkārajjamakāsi so.

Thus Duṭṭhagāmaṇi, having conquered thirty-two Damiḷa kings, brought the kingdom of Laṅkā under a single parasol.

76.

76.

Vijite nagare bhinne, yodho so dīghajattuko;

Eḷārassa nivedetvā, bhāgineyyassa yodhataṃ.

When the city was conquered and broken, that warrior Dīghajantuka, having informed Eḷāra's nephew of the state of the war,

77.

77.

Tassa halluka nāmassa, bhāgineyyassa attano;

Pesayī cāgamatthāya, tassa sutvāna halluko.

sent to his own nephew, Bhalluka by name, that he should come; and Bhalluka, having heard this,

78.

78.

Eḷāradaḍḍhadivasā, sattame divase idha;

Purisānaṃ sahassehi, saṭṭhiyā saha otari.

On the seventh day from the day Eḷāra was burned, he landed here with sixty thousand men.

79.

79.

Otiṇṇo so suṇitvāpi, patanaṃ tassa rājino;

“Yujjhissāmī”ti lajjāya, mahātitthaṃ idhāgamā.

Although he had landed and heard of that king's fall, out of shame he declared, “I will fight,” and came here to Mahātittha.

80.

80.

Khandhāvāraṃ [M 0.0149] nivesesi, gāme koḷambahālake;

Rājā tassā’gamaṃ sutvā, yuddhāya abhinikkhami.

He set up camp in the village of Koḷambahālaka. The king, hearing of his arrival, marched out for battle.

81.

81.

Yuddhasannaha sannaddho, hatthimāruyha kaṇḍulaṃ;

Hatthassa rathayo dhehi, pantīhi ca anunako.

Clad in the armor of war, mounted on the elephant Kaṇḍula, he was accompanied by warriors on elephants, horses, and in chariots, and by lines of foot-soldiers.

82.

82.

Ummādaphusso devo so, dīpe aggadhanuggaho;

Dasaḍḍhāyudhasanaddho, sesayodhā ca anvaguṃ.

That Phussadeva, the foremost archer on the island, armed with his array of weapons, and the remaining warriors followed.

83.

83.

Pavatte tumūle yuddhe, sannaddho bhalluko tahiṃ;

Rājābhimukha māyāsi, nāgarājā tu kaṇḍulo.

When the tumultuous battle was raging, the armored Bhalluka advanced towards the king; but the elephant-king Kaṇḍula,

84.

84.

Taṃ vegamandibhāvatthaṃ, paccosakki saniṃ saniṃ;

Senāpi saddhiṃ teneva, paccosakki saniṃ saniṃ.

To lessen his momentum, it retreated slowly, slowly; the army also, along with it, retreated slowly, slowly.

85.

85.

Rājāha “pubbe yuddhesu, aṭṭhavīsatiyā ayaṃ;

Na paccosakki kiṃ etaṃ, phussadevā”ti āha so.

The king said: “In twenty-eight battles before, this one never retreated. What is this, Phussadeva?”

86.

86.

Jayo no paramo deva, jayabhūmi mayaṃ gajo;

Paccosakkati pekkhanto, jayaṭhānamhi ṭhassati.

“Victory is ours, O Deva! This elephant retreats, seeking the ground for victory; it will stand in the place of victory.”

87.

87.

Nāgo’tha paccosakkitvā, phussadevassa passato;

Mahāvihārasīmante, aṭṭhāsi suppatiṭṭhito.

Then the elephant, having retreated while Phussadeva watched, stood firmly established at the boundary of the Mahāvihāra.

88.

88.

Tatraṭṭhito nāgarājā, bhalluko damiḷo tahiṃ;

Rājābhimukhamāgantvā, uppaṇḍesi mahīpati.

As the elephant-king stood there, the Damiḷa Bhalluka came towards the king and taunted the lord of the earth.

89.

89.

Mukhaṃ pidhāya khaggena, rājā akkosi taṃ pana;

“Rañño mukhamhi pātemi”, iti kaṇḍañca so khipi.

Covering his face with his sword, the king then rebuked him; and he, saying, 'I shall strike the king's face,' hurled an arrow.

90.

90.

Āhacca so khaggatalaṃ, kaṇḍo papati bhūmiyaṃ;

“Mukhe viddho”ti saññāya, ukkaṭṭhiṃ bhalluko akā.

Having struck the flat of the sword, the arrow fell to the ground. Perceiving, 'He is pierced in the mouth,' Bhalluka raised a shout of triumph.

91.

91.

Rañño pacchā nisinno bho, phussadevo mahabbalo;

Kaṇḍa khipimukhe tassa, ghaṭṭento rājakuṇḍalaṃ.

Behind the king sat Phussadeva, of great strength; he shot an arrow into his (Bhalluka's) mouth, grazing the king's earring.

92.

92.

Rājānaṃ pādato katvā, patamānassa tassa tu;

Khipitvā aparaṃ kaṇḍaṃ, vijjhitvā tassa jaṇḍukaṃ.

As that one (Bhalluka) was falling, having aimed from the line of the king's feet, he shot another arrow, piercing his knee.

93.

93.

Rājānaṃ sīsato katvā, pātesī lahuhatthako;

Bhalluke patite tasmiṃ, jayanādo pavattatha.

Having aimed from the line of the king's head, the swift-handed one struck him down; when that Bhalluka had fallen, a shout of victory arose.

94.

94.

Phussadevo [M 0.0150] tahiṃyeva, ñāpetuṃ dosa mattano;

Kaṇḍavalliṃ sakaṃ chetvā, pasataṃ lohitaṃ sayaṃ.

Phussadeva, right there, to make known his own fault, having cut his own bowstring, himself presented a handful of blood.

95.

95.

Radhaññā dassesi taṃ disvā, rājā taṃ pucchi“kiṃ”iti;

Rāja daṇḍo kato meti, so avoca mahīpati.

He showed it to the king. Seeing that, the king asked him, 'What is this?' 'The royal punishment has been inflicted upon me,' he said to the lord of the earth.

96.

96.

Kodho dosoti vuttova,

Āha kuṇḍala ghaṭṭanaṃ;

Adosaṃ dosamaññāya,

Kimetaṃ kari bhātika.

‘Anger is indeed called a fault,’ he said concerning the grazing of the earring. ‘Mistaking a non-fault for a fault, what is this you have done, brother?’

97.

97.

Iti vatvā mahārājā, kataññu idha māha ca;

“Kaṇḍānucchaviko tuyhaṃ, sakkāro hessate mahā.

Having spoken thus, the great king, being grateful, said: 'A great honor, worthy of your arrow, shall be yours.'

98.

98.

Ghātetvā damiḷe sabbe, rājā laddhajayo kato;

Pāsāda talamāruyha, sīhāsanagato tahiṃ.

Having slain all the Damiḷas, the king, having gained the victory, ascended the palace terrace and went to the lion throne there.

99.

99.

Nāṭakāmacca majjhamhi, phussadevassa taṃ saraṃ;

Āṇāpetvā ṭhapāpetvā, puṃkhena ujukaṃ tale.

In the midst of the actors and ministers, he commanded that arrow of Phussadeva to be brought and had it placed upright on the floor by its feathered end.

100.

100.

Kahāpaṇehi kaṇḍaṃ taṃ, āsitte’yu parūpari;

Chādāpetvā dāpesi, phussadevassa taṃ khaṇe.

With kahāpaṇas poured one upon another, he had that arrow covered; having had it covered, he gave it to Phussadeva at that moment.

101.

101.

Narindapāsādatale, narindotha alaṅkate;

Sugandhadīpujjalite, nānāgandhasamāyute.

On the floor of the king's palace, adorned by the lord of men, lit with fragrant lamps, and filled with various scents.

102.

102.

Nāṭaka janayogena, accharāhi ca bhūsite;

Anagghattharaṇatthiṇṇe, muduke sayane subhe.

Adorned with a company of actors and people, and embellished with celestial nymphs; spread with priceless coverings, on a soft, beautiful bed.

103.

103.

Sayito sirisampattiṃ, mahatiṃ apipekkhiya;

Kataṃ akkhobhiṇighātaṃ, saranto na sukhaṃ labhi.

Lying down, though beholding his great prosperity, remembering the slaughter of an akkhobhiṇī that had been wrought, he did not obtain happiness.

104.

104.

Yiyaṅgudīpe arahanto, ñatvā taṃ tassatakkitaṃ;

Aṭṭhā’rahante pāhesuṃ, tamassāsetumissaraṃ.

The Arahants on the island of Yiyaṅgu, knowing that thought of his, sent eight Arahants to console that lord.

105.

105.

Āgamma te majjhāyāme, rāja dvāramhi otaruṃ;

Nivedi tabbhāgamanā, pāsāda talemāruhuṃ.

Having come, they descended at the palace gate in the middle watch of the night. Their arrival having been announced, they ascended to the palace terrace.

106.

106.

Vanditvā [M 0.0151] te mahārāja, nisīdāpiya āsane;

Katvā vividhasakkāraṃ, pucchi āgatakāraṇaṃ.

The great king paid homage to them, had them seated on seats, and performed various honors; then he asked the reason for their coming.

107.

107.

Piyaṅgudīpe saṅghena, pesitaṃ manujādhipa;

Tamassā sayituṃ amhe, iti rājā punā’hate.

'O lord of men, we were sent by the Saṅgha on Piyaṅgu Island to console you.' Thus they spoke.

108.

108.

“Kathaṃ nu bhante assāso, mama hessati yena me;

Akkhobhiṇimahāsena, ghāto kārāpito”iti.

‘Venerable sirs, how can there be solace for me, by whom the slaughter of a great army, an akkhobhiṇī, was caused to be done?’

109.

109.

“Saggamaggantarāyo ca, natthi te tena kammunā;

By that deed, there is no obstacle for you to the path to heaven.

Dīyaḍḍhamanujā ce’ttha, ghātitā manujādhipa.

Only one and a half human beings were slain here, O lord of men.

110.

110.

Saraṇesu ṭhito eko, pañcasīlepi cā’paro;

Micchādiṭṭhi ca dussīlo, sesā pasusamāmatā.

One was established in the refuges, and another in the five precepts. The rest, of wrong view and immoral, were considered equal to beasts.

111.

111.

Jotayissasi ceva tvaṃ, bahudhā buddhasāsanaṃ;

Manovilekhaṃ tasmā tvaṃ, vinodaya narissara.

You will indeed illuminate the Buddha's Dispensation in many ways; therefore, O ruler of men, dispel the agitation of your mind.

112.

112.

Iti vutto mahārājā, tehi assāsamāgato;

Vanditvā te visajjetvā, sayito puna cintayi.

Thus addressed by them, the great king was comforted. Having paid homage to them and dismissed them, he lay down and reflected once more.

113.

113.

Vinā saṅghena āhāraṃ, mābhuñjetha kadācipi”;

Iti mātāpitā’hāre, sapiṃsu dahare’ vano.

‘Never eat food without the Saṅgha.’ Thus his parents had instructed the young one concerning food.

114.

114.

Adatvā bhikkhusaṅghassa, bhuttaṃ atthi nukho iti;

Addasa pātarāsamhi, ekaṃ maricavaṭṭikaṃ.

He reflected, 'Is there anything I have eaten without giving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?' He recalled a single chili-pod at his morning meal.

115.

115.

Saṅghassa aṭṭhapetvāva paribhuttaṃ satiṃ vinā;

Tadatthaṃ daṇḍakammaṃ me, kattabbanti ca cintayi.

It had been consumed without mindfulness and without having been set aside for the Saṅgha. And he thought, 'For that, a penalty should be undertaken by me.'

116.

116.

Ete tenekakoṭi idha manujagaṇe ghātite cintayitvā,

Kāmānaṃ hetu etaṃ manasi ca kayirā sādhu ādīnavaṃ taṃ;

Sabbesaṃ ghātaniṃ taṃ manasi ca kayirā’ niccataṃ sādhu sādhu,

Evaṃ dukkhā pamokkhaṃ subhagati mahavā pāpuṇeyyā’cīrenāti.

Having reflected that here many crores of the human multitude were slain, let one well consider in the mind the danger of this, which is for the sake of sensual pleasures; and let one consider well in the mind that this is the slayer of all, and its impermanence. Thus may the great one quickly attain liberation from suffering and a good destiny.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Great Chronicle, composed for the serene faith and spiritual urgency of the virtuous.

Duṭṭhagāmaṇivijayo nāma

The Victory of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi

Pañcavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-fifth Chapter.

Chabbīsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-sixth Chapter

Maricavaṭṭikavihāramaho

The Great Festival of the Maricavaṭṭika Monastery

1.

1.

Ekacchattaṃ [M 0.0152] karitvāna, laṃkārajjaṃ mahāyaso;

Nānantaraṃ saṃvidahi, yodhānaṃ so yathārahaṃ.

Having brought the kingdom of Laṅkā under one umbrella, the greatly renowned one immediately thereafter made arrangements for the warriors as was fitting.

2.

2.

Theraputtābhayo yodho, diyyamānaṃ na icchitaṃ;

Pucchitova kimatthanti, yuddhamatthīti abravi.

The warrior Theraputtābhaya did not desire what was being given. When asked, 'For what purpose?', he replied, 'There is a battle.'

3.

3.

Ekarajje kate yuddhaṃ, kināmattīti pucchito;

Yuddhaṃ kilesa corehi, karissāmi sudujjayaṃ.

When asked, 'Now that the kingdom is made one, what battle is there?', he replied, 'I shall wage the battle with the thieves that are the defilements, a battle most difficult to win.'

4.

4.

Icceva māha taṃ rājā, punappunaṃ nisedhayi;

Punappunaṃ soyācitvā, raññonuññāya pabbaji.

Thus the king spoke to him and again and again forbade him; but he entreated again and again, and with the king's consent, he went forth into homelessness.

5.

5.

Pabbajitvā ca kālena, arahattamapāpuṇi;

Pañcakhīṇāsavasata-parivāerā ahosi ca.

Having gone forth, in due time he attained Arahantship; and he had a retinue of five hundred Arahants whose cankers were destroyed.

6.

6.

Chattamaṅgala sattāhe, gate gatabhayo’ bhayo;

Rājā katā bhisekova, mahatā vibhavena so.

When the seven days of the Umbrella Festival had passed, the king, his fear departed, became fearless; as if consecrated, he reigned with great magnificence.

7.

7.

Tissavāpi’magā kīḷa-vidhinā samalaṅka taṃ;

Kīḷituṃ abhisittānaṃ, cārittañcā nurakkhituṃ.

He went to the Tissavāpi, which he had adorned with festive arrangements, for the consecrated to engage in sport and to uphold the tradition.

8.

8.

Rañño paricchadaṃ sabbaṃ, upāyanasatāni ca;

Maricavaṭṭivihārassa, ṭhānamhi ṭhapayiṃsu ca.

All the king's regalia, and hundreds of offerings, they placed on the site of the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery.

9.

9.

Tattheva thūpaṭhānamhi, sadhātuṃ kuntamuttamaṃ;

Ṭhapesuṃ kuntadharakā, ujukaṃ rājamānusā.

There, at the very site of the stupa, the royal men, the spear-bearers, erected the excellent relic-bearing spear upright.

10.

10.

Sahorodho mahārājā, kīḷitvā salile divā;

Sāyamāhaṃ gamissāma, kuntaṃ vaḍḍhetha bho”iti.

The great king with his harem, having played in the water by day, said in the evening: 'We shall go; sirs, take up the spear!'

11.

11.

Cāletuṃ taṃ na sakkhiṃsu, kuntaṃ rājādhikārikā;

Gandhāmālāhi pūjesuṃ, rājasenāsamāgatā.

The royal officers could not move the spear; the royal army, having assembled, honored it with perfumes and garlands.

12.

12.

Rājā [M 0.0153] mahantaṃ accheraṃ, disvā taṃ haṭṭhamānaso;

Vidhāya tattha ārakkhaṃ, pavisitvā puraṃ tato.

The king, seeing that great marvel, with a joyful mind, arranged for a guard to be placed there, and then entered the city.

13.

13.

Kuntaṃ parikkhipāpetvā, cetiyaṃ tattha kārayi;

Thūpaṃ parikkhipāpetvā, vihārañca akārayi.

Having had the spear encircled, he had a cetiya built there; having had the stupa encircled, he also had a monastery constructed.

14.

14.

Tīhi vassehi niṭhāsi, vihāro so narissaro;

Saṅghaṃ sasannipātesi, viharamahākāraṇā.

In three years that monastery was completed. The ruler of men then assembled the Saṅgha for the great festival of the monastery.

15.

15.

Bhikkhunaṃ satasahassāni, tadā bhikkhuniyo pana;

Navuti ca sahassāni, abhaviṃsu samāgatā.

One hundred thousand bhikkhus and ninety thousand bhikkhunīs were gathered there at that time.

16.

16.

Tasmiṃ samāgame saṅghaṃ, idamāka mahīpati;

“Saṅghaṃ bhante visaritvā, bhuñjiṃ maricavaṭṭikaṃ.

At that gathering, the king addressed the Saṅgha thus: 'Venerable sirs, having forgotten the Saṅgha, I ate a pepper pod.'

17.

17.

Hasse’taṃ daṇḍakammaṃ me, bhavatūti akārayi;

Sacetiyaṃ maricavaṭṭi-vihāraṃ sumanoharaṃ.

He had this most delightful Maricavaṭṭi monastery with its cetiya built, saying, 'Let this be the penance for my fault.'

18.

18.

Patiggaṇhātu taṃ saṅgho, iti so dakkhiṇodakaṃ;

Pātitvā bhikkhusaṅghassa, vihāraṃ sumano adā.

Saying, 'May the Saṅgha accept it!', he poured the water of dedication and, with a joyful mind, gave the monastery to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

19.

19.

Vihāre taṃ samantāpi, mahantaṃ maṇḍapaṃ subhaṃ;

Kāretvā tattha saṅghassa, mahādānaṃ pavattayi.

All around that monastery, he had a great and beautiful pavilion constructed, and there he initiated a great offering to the Saṅgha.

20.

20.

Pāde patiṭṭhāpetvāpi,

Jale abhayavāpiyā;

Kato so maṇḍapo āsi,

Seso kāse kathāvakā.

That pavilion was so made that its posts were established even in the water of the Abhayavāpi; what need be said of the part on dry land?

21.

21.

Sattāhaṃ annapānādiṃ, datvāna manujādhipo;

Adā sāmaṇakaṃ sabbaṃ, parikkhāraṃ mahārahaṃ.

For seven days, the lord of men, having given food, drink, and so forth, gave all the monastic requisites, of great value.

22.

22.

Ahu satasahassaggho, parikkhāro sa ādiko;

Ante sahassagghanako, sabba saṅgho ca taṃlabhi.

The first set of requisites was worth a hundred thousand, and the last was worth a thousand; the entire Saṅgha received them.

23.

23.

Yuddhe dāne ca sūrena, sūrinā ratanattaye;

Pasannāmalacittena, sāsanujota natthinā.

By him who was a hero in battle and in giving, wise concerning the Triple Gem, with a mind clear and pure, and who desired to illuminate the Dispensation.

24.

24.

Raññā [M 0.0154] kataññunā tena, thūpakārāpanādito;

Vihāra mahanantāni, pūjetuṃ ratanattayaṃ.

By that grateful king, beginning with the building of stupas, great and endless monasteries were made to honor the Triple Gem.

25.

25.

Pariccattadhanāne’ttha, anagghāni vimuñciya;

Sesāni honti ekāya, ūnavīsatikoṭiyo.

Here, leaving aside the priceless wealth that was given, the remainder amounted to nineteen crores.

26.

26.

Togā dasaddhavidha dosavidūsitāpi,

Paññāvisesa sahitehi janehi pattā;

Honteva pañcaguṇayoga gahitasāraṃ,

Iccassa sāragahaṇe matimāyateyyāti.

Though this work may have various faults, its essence is grasped by those endowed with special wisdom; therefore, one should apply the mind to grasping this essence.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Great Chronicle, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of the good.

Maricavaṭṭikavihāramahonāma

The Great Maricavaṭṭika Monastery.

Chabbīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-sixth Chapter.

Sattavīsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-seventh Chapter.

Lohapāsādamaho

The Great Brazen Palace.

1.

1.

Tato rājā vicintesi, vissutaṃ sussutaṃ sutaṃ;

Mahāpañño sadā puñño, paññāya katanicchayo.

Then the king reflected, he of great wisdom, ever meritorious, whose decisions are made by wisdom: 'Famed, having heard well, and learned.'

2.

2.

“Dīpappasādako thero, rājino ayyakassa me;

Evaṃ kirāhanattā te, duṭṭhagāmaṇibhūpati.

The elder who brought faith to the island thus indeed said to my royal ancestor: 'O grandson, you, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī...'

3.

3.

Mahāpuñño mahāthūpaṃ, soṇṇamāliṃ manoramaṃ;

Vīsaṃhatthasataṃ uccaṃ, kāressati anāgate.

The greatly meritorious one will, in the future, cause a great stupa to be built, the delightful Soṇṇamāli, one hundred and twenty cubits high.

4.

4.

Puno uposathāgāraṃ, nānāratanamaṇḍitaṃ;

Navabhūmaṃ karitvāna, lohapāsāda meva ca.

Furthermore, having made a nine-storied Uposatha hall adorned with various jewels, which is the Lohapāsāda itself.

5.

5.

Iti cintiya bhūmindo, likhitvevaṃ ṭhapāpitaṃ;

Pekkhāpento rājagehe, ṭhitaṃ eva karaṇḍake.

Thus reflecting, the lord of the earth had this written down and so placed; he had it displayed in the royal house, where it remained within a casket.

6.

6.

Sovaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ laddhāna, lekhaṃ tattha avācayi;

“Cattālīsasataṃ vassaṃ, atikkamma anāgate.

Having obtained the golden plaque, he read the inscription there: 'One hundred and forty years having passed, in the future...'

7.

7.

Kākavaṇṇasuto [M 0.0155] duṭṭha-gāmaṇimanujādhipo;

Idañcidañca evañca, kāressatī”ti vācitaṃ.

'Kākavaṇṇa's son, the lord of men Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, will cause this and that to be done in such a way'—thus it was read.

8.

8.

Sutvā haṭṭho udānetvā, appoṭṭhesi mahīpati;

Tato pāto’va gantvāna, mahāmeghavanaṃ subhaṃ.

Hearing this, the delighted king uttered a cry of joy and clapped his hands; then, at dawn, he went to the beautiful Mahāmegha Grove.

9.

9.

Sannipātaṃ kārayitvā, bhikkhusaṅghassa abravi;

“Vimānatulyaṃ pāsādaṃ, kārayissāmi vo ahaṃ.

Having convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he said: 'I shall have a palace built for you, like a celestial mansion.'

10.

10.

Dibbaṃ vimānaṃ pesetvā, tadā lekhaṃ adātha me”;

Bhikkhusaṅgho visajjesi, aṭṭha khīṇāsave tahiṃ.

'Send for a model of a celestial mansion and then give me the plan.' The Saṅgha of bhikkhus thereupon dispatched eight Arahants.

11.

11.

Kassapamunino kāle, asoko nāma brāhmaṇo;

Aṭṭha salākabhattāni, saṅghassa pariṇāmiya.

In the time of the sage Kassapa, a brahmin named Asoka, having dedicated eight ticket-portions of food to the Saṅgha,

12.

12.

Bharaṇiṃ nāma dāsiṃ so, “niccaṃ dehī”ti abravi;

Datvā sā tāni sakkaccaṃ, yāvajīvaṃ tato cutā.

told a slave woman named Bharaṇī, 'Give these always.' She, having given them faithfully throughout her life, passed away from that existence.

13.

13.

Ākāsaṭṭhavimānamhi, nibbattirucire subhe;

Accharānaṃ sahassena, sadā’si parivāritā.

She was reborn in a beautiful, delightful celestial mansion standing in the sky; she was always surrounded by a thousand nymphs.

14.

14.

Tassā ratanapāsādo, dvādasayojanuggato;

Yojanānaṃ parikkhepo, cattālīsañca aṭṭha ca.

Her jeweled palace was twelve yojanas in height, and its circumference was forty-eight yojanas.

15.

15.

Kūṭāgārasahassena, maṇḍito navabhūmiko;

Sahassagabbhasampanno, rājamāno catummukho.

It was nine-storied, adorned with a thousand peaked chambers, endowed with a thousand rooms, resplendent, and with four facades.

16.

16.

Sahassasaṅkhasaṃvutti, sīhapañjara nettavā;

Sakiṅkaṇikajālāya, sajjito vedikāya ca.

With a thousand conch-shell ornaments, having lion-windows and lattices, fitted with nets of small bells, and adorned with a railing.

17.

17.

Ambalaṭṭhikapāsādo, tassa majjhe ṭhito ahu;

Santamato dissamāno, paggahitadhajākulo.

In its midst stood the Ambalaṭṭhika Palace; though crowded with raised banners, it appeared peaceful.

18.

18.

Tāvatiṃsañca gacchantā, disvā theraṃ tameva te;

Hiṅgulena tadā lekhaṃ, lekhayitvā paṭe tato.

They, going to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and seeing that palace, then had a drawing made with vermilion upon a cloth.

19.

19.

Nivattitvāna āgantvā, paṭaṃ saṅghassa dassayuṃ;

Saṅgho paṭaṃ gahetvā taṃ, pāhesi rājasantikaṃ.

Returning, they came and showed the cloth to the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha, taking that cloth, sent it to the king's presence.

20.

20.

Taṃ [M 0.0156] disvā sumano rājā, āgammārāma muttamaṃ;

Ālekhatulyaṃ kāresi, lohapāsāda muttamaṃ.

Seeing it, the joyful king went to the excellent monastery and had the magnificent Lohapāsāda built according to the drawing.

21.

21.

Kammārambhanakāleva, catudvāramhi bhogavā;

Aṭṭhasatasahassāni, hiraññāni ṭhapāpayi.

At the very start of the work, the wealthy one had eight hundred thousand pieces of gold placed at the four gates.

22.

22.

Puṭasahassa vatthāni, dvāre dvāre ṭhapāpayi;

Guḷa telasakkharamadhu-purā cāneka cāṭiyo.

He had a thousand bundles of cloth placed at each gate, and many jars filled with molasses, oil, sugar, and honey.

23.

23.

“Amūlakakamma mettha, na kātabba”nti bhāsiya;

Agghāpetvā kataṃ kammaṃ, tesaṃ mūlamadāpayi.

Having declared, 'No unpaid work is to be done here,' he had the completed work valued and caused their wages to be paid.

24.

24.

Hatthasataṃ hatthasataṃ, āsi ekeka passato;

Uccato tattakoyeva, pāsādo hi catummukho.

Each side of the four-faced palace was one hundred cubits, and it was of exactly the same height.

25.

25.

Tasmiṃ pāsāda seṭṭhasmiṃ, ahesuṃ navabhūmiyo;

Ekekissā bhūmiyā ca, kūṭāgārasatāni ca.

In that supreme palace, there were nine stories; and on each story, there were one hundred peaked chambers.

26.

26.

Kūṭāgārāni sabbāni, sajjhunā khacitā na’yuṃ;

Pavālavedikā tesaṃ, nānāratana bhūsitā.

All the peaked-roof chambers were inlaid with silver; their railings of coral were adorned with various jewels.

27.

27.

Nānāratana cittāni, tāsaṃ padumakāni ca;

Sajjhakiṃkiṇikāpanti-parikkhittāva tā ahu.

Their lotus ornaments were adorned with various jewels, and they were indeed surrounded by rows of silver tinkling bells.

28.

28.

Sahassaṃ tattha pāsādo, gabbhā āsuṃ susaṅkhatā;

Nānāratana khacitā, sīhapañjaranettavā.

A thousand mansions were there, their inner chambers well-arranged, inlaid with various jewels, and having windows like lions' cages.

29.

29.

Nārivāhanayānantu, sutvā vessavaṇassa so;

Tadā kāramakāresi, majjhe ratanamaṇḍapaṃ.

Having heard of the celestial vehicle of Vessavaṇa borne by women, he then had a jeweled pavilion built in the middle.

30.

30.

Sīhabyagghādirūpehi, devatā rūpakehi ca;

Ahu ratanamayohe’sa, thambhehi ca vibhūsito.

With figures of lions, tigers, and other such beasts, and with images of deities, it was made of jewels and adorned with pillars.

31.

31.

Muttājālaparikkhepo, maṇḍapante samantato;

Pavālavedikā cettha, pubbe vuttavidhā ahu.

All around the edge of the pavilion was a surrounding net of pearls; and here the coral railing was of the kind previously described.

32.

32.

Sattaratana cittassa, vemajjhe maṇḍapassa tu;

Ruciro dantapallaṅko, rammo phalikasantharo.

In the very middle of the pavilion, which was adorned with the seven kinds of jewels, was a splendid ivory couch, delightful with a crystal covering.

33.

33.

Dantamayāpassaye’ttha, suvaṇṇamaya sūriyo;

Sajjhumaye candimā ca, tārā ca muttakā mayā.

Here were supports of ivory, a sun of gold, a moon of silver, and stars made of pearls.

34.

34.

Nānāratana [M 0.0157] padumāni, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ;

Jātakāni ca tattheva, āsuṃ soṇṇalatantare.

Lotuses of various jewels were there, each in its appropriate place; and depictions of the Jātakas were also there, amidst a network of golden creepers.

35.

35.

Mahagghapaccattharaṇe, pallaṅke’ti manorame;

Manoharā’siṭṭhapitā, ruciraṃ dantabījanī.

Upon a costly covering on that delightful couch, a charming ivory fan was beautifully placed.

36.

36.

Pavālapādukā tattha, phalikamhi patiṭṭhitā;

Setacchattaṃ sajjhudaṇḍaṃ, pallaṅko’parisobhatha.

There, coral sandals were placed on crystal; a white parasol with a silver handle adorned the couch from above.

37.

37.

Sattaratana mayānettha, aṭṭhamaṅgalikāni ca;

Catuppadānaṃ pantī ca, maṇimuttantarā ahuṃ.

Here were the eight auspicious symbols made of the seven kinds of jewels; and there were rows of four-footed animals interspersed with gems and pearls.

38.

38.

Rajatānañca ghaṇṭānaṃ, pantī bhattantalambitā;

Pāsādachattapallaṅka-maṇḍapā’suṃ anagghikā.

A row of silver bells hung from the cornice; the palace, parasol, couch, and pavilion were priceless.

39.

39.

Mahaggha paññapāpesi, mañcapīṭhaṃ yathārahaṃ;

Tatheva bhūmattharaṇaṃ, kambalañca mahārahaṃ.

He had costly couches and chairs prepared, each in its proper place, and likewise exquisite floor coverings and valuable woolen blankets.

40.

40.

Ācāma kumbhisovaṇṇā, uluṅko ca ahu tahiṃ;

Pāsāda paribhogesu, sesesu ca kathā’ vakā.

Golden water pots for rinsing and a ladle were there; as for the remaining furnishings of the palace, what more is there to say?

41.

41.

Cārupākāra parivāro,

So catudvārakoṭṭhako;

Pāsādo’laṅkato sobhi,

Tāvatiṃsa sabhā viya.

Surrounded by a beautiful wall, with four gate-towers, the adorned palace shone like the assembly hall of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

42.

42.

Tamba lohiṭṭhakāhe’so,

Pāsādo chādito ahu;

Loha pāsāda vohāro,

Tena tassa ajāyatha.

This palace was roofed with tiles of copper, and for that reason the name 'Lohapāsāda' (Brazen Palace) arose for it.

43.

43.

Naṭṭhite lohapāsāde, so saṅghaṃ sannipātayi;

Rājā saṅgho sannipati, maricavaṭṭimahe viya.

When the Lohapāsāda was completed, he gathered the Sangha. The king and the Sangha assembled as at the festival for the Maricavaṭṭi Cetiya.

44.

44.

Puthujjanā’va aṭṭhaṃsu, bhikkhū paṭhamabhūmiyaṃ;

Tepiṭakā dutiyāya, sotāpannādayo pana.

The ordinary bhikkhus stood on the first floor, those versed in the Tipiṭaka on the second, and next the stream-enterers and others.

45.

45.

Eke [M 0.0158] keyeva aṭṭhaṃsu, tatiyādīsu bhūmisu;

Arahanto ca aṭṭhaṃsu, uddhaṃ catūsu bhūmisu.

They stood on the third and subsequent floors, while the Arahants stood on the upper four floors.

46.

46.

Saṅghassa datvā pāsādaṃ, dakkhiṇambupurassaraṃ;

Rājā’dattha mahādānaṃ, sattāhaṃ pubbakaṃ piya.

Having given the palace to the Sangha, preceded by the water of dedication, the king gave a great donation for seven days, rejoicing in this meritorious deed.

47.

47.

Pāsāda mahacattāni, mahācāgena rājinā;

Anagghāni ṭhapetvāna, ahesuṃ tiṃsakoṭiyo.

The great expenditure for the palace by the king of great generosity, setting aside the priceless items, amounted to thirty crores.

48.

48.

Nissāre dhananicaye visesasāraṃ,

Ye dānaṃ parigaṇayanti sādhupaññā;

Te dānaṃ vipulamapeta cittasaṅgā,

Sattānaṃ hitaparamā dadanti evaṃti.

Those of good wisdom, who discern that giving is the special essence in the worthless accumulation of wealth, give a vast gift, their minds free from attachment, for the supreme welfare of beings.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the faith and spiritual urgency of good people.

Lokahapāsādamaho nāma

The chapter named 'The Great Work of the Lohapāsāda'.

Sattavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-seventh Chapter.

Aṭṭhavīsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-eighth Chapter.

Mahā thūpasādhana lābho

The Acquisition of Materials for the Great Stupa.

1.

1.

Tato satasahassaṃ so, vissajjetvā mahīpati;

Kārāpesi mahābodhi-pūjaṃ suḷāramuttamaṃ.

Then that lord of the earth, having spent a hundred thousand, caused a magnificent and supreme worship of the Great Bodhi to be performed.

2.

2.

Tato puraṃ pavisinto, thūpaṭhāne nivesitaṃ;

Passitvāna sīlāyūpaṃ, saritvā pubbakaṃ sutiṃ.

Then, upon entering the city, having seen the stone pillar established at the site of the stupa, he remembered the ancient tradition.

3.

3.

“Kāressāmi mahāthūpaṃ”, iti haṭṭho mahātalaṃ;

Āruyha rattiṃ bhuñjitvā, sayito iti cintayi.

“I will have a great stupa built,” thus elated, he ascended to the upper palace; having eaten at night, he lay down and thought thus.

4.

4.

“Damiḷe [M 0.0159] maddamānena, loko’yaṃ pīḷito mayā;

Na sakkā balimuddhattuṃ, taṃ vajjiya baliṃ ahaṃ.

“By crushing the Damiḷas, this populace was oppressed by me. It is not possible to levy tribute; therefore, avoiding that tribute, I shall...

5.

5.

Kārayanto mahāthūpaṃ, kataṃ dhammena iṭṭhikā;

Uppādessāmi “iccevaṃ, cintayantassa cintitaṃ.

...while having the great stupa built, produce bricks made righteously.” Thus was the thought of him who was thinking.

6.

6.

Chattamhi devatājānī, tato kolāhalaṃ ahu;

Devesu ñatvā taṃ sakko, vissakammāna mabravi.

The deity in the parasol knew, and from that a commotion arose. Sakka, having learned of this among the gods, spoke to Vissakamma.

7.

7.

“Iṭṭhakattaṃ cetiyassa, rājā cintesi gāmaṇi;

Gantvā purā yojanamhi, gambhīra nadī yantike.

“King Gāmaṇi has thought of the brickwork for the cetiya. Go to a place one league from the city, near a deep river.

8.

8.

Māpehi iṭṭhikā tattaṃ’, iti sakke na bhāsito;

Vissakammo idhāgamma, māpesi tattha iṭṭhikā.

‘Create bricks there.’ Thus spoken by Sakka, Vissakamma came here and created bricks in that place.

9.

9.

Pabhāte luddako tattha, sunakhehi vanaṃ agā;

Vodhārūpena dassesi, luddakaṃ bhummadevatā.

At dawn, a hunter went there into the forest with his dogs; an earth-deity showed herself to the hunter in the form of a monitor lizard.

10.

10.

Luddako taṃ’nubandhanto, gantvā disvāna iṭṭhakā;

Antarahitāya godhāya, iti cidhantasi so tahiṃ.

The hunter, following it, went and saw the bricks; when the monitor lizard had disappeared, he thought thus at that place.

11.

11.

“Kāretu kāmo kira no, mahāthūpaṃ mahīpati;

Upāyanamidaṃ tassaṃ’, iti gantvā nivedayi.

“It seems our king desires to have a great stupa built; this is a gift for him.” Thus thinking, he went and informed the king.

12.

12.

Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, piyaṃ janahi tappiyo;

Rājā kāresi sakkāraṃ, mahantaṃ tuṭṭhamānaso.

Hearing his words, which were pleasing and dear, the king, with a joyful heart, bestowed upon him a great honor.

13.

13.

Purāpubbuttare dese, yojanattaya matthake;

Ācāra viṭṭhigāmamhi, soḷasakarīse kale.

In the northeastern region of the city, at a distance of three leagues, in the village of Ācāraviṭṭhi, in a field of sixteen karīsas,

14.

14.

Sovaṇṇa bījānu’ṭṭhiṃsu, vividhāni pamāṇato;

Vidatthukkaṭṭha māṇāni, aṅgulimāṇā niheṭhato.

golden nuggets of various sizes arose: the largest measured a span, and the smallest a finger-breadth.

15.

15.

Suvaṇṇa puṇṇaṃ taṃ bhūmiṃ, disvā saṅgāmavāsikā;

Suvaṇṇa pāhiṃ ādāya, gantvā rañño nivedayuṃ.

Seeing that land filled with gold, the villagers, taking a bowl of gold, went and informed the king.

16.

16.

Purāpācina passamhi, satta yojana matthake;

Gaṅgāpāre tambapiṭṭhe, tambalohaṃ samuṭṭhahi.

In the eastern region of the city, at a distance of seven leagues, beyond the river in Tambapiṭṭha, copper arose.

17.

17.

Taṅgāmikā tambaloha-bījamādāya pātiyā;

Rājāna mupasaṅkamma, tamatthañca nivedayuṃ.

The villagers of that place, taking nuggets of copper in a bowl, approached the king and informed him of the matter.

18.

18.

Pubbadakkhiṇadesamhi, purato catuyojane;

Sumana vāpi gāmamhi, uṭṭhahiṃsu maṇībahū.

In the southeastern region, four leagues from the city, in the village of Sumanavāpi, many jewels arose.

19.

19.

Upala [M 0.0160] kuruvindehi, missakāneva gāmikā;

Ādāya pātiyāeva, gantvā rañño nivedayuṃ.

The villagers, finding them mixed with sapphires and rubies, taking them in a bowl, went and informed the king.

20.

20.

Purato dakkhiṇe passe, aṭṭhayojanamatthake;

Ambaṭṭha kolaleṇamhi, rajataṃ upapajjatha.

In the southern region, eight leagues from the city, in the Ambaṭṭhakola cave, silver appeared.

21.

21.

Nagare vāṇijo eko, ādāya sakaṭe bahū;

Malayā siṅgīverādiṃ, ānetuṃ malayaṃ gato.

A certain merchant in the city, taking many carts, went to Malaya to bring back ginger and other such goods from there.

22.

22.

Leṇassa avidūramhi, sakaṭāniṭṭha pāpiya;

Patodādārunicchanto, āruḷho taṃ mahīdharaṃ.

Not far from the cave, having caused the carts to be stopped, and desiring wood for a goad, he climbed that mountain.

23.

23.

Cāṭippamāṇa taṃ tattha, pakkabhārena nāmi taṃ;

Disvā pana salaṭṭhiñca, pāsāṇaṭṭhañca taṃ phalaṃ.

There he saw on a sala tree a fruit the size of a water pot, bent down by its ripe weight and resting on a rock.

24.

24.

Vaṇṭe taṃ vāsiyā chetvā, dassāma’gganti cintiya;

Kālaṃ ghosesi saddhāya, cattāro’nāsavāgamuṃ.

Having cut it at the stem with an adze, and thinking, ‘I will give the first portion,’ with faith he announced the time for a meal. Four Arahants, free from cankers, arrived.

25.

25.

Haṭṭho so te’bhivādetvā, nisīdāpiya sādaro;

Vāsiyā vaṇṭasāmantā, tacaṃ chetvā apassayaṃ.

Delighted, he paid homage to them and respectfully had them take a seat. With the adze, he cut the skin around the stem and looked inside.

26.

26.

Muñjitvā’vāṭa puṇṇaṃ taṃ, yūsaṃ pattehī ādiya;

Cattāro yūsa pūrete, patte tesamadāsiso.

Having opened the full hollow, he took the juice in their bowls; he gave to them the four bowls filled with juice.

27.

27.

Te taṃ gahetvā pakkāmuṃ,

Kālaṃ ghosesi so puna;

Aññe khiṇāsavā therā,

Cattāro tattha āgamuṃ.

They took it and departed. He again announced the time. Four other elders, who had destroyed the cankers, arrived there.

28.

28.

Tesaṃ patte gahetvā so, pattāmiñjahi pūriya;

Adāsi tesaṃ pakkāmuṃ, tayo eko napakkami.

Taking their bowls, he filled them with the pulp and gave it to them. Three departed, but one did not depart.

29.

29.

Rajataṃ tassa dassetuṃ, orohitvā tato hi so;

Nisajja leṇāsannamhi, tāmiñjā paribhuñjatha.

In order to show him the silver, that elder descended from there. Sitting near the cave, he partook of the pulp.

30.

30.

Sesāmiñjā vāṇijo’pi, bhuñjitvā yāvadatthakaṃ;

Bhaṇḍikāya gahetvāna, sesatherapadānugo.

The merchant also, having eaten the remaining pulp to his satisfaction, took his bundle and followed in the footsteps of the remaining elder.

31.

31.

Añjasā [M 0.0161] iminā tvampi, gaccha dānī upāsaka;

Gantvāna theraṃ passitvā, veyyāvacca mahāsi ca.

“Lay devotee, you too go now by this direct path. Having gone and seen the elder, you shall render him great service.”

32.

32.

Thero ca leṇadvārena, tassa magga amāpayi;

Theraṃ vandiya so tena, gacchanto leṇamaddasa.

And the elder, at the cave entrance, created a path for him. Having paid homage to the elder, he went along that path and saw the cave.

33.

33.

Leṇa dvāramhi ṭhatvāna, passitvā rajatampi so;

Vāsiyā āhanitvāna, rajatati vijāniya.

Standing at the entrance of the cave, he saw silver; and having struck it with an adze, he recognized it as silver.

34.

34.

Gahetvekaṃ sajjhupiṇḍaṃ, gantvāna sakaṭantikaṃ;

Sakaṭāni ṭhapāpetvā, sajjhupiṇḍaṃ tamādiya.

Having taken a single lump of silver, he went to the carts; and having caused the carts to be stopped, he took that lump of silver.

35.

35.

Lahuṃ anurādha puraṃ, āgamma varavāṇijo;

Dassetvā rajataṃ rañño, tamatthampi nivedayi.

Swiftly reaching Anurādhapura, the excellent merchant, having presented the silver to the king, informed him of the matter.

36.

36.

Purato pacchime passe, pañcayojana matthake;

Uruvelapaṭṭane muttā, mahāmalaka mattiyo.

In front, on the western side, at a distance of five yojanas, in the port of Uruvela, pearls the size of large myrobalan fruits appeared.

37.

37.

Pavālantarikā saddhiṃ, samuddāthalamokkamuṃ;

Kevaṭṭā tā samekkhitvā, rāsiṃ katvāna ekato.

Interspersed with coral, they came up to the sea-shore. The fishermen, having seen them, made them into one heap.

38.

38.

Pātiyā ānayitvāna, muttā saha pavālakā;

Rājāna mupasaṅkamma, tamatthampi nivedayuṃ.

Having brought the pearls together with the coral in a bowl, they approached the king and informed him of the matter.

39.

39.

Purato uttare passe, satta yojana matthake;

Peḷivāpika gāmassa, vāpipakkhantakandare.

In front, on the northern side, at a distance of seven yojanas, in a cave on the bank of the reservoir of the village of Peḷivāpika.

40.

40.

Jāyiṃsu vālukāpiṭṭhe, cattāro uttamā maṇī;

Nīsada potappamāṇā, ummāpupphanibhāsubhā.

On the sandy surface arose four excellent gems, the size of a small grindstone, lovely and radiant as ummā flowers.

41.

41.

Te disvā sunakho luddo, agantvā rājasantikaṃ;

“Evarūpā maṇīdiṭṭho, mayā”iti nivedayi.

Having seen them, the hunter Sunakha came into the king's presence and reported thus: 'Gems of such a kind have been seen by me.'

42.

42.

Iṭṭhakādīni etāni mahāpuñño mahāmati;

Mahāthūpatthamuppannā-na’ssosi tadaheva so.

The one of great merit and great wisdom did not hear on that very day that these things, bricks and so forth, had arisen for the sake of the Great Stupa.

43.

43.

Yathānurūpaṃ sakkāraṃ, tesaṃ katvā sumānato;

Ete vā rakkhake katvā, sabbāni āharāpayi.

Having paid them due honor with a joyful mind, and having appointed these men as guards, he had all the treasures brought to him.

44.

44.

Khedampi [M 0.0162] kāyajamasayhamacintayitvā,

Puññaṃ pasannamanaso pacita hi evaṃ;

Sādheti sādhana satāni sukhā karāni,

Tasmā pasannamanaso’va kareyya puññanti.

Not considering even the unbearable weariness of the body, one with a serene mind thus accumulates merit. One accomplishes hundreds of means that bring happiness. Therefore, with a serene mind, one should indeed perform meritorious deeds.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people.

Mahāthūpasādhanalābho nāma

Named 'The Gaining of Materials for the Great Stupa'

Aṭṭhavīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Eighth Chapter.

Ekūnatiṃsatima pariccheda

The Twenty-Ninth Chapter.

Thūpārambho

The Commencement of the Stupa.

1.

1.

Evaṃ samatte sambhāre, vesākhapuṇṇamāsīyaṃ;

Patte visākhanakkhatte, mahāthūpatthamārabhi.

Thus, when the materials were complete, on the full-moon day of Vesākha, when the Visākha constellation had appeared, he began the work for the Great Stupa.

2.

2.

Hāretvāna tahiṃ thūpaṃ, thūpaṭhānamakhāṇayi;

Satthahattho mahīpālo, thirī kātuṃ manekadhā.

Having had the stupa that was there removed, the ruler excavated the stupa site to a depth of seven cubits in order to make it firm in many ways.

3.

3.

Yodhehi āharāpetvā, guḷapāsāṇake tahiṃ;

Kūṭehi āhanāpetvā, pāsāṇe cuṇṇite atha.

Having caused warriors to bring round stones there, and having caused them to be broken with hammers, the stones were then pulverized.

4.

4.

Cammavanaddha pādehi, mahāhatthīhi maddayi;

Bhūmiyā thirībhāvatthaṃ, atthānatthavicakkhaṇo.

For the sake of the earth's stability, the king, discerning what was advantageous and what was not, had the ground trampled by great elephants whose feet were bound in leather.

5.

5.

Ākāsa gaṅgāpatita-ṭṭhāne satatatintake;

Mattikā sukhumā tattha, samantā tiṃ sayojane.

In a place where the celestial Ganges had once fallen, which was perpetually moist, the clay there was fine, for thirty yojanas all around.

6.

6.

Navanīta mattikā’tesā, sukhumattā papuccati;

Khīṇāsavā sāmaṇerā, mattikā āharuṃ tato.

That clay is called 'butter-clay' on account of its fineness. The novices who were free from cankers brought the clay from there.

7.

7.

Mattikā attharāpesi, tattha pāsāṇakoṭṭime;

Iṭṭhakā attharāpesi, mattiko pariissaro.

The lord had clay spread there on the stone pavement; then he had bricks spread, and clay on top of them.

8.

8.

Tasso [M 0.0163] parikharasudhaṃ, kuruvindaṃ tatopari;

Tasso pariayojālaṃ, marumbantu tatoparaṃ.

On top of that, rough plaster; on top of that, kuruvinda stone; on top of that, an iron net; and after that, fine gravel.

9.

9.

Āhaṭaṃ sāmaṇerehi, himavantā sugandhakaṃ;

Santharāpesi bhūmindo, phaḷikantu tatopari.

The lord of the earth had a fragrant substance, brought by the novices from the Himālaya, spread out, and on top of that, a layer of crystal.

10.

10.

Sīlāyo santharāpesiccha phaḷikasantharo pari;

Sabbattha mattikākicce, navanītavhayā ahu.

On top of the crystal layer he had stone slabs spread. In all the work involving clay, the clay used was that called 'butter-clay'.

11.

11.

Niyyāsena kapiṭṭhassa, sannitena rasodake;

Aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ bahalaetā, lohapaṭṭaṃ sīlopari.

On top of the stone slab, an iron plate eight fingers thick was laid, cemented with the resin of the wood-apple tree mixed with mercury.

12.

12.

Manosilāyatilate-lasannitāya tato pari;

Sattaṅgulaṃ sajjupaṭṭaṃ, santharesi rathesabho.

On top of that, the lord of chariots spread a silver plate seven fingers thick, using a cement of red arsenic mixed with sesame oil.

13.

13.

Mahāthūpa patiṭṭhāna-ṭhāne evaṃ mahīpati;

Kāretvā parikammāni, vippasannena cetasā.

Thus, at the site for the foundation of the Great Stūpa, the great king, having had the preliminary work performed, with a perfectly serene mind,

14.

14.

Āsaḷhī sukkapakkhassa, divasamhi catuddase;

Kāretvā bhikkhusaṅghassa, sannipātamidaṃ vadi.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āsāḷhī, having convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he spoke thus.

15.

15.

Mahācetiya matthāya, bhadantāmaṅgaliṭṭhakaṃ;

Patiṭṭhāpessaṃ sve ettha, sabbo saṅgho sametuno.

For the sake of the Great Cetiya, venerable sirs, I shall establish the auspicious brick here tomorrow; may the entire Saṅgha assemble.

16.

16.

Buddha pūjā payogena, mahājanahītatthiko;

“Mahājano’ posathiko, gandhamālādigaṇhiya.

Desiring the welfare of the great multitude, by means of the performance of Buddha-worship, the great multitude, observing the Uposatha, having taken perfumes, garlands, and so forth,

17.

17.

Mahāthūpa patiṭṭhāna-ṭhānaṃ yātu suve”iti;

Cetiya ṭhāna bhūsāya, amacce ca niyojayi.

‘May they go to the site for the establishment of the Great Stūpa tomorrow!’ Thus, he appointed ministers for the adornment of the Cetiya site.

18.

18.

Āṇāpitā narindena, munino piyagāravā;

Anekehi pakārehi, te taṃ ṭhānamalaṅkaruṃ.

Commanded by the king, out of affection and respect for the Sage, they adorned that place in many ways.

19.

19.

Nagaraṃ sakalañceva, maggañceva idhāgataṃ;

Anekehi pakārehi, alaṅkārayi bhūpati.

The king adorned the entire city and the roads leading here in many ways.

20.

20.

Pabhāte ca catudvāre, nagarassa ṭhapāpayi;

Nahāpite nahāpake ca, appake ca bahūtathā.

And at dawn, at the four gates of the city, he had placed barbers and bath attendants, both few and many.

21.

21.

Vatthāni [M 0.0164] gandhamālā ca, annāni madhurāni ca;

Mahājanatthaṃ bhūmindo, mahājanahite rato.

Clothes, perfumes, garlands, and sweet foods for the sake of the great multitude; the ruler of the land, delighting in the welfare of the great multitude.

22.

22.

Paṭiyattāni etāni, sādiyitvā yathāruci;

Porājānapadāceva thūpaṭhānamupāgamuṃ.

Having enjoyed these prepared things according to their liking, the citizens and country-folk approached the site of the Stūpa.

23.

23.

Sumaṇḍitehi nekehi, ṭhānantara vidhānato;

Ārakkhito amaccehi, yathāṭhānaṃ mahīpati.

Guarded by many well-adorned ministers according to their various stations, the king was in his proper place.

24.

24.

Sumaṇḍitāhi nekāhi, devakaññūpamāhi ca;

Nāṭakīhi paribbuḷho, sumaṇḍita passādhito.

Surrounded by many beautifully adorned dancers, like unto celestial maidens, he was himself splendidly attired and well-equipped.

25.

25.

Cattālīsa sahassehi, narehi parivārito;

Nānā tūriya saṅghuṭṭho, devarāja vilāsavā.

Surrounded by forty thousand men, amidst the resounding of various musical instruments, he possessed the splendor of a king of gods.

26.

26.

Mahāthūpa patiṭṭhānaṃ, ṭhānāṭhāna vicakkhaṇo;

Aparaṇhe upāgañchi, nandayanto mahājanaṃ.

Discerning what was proper and improper for the establishment of the Great Stūpa, he arrived in the afternoon, delighting the great multitude.

27.

27.

Aṭṭhuttarasahassaṃ so, sāṭakāniṭṭhapāpiya;

Puṭabaddhāni majjhamhi, catupasse tato pana.

Having had one thousand and eight garments, bound in bundles, placed in the middle, he then had them placed on the four sides.

28.

28.

Vatthāni rāsīṃkāresi, anekāni mahīpati;

The lord of the earth had many kinds of cloth heaped up; and for auspicious purposes, he had honey, ghee, molasses, and so forth, placed there.

29.

Nānādesehipā’gañchuṃ, bahavo bhikkhavo idha;

Many bhikkhus came here from various countries; what need is there to speak of the Saṅgha residing on this island, regarding their coming here?

30.

30.

Thero’ sīti sahassāni, bhikkhū ādāya āgamā;

The great leader, Elder Indagutta, came from the vicinity of Rājagaha, leading eighty thousand bhikkhus.

31.

31.

Sahassāni’sipatanā, bhikkhūnaṃ dvādasā’diya;

The great elder Dhammasena came to the Cetiya site from Isipatana, leading twelve thousand bhikkhus.

32.

32.

33.

34.

34.

Kosambī ghositārāmā, theroru dhammarakkhito;

35.

36.

37.

38.

39.

40.

40.

41.

41.

42.

42.

Candagutto mahāthero, vanavāsapadesato;

43.

43.

Sūriyaguttomahāthero, kelāsamhā vihārato;

44.

44.

45.

45.

46.

47.

48.

49.

49.

having caused it to be held by a well-born, adorned, and exceedingly auspicious minister, [the king was] intent on the welfare of beings.

51.

52.

53.

“Evaṃ mahantaṃ thūpañca, ayaṃ rājā’rabhissati;

54.

55.

56.

57.

58.

60.

61.

62.

63.

64.

65.

66.

67.

68.

69.

70.

Knowing that the supreme achievement of the world's welfare is thus brought about by one like him, whose mind is serene towards the Triple Gem, and by people whose minds are liberated through generosity, one should take delight in cultivating the many virtues beginning with faith.

2.

3.

4.

5.

6.

7.

Khepayissāmi ekkā’haṃ, taṃ rājā paṭibāhayi;

8.

9.

“Udukkhale koṭṭayitvā, ahaṃ suppehi vaṭṭitaṃ;

10.

Iti vutto anuññāsi, tiṇādinetthano siyuṃ;

11.

11.

12.

13.

14.

15.

“Iṭṭhakā āhārāpessaṃ, apīḷento kathaṃ nare”;

16.

Having brought bricks to the four gates of the cetiya, they placed them night after night, a sufficient portion for each day.

17.

Taṃ sutvā sumanorājā, cetiye kammamārabhi;

Hearing this, the pleased king began the work on the cetiya. He made it known that no work should be done there without payment.

18.

Ekekasmiṃ duvārasmiṃ, ṭhapāpesi kahāpaṇe;

19.

20.

“Yathārucitaṃ gaṇhantu, kammaṃ katvā yathāruciṃ;

21.

22.

23.

24.

25.

26.

26.

Ekobalatthaṃ dassetuṃ, mattikā dāyakaṃ yatiṃ;

27.

28.

28.

29.

29.

Kelivāte janapade, piyaṅgallanivāsiko;

30.

30.

31.

31.

32.

32.

Rājā sutvāva’ taṃ āha, “ñātuṃ sakkā tamiṭṭhikaṃ”;

33.

33.

“Jānāsi taṃ tvaṃ theraṃti”,

“Do you know that elder?” he was asked. Being spoken to, he replied, “Yes.” To inform the elder, the king sent Balattha to him.

34.

34.

35.

36.

37.

38.

38.

39.

39.

40.

40.

Kulūpagassa [M 0.0171] therassa, gahitā me ime mayā;
