Then, greatly enraged, he sent them again and again. 'It would be good to see my friend and, after bathing in the Kāḷavāpi...'

93.

93.

Parissāmīti cintetvā, āha dūte sace mamaṃ;

Kāḷavāpiṃsamāpeti, sakkā ñātunti te gatā.

Thinking, 'I shall perish,' he told the messengers, 'If he has me brought to the Kāḷavāpi, it will be possible to know.' They went.

94.

94.

Rañño āhaṃsu rājāpi, tuṭṭhahaṭṭho dhanatthiko;

Pesesi dūte datvāna, rathaṃ jiṇṇena vājinā.

They told the king. The king, pleased and delighted and desiring wealth, sent messengers, having given them a chariot with an old horse.

95.

95.

Evaṃ gacchati bhūpāle, pājento rathiko rathaṃ;

Khādanto lājamassāpi, kiñci mattaṃ adāsi so.

As the king was thus going, the charioteer was driving the chariot. While eating parched grain, he also gave a small amount to the horse.

96.

96.

Taṃ khāditvā pasīditvā, tasmiṃ pāṇamadā tadā;

Moggallānassa taṃ kātuṃ, saṅgahaṃ dvāranāyakaṃ.

Having eaten that and being pleased, he then gave him life. That favor for Moggallāna was to be done by the gate-chief.

97.

97.

Evaṃ sampattiyo nāma, calā vijjullatopamā;

Tasmā tāsu pamajjeyya, ko hi nāma sacetano.

Thus, worldly success is fleeting, like a flash of lightning. Therefore, what person of sound mind would be heedless in regard to it?

98.

98.

Rājā etītisutvāna, thero so tassa soha do;

Laddhā māsodanaṃ maṃsaṃ, sāṇuṇañca varaṃ saraṃ.

Hearing, 'The king is coming,' that elder, who was his friend, having received rice with beans and meat, and excellent spiced liquor,

99.

99.

Rājā roceti etanti, gopayitvā upāvisi;

Gantvā rājāpi vanditvā, ekamantamupāvisī.

Thinking, 'The king will like this,' he kept it safe and sat down. The king also, having approached and paid homage, sat down to one side.

100.

100.

Evaṃ nisinnā sampatta-rajjā viya ubhopi te;

Aññamaññā’bhilāpena, nibbāpesuṃ mahādaraṃ.

Thus seated, they both were like those who had attained a kingdom. With mutual conversation, they extinguished their great sorrow.

101.

101.

Bhojayitvāna taṃ thero, ovaditvā anekadhā;

Appamāde niyojesi, dassetvā lokadhammataṃ.

Having fed him, the elder advised him in many ways, and showing him the nature of worldly conditions, urged him to be diligent.

102.

102.

Tato [M 0.0253] vāpī mupagamma, oggayhitvā yathā sukhaṃ;

Nhayitvā pivitvā ca, āhevaṃ rājasevake.

Then, approaching the reservoir, plunging in as he pleased, and having bathed and drunk, he spoke thus to the king’s servants:

103.

103.

Ettakaṃ me dhanaṃ bho’ti, sutvā taṃ rājasevakā;

Āparitvā puraṃrañño, nivedesuṃ nirissaro.

'Sirs, this much is my wealth.' Hearing this, the king’s servants returned to the city and reported to the lordless king.

104.

104.

Dhanaṃ rakkhati puttassa, dīpe bhindati mānuse;

Jīvanto’yaṃtī kujjhitvā, āṇāpesi camūpatiṃ.

'He protects the wealth for his son; he creates division among the people of the island! As long as this man lives...' Thinking thus, he became enraged and ordered the army commander:

105.

105.

Mārehi pitaraṃ meti, diṭṭhā piṭṭhīti verino;

Haṭṭhatuṭṭho tiruṭṭhoso, sabbālaṅkaramaṇḍito.

'Kill my father!' he ordered. Thinking, 'The back of my enemy is seen!', that man, joyful, pleased, and very angry, adorned with all his ornaments,

106.

106.

Rājānamupasaṅkamma, purato ca’ssa caṅkami;

Rājādisvā ca cintesi, pāpiyo’yaṃ mataṃ mama.

Having approached the king, he paced back and forth before him. And the king, seeing him, thought: 'This wicked man is my death.'

107.

107.

Kāyaṃ viya dukkhāpetvā, narakaṃ hetu micchati;

Rosuppādena tasseva, kiṃpuremi manorathaṃ.

He wishes to torment my body and thereby desires hell. Why, by the arising of anger in myself, should I fulfill his wish?

108.

108.

Iti mettāyamāno taṃ, āha senāpatiṃ pati;

Moggallāne tvayiceva, ekacitto ahaṃ iti.

Thus, extending loving-kindness towards him, the lord said to the commander: 'Towards Moggallāna and towards you, I am of the same mind.'

109.

109.

Hasaṃcālesi sīsaṃso, disvā taṃ jānibhūpati;

“Nūna māreti ajjā”ti, tadā sāhasikopi so.

He laughed and shook his head. Seeing that, the king, lord of men, even that reckless one, then thought: 'Surely he will kill me today.'

110.

110.

Naggaṃ katvāna rājānaṃ, sasaṅkhalika bandhanaṃ;

Puratthābhimukhaṃ katvā, antobandhiya bhittiyaṃ.

Having stripped the king naked and bound him with chains, he made him face the east and walled him in, having bound him.

111.

111.

Mattikāya vilimpesi, evaṃ disvāpi paṇḍito;

Ko hi rajjeyya bhogesu, jīvitepi yasepi vā.

He plastered him over with clay. Seeing this, what wise person would be attached to possessions, to life, or to fame?

112.

112.

Dhātuseno narindo so, evaṃ puttahato gato;

Aṭṭhārasahi vassehi, devarājassa santikaṃ.

Thus King Dhātusena, slain by his son, went, after a reign of eighteen years, into the presence of the king of the gods.

113.

113.

Kāḷavāpī mayaṃ rājā, kārāpento samāhitaṃ;

Passitvā bhikkhumetantu, vuṭṭhāpetuṃ samādhito.

I, King Kāḷavāpi, while diligently having a tank constructed, saw this monk and sought to rouse him from his concentration.

114.

114.

Asakkonto khipāpesi, paṃsuṃ bhikkhussa matthake;

Sandhiṭṭhiko vipākoyaṃ, tassa kammassa dīpito.

Being unable to do so, he had dust thrown upon the monk’s head. The immediate result of that action was thus made manifest.

115.

115.

Dasāpite [M 0.0254] rājavarā sabhogā,

Upāgamuṃ maccumukhaṃ sabhovā;

Aniccataṃ bhogavato dhane ca,

Disvā sapañño vibhavaṃ icche.

Those ten excellent kings, with all their possessions, went to the mouth of death. Seeing the impermanence of the wealthy and of wealth, a wise person should desire non-becoming.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Great Chronicle, composed for the serene joy and emotion of the virtuous.

Dasarājako nāma

The Chapter of the Ten Kings.

Aṭṭhatiṃsatiemā paricchedo.

The Thirty-Eighth Chapter.

Ekūnacattālīsatima pariccheda

The Thirty-Ninth Chapter.

Rājadvayadīpano

The Elucidation of the Two Kings.

1.

1.

Tato kassapanāmo so, pāpako narapālako;

Assa go pañcasūdañca, pesayitvāna bhātikaṃ.

Then that wicked ruler named Kassapa, having sent his brother with horses, cattle, and five butchers,

2.

2.

Mārāpetuṃ asakkonto, bhīto sīhagiriṃ gato;

Durārohaṃ manussehi, sodhāpetvā samantato.

Unable to have him killed, he went in fear to Sīhagiri. Having cleared it all around and made it difficult for men to ascend,

3.

3.

Pākārena parikkhippa, sīhākārena kārayi;

Tattha nisseṇi gehāni, tena taṃ nāmako ahū.

Having enclosed it with a rampart, he had it made in the shape of a lion. There were stairways and houses there; hence it was so named.

4.

4.

Saṃharitvā dhanaṃ tattha, nidahitvā sugopitaṃ;

Attano nihitānaṃ so, rakkhaṃ datvā tahiṃ tahiṃ.

Having gathered wealth there and hidden it securely, he assigned guards here and there to his own deposits,

5.

5.

Katvā rājagharaṃ tattha, dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ;

Dutiyālakamandaṃva, kuverova tahiṃ vasi.

Having made a royal residence there, beautiful and delightful, he lived there like Kuvera, as if in a second Ālakamandā.

6.

6.

Migāro nāma kāresi, senāpati sanāmakaṃ;

Pariveṇaṃ tathāgeha-mabhisekajinissa ca.

He had a monastic college built, named Migāra after the general, and likewise a shrine for the Buddha of the Consecration.

7.

7.

Tassābhisekaṃ yācitvā, silāsambuddhato’dhiraṃ;

Aladdhāsāmi no rajje, jānissāmīti saṇṭhahi.

Having requested his consecration from the Stone Sambuddha and receiving no firm reply, he resolved, 'I shall know whether or not I am master in this kingdom.'

8.

8.

Hutvā vippaṭisārī so, attanā katakammanā;

Muccissāmi kataṃ nu’ti, puññaṃ kāsi anappakaṃ.

Becoming remorseful for the deed he himself had done, he performed abundant merit, thinking, 'Shall I be freed from what I have done?'

9.

9.

Mahā [M 0.0255] vatthuni kāresi, dvāresu nagarassa so;

Ambuyyāne ca kāresi, dīpe yojana yojane.

He had great edifices built at the city gates, and in the island, he had parks with ponds constructed at every yojana.

10.

10.

Issarasamaṇārāmaṃ, kāretvā pubbavatthuto;

Adhikaṃ bhogagāme ca, adhikaṃ tassa dāpayi.

Having had the Issarasamaṇa monastery built, making it grander than the former foundation, he also had additional revenue villages given to it.

11.

11.

Bodhi uppalavaṇṇā ca, tassāsuṃ dhītaro duve;

Vihārassa’ssa kāresi, nāmaṃ tāsañca attano.

His two daughters were Bodhi and Uppalavaṇṇā. He had a monastery built and gave it a name combined from theirs and his own.

12.

12.

Dente tasmiṃ na icchiṃsu, samaṇā theravādino;

“Pitughātissa kamma”nti, lokagārayha bhīruno.

When it was offered, the Theravāda monks did not accept it, fearing worldly censure and saying, 'It is the work of a patricide.'

13.

13.

Dātukāmosa tesaṃ’va, sambuddha paṭimāya’dā;

Bhikkhave adhivāsesuṃ, bhogo no satthuno iti.

Desiring to give it to them, he gave it to an image of the Sambuddha. The monks then consented, saying, 'This property belongs to the Teacher, not to us.'

14.

14.

Kathā niyyanti uyyāne, samīpe pabbatassa so;

Kārāpesi vihāraṃ so, tesaṃ nāmo tato ahu.

He had a monastery built in the park near the mountain, and from that it received its name.

15.

15.

Adā dhammarucinaṃ taṃ, sampatta catupaccayaṃ;

Vihārañceva uyyānaṃ, disābhāgamhi uttare.

He gave it—the monastery and the park, endowed with the four requisites—to the Dhammarucikas, in the northern quarter.

16.

16.

Bhattaṃ sanīrapakkaṃ so, bhuñjitvā dinnamitthiyā;

Sappiyuttaṃ manuññehi, sūpehi abhisaṅkhataṃ.

Having eaten a meal of boiled rice given by a woman, which was mixed with ghee and seasoned with delightful curries,

17.

17.

Manuññamidamayyānaṃ, dassamevanti tādisaṃ;

Bhattaṃ pādāsi bhikkhūnaṃ, sabbesañca sacīvaraṃ.

Thinking, 'This is pleasing to the noble ones; I shall give just such a meal,' he gave such food to all the monks, together with robes.

18.

18.

Uposathamadhiṭṭhāsi, appamaññañca bhāvayi,

Samādiyi dhutaṅge ca, likhāpesi ca potthake.

He undertook the Uposatha observance, developed the immeasurables, took up the ascetic practices, and had books written.

19.

19.

Paṭimādāna sālādiṃ, kārāpesi anappakaṃ;

Bhito so paralokamhā, moggallānā ca vattati.

He had many image-houses, alms-halls, and other such buildings constructed. He lived in fear of the next world and also of Moggallāna.

20.

20.

Tato aṭṭhārase vasse, moggallāno mahābhaṭo;

Ādesena nigaṇṭhānaṃ, dvādasaggasahāya vā.

Then, in the eighteenth year, Moggallāna, the great warrior, with twelve chief companions, at the behest of the Nigaṇṭhas,

21.

21.

Jambudīpā idhāgamma, dese ambaṭṭhakolake;

Kuḷārī nāme bandhittha, vihāre balasañcayaṃ.

Having come here from Jambudīpa, in the region of Ambaṭṭhakolaka, he gathered an army at the monastery named Kuḷārī.

22.

22.

Rājā sutvā gahetvā taṃ, bhañjissāmiti nikkhami;

Nemittehi na sakkāti, vadantepi mahābalo.

The king, hearing of this, went forth thinking, 'I will seize and crush him.' He, the mighty one, went forth even though the soothsayers said it was not possible.

23.

23.

Moggallānopi sannaddha balo sūrasahāya vā;

Gacchanto surasaṅgāmaṃ, devo viya sujampati.

Moggallāna also, armed and strong, with heroic companions, went to the divine battle like the god Sujampati.

24.

24.

Aññamaññaṃ [M 0.0256] upāgamma, bhinnavelāva sāgarā;

Ārabhiṃsu mahāyuddhaṃ, balakāyā ubhopi te.

Having approached one another, those two armies, like oceans that have broken their shores, began a great battle.

25.

25.

Kassapo purato disvā, mahantaṃ kaddamāsayaṃ;

Gantumaññena maggena, parivattesi dantinaṃ.

Kassapa, having seen a great muddy mire ahead, turned the elephant to go by another path.

26.

26.

Disvā taṃ sāmikono’yaṃ, palāyati bhaṇe iti;

Balakāyo pabhijjittha, “diṭṭhaṃ piṭha”nti ghosayuṃ.

Seeing this, the army broke apart, thinking, 'Our master flees!', and shouting, 'His back is seen!'

27.

27.

Moggalāna balārājā, chetvā nikaraṇena so;

Sīsaṃ ukkhipiyā’kāsaṃ, churikaṃ kosiyaṃ khipi.

He, Moggallāna, the king of the army, having cut with a weapon, and lifting his head to the sky, threw a dagger at Kosiya.

28.

28.

Katvā’ḷāhana kiccaṃ so, tassa kamme pasīdiya;

Sabbaṃso dhanamādāya, āgañchi nagaraṃ varaṃ.

He, having performed the cremation rites for him, and being pleased with that deed, took all the wealth and came to the excellent city.

29.

29.

Bhikkhū sutvā pavattiṃ taṃ, sunivatthā supārutā;

Sammajjitvā vihārañca, aṭṭhaṃsu paṭipāṭiyā.

The monks, having heard of this event, well-robed and cloaked, swept the monastery and stood in order.

30.

30.

Mahāmeghavanaṃ patvā, devarājāva nandanaṃ;

Mahāsena nivattetvā, hatthipākārato bahi.

Having reached the Mahāmeghavana, like the king of gods reaching the Nandana grove, he turned back the great army outside the elephant-wall.

31.

31.

Upasaṅkamma vanditvā, saṅghe tasmiṃ pasīdiya;

Chattattena saṅghaṃ pūjesi, saṅgho tasseva taṃ adā.

Having approached, paid homage, and gained faith in that Sangha, he honored the Sangha with the royal umbrella, and the Sangha gave it back to him.

32.

32.

Taṃ ṭhānaṃ chattavaḍḍhīti, vohariṃsu tahiṃ kataṃ;

Pariveṇampi taṃ nāmaṃ, ahosi puramāgato.

They called that place 'Chattavaḍḍhi' on account of what was done there. The pariveṇa there, founded by the one who had come to the city, also received that name.

33.

33.

Vihāre dvepi gantvāna, saṅghaṃ tatthā’bhivandiya;

Pāpuṇitvā mahārajjaṃ, lokaṃ dhammena pālayi.

Having gone to both monasteries and paid homage to the Sangha there, having attained the great kingdom, he ruled the world with Dhamma.

34.

34.

Kuddho nīhari dāṭhaṃso, ghātakaṃ pituno mama;

Anuvattitvā maccāti, tena rakkhasa nāma vā.

Angry, he drove out Dāṭha, the murderer of my father. Because he pursued him like death, he was therefore named Rakkhasa.

35.

35.

Atirekasahassaṃ so, amaccānaṃ vināsayi;

Kaṇṇanāsādi chedesi, pabbājesi tathā bahū.

He destroyed over a thousand ministers. He cut off ears, noses, and so forth, and likewise banished many.

36.

36.

Tato sutvāna saddhamma-mupasanno sumānaso;

Mahādānaṃ pavattesi, megho viya mahītale.

Then, having heard the Good Dhamma, devout and with a gladdened mind, he instituted great almsgiving, like a great cloud upon the earth.

37.

37.

Phussapuṇṇamīyaṃ dāna-manuvassaṃ pavattayi;

Tato paṭṭhāya taṃ dānaṃ, dīpe ajjāpi vattati.

On the full moon day of Phussa, he established an annual almsgiving. From that time onwards, that almsgiving continues on the island even today.

38.

38.

Sopi sārathiko lāja-dāyako piturājino;

Ānetvā pitusande saṃ, moggallānassa dassayi.

That charioteer also, the giver of roasted grain for the father-king, having brought the father's message, showed it to Moggallāna.

39.

39.

Taṃ [M 0.0257] disvā paridevitvā, pituno pema mattanī;

Vaṇṇetvā tassa pādāsi, dvāranāyakataṃ vibhū.

Seeing that, he lamented, his mind overcome with love for his father. Having praised him, the powerful one bestowed upon him the position of chief of the gate.

40.

40.

Senāpati migārohi, nivedetvā yathā vidhiṃ;

Abhiseka jinassā’kā, abhisekaṃ yathāruciṃ.

The general Migāra, having made the announcement according to custom, performed the consecration for the victor, an anointing according to his wish.

41.

41.

Sīhā’cale daḷhanāmaṃ, dāṭhā koṇḍaññakampi ca;

Vihāraṃ dhammarucinaṃ, sāgalinañca dāpayi.

He had the vihāra named Daḷha on Sīhācala built, and also the Dāṭhākoṇḍañña. He also had a vihāra given to the Dhammarucis and the Sāgaliyas.

42.

42.

Pabbatantu vihāraṃso, katvā therassa dāpayi;

Mahānāmasanāmassa, dīghasaṇḍa vihārake.

Having built the Pabbata Vihāra, he had it given to the elder named Mahānāma at the Dīghasaṇḍa Vihāra.

43.

43.

Rājinināmakañceva, katvā bhikkhunupassayaṃ;

Adā sāgalikānaṃ so, bhikkhunīnaṃ mahāmati.

He also built a nunnery named Rājinī and, being great-minded, gave it to the Sāgaliya nuns.

44.

44.

Lambakaṇṇakagottopi, dāṭhā pabhuti nāmako;

Kassapassa upaṭhāne, koci nibbinna mānaso.

A certain one of the Lambakaṇṇa clan, named Dāṭhāpabhuti, who was in the service of Kassapa, became disenchanted in mind.

45.

45.

Gantā me reliyaṃ vaggaṃ,

Vāsaṃ tattheva kappayi;

Ahosi putto tasseko,

Silākā loti pissuto.

Having gone to the Mereliya district, he established his residence there. He had one son, who was well-known as Silākāḷa.

46.

46.

Sopi kassapato bhīto, ñātakena saha’ttano;

Moggallānena gantvāna, jambudīpatalaṃ ito.

He too, fearing Kassapa, went from here to the land of Jambudīpa with his own kinsman and with Moggallāna.

47.

47.

Bodhipaṇḍavihārampi, pabbajjaṃ samupāgato;

Karonto saṅghakiccāni, sādaro so supesalo.

He undertook ordination at the Bodhimaṇḍa Vihāra. Performing the duties of the Sangha, he was respectful and very skillful.

48.

48.

Ammaṃ saṅghassa pādāsi, saṅgho tasmiṃ pasīdiya;

Āha’mba sāmaṇero’ti, tena taṃ nāmako ahu.

He gave a mango to the Sangha. The Sangha, pleased with him, said, 'Ambasāmaṇera.' Thus he became known by that name.

49.

49.

So kesadhātuvaṃsamhi, vuttena vidhinā tato;

Kesadhātuṃ labhitvāna, tassa rajje idhā’nayi.

He, having obtained the hair relic according to the method stated in the Kesadhātuvaṃsa, brought it here to his kingdom.

50.

50.

Tassa katvāna sakkāraṃ, gahetvā kesa dhātuyo;

Mahagghe nidahitvāna, karaṇḍe phalikumbhavhe.

Having paid homage to it, he took the hair relics and enshrined them in a valuable casket called a crystal urn.

51.

51.

Dīpaṅkarassa nāthassa, paṭimāya ghare vare;

Vaḍḍhetvā parihārena, mahāpūjaṃ pavattayi.

In the excellent image-house of the Lord Dīpaṅkara, having increased its endowments, he instituted a great ceremony of worship.

52.

52.

Mātulaṃ bhariyañca’ssa, katvā sovaṇṇayaṃ tahiṃ;

Ṭhapesi paṭimāyo ca, assa bimbañca cārukaṃ.

He had golden images of his maternal uncle and his wife made there, and he also placed a beautiful image of himself.

53.

53.

Kesadhātukaraṇḍañca[M 0.0258], chattaṃ ratanamaṇḍapaṃ;

Sāvakaggayuṃgaṃ vāḷa-bījaniñca sakārayi.

He had the hair-relic casket, the umbrella, the jeweled pavilion, the pair of chief disciples, and the fly-whisk made.

54.

54.

Parihārañca tassa’dā, rājā adhikamattano;

Silākāḷa masiggāhaṃ, katvā rakkhāya yojayi.

The king granted him a retinue, even greater than his own; and having made Silākāḷa his sword-bearer, he appointed him for protection.

55.

55.

Asiggāhasilākāḷo, iti tenā’si vissuto;

Bhaginiñca’ssa pādāsi, saddhiṃ bhogena bhūmipo.

Thus he became known as Silākāḷa the Sword-bearer. The lord of the land also gave him his sister, together with possessions.

56.

56.

Vutto’yamati saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana sabbaso;

Kesadhātukavaṃsamhā, gahetabbo vibhāvinā.

This has been stated very briefly; but the full detail should be taken from the Kesadhātukavaṃsa by the discerning.

57.

57.

Bandhitvā sāgarā rakkhaṃ, dīpañca kāsinibbhayaṃ;

Dhammakammana sodhesi, sadhammaṃ jinasāsanaṃ.

Having established protection from the ocean and made the island fearless, he purified the true Dhamma, the Conqueror's Dispensation, by means of righteous action.

58.

58.

Senāpatisa nāmaṃ’kā, padhānaghara muttaro;

Katvā’ṭṭhārasame vasse, so puññāni khayaṃ gato.

He made a principal dwelling to the north, named Senāpati. In his eighteenth year, having performed meritorious deeds, he went to the exhaustion of his merits.

59.

59.

Kassapato jito atibali puññakkhaye saṅkhate;

Jetuṃ no visahittha maccumupagaṃ so yevadāsoviya;

Tasmā maccubalaṃ nihacca sukhino hessanti medhāvino;

Nibbānaṃ paramaccutaṃ sivapadaṃ pattabbamattaññunā.

Kassapa, though very mighty, was conquered when the exhaustion of his merit came to pass. He could not conquer approaching death, just like a slave. Therefore, the wise, having destroyed the power of death, will be happy. Nibbāna, the supreme, imperishable, auspicious state, is to be attained by one who knows what is for his own good.

Sujanappasāda saṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the faith and spiritual urgency of good people.

Rājadvayadīpano nāma

Named the Illuminator of the Two Kings.

Ekūnacattālīsatimo paricchedo.

The Thirty-ninth Chapter.

Cattālīsatima pariccheda

The Fortieth Chapter.

Aṭṭharājako

The Eight Kings.

1.

1.

Tassaccaye kumārādi-dhātusenoti vissuto;

Ahu tassa suto rājā, devarūpo mahābalo.

Upon his demise, his son, known as Kumāradhātusena, became king, being of divine form and great power.

2.

2.

Kārite pitarā’kāsi, vihāre navakammakaṃ;

Kāretvā dhammasaṅgītiṃ parisodheti sāsanaṃ.

He undertook the new work on the vihāra that had been founded by his father. Having sponsored a recitation of the Dhamma, he purified the Dispensation.

3.

3.

Santappesi [M 0.0259] mahāsaṅghaṃ, paccayehi catūhipi;

Katvā puññāni’nekāni, navame hāyane’tigā.

He satisfied the great Sangha with the four requisites. Having performed many meritorious deeds, he passed away in his ninth year.

4.

4.

Tittiseno suto tassa, rājā hutvā anekadhā;

Katvā puññāni rajjaṃ taṃ, māsampi navame jahi.

His son, Tittisena, became king and performed meritorious deeds in many ways. He passed from that kingdom in the ninth month.

5.

5.

Sivo taṃ mātulo hantvā, hutvā rājā anappakaṃ;

Puññaṃ katvo’patissena, pañcavīsa dine hato.

His maternal uncle Siva, having killed him, became king. Having performed no small amount of merit, he was slain by Upatissa in twenty-five days.

6.

6.

Upatisso tato āsi, rājā hantvāna sīvakaṃ;

Moggallānassa bhaginī, sāmiko dhajinīpati.

Then Upatissa, the commander of the army and husband of Moggallāna's sister, became king, having slain Sivaka.

7.

7.

Rājā ṭhānantarādīhi, katvāna janasaṅgahaṃ;

Sīlākāḷassa pādāsi, saha bho kanadhīvaraṃ.

The king, having won the support of the people by bestowing high offices and so forth, gave gifts to Silākāḷa and to the fisherman Kana.

8.

8.

Eko putto ahu rañño, upatissassa kassapo;

Sasoḷasa sahāyehi, sūro sūpehi saññuto.

King Upatissa had one son, Kassapa, a hero accompanied by sixteen companions and furnished with provisions.

9.

9.

Eka vuttisahāyehi, dānamāna mahādhano;

Dhammaṭṭho vīriyājīvi, sādhu jeṭṭhapacāyako.

He and his companions were of like conduct; he was generous and respectful, of great wealth, established in the Dhamma, living energetically, virtuous, and reverent towards his elders.

10.

10.

Silā kāḷotato rajja-lobhavañcita mānaso;

Dakkhiṇaṃ malayaṃ gantvā, saṅgaṇhitvā mahā balaṃ.

Then Silākāḷa, his mind deceived by greed for the kingdom, went to southern Malaya and amassed a great force.

11.

11.

Vilumpamāno paccanti, sampatto nagarantikaṃ;

Taṃ sutvā kassapo jeṭṭho, varamāruyha kuñjaraṃ.

Plundering the border regions, he reached the vicinity of the city. Hearing this, the elder Kassapa mounted a choice elephant.

12.

12.

Assā setvāna pitaraṃ, samādāya sahāyake;

Nikkhamma nagarā gacchi, silākālassa dassanaṃ.

Having encouraged his father and taking his companions with him, he went forth from the city to confront Silākāḷa.

13.

13.

Evaṃ satta’ṭṭha vāresu, palāto līnavuttiko;

Hatthe katvā upāyena, dese pācina pacchime.

Thus, on seven or eight occasions he was put to flight and went into hiding. Then, by means of a stratagem, he took control of the eastern and western regions.

14.

14.

Yujjhituṃ puna pācina-tissa pabbatamāgami;

Kassapopi sahāyehi, saddhimāruyha dantinaṃ.

To fight again, he came to the Eastern Tissa Mountain. Kassapa also, together with his companions, mounted an elephant.

15.

15.

Tattha gantvā palāpetvā, coraṃ pabbatamatthakaṃ;

Āropesi mahānāgaṃ, tenā’si girikassapo.

Having gone there and driven away the rebel, he made the great elephant ascend to the mountain peak; for that reason he became known as Girikassapa.

16.

16.

Mānatthaddho silākāḷo, bhiyyo raṭṭhaṃ pabhindiya;

Sabbaṃ hatthagataṃ katvā, ajeyya balavāhano.

Proud and stubborn, Silākāḷa further ravaged the kingdom. Having brought everything under his control, his army and transport became invincible.

17.

17.

Āgamma nagaraṃ rundhi, satthāhaṃ rājasevakā;

Yujjhitvā viralā āsuṃ, tato cintesi kassapo.

Having approached the city, he besieged it for seven days. The king's servants fought, but became few. Then Kassapa reflected:

18.

18.

Ete [M 0.0260] nagararodhena, sabbe bhijjanti pāṇino;

Parihīnaṃ balaṃ rājā, andhako ca mahallako.

‘By this siege of the city, all living beings are afflicted. The king’s strength is diminished, and he is blind and old.’

19.

19.

Merukandarake katvā, mātaraṃ pitarañca me;

Aṅgahetvā balaṃ pacchā, coro niggaṇhi yo iti.

Having made a cave on Meru, and later having gathered a force, he subdued the thief who had seized my mother and father.

20.

20.

Rattiyaṃ so sahāye ca, rājasādhanamevaca;

Ādāya pitaro ceva, malayaṃ gantumārabhi.

At night, taking his companions, the royal treasure, and also his parents, he set out for Malaya.

21.

21.

Tadā maggamajānantā, sammūḷā maggadesakā;

Nagarassa samīpeva, sambhamiṃsu ito tato.

Then, not knowing the way, the guides were confused; near the city itself, they wandered here and there.

22.

22.

Silākāḷo pavattiṃ taṃ, sutvā saṅgamma vegasā;

Parivāresi saṅgāmo, tattha bhiṃsanako ahu.

Silākāla, hearing that news, quickly assembled his forces and surrounded them; a frightening battle took place there.

23.

23.

Devāsuraraṇākāre, vattamāne mahāhave;

Patitesu sahāyesu, sīdamāne mahāgaje.

While the great battle, in the manner of the war between gods and asuras, was proceeding, as his comrades fell and the great elephant weakened,

24.

24.

Hatthārohassa datvā, chinditvā sīsamattano;

Puñchitvā lohitaṃ katvā, kosiyaṃ asi puttikaṃ.

Having given (the sword) to the elephant rider, having cut his own head, having wiped the blood, he made a sheath for the small sword.

25.

25.

Hatthikumbhe ubho hatthe, ṭhapetvāna avatthari;

Upatissopi taṃ sutvā, sokasallāhato mari.

Placing both hands on the elephant's forehead, he collapsed. Upatissa, hearing of this, died, struck by the arrow of sorrow.

26.

26.

Evaṃ diyaḍḍhavassena, upatisse divaṃgate;

Rājā’hosi silākāḷo, pubbanāmena ekato.

Thus, after one and a half years, when Upatissa had gone to heaven, Silākāla became king, together with his former name.

27.

27.

Taṃ ambasāmaṇerādi-silākāḷoti voharuṃ;

Titthaṃ terasavassāni, dipaṃ dhammena pālayi.

They addressed him as Ambasāmaṇera Silākāla. For thirteen years, he ruled the island righteously.

28.

28.

Mahāpāḷimhi dāpesi, paccagghaṃ rājabhojanaṃ;

Vejjasālāsu bhoge ca, vaḍḍhesi janatāhito.

In the Mahāpāli alms-hall, he provided costly royal food; and in the hospitals, he increased the provisions for the welfare of the people.

29.

29.

Anvahaṃ pūjayi bodhiṃ, paṭimāyo ca kārayi;

Sabbesaṃ dīpavāsīnaṃ, bhikkhūnaṃ’dā ticīvaraṃ.

Daily he honored the Bodhi tree and had images made; he gave the triple robe to all the monks dwelling on the island.

30.

30.

Māghātaṃ kārayidīpe, sabbesaṃyeva pāṇinaṃ;

Ānitaṃ attanā kesa-dhātuṃ sammā apūjayi.

He established on the island a prohibition on killing for all living beings; and he properly venerated the hair relic that he himself had brought.

31.

31.

Raheradakavārañca, adāsi abhayuttare;

Puratthimā therīyānaṃ, vihārakunthanāma so.

He also gave the Rahera water channel to the Abhayuttara vihara; and for the eastern nuns, he gave the monastery named Kuntha.

32.

32.

Ānetvā āsanaṃ tattha, ṭhapesi dumarājake;

Yāvajīvaṃ pavattesi, puññakammamasaṅkhiyaṃ.

Having brought a seat there, he placed it at the king of trees; throughout his life, he performed innumerable meritorious deeds.

33.

33.

Moggallāno [M 0.0261] tathā dāṭhā, pabhuti co’patissako;

Putto tassā’sumaggassa, desaṃ datvā puratthimaṃ.

His sons were Moggallāna, Dāṭhāpabhuti, and Upatissa. Having given the eastern region to the eldest son,

34.

34.

Datvā ṭhānantarañcādi-pādasaññaṃ visajjayi;

Gantvā tattha vasāhīti, sopi gantvā tahiṃ vasi.

Having also given him a suitable domain and the title of Ādipāda, he dispatched him, saying, 'Go and dwell there.' And so he went and dwelt there.

35.

35.

Ṭhānaṃ malayarājaggaṃ, desaṃ datvāna dakkhiṇaṃ;

Rakkhaṇatthaṃ samuddassa, majjhimaṃ tu niyojayi.

Having given the southern region and the governorship of the Malaya country for the protection of the sea, he appointed the middle son.

36.

36.

Upatissaṃ tu vāsesi, santikeyeva attano;

Visesena mamāyanto, yūnaṃ kalyānadassanaṃ.

Upatissa, however, he had dwell near to himself, cherishing with special affection the handsome youth.

37.

37.

Tassa dvādasame vasse, ito kāsi puraṃ gato;

Dhammātu midhā’nesi, tato vāṇija māṇavo.

In his twelfth year, a young merchant, having gone from here to the city of Kāsī, brought hither from there a Dhammadhātu.

38.

38.

Rājā disvā’samattho so, dhammādhammavicāraṇe;

Hemasaññāya dīpamhi, patanto salabho viya.

The king, being incapable of discerning between Dhamma and non-Dhamma, was like a moth that, perceiving it as gold, falls into a flame.

39.

39.

Buddhadhammoti saññāya, taṃ gahetvāna sādhukaṃ;

Katvā sakkārasammānaṃ, gehe rājagharantike.

Perceiving it as the Buddha’s Dhamma, taking it carefully, and having made offerings and shown honor, he placed it in a house near the royal palace.

40.

40.

Ṭhapetvā anuvassaṃ tu, netvā jetavanaṃ mahaṃ;

Kātuṃ kāresi cārittaṃ, hitaṃ mantvāna pāṇinaṃ.

Having placed it there, and considering it a benefit to beings, he established the custom of taking it annually to the great Jetavana vihara.

41.

41.

Evaṃ katvā silākāḷo, puññakammamanappakaṃ;

Patte terasame vasse, yathākammamupāgami.

Thus Silākāla, having done much meritorious work, upon reaching his thirteenth year, passed away according to his kamma.

42.

42.

Dāṭhappabhutiko rajjaṃ, gahetvā bhātaraṃsakaṃ;

Akkamoti nivārentaṃ, mārāpesi vibuddhiko.

Dāṭhāpabhuti, having seized the kingdom, that foolish one had his own brother killed, who was trying to prevent him, saying, 'Do not transgress!'

43.

43.

Moggallāno’tha taṃ sutvā, appattaṃ rajjamaggahi;

Akāraṇe me māresi, kaṇiṭṭhaṃ dhammavādīnaṃ.

Then Moggallāna, hearing that, laid claim to the kingdom that was not his, saying: 'For no reason you have killed my youngest brother, a speaker of Dhamma.'

44.

44.

Kārāpessāmahampajja, rajjanti parikuppiya;

Samādāya mahāsenaṃ, agārāhera pabbataṃ.

Greatly enraged, he thought, 'Today I will make you pay!' and taking a great army, he advanced from his home to the Hera mountain.

45.

45.

Rājāpi sutvā sannaddha-balakāyo karindake;

Pabbate siviraṃ bandhi, moggallāno nisammataṃ.

The king also, hearing this, with his forces and elephants arrayed, pitched camp on Karindaka mountain. Moggallāna, hearing of this,

46.

46.

Sāparādhāna te me vā, manussā dīpavāsino;

Ekasmiñca mate rajja-mubhinnaṃyeva nosiyā.

'These island-dwellers are at fault neither to you nor to me. If one of us is slain, the kingdom will no longer belong to both of us.'

47.

47.

Tasmā aññena yujjhantu, ubhoyeva mayaṃ idha;

Hatthiyuddhaṃ karomāti, rañño pesesi sāsanaṃ.

'Therefore, let others not fight. Let us two, and us two alone, engage in elephant combat here.' Thus he sent a message to the king.

48.

48.

Sopi [M 0.0262] sādhūti vatvāna, baddhapañcāyudho gajaṃ;

Āruyha munino māro viya otthari tāvade.

He too, saying, 'Good!', agreed. Armed with the five weapons, he mounted an elephant and descended upon him, like Māra upon the Sage.

49.

49.

Moggallānopi sannaddho, āruyha karīnaṃ varaṃ;

Tatthā’go aññamaññaṃ te, pāpuṇiṃsu mahāgajā.

Moggallāna, also armored, mounted a superb elephant. There he went, and those great elephants came upon one another.

50.

50.

Saddo sūyittha saṅghaṭṭe, asanirāva sannibho;

Dantaghātena uṭṭhāsi, jālā vijjullatā viya.

The sound of the collision was heard, like the sound of a thunderbolt. From the clash of tusks, flames arose like a flash of lightning.

51.

51.

Sañjhāghanasabhāgā’suṃ, gajā lohitamakkhitā;

Moggallānagajāviddho, raññoosakki kuñjaro.

The elephants, smeared with blood, were like evening clouds. Pierced by Moggallāna’s elephant, the king’s elephant retreated.

52.

52.

Rājā ārabhi taṃ disvā, chindituṃ sīsamattano;

Moggallāno’tha vandanto, yāci’me’vaṃ kirīiti.

The king, seeing this, began to cut off his own head. But Moggallāna, paying homage, begged him thus, “Do not do this!”

53.

53.

Yācamānepi somānaṃ, mānento chindikandharaṃ;

Chaḍḍesi chahi so rajjaṃ, māsehi divasehi ca.

Though entreated, upholding his honor, he severed his own neck. He thus abandoned the kingdom after six months and six days.

54.

54.

Moggallāno tato rājā, āsi dīpe mahābalo;

Mātulañca paṭiccemaṃ, cūlanāmena voharuṃ.

Then Moggallāna, of great strength, became king on the island. And on account of his maternal uncle, they called him by the name Cūla.

55.

55.

Āsādhāraṇakāveyyo, vatthuttaya parāyaṇo;

Dānasaṃyama soceyyo, soraccādiguṇālayo.

He was of uncommon poetic skill, devoted to the Triple Gem, possessed of generosity, self-restraint, and purity, a repository of virtues such as gentleness.

56.

56.

Dānena piyavācāya, atthassa cariyāya ca;

Samānattassabhāvena, saṅgahesi mahājanaṃ.

Through generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality, he won over the great populace.

57.

57.

Piṇḍapātavihārehi, bhesajjacchādanehi ca;

Bhikkhusaṅghañhi saṅgaṇhi, dhammikāya ca guttiyā.

With alms-food, dwellings, medicines, and robes, he supported the community of monks, and with righteous protection.

58.

58.

Atirekāya pūjāya, pūjetvā dhammabhāṇake;

Piṭake tīṇi vācesi, saddhimaṭṭhakathāya so.

With extraordinary honor, he revered the preachers of the Dhamma, and had the three Piṭakas recited, together with the commentaries.

59.

59.

Kumāre upalāletvā, nivāpena yathāruciṃ;

Sajjhāpesi sadā dhammaṃ, dhammadīpo mahāmati.

Cherishing the princes with affection and providing for them as they wished, that great-minded one, a lamp of the Dhamma, constantly had them study the Dhamma.

60.

60.

Dhammadīpañca so katvā, kuñjarasekhareni sā;

Dhammāvāsāne vācesi, puramhi purisuttamo.

That foremost of men, having composed the Dhammadīpa, had it and the Kuñjarasekhara recited in the monasteries of the city.

61.

61.

Bandhāpesi kadambañca, nadiṃpabbatamajjhato;

Pattapasāṇavāpiñca, dhanavāpiṃ garitaraṃ.

He had the Kadamba river dammed from the middle of the mountain, and also built the Pattapāsāṇa tank and the very large Dhanavāpi tank.

62.

62.

Gaṇhāpesi sadīghāyu-hetu kammanti sādaro;

Likhāpesi ca saddhammaṃ, vatthupūjañca kārayi.

With reverence, he had deeds performed for the sake of his own long life, had the True Dhamma inscribed, and caused offerings to be made to the sacred relics.

63.

63.

Lokaṃ [M 0.0263] so anukampitvā, mātāputtaṃva orasaṃ;

Datvā bhutvā yathākāmaṃ, vasse vīsatime mari.

Having compassion for the world, like a mother for her own son, he gave and enjoyed as he wished, then died in his twentieth year.

64.

64.

Mahesī tassa ghātetvā, visayogena ñātake;

Puttaṃ rajje’bhisiñcitvā, sayaṃ rajjaṃ vicārayi.

His queen, having had him killed by relatives by means of poison, anointed her son to the kingdom and administered the realm herself.

65.

65.

Tathābhisitto so kitti-sirimegho narādhipo;

Tipupattehi chādesi, dumindadharamādito.

Thus anointed, that king, Kittisirimegha, from the outset covered the terrace of the Lord of Trees with plates of tin.

66.

66.

Kapaṇaddhivaṇibbānaṃ, mahādānaṃ pavattayi;

Maggapālo tathākāro, ahu sabbopabhogiyo.

He instituted a great almsgiving for the poor, travelers, and beggars; and Maggapāla, in like manner, became one who enjoyed all requisites.

67.

67.

Mahesī sā sadā āsi, padhānā sabbakammasu;

Rajjaṃ tassā’si teneva, heṭṭhupariyavattikaṃ.

That queen was always pre-eminent in all affairs; for that very reason, the kingdom was hers, and it was turned upside down.

68.

68.

Rājāpādā mahāmaccā’-hesuṃ lañcaparāyanā;

Dubbale ca viheṭhesuṃ, balī jānapadā narā.

The royal officials and great ministers were devoted to bribes, and the strong men of the countryside oppressed the weak.

69.

69.

Silākāḷassa kālamhi, gāme saṅgillanāmake;

Bhayavasīvhayo poso, ahu moriyavaṃsajo.

In the time of Silākāḷa, in the village named Saṅgilla, there was a man named Bhayavasī, born of the Moriya clan.

70.

70.

Ahosi putto sīvassa, aggabodhi sanāmako;

Bhāgineyyopi tassāsi, mahānāgoti vissuto.

There was a son of Sīva, Aggabodhi by name; and his nephew was the renowned Mahānāga.

71.

71.

Bhāgineyo mahānāgo, aggabodhi ca sundaro;

Uḷārajjhāsayattā so, mahānāgo mahabbalo.

The nephew Mahānāga, and the handsome Aggabodhi; because of his magnanimous disposition, this Mahānāga was very powerful.

72.

72.

Hitvā kassakakammāni, corakammamakā vane;

Godhaṃ laddhāna pesesi, mātulāniya santikaṃ.

Abandoning the work of a farmer, he practiced thievery in the forest; having obtained a monitor lizard, he sent it to his maternal aunt.

73.

73.

Godhaṃ disvā’vasā ñatvā, dhaññapacchimapesayi;

Kammārassā’pi pesesi, sasaṃ sopi tathevakā.

The aunt, seeing the lizard and knowing it was female, sent the last of her grain. She also sent a hare to the smith, and he too did likewise.

74.

74.

Bījaṃ bhaginī māyāci, bījagāhañca tassa sā;

Dāsañca ñatvā pesesi, annapānādinā raho.

His sister did not ask for seed, nor did she accept seed from him; but recognizing the servant, she secretly sent food, drink, and other provisions.

75.

75.

Tadā dubbhikkhakālamhi, eko mantadharo naro;

Bhikkhālābhāya saddhehi, bhikkhuvesena bhikkhati.

Then, in a time of famine, a man who knew mantras begged in the guise of a monk to obtain alms from the faithful.

76.

76.

Taṃ gāmaṃ pavisitvā so, aladdhā kiñci bhojanaṃ;

Abhibhūto jighacchāya, kampamāno nigacchati.

Entering that village, he obtained no food at all; overcome by hunger, trembling, he departed.

77.

77.

Taṃ disvā karuṇāyanto, mahānāgo mahādayo;

Pattamādāya gāmanta-māhiṇḍitvāpi sabbaso.

Seeing him, Mahānāga, of great compassion, felt pity; taking a bowl, he wandered through the entire village vicinity.

78.

78.

Yāgumattampi [M 0.0264] nālattha, tato uttarasāṭakaṃ;

Datvā āhari āhāraṃ, so taṃ bhutvā pasīdiya.

He did not obtain even a measure of gruel; then, giving his upper garment, he brought food. The man, having eaten that, was pleased.

79.

79.

Rajjārahamimaṃ dīpe, karissāmīti cintiya;

Tamādāya khaṇenā’gā, gokaṇṇakamahaṇṇavaṃ.

Thinking, 'I will make him king of this island,' he took him and in a moment went to the great ocean of Gokaṇṇa.

80.

80.

Atha tattha nisīditvā, sañjapanto yathāvidhiṃma;

Mantonā’nesi nāgindaṃ, phussapuṇṇamarattiyaṃ.

Then, sitting there, reciting the mantra according to custom, by the power of the mantra, he summoned the Nāga king on the full moon night of Phussa.

81.

81.

Mahānāgaṃ phusāhīti, mahānāgaṃ niyojayi;

So bhīto purime yāme, āgataṃ taṃ na sambhusī.

'Touch the great Nāga!' thus he commanded the great Nāga. But he, being afraid, did not touch him when he came in the first watch.

82.

82.

Tathā majjhimayāmepi, pacchime pana naṅgale;

Gahetvā khipi tīheva, aṅgulīhi sataṃ chupi.

Likewise in the middle watch. But in the last watch, he seized a plough, struck him three times, and touched him with a hundred fingers.

83.

83.

So taṃ byākāsi taṃ ditvā, sabalaṃ me parissamaṃ;

Tīhi rājūhi yujjhitvā, catutthaṃ tvaṃ nighātiya.

Seeing this, the Nāga declared to him: 'My effort is fruitful. Having fought with three kings and having slain the fourth...

84.

84.

Vuḍḍho tīṇeva vassāni, rājā hutvā na jīvasi;

Tathā hessanti rājāno, tayo te vaṃsajā narā.

...as an old man, having become king, you will live for only three years. Likewise, three men born of your lineage will become kings.

85.

85.

Gantvā sevassu rājānaṃ, pacchā passasi mekhalaṃ;

Iti vatvāna pesesi, sopi gantvā narissaraṃ.

'Go and serve the king; afterwards you will see the girdle.' Having spoken thus, he sent him away. He too, having gone to the lord of men...

86.

86.

Passitvā tamupaṭṭhāsi, rājā rohaṇakammikaṃ;

Taṃ akāsi taduṭṭhānaṃ, bhaṇḍamāhari so bahuṃ.

Having seen the king, he served him. The king made him the official for Rohaṇa. Arising from that position, he brought much wealth.

87.

87.

Rājā tasmiṃ pasīditvā, andhasenāpativhayaṃ;

Datvā ṭhānantaraṃ tassa, gantuṃ tattheva yojayi.

The king, being pleased with him, gave him the rank named Andhasenāpati and appointed him to go there.

88.

88.

Bhayasīvassa puttañca, bhāgineyyañca attano;

Ādāya gantvā taṃ desaṃ, parivattesi sabbaso.

Taking the son of Bhayasīva and also his own nephew, he went to that country and transformed it completely.

89.

89.

Paccekabhogaṃ katvāna, rohaṇaṃ tattha so vasaṃ;

Dāṭhappabhūtinā kātuṃ, yuddhaṃgantvā mahabbalo.

Having established it as his individual domain, he resided there in Rohaṇa; a man of great strength, he went to wage war with Dāṭhappabhūti.

90.

90.

Moggallānabhayā gantvā, rohaṇañca tahiṃ vasī;

Sutvā kittisirīmeghavaṇṇa-rañño rajje samañjasaṃ.

Out of fear of Moggallāna, he went and dwelt there in Rohaṇa. Having heard of the prosperous reign of King Kittisirīmeghavaṇṇa,

91.

91.

Rajjaṃ gahetuṃ kāloti, sīghaṃ āgamma rohaṇā;

Ekūnavise divase, mārayitvā mahīpatiṃ.

thinking, 'It is time to seize the kingdom,' he came swiftly from Rohaṇa and, on the nineteenth day, slew the king.

92.

92.

Sayaṃ hutvā mahīpālo, desaṃ katvā yathā pure;

Bhāgineyyassa pāhesi, paṇṇamāgacchatūti so.

Becoming king himself and administering the country as it was before, he sent a message to his nephew, saying, 'Let him come.'

93.

93.

Āgacchanto [M 0.0265] nimittena, nivattitvā marittha so;

Tato mātulaputtaṃ’kā, uparajjaṃ kataññuko.

While coming, because of an omen, he turned back and died. Then the grateful king made his maternal uncle's son the viceroy.

94.

94.

Ālavālaṃ dumindassa, katvā hemamayaṃ gharaṃ;

Chādāpesi munindassa, paṭimāyo ca sandahi.

He made a golden house for the enclosure of the king of trees and had it roofed; and he set up images of the Lord of Sages.

95.

95.

Mahācetittaye kāsi, sudhākammañca cumbaṭaṃ;

Hatthivediñca kāretvā, cittakammamakārayi.

On the three great cetiyas, he did plaster-work and made the coping-rings; and having had the elephant-terrace made, he caused it to be adorned with paintings.

96.

96.

Pesakārakagāmaṃ so, jambelavhayamuttare;

Mahāvihārecābandhi, gāmaṃ tintiṇikavhayaṃ.

He dedicated the weavers' village named Jambela in the north, and the village called Tintiṇika, to the Mahāvihāra.

97.

97.

Uddhagāmamhi vasabha-gāmaṃ jetavanassa’dā;

Vatthadānaṃ nikāyesu, tīsu ceva pavattayi.

He gave the village of Vasabha in Uddhagāma to the Jetavana monastery; and he instituted the giving of robes to the three fraternities.

98.

98.

Khettānaṃ hisataṃ datvā, vihāre jetanāmake;

Yāguṃ tattha pavattesi, bhikkhūnaṃ sabbakālikaṃ.

Having given a hundred fields to the monastery named Jetana, he provided rice gruel there for the monks at all times.

99.

99.

Sahassa dūratissavhā, khettaṃ datvā tapassinaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, yāguṃ niccaṃ pavattayi.

Having given the field named Sahassa-dūratissa to the ascetics residing in the Mahāvihāra, he constantly provided rice gruel for them.

100.

100.

Ciramātikavārañca, tattheva’dā guṇe rato;

Mayūrapariveṇe ca, navakammamakārayi.

Delighting in virtue, he also gave Ciramātikavāra there; and he caused renovations to be done in the Mayūrapariveṇa.

101.

101.

Kāsikhaṇḍe mahādeva-rattakuravanāmake;

Vihāre anurārāmaṃ, jiṇṇañca paṭisaṅkharī.

In Kāsikhaṇḍa, in the monastery named Mahādeva-Rattakuravana, he repaired the dilapidated Anurārāma.

102.

102.

Kamaṃ sovaggikaṃ katvā, evamādiṃ narissaro;

Agamā tīhi vassehi, devarājasahabyataṃ.

Having performed such deeds leading to heaven, that lord of men, after three years, went to the companionship of the king of gods.

103.

103.

Aṭṭhete kuṭṭhacittā’parimitavibhavā rājarājenarūpā;

Rājāno rājamānā narakarituragāsūrasenārathehi;

Ante hitvā’khilaṃ taṃ vigataparijanā’ḷāhanaṃ saṅkhatāsuṃ;

Sappañño taṃ saranto bhavatu bhavasukhaṃ vantukāmo hitesī.

These eight kings, with minds like lepers, of boundless splendor, in form like the king of kings; proud kings with armies of men, elephants, horses, asuras, and with chariots; in the end, abandoning all that, bereft of retinue, they went to the cremation ground. The wise one, remembering this, desiring to renounce the bliss of existence, should be intent on his own welfare.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the faith and spiritual urgency of the virtuous,

Aṭṭharājako nāma

The Chapter on the Eight Kings

Cattālīsatimo paricchedo.

The Fortieth Chapter.

Ekacattālīsatima pariccheda

The Forty-First Chapter

Dvirājako

The Two Kings

1.

1.

Mahānāganarindassa[M 0.0266], bhāgineyyo subhāgiyo;

So aggabodhirājāsi, aggabodhigatāsayo.

The nephew of King Mahānāga, who was indeed fortunate, was King Aggabodhi, with a mind inclined toward supreme enlightenment.

2.

2.

Tejena bāhuṃ sommena, candaṃ sampuṇṇamaṇḍalaṃ;

Sumerumacalantena, gambhirena mahodadhiṃ.

In his splendor, he was like the sun; in his gentleness, like the full-orbed moon; in his immovability, like Mount Sumeru; in his depth, like the great ocean.

3.

3.

Vasundharā pakampena, mārutaṃ sampavuttiyā;

Buddhiyāmaramantāraṃ, suddhiyā saradambaraṃ.

In his power to shake, he was like the earth; in his movement, the wind; in his wisdom, the counsellor of the immortals; in his purity, the autumn sky.

4.

4.

Kāmabhogena devinda, matthena ca narissaraṃ;

Dhammena suddhavāseṭṭhaṃ, vikkamena migādhipaṃ.

In his enjoyment of sensual pleasures, he was like the lord of gods; in his eminence, the lord of men; in his righteousness, the foremost of the Suddhāvāsa deities; in his valor, the lord of beasts.

5.

5.

Rājadhammehi rajjehi, cakkavattinarissaraṃ;

Vessantarañca dānena, anugantvā jane suto.

In his royal virtues and his reign, he was like a wheel-turning monarch; and in generosity, following Vessantara, he was renowned among the people.

6.

6.

Mātulaṃ uparājavhe, bhātaraṃ yuvarājake;

Bhāgineyyañca malaya-rājaṭhāne ṭhapesi so.

He appointed his maternal uncle to the office of viceroy, his brother to the office of crown prince, and he installed his nephew in the kingdom of Malaya.

7.

7.

Ṭhānantare yathāyogaṃ-seṭṭhāmacce ṭhapesi ca;

Janaṃ saṅgahavatthūhī, rājadhammehi caggahi.

He appointed chief ministers to other suitable positions, and he won over the people with the bases of sympathy and with the royal virtues.

8.

8.

Desaṃ sayoggaṃ pādāsi, yuvarājassa dakkhiṇaṃ;

Vasaṃ tattha sirīvaḍḍha-mānavāpiṃ sagāhayi.

He bestowed a suitable country, the southern region, upon the crown prince; dwelling there, the latter had the Sirivaḍḍhamānavāpi tank constructed.

9.

9.

Katvā girivihārañca, saṅghikaṃ tassa dāpayi;

Khettānaṃ dvisataṃ saṅgha-bhogatthāya mahāmati.

Having built a mountain monastery, the great wise one had it given to the Sangha, along with two hundred fields for the Sangha's use.

10.

10.

Adā malayarājassa, dāṭhānāmaṃ sadhītaraṃ;

Pariveṇaṃ sīrisaṅgha-bodhināmañca kārayi.

He gave his daughter named Dāṭhā to the king of Malaya, and he had a monastic college named Sīrisaṅghabodhi built.

11.

11.

Mahāsivassa kāresi, pariveṇaṃ sanāmakaṃ;

Parivāro’pi tassāsi, evaṃ puññaparāyano.

He had a monastic college bearing his own name built for Mahāsiva; and his retinue was also thus devoted to merit.

12.

12.

Katvā sādhupacārena, porāṇaṃ saṅgahaṃ vidhiṃ;

Antarāyaṃ visodhetuṃ, jiṇṇañca paṭisaṅkhari.

Having performed the ancient custom of patronage with proper service, he also repaired what was dilapidated in order to purify obstacles.

13.

13.

Kavayo [M 0.0267] tassa rajjamhi, sīhaḷāya niruttiyā;

Kāveyye bahuke’kāsuṃ, vicitranayāsālino.

In his kingdom, poets endowed with varied styles composed many poetic works in the Sinhalese language.

14.

14.

Vihāre dakkhiṇe kāsi, pāsādaṃ sumanoharaṃ;

Akā navahi vassehi, dipe kaṇṭakasodhanaṃ.

In the southern monastery, he built a most delightful palace; and in nine years, he performed the clearing of thorns on the island.

15.

15.

Kurundanāmaṃ kāretvā, vihāraṃ sabbasaṅghikaṃ;

Vāpiṃ tannāmakaṃ nāḷi-kerārāmaṃ tiyojanaṃ.

Having had a monastery named Kurunda built for the entire Sangha, he also established a tank of the same name and a coconut grove three leagues in extent.

16.

16.

Mahāsivavhaye ceva, sassaṃ kārayituṃ adā;

Lābhasakkārasammāna-mārāmikasataṃ tadā.

He also gave lands in the place called Mahāsiva for the cultivation of crops; and at that time, he provided gain, offerings, and honor for a hundred monastery attendants.

17.

17.

Vihāraṃ taṃ samīpamhi, katvā ambilapassavaṃ;

Gāmaṃ tannāmakaṃ cādā, theriyānaṃ tapassīnaṃ.

Near that monastery, having established a place for distributing sour gruel, he also gave a village of the same name to the ascetic elder nuns.

18.

18.

Uttaravallivihārassa, ratanaṃ dīghavaṇṇitaṃ;

Datvā gāmaṃ patiṭṭhesi, satthubimbaṃ silāmayaṃ.

To the Uttaravalli monastery, he gave a jewel and a long, decorated hall; and having given a village, he established a stone image of the Teacher.

19.

19.

Keḷivāte ca kāresi, sumanaṃ nāma pabbataṃ;

Mahātelavaṭaṃbodhi-ghare pāsāṇavedikaṃ.

At Keḷivāta, he had a mountain named Sumana constructed, and a stone platform in the great Telavaṭa Bodhi-house.

20.

20.

Kāretvā lohapāsādaṃ, pāsādamahane adā;

Chattiṃsānaṃ sahassānaṃ, bhikkhūnaṃ so ticīvaraṃ.

Having had the Lohapāsāda built, he held a festival for the palace; and he gave the triple robe to thirty-six thousand monks.

21.

21.

Gāmaṃ datvā niyojesi, ārakkhaṃ dhītu nāmakaṃ;

Hatthikucchivihārepi, pāsādaṃ kāsi buddhimā.

Having given a village, he assigned it for the maintenance of his daughter; and the wise man also built a palace at the Hatthikucchi monastery.

22.

22.

Dāṭhā sivassa ṭhatvāna, ovāde sādhu bhikkhuno;

Samācaranto dhammena, sakkaccaṃ tamupaṭṭhahi.

Abiding well in the advice of the monk Dāṭhāsiva, and conducting himself righteously, he attended to him with devotion.

23.

23.

Mūgasenāpatiṃ cākā, vihāraṃ so visālakaṃ;

Gāmaṃ lajjikametassa, dāsa bhogāya’dāsi ca.

The general Mūga also built a large monastery; and he (the king) gave to him the village of Lajjika and slaves for his support.

24.

24.

Mahānāgassa puññatthaṃ, rañño taṃnāmakaṃ akā;

Mahātherassa tañcā’dā, rājā tepiṭakassa so.

For the merit of King Mahānāga, he built a monastery bearing his name; and that king, a master of the Tipiṭaka, gave it to a great elder.

25.

25.

Attano sadisānañca, yogīnaṃ vigatālayo;

Bhikkhūnaṃ catusaṭṭhīnaṃ, vihāraṃ taṃ tadā adā.

He, being without attachment, then gave that monastery to sixty-four monks, yogis who were like himself.

26.

26.

Katvā tasseva mahā-pariveṇanivāsino;

Bhinnorudīpaṃ datvāna, vaṭṭakākārapiṭṭhito.

Having made it for the dwellers of that very great monastic college, and having given the island of Bhinnoru, which was behind the circular terrace.

27.

27.

Dakkhiṇagīridaḷhavhe, mahānāge ca pabbate;

Kāḷavāpādike cā’kā, vihāre posathālaye.

At Dakkhiṇagiri, Daḷhavha, the Mahānāga mountain, Kāḷavāpi, and other such places, he built monasteries and Uposatha halls.

28.

28.

Vihāre [M 0.0268] abhaye’kāsi, mahāpokkharaṇiṃ tathā;

Cetiyapabbate cākā, nāgasoṇḍiṃ thirodikaṃ.

Likewise, in the Abhaya monastery he made a great lotus pond; and on Cetiyapabbata he made the Nāgasoṇḍi pond with its lasting water.

29.

29.

Mahindataṭavāviñca, kārāpetvāna sādhukaṃ;

Etissā mariyādāya, theraṃ netuṃ niyojayi.

Having had the Mahindataṭa tank well constructed, he appointed someone to bring the Elder for its demarcation.

30.

30.

Mahāmahinda theramhi, taṃṭhānasamupāgato;

Taracchā eva netunti, katikañceva kārayi.

When the great elder Mahinda arrived at that place, he had an agreement made, saying: “He is to be brought just like a hyena.”

31.

31.

Chattaṃ soṇṇañca kāresi, nikāyesupi tīsu so;

Sattāṭṭhanava vāresu, mahaggharatanehi ca.

He had a golden parasol made for the three Nikāyas, and on seven, eight, or nine occasions, also one with priceless jewels.

32.

32.

Mahātūpe catubbīsa-bhāraṃ chattaṃ suvaṇṇayaṃ;

Tattha tattha ca pūjesi, mahagghaṃ ratanuttamaṃ.

For the Great Thūpa, he had a golden parasol made weighing twenty-four bhāras, and he offered worship there with priceless and most excellent gems.

33.

33.

Dāṭhādhātugharaṃ katvā, vicitraratanujjalaṃ;

Kāsi hemakaraṇḍañca, lohanāvañca pāḷiyaṃ.

Having built a house for the Tooth Relic, resplendent with various jewels, he made a golden casket and a bronze ship in its enclosure.

34.

34.

Maṇimekhalanāmañca, bandhāpesi sabandhanaṃ;

Mahāmātiñca gaṇhesi, maṇihīrakavāpiyaṃ.

He had the jeweled girdle named Maṇimekhalā made, complete with its fastenings. He also seized the great minister, along with the Maṇihīrakavāpi tank.

35.

35.

Tadā eko mahāthero, jotipālakanāmako;

Parājesi vivādena, dīpe vetullavādino.

At that time, a great elder named Jotipāla defeated the Vetullavādins on the island in debate.

36.

36.

Dāṭhāpabhutināmo’tha, ādipādo’tilajjito;

Hatthamukkhippi taṃ hantuṃ, gaṇḍo sañjāyi taṃkhaṇe.

Then the Ādipāda named Dāṭhāpabhuti, being greatly ashamed, raised his hand to strike him, and a boil instantly arose.

37.

37.

Rājā tasmiṃ pasīditvā, vihāreyeva vāsayi;

Mānena taṃ anāgamma, dāṭhāpabhūmato kira.

The king, pleased with that elder, had him reside in the monastery itself. It is said that Dāṭhāpabhuti, out of pride, did not approach him.

38.

38.

Datvā mahādipādattaṃ, bhāgineyyaggabodhino;

Rakkhituṃ taṃ niyojesi, theraṃ sopi tamācari.

Having given the rank of Great Heir Apparent to his nephew Aggabodhi, he appointed him to protect the elder, and he acted accordingly.

39.

39.

Nīlagehaparicchedaṃ, katvā tasseva so adā;

Katvevaṃ bahudhā puññaṃ, catuttiṃse same mato.

He made the Nīlageha enclosure and gave it to that same elder. Having thus performed merit in many ways, he died in his thirty-fourth year.

40.

40.

Aggabodhi tato āsi, rājā pubbassa rājino;

Mahallakattānaṃ khudda-nāmena paridīpayuṃ.

Then Aggabodhi, nephew of the former king, became king. They designated him by the nickname 'the Small'.

41.

41.

So dīpaṃ paripālesi, pubbacārittakovido;

Akāsi ca mahesiṃ so, mātuladhītumattano.

He protected the island, being skilled in the customs of his predecessors; and he made his own maternal uncle's daughter his chief queen.

42.

42.

Saṅghabhaddaṃ asiggāhaṃ, kāsi bandhuṃ mahesiyā;

Yathārahamadā ceva, ṭhānantaramanālayo.

He made Saṅghabhadda the sword-bearer a kinsman of the chief queen and, being generous, gave him a fitting rank.

43.

43.

Katvā [M 0.0269] veḷuvanaṃ rājā, sāgalīnaṃ niyojayī;

Jamburantaragallañca, kāsi mātikapiṭṭhikaṃ.

The king built the Veḷuvana monastery and assigned it to the Sāgaliyas. He also built the Jamburantaragalla and Mātikapiṭṭhika monasteries.

44.

44.

Rañño tasse’va rajjamhi, kāliṅgesu mahīpati;

Sattānaṃ maraṇaṃ yuddhe, disvā saṃviggamānaso.

During the reign of that very king, the lord of the Kalingas, seeing the death of beings in battle, became deeply stirred in mind.

45.

45.

Imaṃ dīpamupāgamma, pabbajjā katanicchayo;

Jotipālamhi pabbaji, rājā sakkāsi taṃ ciraṃ.

Having come to this island, resolved on going forth, he went forth under Jotipāla. The king honored him for a long time.

46.

46.

Padhānaṭhānaṃ tassa’kā, vihāre mattapabbate;

Tassāmacco mahesī ca, tathevā’gamma pabbajuṃ.

He made a place for striving for him at the Mattapabbata monastery. His minister and chief queen also came there and likewise went forth.

47.

47.

Rañño mahesī sutvāna, tassa pabbajjamuttamaṃ;

Sakkaccaṃ tamupaṭṭhāsi, ratanavhañca kārayi.

When the king's chief queen heard of his supreme going forth, she attended on him respectfully and had a jewel-house built.

48.

48.

Adā rājā amaccassa, pācīnakaṇḍarājiyaṃ;

Vettavāsavihārañca, so’dā saṅghassa taṃ yati.

The king gave the Pācīnakaṇḍarājiya district to the minister, and also the Vettavāsa monastery. That ascetic, in turn, gave the monastery to the Sangha.

49.

49.

Rājattheremate rājā, socitvā parideviya;

Padhānaṭhānaṃ kāresi, cūḷagallavihārake.

At the death of the royal elder, the king grieved and lamented. He had a place for striving established at the Cūḷagalla monastery.

50.

50.

Palaṃnagaragañceva, tassa ṭhānañhi kārayi;

Evaṃ tadatthaṃ puññāni, bahūni’pi mahīpati.

He had the village of Palaṅganagara made, and a residence for him. Thus the lord of the earth performed many meritorious deeds for his sake.

51.

51.

Jotipālita theramhi, tūpārāmamhi cetiyaṃ;

Vandamāne pabhijjitvā, bhāgo taṃ purato pati.

When the elder Jotipālita was venerating the cetiya at Tūpārāma, a part of it broke off and fell before him.

52.

52.

Pakkositvāna rājānaṃ, thero dassesi dukkhito;

Rājā disvāva saṃviggo, kammaṃ paṭṭhapi taṃkhaṇe.

The elder, being distressed, summoned the king and showed it to him. The king, upon seeing it, was deeply stirred and immediately began the work.

53.

53.

Dakkhiṇakkhakadhātuṃ so, lohapāsādakucchiyaṃ;

Sārakkhaṃ ṭhapayitvāna, rattindivamapūjayi.

Having placed the right collarbone relic under guard in the interior of the Lohapāsāda, he venerated it day and night.

54.

54.

Navakamme cirāyante, thūpārāmamhi devatā;

Supinaṃ tassa dassesuṃ, rattimārāmikā viya.

While the new work at Tūpārāma was taking a long time, deities there showed him a dream, appearing like monastery attendants at night.

55.

55.

Sace rājā papañceti, kātuṃ dhātugharaṃ mayaṃ;

Dhātuṃ gahetvā gacchāma, yatthatatthā’ti taṃkhaṇe.

“If the king delays in making the relic-house,” they said, “we will take the relic and go just anywhere.”

56.

56.

Rājā pabuddho saṃviggo, na cireneva kārayi;

Kammaṃ dhātugharesabbaṃ, cittakammādisaññuttaṃ.

Awakened and stirred, the king had all the work on the relic-house, complete with paintings and other decorations, finished without delay.

57.

57.

Catasso paṭimāyo ca, pallaṅke ca silāmaye;

Hemacchattaṃ silādanta-kammaṃ gehamhi sabbaso.

He also had made four images, stone couches, a golden parasol, and stone and ivory work throughout the entire house.

58.

58.

Mahāmaccādayo’kaṃsu[M 0.0270], karaṇḍānaṃ sataṃ nava;

Devānaṃpiyatissassa, kammañca nikhilaṃ navaṃ.

The great ministers and others made a hundred new caskets. And all the work of Devānampiyatissa was made new.

59.

59.

Sabbussāhena kāretvā, mahāpūjaṃ yathārahaṃ;

Ānetvā lohapāsādā, dhātuṃ sabbādarena so.

Having had the work done with all diligence and having made a great offering as was fitting, he, with all reverence, brought the relic from the Lohapāsāda.

60.

60.

Jotipālaṃ mahātheraṃ, sasaṅghaṃ parivāriya;

Parihārena vaḍḍhesi, dhātuṃ dhātukaraṇḍake.

Having surrounded the great elder Jotipāla together with the Sangha, he honored them with requisites and enshrined the relic in the relic casket.

61.

61.

Dhātugehassa pādāsi, laṅkādīpaṃ sahattanā;

Lābhaggāma-madā tassā, rakkhakānaṃ mahesiyā.

The chief queen, with her own hand, gave the island of Laṅkā to the relic-house. For its guardians, she gave the village of Lābhaggāma.

62.

62.

Nāgadīpamhi gehañca, rājāyatanadhātuyā;

Uṇṇalomagharañceva, chattamāmalacetiye.

He built a house for the Rājāyatana relic at Nāgadīpa, a house for the Uṇṇaloma relic, and placed an umbrella on the Āmalaka Cetiya.

63.

63.

Tattha gāmaṃ vihārassa, yāgudānāya’dāsi ca;

Vihārassa’bhayassā’dā, gāmamaṅgaṇasālakaṃ.

There she gave a village to the monastery for the provision of rice-gruel. She also gave the village of Aṅgaṇasālaka to the Abhaya monastery.

64.

64.

Nāmaṃ katvāna so’kāsi, attano ca mahesiyā;

Dāṭhaggabodhimāvāsaṃ, vihāre atayuttare.

He built the Dāṭhāggabodhi residence in the far northern monastery, naming it after himself and his chief queen.

65.

65.

Devī kapālanāgaṃ sā, vihāraṃ sādhukāriya;

Tasse’vādā vihārassa, sampannacatupaccayaṃ.

That queen had the Kapālanāga monastery well built and provided that very monastery with an abundance of the four requisites.

66.

66.

Gehaṃ jetavane kāsi, rājā rājatacumbaṭaṃ;

Udapānaṃ maṇāpesi, sova bodhigharantike.

The king built a house in Jetavana and a silver reliquary. He also had a beautiful well constructed near the Bodhi-house.

67.

67.

Gaṅgātaṭaṃ valāhassaṃ, vāpiṃ giritaṭañcakā;

Mahāpāḷiṃpi vaḍḍhesi, bhatanāvañca kārayi.

He built the Valāhassa on the bank of the Gaṅgā, and a tank on a mountain slope. He also enlarged the Mahāpāli Hall and had a food-boat made.

68.

68.

Bhikkhūnīnaṃ mahesī ca, bhattavaṃsaṃ samādisi;

Evaṃ puññāni katvā so, divaṃ’gā dasame same.

The chief queen also established a regular provision of food for the bhikkhunīs. Having thus performed meritorious deeds, he passed away to heaven in his tenth year.

69.

69.

Evaṃ puññaratā narādhipatayo sampannabhogā gamuṃ;

Maccusseva vasaṃ tatohi matimā sammā bhavassīdisaṃ;

Passanto niyamaṃ vihāya vidhinā sabbaṃ bhave saṅgatiṃ;

Nibbānābhimukho careyya dhitimā pabbajjamajjhūpago.

Thus kings who delighted in merit and possessed abundant wealth all came under the sway of death. Therefore, a wise person, rightly seeing this fixed nature of existence, should properly abandon all attachment in worldly existence. Resolute, facing Nibbāna, having embraced the renunciant life, one should fare on.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene faith and spiritual urgency of good people.

Dvirājako nāma

The Two Kings

Ekacattālīsatimo paricchedo.

The Forty-first Chapter.

Dvicattālīsatima pariccheda

The Forty-second Chapter.

Cha rājako

The Six Kings

1.

1.

Saṅghatisso [M 0.0271] tato āsi, asiggāho mahīpati;

Sāsanassa ca raṭṭhassa, vuddhikāmo naye rato.

Then there was the king Saṅghatissa, the Sword-bearer. Desiring the welfare of the Dispensation and the kingdom, he was devoted to just policy.

2.

2.

Ṭhānantaraṃ yathārahaṃ, datvā saṅgaṇhiso janaṃ;

Tadā khuddakarājassa, moggallāno camūpati.

Having given positions to people according to their worth, he won their support. At that time, Moggallāna was the army commander of the sub-king.

3.

3.

Vasanto rohaṇe sutvā, saṅghatissassa rājataṃ;

Khandhavāraṃ sayuddhatthaṃ, mahāgalle nivesayi.

Dwelling in Rohaṇa and hearing of Saṅghatissa's kingship, he established a fortified camp at Mahāgalla in order to do battle.

4.

4.

Saṅghatisso ca sutvā taṃ, balakāyamapesayi;

Yujjhituṃ tena tajjesi, moggallāno mahabbalo.

When Saṅghatissa heard this, he sent out an army. The very powerful Moggallāna challenged it to fight with him.

5.

5.

Tato hatthassamādāya, gantvā rattivihārakaṃ;

Balaṃ so sannipātento, vāsaṃ tattheva kappayi.

Then, taking his elephants and horses, he went to the Rattivihāraka. Assembling his forces, he took up his quarters right there.

6.

6.

Rājā sutvā punā’gantvā, kadallādīnivātake;

Yujjhitvā taṃ palāpetvā, pesetvā balamattano.

The king, hearing of this, came again to Kadallādinivātaka. Having fought and put him to flight, he sent his own army after him.

7.

7.

Sayaṃ puramupāgañchi, sopi naṭṭhaṃ savāhiniṃ;

Puna pākatikaṃ katvā, kareheramupāgami.

He himself went up to the city. But the other, his army having been shattered, restored it to its former state and went to Karehera.

8.

8.

Rañño senāpati puttaṃ, pesetvā corasantikaṃ;

Yena kenaci lesena, sayaṃ dukkhiva dummano.

The king's general, having sent his son to the rebel on some pretext, became as if sorrowful and dejected himself.

9.

9.

Āturo viya bāḷhaṃ so, hosi mañcaparāyano;

Rājā sutvā pavattitaṃ, upasaṅkamma taṅkhaṇe.

He became as if gravely ill and was confined to his bed. The king, hearing of this matter, approached him at that very moment.

10.

10.

Mā tvaṃ soci kumārassa, sammānetvānusāsiya;

Handa tvaṃ nagaraṃ rakkha, nate sakkā mayā saha.

“Do not grieve for the boy; I will honor and instruct him. Come now, you protect the city, for it is not possible for you to come with me

11.

11.

Yuddhamaṇḍalamāgantuṃ, gilānattāti yojayi;

Ubbāsite jane sabbe, vicchinne rājabhojane.

to the battlefield, being ill,” he arranged. When all the people had been dismissed and the royal meal was interrupted,

12.

12.

Mahāpāḷimhi sampakkaṃ, rañño bhojanamāharuṃ;

Rājā dvisvā’ti nibinno, yāva mando na hessati.

they brought the king his well-cooked food from the Mahāpāli Hall. But the king, disgusted with those two, thought: “So long as that fool is not dealt with...”

13.

13.

Ekko [M 0.0272] pīti vicintetvā, yuddhāya samāsā’gamā;

Saddhiṃ puttena āruyha, hatthiṃsannaddhavāhano.

Thinking, “I will go even alone,” he went forth to battle. With his mount fully caparisoned, he mounted an elephant together with his son.

14.

14.

Thokeneva balenāgā, pācinatissapabbataṃ;

Evaṃ ubhayato cūḷa-saṅgāme paccupaṭṭhite.

He went to the Pācīnatissapabbata mountain with only a small force. Thus a minor battle between the two sides became imminent.

15.

15.

Senāpatisamittaddu, yuddhamārabhi pacchato;

Putto disvā narindassa, ghātessāmi imaṃ iti.

That treacherous general began the battle from the rear. The king's son, seeing him, thought, “I will kill him!”

16.

16.

Āha rājā nivāresi, mā te rucci balaṃ idaṃ;

Neva sakkā’dhivāsetuṃ, atimandaṃ hanissati.

The king stopped him, saying: “Do not be eager for this force. It is not able to withstand them; being too weak, it will be destroyed.”

17.

17.

Duvinnaṃ balakāyānaṃ, rājāmajjhagato ahu;

Tato senā dvidhā’hosi, corasenāpatīpati.

The king was caught between the two armies. Then the army split in two, going over to the rebel general.

18.

18.

Rañño nāgo madhukavha rukkhacchāyaṃ samāvisi;

Tadā chattaṃ patitassa, sākhamāhacca bhūmiyaṃ.

The king's elephant, named Madhuka, entered the shade of a tree. Then the king's parasol, striking a branch, fell to the ground.

19.

19.

Corassa senā taṃ ditvā, haritvā sāmino adā;

So taṃ ussāpayichattaṃ, ṭhatvāpabbatamuddhani.

The rebel's soldiers, seeing it, seized it and gave it to their master. He had that parasol raised while he stood on the mountain peak.

20.

20.

Tadā rājabalaṃ rājā, nunamesoti cintiya;

Gantvā taṃ parivāresi, rājā āsi tadekako.

Then the king, thinking his royal army was lost, went to surround him; the king was then alone.

21.

21.

Hatthikkhandhā tadoruyha-puttaṃ’maccañca sohadaṃ;

Upāvisi samīpamhi, merumajjarakānanaṃ.

Then, dismounting from the elephant's back with his son and his loyal minister, he sat down near the Merumajjara forest.

22.

22.

Moggallāno tato laddha-jayo vāhanamādiya;

Senāpatiṃca mittadduṃ, tassa puttañca pāpinaṃ.

Then Moggallāna, having gained the victory, taking his mount, the treacherous general, and his wicked son,

23.

23.

Upāgamma puraṃ rājā, āsī laṅkā talādhipo;

Tato cintesi jīvante, sattumhi na sukhaṃ iti.

approached the city and became king, the lord of the land of Laṅkā. Then he thought: 'While my enemy lives, there is no happiness for me.'

24.

24.

So sutvā pubbarājassa, putto etthāti kujjhiya;

Āṇāpesi ca tassā’su, hatthapādāni chindituṃ.

When he heard that the son of the former king was there, he became enraged and immediately gave the order to cut off his hands and feet.

25.

25.

Upakkami tadā raññā, āṇatto puriso khaṇe;

Chindituṃ hatthapādaṃ so, kumāro rodi dummano.

Then a man, commanded by the king, immediately set about to cut off his hands and feet. That prince, in despair, began to weep.

26.

26.

Pūvakhādakahatthaṃ me, chindeyyaṃ ce tadā ahaṃ;

Khādisaṃ tena pūveti, haṃ sutvā rājakammiko.

The prince cried out: 'If you cut off this hand of mine that eats cakes, how then could I eat cakes?' The king's officer heard him.

27.

27.

Roditvā paridevitvā, rājāṇāya dukhaddito;

Vāmaṃ hatthañca pādañca, tassa chindi narādhamo.

Weeping and lamenting, tormented by the king's command, that wretched man cut off the prince's left hand and foot.

28.

28.

Jeṭṭhatisso [M 0.0273] palāyitvā, rañño putto’paro agā;

Aññato malayaṃ desaṃ, merukandaranāmakaṃ.

The king's other son, Jeṭṭhatissa, fled and went elsewhere to the Malaya region, to a place named Merukandara.

29.

29.

Rājā’tha sasutā’macco, gantvā veḷuvanaṃ raho;

Codito tattha bhikkhūhi, kāsāvāni samādiyi.

Then the king, with his son and minister, went secretly to the Veḷuvana. There, urged by the bhikkhus, he took up the saffron robes.

30.

30.

Bhikkhuvesaṃ gahetvāna, rohaṇaṃ gantumānaso;

Maṇihīraṃ samāgañchi, tatraṭhā rājasevakā.

Having taken on the guise of a bhikkhu and intending to go to Rohaṇa, he arrived at Maṇihīra, where the king's servants were stationed.

31.

31.

Sañjānitvā tayopete, tesaṃ pādevarujjhiya;

Sāsanaṃ tassa pesesuṃ, rājā sutvā visesato.

Recognizing the three fugitives, they seized them and sent a message to the king. The king, hearing the news, was especially pleased.

32.

32.

Tuṭṭho āṇāpayi gantvā, sīghamādāya tejane;

Tato sīhagiriṃnetvā, tissaṅkaṃ nirupaddavaṃ.

Pleased, he ordered his men to go and bring those people quickly. Then, having had them brought to Sīhagiri, he made himself free from that danger.

33.

33.

Sīsaṃ gaṇhatha tattheva, rañño ca tanayassa ca;

Amaccaṃ pana jīvanta-māneyyātha mama’ntikaṃ.

Take the heads of both the king and his son right there, but bring the minister to me alive.

34.

34.

Manussā evamāṇattā, te gahetvā tayojane;

Netvā sīhagiriṃkātuṃ, yathāvuttamupakkamuṃ.

The men, having been thus commanded, seized those three persons and, leading them to Sīhagiri, proceeded to do as they had been instructed.

35.

35.

Tato rājasuto āha, purise kammakārake;

Sīsaṃ me paṭhamaṃ chetvā, detha mayhaṃ sukhaṃ iti.

Then the prince said to the executioners: 'First cut off my head and grant me happiness.'

36.

36.

Rājaposā tathā’kāsuṃ, pacchāchindiṃsu rājino;

Sīsaṃ passatha bālānaṃ, kammaṃ kammavidūjanā.

The king's men did so, and afterwards they cut off the king's head. O you who understand action, behold the deed of fools!

37.

37.

Evaṃ aniccā bhogāhi, adhuvā asayaṃvasī;

Tattha laggā kathaṃ niccaṃ, sukhaṃ bho na gavesatha.

Thus, possessions are indeed impermanent, unstable, and not under one's own control. Being attached to them, sirs, why do you not seek lasting happiness?

38.

38.

Rañño sāsanamāhaṃsu, amaccassa hitesino;

Taṃ sutvāna hasitvāna, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

They announced the king's order to the minister, the well-wisher. Having heard it, he laughed and spoke these words:

39.

39.

Chinnasīso mayā diṭṭho, mayi jīvati sāmiko;

Ṭhapetvā hampi sevāmi, aho aññañhi sāmikaṃ.

By me has my master been seen with his head cut off, yet he lives on in me. Should I set him aside and serve another master? Oh, what a different master indeed!

40.

40.

Idha taṃ mārayitvāna, chāyaṃ tassa harissatha;

Aho aññāṇakā tumhe, maññe ummattakā iti.

If you kill me here, you will only carry off his shadow. Oh, how ignorant you are! I think you are mad.

41.

41.

Iti vatvāna so pāde, gahetvā sāmino sayi;

Tassa te haraṇopāyaṃ, apassantā yathā tathā.

Having spoken thus, he grasped his master's feet and lay down. They, seeing no way to remove him, acted accordingly.

42.

42.

Tassāpi sīsaṃ chetvāna, maccā ādāya tīṇi’pi;

Rañño dassetumāhacca, rājā tusittha nibbhayo.

Having cut off his head as well, the men took all three heads and, having come, showed them to the king. The king was pleased and without fear.

43.

43.

Duṭṭhasenā [M 0.0274] patissā’dā, tato malayarājataṃ;

Asiggāhakaṭhānamhi, tassa puttaṃ ṭhapesi ca.

Then he gave the kingship of Malaya to the wicked general, and appointed his son to the position of sword-bearer.

44.

44.

Thūpattayampi chādesi, vatthehi ahatehi so;

Tathā laṅkātale sabbe, thūpekāsi mahussavaṃ.

He also covered the three great stūpas with new cloth, and likewise, he held a great festival at all the stūpas throughout the land of Laṅkā.

45.

45.

Kesadhātuñca nāthassa, dāṭhādhātuṃ tatheva ca;

Mahābodhiṃ sasakkaccaṃ, mahāpūjāya sakkari.

With reverence, he honored the Protector's hair-relic and likewise the tooth-relic and the Great Bodhi tree with a great festival of offerings.

46.

46.

Sabbaṃ vesākhapūjādiṃ, cārittaṃnugataṃ akā;

Dhammakammena sodhesi, sabbaṃ sugatasāsanaṃ.

He performed all the customary ceremonies, such as the Vesākha festival, in accordance with tradition. By means of righteous acts, he purified the entire Dispensation of the Sugata.

47.

47.

Piṭakānañca sajjhāyaṃ, mahāpūjāya kārayi;

Lābhaṃ datvā tirekena, pūjayittha bahussute.

He sponsored a recitation of the Piṭakas with a great festival of offerings. Giving requisites in abundance, he honored the very learned monks.

48.

48.

Bhikkhūnaṃ dīpavāsīnaṃ, sabbesaṃ cīvaraṃ agā;

Āvāsesu ca sabbesu, kathinaṃ attharāpayi.

He gave robes to all the monks dwelling on the island, and in all the monasteries he sponsored the spreading of the kathina cloth.

49.

49.

Paṭimāyo ca kāresi, jiṇṇañca paṭisaṅkhari;

Loṇakkhettañca pādāsi, saṅghassa tisatādhikaṃ.

He had images made and restored those that were dilapidated. He also gave to the Sangha a salt-field of more than three hundred units in extent.

50.

50.

Kārapiṭṭhimhi kāresi, moggallāna vihārakaṃ;

Vihārā piṭṭhigāmañca, sagāmaṃ vaṭagāmakaṃ.

He had the Moggallāna monastery built at Kārapiṭṭhi. He also endowed the Piṭṭhigāma monastery and the Vaṭagāmaka monastery, together with its village.

51.

51.

Tathā cetiyagehañca’-kāsi rakkhavihārake;

Vihāraṃ naṃ bahunnaṃ so, bhogagāme bahū adā.

Likewise, he built a shrine-house at the Rakkhavihāra. He also gave many revenue-villages to many monasteries.

52.

52.

Evaṃ puññānī so’kāsi, appameyyāni bhūmipo;

Sampattīnamanicattaṃ, saranto pubbarājino.

Thus the lord of the land performed immeasurable meritorious deeds, all the while remembering the impermanence of the fortune of the former king.

53.

53.

Tadā kenaci dosena, kuddhomalayarājino;

Saritvā pubbarājassa, kataṃ tena virūpakaṃ.

Then, due to some fault, the king grew angry with the king of Malaya, remembering the disfigurement that had been done by him to the former king.

54.

54.

Upāyena gahetvāna, hatthapādañca chedayi;

Taṃ sutvā so asiggāho, saputto rohaṇaṃgato.

Seizing him by a stratagem, he had his hands and feet cut off. Hearing of this, the Sword-bearer, together with his son, went to Rohaṇa.

55.

55.

Vasanto tattha so katvā, hatthe janapadaṃ lahuṃ;

Jeṭṭhasissamupagañchi, nilīnaṃ malaye ṭhitaṃ.

Dwelling there, he quickly brought the countryside under his control. He then approached Jetthatissa, who was staying hidden in the Malaya region.

56.

56.

Saddhiṃ tenasaghātento, raṭṭhaṃ janapadaṃ khaṇe;

Doḷapabbatamāgamma, khandhāvāraṃ nivesayi.

Joining forces with him and striving for the kingdom and the countryside, he swiftly came to Doḷapabbata mountain and established a fortified camp.

57.

57.

Rājā sutvāna taṃ sabbaṃ, sannaddhabalavāhano;

Khandhāvāraṃ nivesesi, gantvā tasseva santikaṃ.

When the king heard all this, he set out with his army and transport fully arrayed, went near to him, and established his own camp.

58.

58.

Tadā [M 0.0275] pajjararogena, manussārājino bahū;

Upaddutā matā āsuṃ, taṃ sutvā so asiggaho.

At that time, many of the king's men were afflicted by a burning disease and died. Hearing of this, the Sword-bearer...

59.

59.

Yuddhamārabhivegena, rañño senātidubbalā;

Pabhijjitvā palāyittha, rājāpacchā palāyi so.

He swiftly began the battle. The king's army, being very weak, was broken and fled. The king himself also fled afterwards.

60.

60.

Disvā ekākinaṃ yantaṃ, sīhapabbatasantike;

Asiggāho mahārājaṃ, mārayittha saparisaṃ.

Seeing the great king going alone in the vicinity of Sīhapabbata, the Sword-bearer slew him along with his retinue.

61.

61.

Ohīnaṃ pacchato jeṭṭha-tissampi pana mārituṃ;

Sāsanaṃ tassa pesesi, ehi rājā bhavāhīti.

Then, in order to kill Jetthatissa, who had been left behind, he sent a message to him, saying: 'Come and be king!'

62.

62.

So taññatvā palāyitvā, nivatto malayaṃ agā;

Kathañhi laddhaṃ kicchena, rajjaṃso deti me iti.

But he, understanding the trick, fled and returned to Malaya, thinking: 'How could he give me the kingdom that he himself has gained with such difficulty?'

63.

63.

Evaṃ kho dallanāmaṃ so, moggallānaṃ narissaraṃ;

Māretvā chahi vassehi, sampattabalavāhano.

Thus, having slain the lord of men Moggallāna, who was known as Dalla, after six years he became possessed of a powerful army and transport.

64.

64.

Athā’gantvā asiggāho, anurādhapuraṃ varaṃ;

Rājā hutvā pavattesi, āṇācakkaṃ mahītale.

Then the Sword-bearer came to the excellent city of Anurādhapura and, having become king, set the wheel of his authority in motion over the face of the earth.

65.

65.

Sa silāmeghavaṇṇavho, saṅghaṃ bodhiñca vandiya;

Thūpattayañca sakkāsi, mahāpāḷiñca vaḍḍhayi.

He, who was known as Silāmeghavaṇṇa, paid homage to the Sangha and the Bodhi tree, honored the three great stūpas, and enlarged the Mahāpāḷi alms-hall.

66.

66.

Pāyāsaṃ’dāsi saṅghassa, sappiphāṇitasaṅkhataṃ;

Chātake atikicchamhi, parissāvanameva ca.

He gave the Sangha rice-porridge prepared with ghee and molasses. During a time of severe famine, he also gave water-strainers.

67.

67.

Sabbadānena saṅgaṇhī, kapaṇaddhivaṇibbake;

Pūvamūladhanaṃcā’dā, kumārānaṃ mahādayo.

With every kind of gift he supported the poor, the needy, and the mendicants. Being greatly compassionate, he also gave a fund for cakes to the young boys.

68.

68.

Vihāre abhaye buddhaṃ, pūjayittha sīlāmayaṃ;

Jiṇṇañca gehaṃ tassā’kā, nānāratanacittikaṃ.

In the Abhayagiri monastery, he honored a stone image of the Buddha. He also restored its dilapidated shrine, making it beautiful with various kinds of gems.

69.

69.

Kolavāpiñca datvāna, ārakkhatthaṃ jinassa so;

Pūjaṃ sabbopahārehi, sabbakālaṃ pavattayi.

Having given the Kolavāpi tank for the maintenance of the Conqueror's shrine, he instituted a perpetual offering with all kinds of tributes.

70.

70.

Evaṃ tasmiṃ mahīpāle, vasante puññabhājane;

Nāyako sirināgavho, jeṭṭhatissassa mātulo.

While that great king, a vessel of merit, was thus reigning, a chieftain named Sirināga, the maternal uncle of Jetthatissa,...

71.

71.

Gantvāna paratīraṃ so, ādāya damiḷe bahū;

Āgantvā uttaraṃ desaṃ, gaṇhituṃ tamupakkami.

...went to the opposite shore, and taking many Damiḷa soldiers, he returned and began to seize the northern province.

72.

72.

Rājāpi sutvā taṃ gantvā, yujjhitvā rājamittake;

Gāme hantvāna taṃ tena, damiḷe saddhimāgate.

The king, hearing of this, also went forth. Having fought in the village of Rājamittaka, he slew him along with the Damiḷas who had come with him.

73.

73.

Hatasese [M 0.0276] gahetvāna, katvā paribhavaṃ bahuṃ;

Adāsi dāse katvāna, vihāresu tahiṃ tahiṃ.

Taking the survivors, he subjected them to much humiliation, made them slaves, and distributed them to the monasteries here and there.

74.

74.

Evaṃsampattavijaye, puramāgammabhūmipe;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ visodhetvā, vasante akuto bhaye.

When the king had thus achieved victory and returned to the capital, he purified the entire kingdom and dwelt there without fear from any quarter.

75.

75.

Bhikkhubodhī sanāmo’tha, vihāre abhayuttare;

Dussīle bahule disvā, pabbajjāya navopi so.

Then a monk named Bhikkhubodhi, at the Abhayuttara monastery, seeing many immoral monks, refused to perform the ordination for new candidates.

76.

76.

Rājānamupasaṅkamma, dhammakammamayācatha;

Rājā te neva kāresi, dhammakammaṃ vihārake.

He approached the king and requested a formal act of the Dhamma, but the king did not have that formal act carried out in the monastery.

77.

77.

Dussīlā nihaṭā tena, sabbe mantiya ekato;

Raho taṃ mārayitvāna, taṃ kammaṃ paṭibāhayyuṃ.

The immoral monks who had been censured by him all conspired together; having secretly killed him, they obstructed that formal act.

78.

78.

Rājā sutvā tadā kuddho, sabbegaṇhiya ekato;

Akā pokkharaṇī pāle, chinnahatthe sabandhane.

Hearing this, the king then became enraged. Seizing them all together, he had them fettered and their hands severed on the bank of the pond.

79.

79.

Aññe tattha sataṃ bhikkhū, jambudīpe khipāpayi;

Saranto tassa ussāhaṃ, parisodhesi sāsanaṃ.

He banished a hundred other monks there to Jambudīpa. Remembering that monk's zeal, he purified the Dispensation.

80.

80.

Bhikkhū theriyavāde so, kātuṃ tehi uposathaṃ;

Ārādhetvā paṭikkhitto, pakuppitvā anādaro.
