He invited the monks of the Theravāda school to perform the Uposatha ceremony with the others, but when he was rejected, he became angry and disrespectful.

81.

81.

Akkositvā ca bhāsitvā, vācāhi pharusāhi so;

Bhikkhū te akkhamāpetvā, dakkhiṇaṃ desamajjhagā.

Having reviled and abused them with harsh words, and without asking for pardon from those monks, he went to the southern region.

82.

82.

Tassa so mahatā phuṭṭho, rogena marisajjukaṃ;

Evaṃ navahi vassehi, pariccaji mahītalaṃ.

Afflicted by a great disease that brought him to the brink of death, he thus relinquished the earth after a reign of nine years.

83.

83.

Tassa putto tato agga-bodhi nāmo kumārako;

Āsi rājāsirisaṅgha-bodhināmena visuto.

His son, the prince named Aggabodhi, thereafter became king, renowned by the name Sirisaṅghabodhi.

84.

84.

Kaṇiṭṭhaṃ bhātaraṃ māṇaṃ, oparajje’bhisañciya;

Tassā’dā dakkhiṇaṃ desaṃ, sayoggabalavāhanaṃ.

Having consecrated his younger brother Māna as viceroy, he gave him the southern region with its troops and transport.

85.

85.

Rājā so pubbarājūnaṃ, pavattaṃ na vināsiya;

Raṭṭhaṃ dhammena pālesi, saṅghañca bahumānayi.

That king, not destroying the tradition of former kings, ruled the kingdom righteously and greatly honored the Sangha.

86.

86.

Jeṭṭhatisso’tha taṃ sabbaṃ, suṇitvā malaye ṭhito;

Ariṭṭhaṃ girimāgamma, saṅgahesi mahājanaṃ.

Then Jeṭṭhatissa, hearing all that while staying in Malaya, went to Ariṭṭha Mountain and won over the populace.

87.

87.

Katvā hatthagate pubba-dakkhiṇe susamānase;

Kamena puramāgantu-mārabhittha mahābalo.

Having brought the well-disposed eastern and southern regions under his control, the mighty one gradually began to approach the capital.

88.

88.

Dāṭhāsiva [M 0.0277] mamaccañca, gahetuṃ pacchimaṃ disaṃ;

Pesayitvā sayaṃ gāme, vasittha siripiṭṭhike.

He sent the minister Dāṭhāsiva to seize the western district, while he himself remained in the village of Siripiṭṭhika.

89.

89.

Rājā nisamma taṃsabbaṃ, uparājaṃ visajjayi;

Sabalaṃ pacchimaṃ desaṃ, so gantvā taṃ palāpayi.

The king, hearing all this, dispatched the viceroy with an army to the western region. The viceroy went and put his foe to flight.

90.

90.

Potakaṃva kulāvamhi, sakkā hantunti dārakaṃ;

Māyettaṃ āgataṃ rājā, kumārā’macca maggahī.

Thinking, 'The boy can be killed like a fledgling in its nest,' the king seized the prince and his ministers who had come with cunning intent.

91.

91.

Jeṭṭhatissaṃpi etaṃva, gaṇhissāmīti cintiya;

Thokeneva balenāgā, nirāsaṅkotivikkamo.

Thinking, 'I will seize Jeṭṭhatissa in the same way,' he came with only a small force, fearless and exceedingly valiant.

92.

92.

Jeṭṭhasissopi taṃ sutvā, sannaddhabalavāhano;

Sāgaro bhinnavelova, rājasenaṃ samotthari.

When Jeṭṭhatissa heard this, with his forces arrayed for battle, he overwhelmed the king's army like the ocean bursting its bounds.

93.

93.

Rājasenā pabhijjittha, rājā āruyha kuñjaraṃ;

Eko aññātavesena, palāyitvā khaṇena so.

The royal army was routed, and the king, mounting an elephant, fled in an instant, alone and in disguise.

94.

94.

Chaṭṭhe māsamhi rajjamhā, nāvamāruyha sajjukaṃ;

Jambudīpamagāhitvā, dhanaṃ desañca ñātake.

In the sixth month since losing his kingdom, he quickly boarded a ship and went to Jambudīpa, leaving behind his wealth, his country, and his kinsmen.

95.

95.

Jeṭṭhatisso tato hutvā, pure rājāyathā pure;

Sabbaṃ kiccaṃ pavattesi, paripālesi sāsanaṃ.

Then Jeṭṭhatissa became king in the capital. Following the custom of old, he conducted all affairs and protected the Dispensation.

96.

96.

Mahādāragiriṃ so’dā, vihāre abhayuttare;

Mahāvihārassā’dāsi, mahāmettavhabodhikaṃ.

He gave the Mahādāragiri shrine to the Abhayuttara monastery, and to the Mahāvihāra he gave the Bodhi-tree shrine named Mahāmetta.

97.

97.

Goṇḍigāmañca pādāsi, rājā jetavanassa so;

Mātulaṅgaṇakañceva, gāmañco dumbaraṅgaṇaṃ.

That king gave to the Jetavana monastery the village of Goṇḍigāma, as well as Mātulaṅgaṇaka and Dumbaraṅgaṇa.

98.

98.

Mahānāgassa pādāsi, padhānagharakassa so;

Kassapassa girissāpi, āhāraṃ ambilāpikaṃ.

He gave support to the meditation house of Mahānāga, and to the Kassapagiri monastery he gave the revenue from the village of Ambilāpika.

99.

99.

Gāmaṃ kakkhalavitthiñca, adāveḷuvanassa so;

Gaṅgāmāti vihārassa, kehetaṃ gāmakaṃ adā.

He gave the village of Kakkhalavitthi to the Veḷuvana monastery, and he gave the village of Keheṭa to the Gaṅgāmāti monastery.

100.

100.

Antarāgaṅgasavhassa, cullamātikagāmakaṃ;

Mayettikassapāvāse, sahanna nagaraṃ adā.

He gave the village of Cullamātika in Antarāganga and the town of Sahanna to the abode of Kassapa of Mayetti.

101.

101.

Kāḷavāpi vihārassa, udavhaṃ gāmamādisi;

Ete caññeca so bhoga-gāmehi paripūrayi.

To the Kāḷavāpi monastery he assigned the village of Udavha. He also endowed these and other monasteries with revenue-villages.

102.

102.

Jiṇṇaṃ satasahassehi, tīhi so paṭisaṅkhari;

Bhikkhūnaṃ dīpavāsīnaṃ, ticīvaramadāsi ca.

He spent three hundred thousand on repairing dilapidated structures, and he gave the triple robe to the monks dwelling on the island.

103.

103.

Jambudīpagatassā’suṃ[M 0.0278], rañño sodariyā narā;

Tattha tattha nilīnā te, desaṃ hantumupakkamuṃ.

The uterine brothers of the king who had gone to Jambudīpa were hiding here and there, and they attempted to destroy the country.

104.

104.

Sutvā taṃ jeṭṭhatisso’tha, kāḷavāpiṃupacca so;

Yujjhanto tehi tattheva, vāsaṃ’kāsi savāhano.

Hearing this, Jeṭṭhatissa went to Kāḷavāpi with his army; fighting them there, he set up his camp.

105.

105.

Paratīraṃ gato rājā, gahetvā damiḷaṃ balaṃ;

Kāḷavāpimupāgamma, kātuṃ yuddhamupakkami.

The king who had gone to the opposite shore returned, having raised a Damiḷa army. He approached Kāḷavāpi and prepared to give battle.

106.

106.

Jeṭṭhatissopi sannaddha balakāyo dhanāyudho;

Jambudīpaṃ gamāpetvā, amaccaṃ dāṭhasivakaṃ.

Jeṭṭhatissa, too, with his troops arrayed and armed with bows, sent his minister Dāṭhasivaka to Jambudīpa.

107.

107.

Vammitaṃ gajamāruyha, yujjhanto attano balaṃ;

Ohīyamānaṃ disvāna, āruḷhaṃ attanā saha.

Mounting his armored elephant, he fought on. But seeing his own army giving way, he spoke to the one who was mounted with him.

108.

108.

Mahāmaccavaco vedaṃ, sandesaṃ me mahesiyā;

Ārocehi yathākāmaṃ, pacchā tava karissati.

The king said: 'Great minister, deliver this message of mine to the queen. Afterwards, you may act as you please.'

109.

109.

Pabbajitvā mahādevī, sajjhāyitvā ca āgamaṃ;

Abhidhammaṃ kathetvāna, pattiṃ dehīti rājino.

'Let the great queen go forth into homelessness, and after reciting the scriptures and teaching the Abhidhamma, let her transfer the merit to the king.'

110.

110.

Iccetaṃ sāsanaṃ datvā, damiḷe āgatāgate;

Yāva yuddhaṃ nihantvāna, āyumhi khayamāgate.

Having given this message, he struck down the Damiḷas as they advanced in battle until his life-span came to its end.

111.

111.

Veḷuppadamiḷaṃ nāma, disvā yujjhitumāgataṃ;

Tambulatthaviyaṃ hatthe, rakkhanto churikaṃ tadā.

Seeing a Damiḷa named Veḷuppa coming to fight, he was then guarding his dagger, with a betel-pouch in his hand.

112.

112.

Tato nikkaraṇiṃ sammā, gahetvā sīsamattano;

Chetvā hatthimhi appetvā, churikaṃ kosiyaṃ khipi.

Then, firmly grasping his sword, he cut off his own head. Having tossed it onto the elephant, he threw his dagger into its sheath.

113.

113.

Ugghosayi mahāsenā, mahāmaccopi so tadā;

Gantvā’bhiyogaṃ vatvāna, sīsacchedamhi rājino.

The great army shouted aloud, and that great minister then went and delivered the message concerning the beheading of the king.

114.

114.

Sandesaṃ deviyā vatvā, tāya pabbajjasāsane;

Samāpito bhidhammamhi, saddhimaṭṭhakathāya hi.

Having delivered the message to the queen, by her instruction on the going-forth he mastered the Abhidhamma together with its commentary.

115.

115.

Dhammāsanā samoruyha, nisīdiya mahītale;

Ehi rañño mahākāraṃ, dassehī’ti niyojito.

Having descended from the Dhamma seat and sat down upon the ground, he was instructed: 'Come, render great honor to the king.'

116.

116.

Nisajja purato tassā, chinditvā sīsamattano;

Khipitvā churikaṃ āha, evaṃ devo mato iti.

Having sat down before her, he cut off his own head, threw down the dagger, and said: 'Thus the king is dead.'

117.

117.

Sā taṃ disvā-tisokena, phāletvā hadayaṃ matā;

Evaṃ pañcahi māsehi, rājā so tidivaṃ gato.

Seeing that, she died with a broken heart from excessive grief. Thus, within five months, that king went to heaven.

118.

118.

Evaṃ [M 0.0279] vijitasaṅgāmo, sattavo abhimaddiya;

Rajjaṃ pākatikaṃ katvā, viharanto pure vare.

Thus, having been victorious in battle and having crushed his enemies, he made the kingdom stable and dwelt in the excellent city.

119.

119.

Uparājassa nāmena, kāritassa pana’ttanā;

Mahallarājā savhassa, padhānagharakassa so.

He, the king known as Mahalla, was the patron of the chief residence, which he himself had caused to be built, but in the name of the viceroy.

120.

120.

Addhā gāmadvayaṃ rājā, haṅkāraṃ sāmugāmakaṃ;

Kehellarājabhāgañca, sabbepi paricārake.

The king indeed granted two villages, Haṅkāra and Sāmugāma, and also the royal share of Kehella, to all his attendants.

121.

121.

Tathā jetavanassa’dā, mahāmaṇikagāmakaṃ;

Mayettikassapāvāsaṃ, sālagāmena pūjayi.

Likewise, he gave the village of Mahāmaṇika to the Jetavana monastery. He honored the residence of Mayettikassapa with the village of Sālagāma.

122.

122.

Ambillapadaraṃ cā’dā, cetiyassa girissa so;

Pulatthinagare kāsi, mahāpānādi dīpakaṃ.

He also gave Ambillapadara to Cetiyagiri. In Pulatthinagara, he provided a great offering of lamps and other things.

123.

123.

Amaccā tassa māresuṃ, māṇavhaṃ yuvarājakaṃ;

Antopure’parajjhitvā, datvāpi samamettikaṃ.

His ministers killed the viceroy named Māṇa after he had committed an offense in the inner palace, even though they had granted him an equal alliance.

124.

124.

Tato kassapanāmaṃ so, kaṇiṭṭhaṃ sakabhātaraṃ;

Pālento santatiṃ rājā, oparajje’bhisecayi.

Then that king, protecting the lineage, consecrated his own younger brother named Kassapa in the office of viceroy.

125.

125.

Māṇassa maraṇaṃ sutvā, gahetvā damiḷe lahuṃ;

Dāṭhāsivo samāgañchi, gāmaṃ tintiṇī nāmakaṃ.

Having heard of Māṇa's death and having quickly gathered the Damiḷas, Dāṭhāsiva came to the village named Tintiṇī.

126.

126.

Tassāgamanamaññāma, nikkhamitvā savāhano;

Yujjhanto dvārase vasse, jambudīpaṃ palātavā.

Learning of his arrival, the king marched out with his army and, fighting in his twelfth year, he fled to Jambudīpa.

127.

127.

Pahāya sabbaṃ gacchanto, saññāṇatthāya attano;

Ekāvaliṃ gahetvāva, ekākī so hi nikkhami.

Abandoning everything, he departed alone, taking only a single string of pearls for his own recognition.

128.

128.

Ekāvaliṃ vināceva, rājā hutvā yathāvidhiṃ;

Ahu dāṭhopatissoti, visuto dharaṇī tale.

Having become king in accordance with custom, even without the single string of pearls, he became famous on the face of the earth as Dāṭhopatissa.

129.

129.

Itaro laddhaokāso, rajjamaggahi yujjhiya;

Aññamaññaṃ palāpesuṃ, evaṃ te antarantarā.

The other, having found an opportunity, seized the kingdom by fighting. Thus they drove each other out from time to time.

130.

130.

Evaṃ ubhinnaṃ rājūnaṃ, saṅgāmenā’bhipīḷito;

Loko upadduto-sabbo vihīnadhanadhaññavā.

Thus the entire populace, afflicted by the conflict of the two kings, was distressed and deprived of wealth and grain.

131.

131.

Dāṭhopatisso nāsesi, sabbaṃ pubbakarājūnaṃ;

Gaṇhī tīsu nikāyesu, sāraṃ dhātugharesu ca.

Dāṭhopatissa destroyed all the property of the former kings. He seized the valuables from the three Nikāyas and from the relic chambers.

132.

132.

Suvaṇṇapaṭimāyo so, suvaṇṇaṃ gaṇhi bhindiya;

Soṇṇamālādikaṃ sabbaṃ, pūjābhaṇḍaṃ nirākari.

He broke the golden images and took the gold. He confiscated all the articles of offering, such as golden garlands and the like.

133.

133.

Thūpārāme [M 0.0280] tathāgaṇhi, sovaṇṇaṃ thupikaṃ ghare;

Mahaggharatanākiṇṇaṃ, chattaṃ bhindittha cetiye.

Likewise, from a building in the Thūpārāma he took the golden finial. He shattered the parasol on the cetiya, which was studded with priceless gems.

134.

134.

Mahāpāḷimhi nāvāyo, damiḷānaṃ sadāpayi;

Rājagehā nijhāpesuṃ, saddhiṃ dhātugharena te.

He had the Damiḷas constantly supplied from the Mahāpāḷi alms hall. They burned down the royal palaces along with the relic chamber.

135.

135.

Pacchā vippaṭisārī so, desetuṃ, pāpamattano;

Kāresi saha bhogena, sākavatthuvihārakaṃ.

Later, becoming remorseful and in order to atone for his own evil deed, he used his wealth to have the Sākavatthu monastery built.

136.

136.

Bhāgineyyopi ratana-dāṭho iti jane suto;

Mahādīpādo hutvāna, sabhogo tamupaṭṭhahi.

His nephew, too, who was known among the people as Ratanadāṭha, became the Mahādipāda and attended upon him with his wealth.

137.

137.

Aggabodhimhi sampatte, rajjaṃ yuddhabalena ca;

Kassapo yuvarājā so, senaṃ rakkhitumattano.

When Aggabodhi had attained the kingdom by the force of battle, the viceroy Kassapa, in order to maintain his own army,

138.

138.

Duppañño sahasā bhetvā, thūpārāmamhi cetiyaṃ;

Devānaṃpiyatissena, khuddarājena ceva hi.

the foolish one, rashly broke the cetiya in the Thūpārāma, which had been built by Devānampiyatissa and also by the lesser king.

139.

139.

Pubbakehica rājūhi, pūjitaṃdhanasārakaṃ;

Aggahesi dunnitīhi, pāpakehi purakkhato.

Urged on by wicked men, he seized by means of bad policies the valuable wealth that had been offered by former kings.

140.

140.

Dakkhiṇassa vihārassa, cetiyaṃ paribhindiya;

Aggahesi dhanaṃ sāraṃ, evamaññepi bhindayi.

Having destroyed the cetiya of the Southern Monastery, he seized its valuable wealth. In the same way he destroyed others too.

141.

141.

Evaṃ karontaṃ taṃ rājā, dunnitikapurakkhataṃ;

Nāsakkhi kira vāretuṃ, aho pāpā nivāriyā.

The king, it is said, was unable to restrain him—who was urged on by bad policy—as he was acting in this way. Alas, how difficult it is to prevent evil deeds!

142.

142.

Taṃ vāretu masakkonto, thūpārāmamhi cetiyaṃ;

Bhinnaṃ tena sakāresi, sahassena samaṅgalaṃ.

Unable to restrain him, the king had the cetiya in the Thūpārāma, which had been broken by that one, repaired with a thousand pieces of gold and with auspicious ceremonies.

143.

143.

Tadā dāṭhopatissena, aggabodhi narissaro;

Jito rohaṇamevā’gā, sajjetuṃ balavāhanaṃ.

Then King Aggabodhi, having been defeated by Dāṭhopatissa, went to Rohaṇa to prepare his forces and transport.

144.

144.

Tatra ṭhito soḷasame, vasse byādhihato mato;

Tadā tassa kaṇiṭṭho so, yuvarājāpi kassapo.

While staying there, he was struck by an illness in his sixteenth year and died. Then his younger brother, the viceroy Kassapa,

145.

145.

Dāṭhopatissa rājānaṃ, jambudīpaṃ palāpiya;

Ekarajjamakādesaṃ, makuṭantu na dhārayi.

having caused King Dāṭhopatissa to flee to Jambudīpa, made the country a unified kingdom, but he did not wear the crown.

146.

146.

Sādhūnaṃ saṅgamene’sa, hutvā vippaṭisārako;

Nāsaṃ pāpassa kammassa, karissāmīti cintiya.

By associating with the virtuous, he became remorseful and thought: 'I will not commit an evil deed again.'

147.

147.

Pupphārāme phalārāme, vāpiyo’pi ca kārayi;

Mahācetittayañcāpi, mahāpūjāhi sakkari.

He had flower parks, fruit parks, and reservoirs built. He also venerated the three great cetiyas with great offerings.

148.

148.

Thūpārāmañca [M 0.0281] pūjetvā, ekaṃgāmañca tassadā;

Sabbāgamiyabhikkhūhi, dhammaṃdesāpayittha ca.

Having honored the Thūpārāma, he gave a village to it. And he had the Dhamma expounded by all the visiting monks.

149.

149.

Katvā maricavaṭṭimhi, pāsādaṃ sutthiraṃ tahiṃ;

Vāsayittha mahātheraṃ, nāgasāla nivāsitaṃ.

Having built a very firm mansion at Maricavaṭṭi, he had the great elder who was a resident of Nāgasāla dwell there.

150.

150.

Tatraṭṭhaṃ tamupaṭṭhāya, paccayeti catūhi’pi;

Abhidhammaṃ kathāpesi, saddhimaṭṭhakathāya so.

He attended upon that elder who was staying there with the four requisites, and he had him recite the Abhidhamma together with its commentary.

151.

151.

Nāgasālakamāvāsaṃ, katvā tasseva’dāsi so;

Mahāniṭṭhilagāmañca, paccayatthāya tassa’dā.

He built the Nāgasālaka residence and gave it to him. He also gave him the village of Mahāniṭṭhila for his support.

152.

152.

Atha dāthopatisso so, jambudīpā idhāgato;

Mahantaṃ balamādāya, karonto tena āhavaṃ.

Then that Dāṭhopatissa returned here from Jambudīpa, and taking a large army, he waged battle with him.

153.

153.

Kassapena susannaddha-vāhanena tato mari;

Dvādasāsuṃ kiretassa, rājabhūtassa hāyanā.

Then Kassapa, who had well-equipped vehicles, died; it is said that twelve years of his reign had passed.

154.

154.

Tassa dāṭhopatissassa, bhāgineyyo sanāmako;

Jambudīpaṃ palāyittha, bhīto tamhā mahāraṇe.

His nephew, who bore the same name, fled to Jambudīpa, being fearful of him in that great battle.

155.

155.

Evaṃ aniccā vata sabbabhogā,

Sudullabhā ceva khaṇeva sobhā;

Tasmāhi etesu ratiṃ vihāya,

Bhaveyya dhammābhimukho hitesī.

Alas, all enjoyments are impermanent, very difficult to obtain, and their splendor is momentary. Therefore, having abandoned delight in them, one who seeks what is beneficial should turn towards the Dhamma.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene confidence and spiritual urgency of good people.

Cha rājako nāma

The Six Kings

Dvicattālīsatimo paricchedo.

The Forty-Second Chapter.

Tecattālīsatima pariccheda

The Forty-Third Chapter

Caturājako

The Four Kings

1.

1.

Tato [M 0.0282] vijitasaṅgāmo, kassapo puritāsayo;

Mahāpāḷimhi saṅghassa, samiddhaṃ bhojanaṃ akā.

Then Kassapa, victorious in battle and with his aspirations fulfilled, provided abundant food for the Saṅgha in the Mahāpāḷi.

2.

2.

Nāgasālā nivāsiṃ so, mahādhammakathiṃ yatiṃ;

Mahāpūjāya pūjetvā, saddhammaṃ tena vācayi.

He honored with a great festival of offerings the ascetic dwelling in Nāgasālā, a great preacher of the Dhamma, and had him recite the good Dhamma.

3.

3.

Vasantaṃ bhātuāvāse, samuddissa likhāpayi;

Kaṭandhakāravāsiṃ so, pāḷi sabbaṃ sasaṅgahaṃ.

He had the entire Pāli with its compendia written down, dedicating it to the dweller in Kaṭandhakāra who was residing in his brother's monastery.

4.

4.

Jiṇṇaṃ saṅkharikammañca, navaṃ kāresi cetiye;

Saṅghabhogamanekañca, tattha tattha pavattayi.

He had repair work done on the old cetiyas and also had new work done. And here and there he established many sources of revenue for the Saṅgha.

5.

5.

Nānāmaṇisamujjotaṃ, kāsi cūḷamaṇittayaṃ;

Sataṃ paṇḍupalāsānaṃ, vatthadānena tappayi.

She had a set of three crest-jewels made, shining with various gems, and she satisfied a hundred monks, who were like withered leaves, with a gift of robes.

6.

6.

Tassāsuṃ bahavo puttā, jeṭṭho tesañca māṇako;

Sabbe te na vayappattā, bālāvigatabuddhino.

She had many sons, the eldest of whom was a youth. All of them had not reached maturity; they were foolish and devoid of wisdom.

7.

7.

Tato so byādhinā phuṭṭho, atekicchena kenaci;

Puttā me bālakā sabbe, ne’te rajjakkhamā iti.

Then he was afflicted by an incurable disease and thought: 'All my sons are children; they are not capable of ruling the kingdom.'

8.

8.

Vasantaṃ rohaṇe dese, bhāgineyyaṃ mahāmatiṃ;

Āhuya sabbaṃ pādāsi, rajjaṃ puttehi attano.

He summoned his wise nephew, who was dwelling in the country of Rohaṇa, and gave him the entire kingdom over his own sons.

9.

9.

Gandhamālādipūjāhi, pūjayitvāna cetiye;

Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ khamādhapasi, datvāna catupaccayaṃ.

Having worshipped the cetiyas with offerings of perfumes, garlands, and so on, and having given the four requisites, he had the Saṅgha of bhikkhus grant him forgiveness.

10.

10.

Evaṃ dhammaṃ caritvāna, mittāmaccajanesu ca;

Gato navahi vassehi, yathākammaṃ narādhipo.

Having thus conducted himself righteously towards his friends, ministers, and people, after nine years that lord of men passed away according to his kamma.

11.

11.

Katvā kattabbakiccaṃ so, mātulassa sagāravo;

Saṅgahanto janaṃ māṇo, damiḷe nīharāpayi.

Māna, being respectful towards his maternal uncle, performed the necessary duties, and while winning over the people, he had the Damiḷas expelled.

12.

12.

Ekato damiḷā hutvā, nibbāsema imaṃ iti;

Tasmiṃ ṭhite bahiddhāva, aggahesuṃ puraṃ sayaṃ.

The Damiḷas, having united, thought, 'Let us expel this man!' And while he was staying outside, they themselves seized the city.

13.

13.

Hatta [M 0.0283] dāṭhassa pesesi, jambudīpagatassa te;

Āgantuṃtava kāloti, sāsanaṃ rajjagāhaṇe.

They sent a message to Hatthadāṭha, who had gone to Jambudīpa, saying: 'It is time for you to come to seize the kingdom.'

14.

14.

Māṇo’pi saṅghaṃ pesesi, sāsanaṃ piturohaṇaṃ;

Pitā sutvāna taṃ āgā, na cīreneva rohaṇā.

Māna also sent the Saṅgha with a message to his father in Rohaṇa. Having heard it, his father came from Rohaṇa without delay.

15.

15.

Ubhe te mantayitvāna, akaṃsu sandhilesakaṃ;

Umiḷehi tato jātā, sabbe te samavuttino.

Those two consulted together and made a written treaty with the Damiḷas; thereupon all parties came to be of one accord.

16.

16.

Tato so pitaraṃ rajje, abhisiñcittha māṇako;

So’bhisitto nikāyānaṃ, sahassānaṃ tayaṃ adā.

Then the youth Māna consecrated his father in the kingdom. Once consecrated, he gave three thousand to the Nikāyas.

17.

17.

Saṅghaṃ raṭṭhañca saṅgayha, sabbaṃ rājakulaṭṭhitaṃ;

Bhaṇḍaṃ pesesi sattūhi, rakkhaṇatthāya rohaṇaṃ.

Having won over the Saṅgha, the country, and all who belonged to the royal family, he sent treasures to Rohaṇa for protection from enemies.

18.

18.

Hatthadāṭhopi sutvāna, damiḷānaṃ tu sāsanaṃ;

Khaṇenā’gā imaṃ dīpaṃ, gahetvā damiḷhaṃ balaṃ.

Hatthadāṭha, having heard the message of the Damiḷas, came to this island in a moment, bringing with him a Damiḷa army.

19.

19.

Tadā te damiḷā sabbe, paribhūtā idha ṭhitā;

Āyantameva taṃ gantvā, parivāresu mañjase.

Then all those Damiḷas who were staying here, having been overpowered, went to meet him as he was coming and surrounded him.

20.

20.

Māṇopi sutvā taṃ sabbaṃ, nāyaṃ kāloti yujjhituṃ;

Pesetvā piturājānaṃ, saddhiṃ sārena rohaṇaṃ.

Māna, too, hearing all that, thought, 'This is not the time to fight,' and sent his father the king to Rohaṇa, together with the elite troops.

21.

21.

Pubbadesaṃ sayaṃ gantvā, saṅgaṇhanto janaṃ vasī;

Laddhā damiḷapakkhaṃ so, gahetvā rājakaṃ puraṃ.

He himself went to the eastern country and dwelt there, winning over the people. That one, having gained the Damiḷa faction, seized the royal city.

22.

22.

Dāṭhopatisso rājāti, nāmaṃ sāveti attano;

Mātulaṃ viya taṃ loko, tena nāmena vohari.

He proclaimed his own name as King Dāṭhopatissa. The people addressed him by that name, just as they had his maternal uncle.

23.

23.

Pitucchaputtamānetvā, aggabodhi sanāmakaṃ;

Ṭhapetvā yuvarājatte, desañcā’dāsi dakkhiṇaṃ.

Having brought his paternal uncle's son, who was named Aggabodhi, he established him as viceroy and gave him the southern country.

24.

24.

Ṭhānantarañca pādāsi, nissitānaṃ yathārahaṃ;

Sāsanassa ca lokassa, sabbaṃ kattabbamācari.

He also gave offices to his dependents according to their merit. He performed everything that ought to be done for the Dispensation and for the world.

25.

25.

Mahāpāḷimhi dāpesi, savatthaṃ dadhibhattakaṃ;

Khīraṃ pāyāsakañceva, dhammaṃ suṇi uposathi.

At the Mahāpāḷi alms hall he had curd-rice with robes given, as well as milk and milk-rice. On Uposatha days he listened to the Dhamma.

26.

26.

Kāretvā sabbapūjāyo, desā petvāna desanaṃ;

Evamādīhi puññehi, attānaṃ’kāsi bhaddakaṃ.

Having had all kinds of worship performed and having had the teaching expounded—by these and other such meritorious deeds, he brought good fortune to himself.

27.

27.

Kassapassa vihārassa, datvāsenavhagāmakaṃ;

Mahāgallañca pādāsi, padhānagharakassa so.

He gave the village of Senavha to the Kassapa Vihāra, and he also granted the village of Mahāgalla for a meditation house.

28.

28.

Pariveṇassa [M 0.0284] morassa, akāsi sakagāmakaṃ;

Thūpārāmassa puṇṇoḷiṃ, datvā sakkāsi cetiyaṃ.

He donated his own village to the Mora Pariveṇa. He gave the village of Puṇṇoḷi to the Thūpārāma and paid homage to its cetiya.

29.

29.

Kappūrapariveṇaṃ so, kāresi abhayuttare;

Vihāraṃ tiputhullavhaṃ, katvā tasseva dāpayi.

He had the Kappūra Pariveṇa built at the Abhayuttara Vihāra. He also built the monastery called Tiputhulla and donated it to that same pariveṇa.

30.

30.

Tasmiṃ karonte vāresuṃ, sīmāyanto’ti bhikkhavo;

Theriyā te kibāhetvā, balaṃ tatheva kārayi.

While he was doing this, the bhikkhus of the Theravāda tradition tried to stop him, saying, 'You are encroaching on the boundary!' But he rejected those elders and had the work done by force.

31.

31.

Atha te te theriyā bhikkhū, dummaññū tattha rājini;

Assaddhaṃ taṃ viditvāna, pattanikkujjanaṃ karuṃ.

Then those bhikkhus of the Theravāda tradition, being displeased with the king and knowing him to be faithless, performed the act of overturning the alms bowl against him.

32.

32.

Vuttañhi muninā tena, assaddho yo upāsako;

Alābhāya ca bhikkhūnaṃ, ceteta’kkosati ca te.

For it has been said by the Sage: 'Whatever lay follower is faithless, strives for the non-receipt of gains by the bhikkhus, and reviles them...'

33.

33.

Pattanikujjanaṃ tassa, kattabbanti tato hi te;

Tassa taṃ kammamakaruṃ, loko maññittha aññathā.

"...the overturning of the bowl should be done to him.' Therefore, they performed that formal act against him, but the world misunderstood it.

34.

34.

Ādāyu kujjitaṃ pattaṃ, caranto bhikkhubhikkhakaṃ;

Nikujjeyya gharadvāre, tassā’ti kathikaṃ karuṃ.

They spread a rumor about this act, saying: 'A bhikkhu, taking an overturned bowl and wandering for alms, would overturn it at the door of that person's house.'

35.

35.

Tasmiṃ so samaye phuṭṭho, byādhinā mahatāmari;

Vassamhi navame rājā, sampatto jīvitakkhayaṃ.

At that time, afflicted by a great illness, the king died, reaching the end of his life in the ninth year of his reign.

36.

36.

Dappulopi tato rājā, gato rohaṇakaṃ sakaṃ;

Vāsaṃ kappesi tattheva, karonto puññasañcayaṃ.

Then King Dappula went to his own Rohaṇa. He took up residence right there, accumulating a store of merit.

37.

37.

Ito paṭṭhāya vakkhāma, tassa vaṃsamanākulaṃ;

Vuccamānamhi ettheva, tasmiṃ hoti asaṅkaro.

From here on we will relate his unconfused lineage, so that when it is spoken of herein, there will be no confusion.

38.

38.

Jāto okkākavaṃsamhi, mahātissoti vissuto;

Āsi eko mahāpuñño, samākiṇṇaguṇākaro.

Born in the Okkāka lineage, there was one renowned as Mahātissa, a man of great merit, a mine of manifold virtues.

39.

39.

Tasse’kā bhariyā āsi, saṅghapivāti vīssutā;

Dhaññapuññaguṇūpetā, dhītā rohaṇasāmino.

He had one wife, renowned as Saṅghapivā. She was the daughter of the lord of Rohaṇa, endowed with the virtues of fortune and merit.

40.

40.

Tassāputtā tayo āsuṃ, paṭhamo aggabedhiko;

Dutiyo dappulo nāma, tatiyo maṇiakkhiko.

She had three sons: the first was Aggabedhika, the second was named Dappula, and the third was Maṇiakkhika.

41.

41.

Ekāva dhītā tassāsi, rājanamagamā ca sā;

Jeṭṭho rohaṇanāmassa, desassā’si sayaṃ vasī.

He had only one daughter, and she was wedded to the king. The eldest son was himself the ruler of the country of Rohaṇa.

42.

42.

Mahāpāḷiṃ sa kāresi, mahāgāme mahādhano;

Dāṭhaggabodhināmañca, pariveṇaṃ tahi vaṃso.

That very wealthy one had the Mahāpāḷi alms hall built in Mahāgāma, and also a monastic college named Dāṭhaggabodhi there.

43.

43.

Kāṇagāmamhi [M 0.0285] kāṇānaṃ, gilānānañca sālake;

Vihāre paṭimāvhe ca, mahantaṃ paṭimāgharaṃ.

In Kāṇagāma, he built a hall for the blind and the sick; and in the monastery called Paṭimā, a large image house.

44.

44.

Patiṭṭhapesi katvāna, buddhatattha silāmayaṃ;

Mahantanāmaṃ sappañño, iddhīhi viya nimmitaṃ.

That wise one had a great stone image of the Buddha made and established there, which seemed as if it were created by psychic powers.

45.

45.

Sālavāṇañca kāresi, vihāraṃ attanāmakaṃ,

Pariveṇavihārañca, tathā kājaragāmakaṃ.

He had the Sālavāṇa Vihāra built, a monastery named after himself, the Pariveṇavihāra, and likewise the Kājaragāmaka Vihāra.

46.

46.

Navakammāni kāretvā, dhammasālavihārake;

Sayaṃ vaccakuṭī esa, tattha sodhesi buddhimā.

Having had new construction work done at the Dhammasāla Vihāra, that wise one himself cleaned the toilet there.

47.

47.

Ucciṭṭhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa, bhojanaṃ paribhuñjiya;

Maṇḍagāmañca saṅghassa, gāmaṃ’dāsi masādavā.

Having partaken of the leftover food of the community of bhikkhus, being of great faith, he gave the village of Maṇḍagāma to the Sangha.

48.

48.

Puññāne’tānicaññāni, katvā tasmiṃ divaṅgate;

Āsī tassā’nujo tattha, sāmi dappulanāmako.

When he had passed away after performing these and other meritorious deeds, his younger brother, named Dappula, became the lord there.

49.

49.

Isseraṃ tattha vattesi, sampamaddiya satta vo;

Mahādānaṃ pavattesi, nissaṅkaṃ rohaṇaṃ agā.

He exercised authority there, having crushed his enemies. He instituted a great largesse and took control of Rohaṇa without challenge.

50.

50.

Tassa tuṭṭho jano āha, mahāsāmīti esano;

Tato paṭṭhāya taṃ loko-mahāsāmīti vohari.

Pleased with him, the people said: "He is our Great Lord!" From that time onwards, the people addressed him as Mahāsāmī.

51.

51.

Sutvāna taṃ silādāṭho, narindo sakadhītaraṃ;

Tassa pādāsi santuṭṭho, guṇehi bahukehi ca.

Hearing of this, King Silādāṭha was pleased with his many virtues and gave him his own daughter in marriage.

52.

52.

Yujarājattamassādā, rajjayoggoti mānituṃ;

Māṇavammādayo tassa, puttā āsuṃ mahāsayā.

Honoring him as worthy of the kingdom, the king gave him the position of heir apparent. His sons, beginning with Mānavamma, were of great resolve.

53.

53.

Pāsāṇadipavāsissa, mahātherassa santike;

Dhammaṃ sutvā pasīditvā, tasmiṃ taṃ bahumānituṃ.

Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the great elder who dwelt at Pāsāṇadīpa, he gained faith in him and wished to show him great honor.

54.

54.

Vihāraṃ rohaṇe katvā, tassa pādāsi sopi taṃ;

Cātuddisiyasaṅghassa, paribhogāya vissajji.

He built a monastery in Rohaṇa and gave it to the elder. The elder, in turn, dedicated it for the use of the Sangha of the four quarters.

55.

55.

Ambamālā vihārādi, vihāre kārayi bahū;

Khadirālivihārañca, katvā deva mapūjayi.

The queen, named Devā, had many monasteries built, such as the Ambamālā Vihāra. Having also built the Khadirālivihāra, she made offerings there.

56.

56.

Pāsādamanurārāmaṃ, muttolambaṃ sujiṇṇakaṃ;

Sīrivaḍḍhañca pāsādaṃ, tathā takkambilaṃ paraṃ.

She repaired the very old Muttolamba Pāsāda with its hanging pearls, which was near the pleasure park, as well as the Sīrivaḍḍha Pāsāda and another at Takkambila.

57.

57.

Sodhetvā bhikkhavo tattha, dvattiṃsa parivāsayi;

Sabbapaccayadānena, santappetvā mahīmati.

Having restored them, the wise queen settled thirty-two bhikkhus there, satisfying them with the gift of all the requisites.

58.

58.

Adā [M 0.0286] kevaṭṭagambhīraṃ, gāmaṃ nāgavihārake;

Tathā rājavihārassa, gonnagāmaṃ samādiyi.

She gave the village of Kevattagambhīra to the Nāgavihāra, and likewise she assigned the village of Gonnagāma to the Rājavihāra.

59.

59.

Adā tīsavihārassa, tathākantikapabbakaṃ;

Cittalapabbatassā’dā, gāmaṃ so gonnaviṭṭhikaṃ.

She gave the Kantikapabbata to the Tissavihāra, and to the Cittalapabbata she gave the village of Gonnaviṭṭhika.

60.

60.

Datvā riyākarassesa, gāmaṃ somālavatthukaṃ;

Akāsi paṭimāgehaṃ, tatheva sumanoharaṃ.

Having given the village of Somālavatthuka to the Ariyākara Vihāra, she also built a very charming image house there.

61.

61.

Tatraṭṭhassa jinassā’kā, uṇṇalomaṃ mahagghiyaṃ;

Hemapaṭṭañca kāresi, sabbaṃ pūjāvidhiṃ sa’kā.

For the Jina image standing there, she made a valuable ūrṇā and also had a golden frontlet made. She performed all the proper rites of worship.

62.

62.

Cetiye parijiṇṇe so, sudhākammena rañjayi;

Tipañcahatthaṃ kāresi, metteyyaṃ sugataṃ paraṃ.

When a cetiya became dilapidated, he had it embellished with plasterwork. He also had a fifteen-cubit image made of the future Sugata, Metteyya.

63.

63.

Evamādini puññāni, appameyyāni so vibhū;

Akāsi ca sayaṃ sādhu, parivārehī kārayi.

Thus that powerful lord performed these and other immeasurable meritorious deeds. He performed them well himself and also had them performed by his retinue.

64.

64.

Parivārā ca tassāsuṃ, bahūpuññakarā narā;

Vihārā nekakā āsuṃ, katā tehi sappaccayā.

His attendants, too, were many men who performed meritorious deeds. Numerous monasteries were built by them, endowed with the necessary requisites.

65.

65.

Kadāci maggaṃ gacchaṃ so, araññamhi agāmake;

Senaṃ saṃvidahitvāna, vāsaṃ kappesi rattiyaṃ.

Once, while he was travelling on a road through a forest that had no villages, he arranged his army in a camp and took up residence for the night.

66.

66.

Sunahātavillitto so, subhuttosayane sukhe;

Nipannesu ghare ramme, niddāyitumupakkami.

Well-bathed and anointed, having eaten well, he lay down on a comfortable couch in a delightful house and tried to fall asleep.

67.

67.

Alabhanto tadā niddaṃ, kinnu kho iti kāraṇaṃ;

Pavattiṃ upadhārento, divase sabbamattano.

Unable to get to sleep, he wondered, "What could be the reason?" He began to reflect on all the events of his day.

68.

68.

Adisvā kāraṇaṃ anto, avassaṃ bahi hessati;

Iti cintiya yojesi, manussetaṃ gavesituṃ.

Not seeing any cause within, he thought, "It must surely be outside." Thinking thus, he dispatched men to investigate.

69.

69.

Evamāha ca nissaṅkaṃ, ayyakā mama rattiyaṃ;

Tementā rukkhamūlasmiṃ, ṭhitā ānetha te iti.

And he said without hesitation: "Sirs, bring those who are standing at the foot of a tree, getting wet in the night."

70.

70.

Tepi gantvā gavesantā, dīpahatthā mahājanā;

Mahāgāmā’gate bhikkhū, rukkhamūlagate tadā.

A great crowd of men, with lamps in their hands, went searching and found the bhikkhus who had come from Mahāgāma, then at the foot of a tree.

71.

71.

Te gantvā sāsanaṃ rañño, ārocesuṃ padhāviso;

Disvā ca bhikkhu santuṭṭho, netvā vāsagharaṃ sakaṃ.

They went and quickly reported the news to the king. The king was pleased to see the bhikkhus and led them to his own dwelling.

72.

72.

Niccadānāya bhikkhūnaṃ, ṭhapite rattacīvare;

Tesaṃ datvāna tintāni, cīvarāni samādiya.

He gave them red robes from the supply set aside for constant giving to bhikkhus, and took their own wet robes.

73.

73.

Sukkhāpiya [M 0.0287] ca katvāna, pādadhovanakādikaṃ;

Nisīdāpiya te sabbe, sayane sādhu santhate.

And having had their robes dried, and having provided for the washing of their feet and so forth, he had them all sit down on well-spread couches.

74.

74.

Bhesajjaṃ paṭiyādetvā, sayamevo’panāmiya;

Paccūsepi ca katvāna, kattabbaṃ bhojanādikaṃ.

Having prepared medicine and brought it himself, and also at dawn having prepared food and other necessary things,

75.

75.

Datvā kappiya kāre’tha, vissajjesi yathāruciṃ;

Evaṃ puññaratasseva, tassā’si divasaṃ gataṃ.

he gave what was allowable, had it made proper, and then dismissed them as they wished. Thus the day passed for him, who delighted in merit.

76.

76.

Evaṃ puññaparetasmiṃ, vasamāne naruttame;

Raṭṭhaṃ janapadaṃ sabbaṃ, yojetvā puññakammesu.

While that best of men, devoted to merit, was dwelling thus, having engaged the whole kingdom and country in meritorious deeds,

77.

77.

Māṇo pācinadesamhi, vasanto balasaṅgahaṃ;

Katvāna pituno senaṃ, dhanaṃ cevā harāpiya.

Māna, dwelling in the eastern country, gathered a force and had his father's army and wealth seized.

78.

78.

Kātuṃ saṅgāmamāgañchi, tipucullasagāmakaṃ;

Dāṭhopatisso taṃ sutvā, tambalaṃgā mahābalo.

He came to the village of Tipucullasa to wage war. Hearing this, the mighty Dāṭhopatissa of Tambalaṅgāma,

79.

79.

Tatthā’kaṃsu mahāyuddhaṃ, aññamaññaṃ samāgatā;

Yodhā dāṭho patissassa, māṇaṃ saṅgaṃva mārayuṃ.

having come together there, fought a great battle with one another. The warriors of Dāṭhopatissa killed Māna in the combat.

80.

80.

Taṃ sutvā dappulo sopi, sokasallahato mari;

Sattāha manurādhamhi, vasaṃ rajjamakārayi.

Hearing that, Dappula too died, struck by the dart of sorrow. He had ruled the kingdom for seven days, dwelling in Anurādhapura.

81.

81.

Rohaṇe tīṇi vassāni, esa rajjamakārayi;

Tasmā tassa kathā āsi, rohaṇamhi idhāpi ca.

This one ruled the kingdom in Rohaṇa for three years; therefore, the story about him was told both in Rohaṇa and here.

82.

82.

Evaṃ paremāriya āhavamhi,

Kicchena laddhāva narena bhogā;

Āsuṃ khaṇe vijjulatopa bhogā,

Ko buddhimā tesu ratiṃ kareyya.

Thus, when possessions are obtained by a person with difficulty after killing others in battle, those possessions are like a flash of lightning, lasting for a moment. What wise person would take delight in them?

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people,

Caturājako nāma

Named The Four Kings,

Tecattālīsatimo paricchedo.

The Forty-Third Chapter.

Catucattālīsatima pariccheda

The Forty-Fourth Chapter

Tirājako

The Three Kings

1.

1.

Accaye [M 0.0288] hatthadāṭhassa, aggabodhikumārako;

Kaṇiṭṭho rājino āsi, sirisaṅghādi bodhiko.

After the death of Hatthadāṭha, the prince Aggabodhi, the king's youngest brother, became king as Sirisaṅghabodhi.

2.

2.

Dhammarājā ayaṃ āsi, sammā dassanasaññuto;

Tasmā so puññakammāni, appameyyāni vattayi.

This one was a righteous king, endowed with right view; therefore he performed immeasurable meritorious deeds.

3.

3.

Nikāyattayavāsīnaṃ, bhattaggamavalokayi;

Mahāpāḷiñca vaḍḍhesi, māghātañceva kārayi.

He inspected the refectory for the residents of the three Nikāyas, enlarged the Mahāpāli alms hall, and established a prohibition on killing.

4.

4.

Ṭhānantarañca dāpesi, yathāraha manālayo;

Sipagottādiyoggehi, saṃgatehi ca saṃgahi.

Without attachment, he bestowed ranks as were deserved. He also gave his patronage to those who were suitable on account of their skills, lineage, and so forth.

5.

5.

Yattha katthaci disvāpi, bhikkhavo so mahāmati;

Sakkatvā sobhaṇāpesi, parittaṃ sāsanogadhaṃ.

That wise one, upon seeing bhikkhus anywhere whatsoever, would honor them and cause them to shine, even if their immersion in the Teaching was but slight.

6.

6.

Theraṃ so upasaṅkamma, nāgasālanivāsinaṃ;

Dāṭhāsivaṃ mahāpaññaṃ, sīlavantaṃ bahussutaṃ.

He approached the elder Dāṭhāsiva, a resident of Nāgasāla, who was of great wisdom, virtuous, and very learned.

7.

7.

Sakkacca naṃ tato sutvā, sammāsambuddhasāsanaṃ;

Dhamme’tīvapasīditvā, sabbasantikaro iti.

Having carefully heard from him the teaching of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha, and having gained extreme confidence in the Dhamma, he thought, 'This brings peace to all.'

8.

8.

Sutvā theriyavādānaṃ, pubbañātīnamattano;

Pāpānaṃ duṭṭhacittānaṃ, apakāre kate bahū.

Having heard that many injuries had been done to the adherents of the Theravāda by his own former relatives, who were evil and corrupt in mind,

9.

9.

Vihāre pariveṇe ca, jiṇṇepākatike akā;

Bhogagāme ca dāpesi, tattha tattha bahūdaye.

he restored the dilapidated monasteries and monastic cells, and he granted here and there revenue villages of great income.

10.

10.

Vicchinnapaccaye cākā, tadātyaṃ kurite viya;

Dāsakepi ca saṅghassa, yathāṭhāne ṭhapāpayi.

He restored interrupted requisites as if providing for the future, and he had the slaves of the Sangha established in their proper places.

11.

11.

Padhānaghara metassa, therassa’kāsanāmakaṃ;

Paṭiggahetvā taṃ so’pi, saṅghassā’dā mahāmatī.

He built a meditation hall for this elder, named after him; that wise one, having accepted it, in turn gave it to the Sangha.

12.

12.

Bhogagāme ca tassā’dā, bharattālaṃ kihimbilaṃ;

Katakañca tulādhāraṃ, andhakārakameva ca.

And he gave to it the revenue villages of Bharattāla, Kihimbila, Kataka, Tulādhāra, and Andhakāraka.

13.

13.

Andhakāraṃ [M 0.0289] antureḷiṃ, bālavaṃ dvāranāyakaṃ;

Mahānikaḍḍhikañceva, peḷahāḷaṃ tathāparaṃ.

Also Andhakāra, Antureḷi, Bālava, Dvāranāyaka, Mahānikaḍḍhika, and another named Peḷahāḷa.

14.

14.

Ete aññe ca so datvā, bhogagāme narissaro;

Dāsi ārāmike ceva, attano kira ñātake.

Having given these and other revenue villages, that lord of men also gave female slaves, monastery workers, and, it is said, his own relatives.

15.

15.

Tathā dvinnaṃ nikāyānaṃ, vihāre mandapaccaye;

Disvāpi ca sutvā vā, bhogagāme bahū adā.

Likewise, for the monasteries of the two Nikāyas that had insufficient requisites, having either seen or heard of their need, he gave many revenue villages.

16.

16.

Bahunā kintuvuttena, nikāyesu’pi tīsu’pi;

Adā gāmasahassaṃ so, bahuppādaṃ nirākulaṃ.

But what is the use of saying much? To the three Nikāyas he gave a thousand villages, rich in produce and free from disturbances.

17.

17.

Anussaranto so tiṇṇaṃ, ratanānaṃ guṇe vare;

Ekāvaliṃ gahetvāna, akkhamāla makā kira.

Recollecting the excellent qualities of the Three Jewels, he took a single-string pearl necklace and made it into a rosary, it is said.

18.

18.

Evaṃ sabbappayogehi, so’hu dhammaparāyano;

Sabbe tamanusikkhantā, hesu dhammakarā narā.

Thus in all his undertakings he was devoted to the Dhamma. Following his example, all the people became practitioners of the Dhamma.

19.

19.

Damiḷo potthakuṭṭhavo, tassa kammakaro tadā;

Māṭambiyavhaṃ kāresi, padhānagharamabbhutaṃ.

At that time his official, the Tamil Potthakuṭṭha, had a wonderful meditation hall called Māṭambiya built.

20.

20.

Būkakalle ambavāpiṃ, tantavāyikacāṭikaṃ;

Gāmaṃ niṭṭhilaveṭṭhiñca, tassā’dā so sadā sakaṃ.

He gave to it from his own property the Ambavāpi tank in Būkakalla, the village of Tantavāyikacāṭika, and Niṭṭhilaveṭṭhi.

21.

21.

Kappūrapariveṇe ca, kurundapillake tathā;

Mahārājaghare ceva, pāsāde so’va kārayi.

He also had palaces built in the Kappūrapariveṇa, in Kurundapillaka, and in the Mahārājaghara.

22.

22.

Aññatthā’dā tayo gāme, vihāresu mahādhano;

Potthasātavhayo pañño, vihāre jetanāmake.

The wise and very wealthy Potthasāta gave three other villages to monasteries. In the Jetavana monastery,

23.

23.

Senāpatirājanāmaṃ, pariveṇaṃ samāpayi;

Mahākando ca damiḷo, pariveṇaṃ sanāmakaṃ.

he completed the pariveṇa named Senāpatirāja. And the Tamil Mahākanda built a pariveṇa named after himself.

24.

24.

Cullapanthaṃ tathā eko, sehālauparājakaṃ;

Uparājā sakāresi, saṅghatisso’pi rājino.

The king's sub-king, Saṅghatissa, had the Cūḷapantha pariveṇa built, and also another one, the Sehālauparājaka.

25.

25.

Aññesu bahavo āsuṃ, vihāre evamādike;

Bhassa rañño’ nuvattantā, evaṃ dhammīhi pāṇino.

Thus there were many other righteous people in these and similar monasteries who followed the example of His Majesty the King.

26.

26.

Pāpaṃ vāpi hi puññaṃ vā,

Padhānoyaṃ karoti yo;

Lo ko taṃ taṃ karoteva,

Taṃ vijaneyya paṇḍito.

For whether it be evil or merit, whatever a leader does, the world does that very same thing. This a wise person should understand.

27.

27.

Jeṭṭhanāmā [M 0.0290] mahāpuññā, mahesī tassa rājino;

Jeṭṭhārāmañca kāresi, bhikkhūnīnamupassayaṃ.

His chief queen, Jeṭṭhā by name, a woman of great merit, had the Jeṭṭhārāma built as a residence for the bhikkhunīs.

28.

28.

Tassā’dāsi ca dve gāme, pakkapāsāṇabhūmiyaṃ;

Tambuddhaṃ bhelagāmañca, ārāmikasataṃ tathā.

He gave to her two villages on land with solid rock, Tambuddha and Bhelagāma, and likewise a hundred monastery attendants.

29.

29.

Akā malayarājāpi, dhātugehaṃ mahārahaṃ;

Maṇḍalagirivihāramhi, cetiyassa mahādhano.

The king of Malaya, a man of great wealth, also built a costly relic-shrine for the cetiya at the Maṇḍalagiri Vihāra.

30.

30.

Lohapāsādake so’va, chādesi majjhakūṭakaṃ;

Bodhitissavihārañca, bodhitasso mahāyaso.

He also covered the central pinnacle of the Lohapāsāda. And the greatly renowned Bodhitissa built the Bodhitissa Vihāra.

31.

31.

Dīpe maṇḍalikā sabbe, tattha tattha yathābalaṃ;

Vihāre pariveṇe ca, kārayiṃsu anappake.

All the provincial chiefs on the island, here and there according to their ability, had a great many vihāras and pariveṇas built.

32.

32.

Tassa kālo narindassa, puññakammamayo idha;

Ativitthārabhītena, sabbaso na vicāritaṃ.

The time of that king here was filled with meritorious deeds, but for fear of excessive length, this has not been described in full.

33.

33.

Pubbakopi kathāmaggo, ākulo viya bhātime;

Yathāpadhānaṃ kathitaṃ, hetūnaṃ upalakkhaṇaṃ.

The previous course of the narrative also seems confused to me. It has been told according to its main points, with an indication of the causes.

34.

34.

Athāparena kālena, pulatthinagaraṃ gato;

Vāsaṃ tattheva kappesi, karonto puññasañcayaṃ.

Then after some time, he went to the city of Pulatthinagara and took up his residence right there, accumulating a store of merit.

35.

35.

Atekicchiyarogena, samphuṭṭho kālamattano;

Maraṇassa viditvāna, tamāhuyamahājanaṃ.

Afflicted by an incurable disease and knowing that his time of death was near, he summoned the people.

36.

36.

Ovaditvāna dhammena, maraṇaṃ so upāgami;

Mahājano mate tasmiṃ, bāḷhasoko parodiya.

Having given admonition in accordance with the Dhamma, he passed away. When he died, the populace, overcome by deep sorrow, wept bitterly.

37.

37.

Katvā āḷahaṇe tassa, kiccaṃ sabbamasesato;

Tassāḷāhaṇabhasmampi, katvā bhesajjamattano.

Having performed all the rites for his cremation completely, the people made even the ashes from his pyre into a medicine for themselves.

38.

38.

Rājā bhaṇḍañca taṃ sabbaṃ, sabbañca balavāhanaṃ;

Sammā ādāya gopetvā, nagaraṃ samupāgami.

The king, having duly taken and secured all the treasures and the entire army with its transport, went to the city.

39.

39.

Evaṃ soḷasame vasse, rājā āsi divaṅgato;

Potthakuṭṭhopi damiḷo, rajjaṃ tassa vicārayi.

Thus in his sixteenth year the king passed away. Then Potthakuṭṭha the Tamil administered his kingdom.

40.

40.

Uparājaṃ gahetvāna, dāṭhāsivaṃ khipāpayi;

Cārako vihituṃ sammā, rakkhāvaraṇa mādisi.

Having seized the Uparāja Dāṭhāsiva, he had him banished and ordered a protective guard to be properly arranged.

41.

41.

Vinā raññā na sakkāti, mediniṃ paribhuñjituṃ;

Ānetvā dattanāmakaṃ, dhanapiṭṭhappadhānakaṃ.

Thinking, 'Without a king it is not possible to rule the earth,' he brought a man named Datta, a chief of Dhanapiṭṭha,

42.

42.

Uppannaṃ [M 0.0291] rājavaṃsamhi, rajje taṃ abhisiñciya;

Tassa nāmaṃ ṭhapetvāna, sayaṃ sabbaṃ vicārayi.

who was born in the royal lineage, and consecrated him as king. Having established his name, he himself administered everything.

43.

43.

Danto so dhanapiṭṭhimhi, vihāraṃ sakanāmakaṃ;

Kārayitvāna puññāni, aññānipi samācini.

That Danta had a vihāra named after himself built at Dhanapiṭṭhi, and he also accumulated other merits.

44.

44.

Samakantu so ṭhatvā’va, vassadvaya mahumato;

Potthakuṭṭho matetasmiṃ, puna aññampi māṇavaṃ.

After he had reigned for two years, he died. When he was dead, Potthakuṭṭha again took another youth,

45.

45.

Hatthadāṭhaṃ samāhūya, uṇhā nagarasambhavaṃ;

Tampi rajje bhisiñcitvā, yathā pubbaṃ sayaṃvasī.

namely Hatthadāṭha, who was born in the city of Uṇhanāgara. Having consecrated him also in the kingship, he himself ruled as before.

46.

46.

Kāḷadīghāvikaṃ katvā, padhānagharakaṃ tathā;

Puññamaññaṃ chamāsehi, so’pi maccuvasaṃ gato.

He built the Kāḷadīghāvika tank and also a meditation house. Having acquired other merit, after six months he too came under the sway of death.

47.

47.

Evaṃ viditvā bahupaddavāni;

Dhanāni dhaññāni ca vāhanāni;

Vihāya rajjesu ratiṃsappaññā;

Manuññapuññābhiratā bhaveyyuṃ.

Thus, understanding the many dangers associated with wealth, grain, and vehicles, the wise should abandon delight in kingdoms and instead delight in pleasing merit.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual emotion of the good.

Tirājako nāma

The Chapter named 'The Three Kings'.

Catucattālīsatimo paricchedo.

The Forty-fourth Chapter.

Pañcacattālīsatima pariccheda

The Forty-fifth Chapter.

1.

1.

Rañño tassaccaye rājā, māṇavammo ahosi so;

Kiṃ gotto kassa putto ca, kathaṃ rajjamapāpuṇi.

On the passing of that king, Māṇavamma became king. Of what clan was he, whose son was he, and how did he attain the kingdom?

2.

2.

Mahāsammatavaṃsamhi, jāto jātiguṇāvaho;

Putto kassapanāmassa, thūpārāmassa bhedino.

He was born in the lineage of Mahāsammata, an enhancer of his clan's virtues, the son of the one named Kassapa, the despoiler of the Thūpārāma.

3.

3.

Dhītā malayarājassa, saṅghanāmassa rājino;

Taṃ labhitvā vasaṃ dese, uttare līnavuttiko.

Having taken to wife the daughter of the king of Malaya, King Saṅgha by name, he lived in obscurity in the northern country.

4.

4.

Hatthadāṭhanarindena, tasmiṃ attheva dhārite;

Jambudīpamupāgamma, narasīhaṃ mahīpati.

When King Hatthadāṭha was slain there, he went to Jambudīpa, to the lord of the earth, a lion among men.

5.

5.

Gantvā vatvā [M 0.0292] sakaṃ nāmaṃ, sevituṃ tamupakkami;

Ārādhesi ca sabbehi, payogehi narādhīpaṃ.

Having gone and announced his name, he began to serve him. And he gratified the lord of men by every possible means.

6.

6.

Viditvā tassa sohajjaṃ, netvā bhariyamattano;

Vāsaṃ tattheva kappesi, sevamāno divānisaṃ.

Recognizing the king's affection for him, he brought his own wife and took up residence right there, serving him day and night.

7.

7.

Sopi ārādhito tena, kaṇḍuveṭṭhi naruttamo;

Sabbaṃ nentova taṃ rajjaṃ, mahābhogamadāpayi.

That best of men, King Kaṇḍuveṭṭhi, being pleased with him, had great wealth bestowed upon him, as if the whole kingdom were being led away.

8.

8.

Tena saṃvāsamanvāya, bhariyā saṅghanāmikā;

Catasso dhītaro putte, cattāropi vijāyatha.

Through living with him, his wife, named Saṅghā, bore four daughters and also four sons.

9.

9.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā, hatthikkhandhavaraṃ gato;

Sañcaranto yathākāmaṃ, māṇavammena ekato.

Then one day the king, mounted on the back of his excellent elephant, was wandering about at will, together with Mānavamma.

10.

10.

Nāḷikeraṃ pivitvāna, tatraṭṭhova pipāsito;

Māṇavammassa pādāsi, maññanto aññameva taṃ.

Having drunk from a coconut, the king, mistaking him for another, gave it to Mānavamma, who stood there thirsty.

11.

11.

So taṃ gahetvā cintesi, sakhaṃ pesa narādhipo;

Ucchiṭṭhaṃ nāma kiṃ hoti, sattānaṃ paramatthato.

Taking it, he thought: 'This lord of men is my friend. In the ultimate sense, what is this thing called a leftover for beings?'

12.

12.

Tasmā yuttaṃ mayāpātu-mīti cintiya taṃ pivi;

Evaṃ honti mahussāhā, detukāmāhi buddhino.

Thinking, 'Therefore it is proper for me to drink it,' he drank it. Thus are the wise who are of great endeavor and wish to be of service.

13.

13.

Rājāpi disvā taṃ bhīto, tassapī tāva sesakaṃ;

Sayaṃ pivi tathāhoti, kammaṃ puññavataṃ sadā.

The king, seeing this, was alarmed and himself drank from the remainder of that same vessel. Such is ever the conduct of the meritorious.

14.

14.

Ṭhapesi sakaveseva, tato paṭṭhāya attano;

Bhojane sayane ceva, parihāre ca vāhane.

From that time onward, he established him as his own equal in food, lodging, attendance, and vehicles.

15.

15.

Evaṃ tesu vasantesu, yuddhatthāyamupakkami;

Vallabho narasīhena, narasīho vicintayi.

While they were dwelling thus, Vallabha prepared for battle with Narasīha. The man-lion, Narasīha, reflected:

16.

16.

Ayaṃ kho mama sevāya, rajjaṃ vaṃsa gataṃ sakaṃ;

Labhissāmīti seveti, rattiṃ diva matandito.

'Thinking, "Through my service, I will obtain my own kingdom, which has come down through my lineage," this man serves me tirelessly day and night.'

17.

17.

Sace sopi mayā gantvā, yujjhanto maraṇaṃ gato;

Takkitaṃ tassa mayhañca, sabbaṃ tamaphalaṃ bhave.

'If he should go with me and die while fighting, then his aspiration and mine would all become fruitless.'

18.

18.

Evaṃ cintiyataṃ rājā, nivattetvā sake pure;

Sayaṃ vallabharājena, kātuṃ saṅgāmamārasi.

Having reflected thus, the king sent him back to his own city and himself set out to do battle with King Vallabha.

19.

19.

Māṇavammopi cintesi, sace’yaṃ mayi jīviti;

Rājā mīyati yuddhamhi, kiṃ phalaṃ mama jīvite.

Māṇavamma for his part reflected: 'If this king should die in battle while I remain alive, of what use is my life?'

20.

20.

Vissāso [M 0.0293] dukkato tena, bhavissati tathāsati;

Saṅgahesi kimatthaṃ maṃ, samānattena attano.

'In that case, his trust would have been misplaced. For what reason did he support me, treating me as his own equal?'

21.

21.

Tasmā yuttaṃ mayā gantuṃ, sahasaṅgāma maṇḍalaṃ;

Sukhañhi saddhiṃ tenettha, jīvitaṃ maraṇaṃpi vā.

'Therefore, it is proper for me to go with him to the battlefield. For with him, it is a blessing, be it life or even death.'

22.

22.

Evaṃ cintiya sannaddha-balo hatthivaraṃ gato;

Gantvā dassesi attānaṃ, so taṃ saṅgāma maṇḍale.

Having reflected thus, armed and with his forces, he mounted a choice elephant. Then he went and presented himself to the king on the battlefield.

23.

23.

Narasīhova taṃ disvā, haṭṭhatuṭṭho samuggiri;

Saho santhavametasmiṃ, kattabbaṃ me kataṃ iti.

When Narasīha saw him, joyful and elated, he exclaimed: 'Ah, the friendship with this one! What was to be done by me has been done!'

24.

24.

Tato mānassa senā ca, senā cevassarājino;

Senaṃ vallabharājassa, viddhaṃsesi samāgatā.

Then the army of Māna and the army of the horse-king, having come together, utterly destroyed the army of King Vallabha.

25.

25.

Māṇavammopi dassesi, tahiṃ surattamattano;

Parakkamanto devānaṃ, raṇe nārāyaṇo viya.

Māṇavamma, too, displayed his own valor there, striving in battle like Nārāyaṇa among the devas.

26.

26.

Narasītopi santuṭṭho, māṇavammassa vikkame;

Āliṅgatvā sinehena, tvaṃ kho me jayado iti.

Narasīha, too, was pleased with Māṇavamma's valor. Embracing him with affection, he said: 'You are indeed the giver of my victory!'

27.

27.

Attano puramāgamma, katvā vijayamaṅgalaṃ;

Māṇavammassa senāya, kattabbaṃ sabbamācari.

Having returned to his own city and held a victory festival, he did everything that needed to be done for Māṇavamma's army.

28.

28.

Athevaṃ cintayi rājā, kattabbaṃ me sahāyako;

Attanā’kāsi sabbañca, anaṇo so mamajjato.

Then the king reflected thus: 'My companion has done all that was to be done by himself. As of today, he is free of debt to me.'

29.

29.

Iṇaṃ mamāpi sodhemi, katvā kattabbamattanā;

Kattaññū katavedīhi, purisā’tīvadullabhā.

'I, too, must clear my debt to him by doing what ought to be done myself. For men who are grateful and mindful of help rendered are exceedingly rare.'

30.

30.

Amacce sannipātetvā, idaṃ vacanamabravi;

Sahāyassa mametassa, kamme tumhepi sakkhino.

Having assembled his ministers, he spoke these words: 'You yourselves are witnesses to the deed of this friend of mine.'

31.

31.

Mayāpi tassa kattabbaṃ, kammaṃ sādhu sukhāvahaṃ;

Upakāro hi sādhūnaṃ, dhammo pubbopakārino.

'I too must do a good and beneficial deed for him. For it is the nature of the virtuous to help one who has helped them before.'

32.

32.

Evaṃ vutte amaccā te, paccāhaṃsu mahīpati;

Yaṃ yamicchati devohi, taṃ taṃ ruccati no iti.

When he had spoken thus, those ministers replied to the lord of the earth: 'Whatever our lord desires, that is pleasing to us.'

33.

33.

Atha so māṇavammassa, senaṃ datvā savāhanaṃ;

Sabbopakaraṇañceva, sabbakammakarepi ca.

Then he gave to Māṇavamma an army with its mounts, all its equipment, and also all the necessary artisans.

34.

34.

Gacchāti vatvā taṃ yantaṃ, sahasenāyapekkhiya;

Paridevittha bhūmindo, vippavutthaṃ’va puttakaṃ.

Having said, 'Go!' the lord of the land watched him departing with his army and lamented as if for a son gone far away.

35.

35.

Māṇavammopi [M 0.0294] āruyha, nāvāyo jaladhītaṭe;

Na cireneva āgamma, samattikkamma vegasā.

Māṇavamma, for his part, embarked on ships at the ocean shore. Having crossed over swiftly, he arrived in no long time.

36.

36.

Saha senāya maddantho, laṅkādīpamupavisī;

Taṃ sutvāna palāyittha, rājā dāṭhopatissako.

Crushing his foes with his army, he entered the island of Laṅkā. Hearing of this, King Dāṭhopatissa fled.

37.

37.

Māṇavammo puraṃ gantvā, ahutvāva narādhipo;

Palātamanubandhittha, padānupadamugato.

Māṇavamma went to the capital, but the ruler was not there. He pursued the fugitive, tracking him footstep by footstep.

38.

38.

Tadā sā damiḷi senā, assosi kira sāmiko;

Mahārogā’bhibhūtoti, sutvā taṃ sā apakkami.

Then that Damila army heard a rumor that their lord was overcome by a great disease. Hearing this, they withdrew.

39.

39.

Sutvā dāṭhopatisso taṃ, samādāya mahābalaṃ;

Māṇavammaṃ upāgamma, kātumārabhi saṃyudhaṃ.

Hearing this, Dāṭhopatissa gathered a great army, approached Māṇavamma, and began to give battle.

40.

40.

Māṇavammo ca cintesi, sabbā senā gatā mama;

Mate mayi samijjheyya, verino me manorathaṃ.

And Māṇavamma reflected: 'My entire army has departed. If I am killed, my enemy's wish will be fulfilled.'

41.

41.

Jambudīpaṃva tasmā’haṃ, gantvā’dāsa balaṃ tato;

Puna rajjaṃ gahessaṃti, tasmā evamakāsi so.

'Therefore I must go back to Jambudīpa, bring a force from there, and take the kingdom again.' And so he did.

42.

42.

Gantvā puna’pi disvāna, sahāyaṃ narasīhakaṃ;

Ārādhahanto nipuṇaṃ, sakkaccaṃ tamupaṭṭhahi.

Having gone and seen his friend Narasīha again, he attended upon him respectfully, skillfully seeking to please him.

43.

43.

Yāva rājacatukkaṃso, māṇāmmo tahiṃ vasi;

Narasīho’tha cintesi, mānatthaddho yasodhano.

Māṇavamma dwelt there for a period of time. Then Narasīha, proud and rich in glory, reflected:

44.

44.

Rajjatthaṃ me sahā yo maṃ, sevantoyeva addhago;

Vuddho hessati taṃ passaṃ, kathaṃ rajjaṃ karomahaṃ.

'This companion of mine, who serves me for the sake of a kingdom, has spent a long time on the road and is growing old. Seeing him thus, how can I enjoy my own rule?'

45.

45.

Imasmiṃ pana vārasmiṃ, pesayitvā balaṃ mama;

Rajjaṃ taṃ na gahessāmi, ko attho jīvitena me.

'But if on this occasion, after I have sent my army, he does not take that kingdom, what is the use of my life?'

46.

46.

Evaṃ cintiya so senaṃ, sannipātiya attano;

Sannāhetvā yathā yogaṃ, dāpetvāna yathāruciṃ.

Having reflected thus, he assembled his own army, equipped them as was fitting, and had gifts given to them according to their desires.

47.

47.

Sayameva tamādāya, samuddataṭamāgato;

Nāvāyo cittarūpāyo, kārayitvā thirā bahū.

He himself, taking the army, went to the seashore, where he had many strong and beautifully decorated ships built.

48.

48.

Amacce āha “etena, saddhiṃ gacchatha bho”iti;

Nāvaṃ ārohituṃ sabbe, na icchiṃsu tadā janā.

He said to his ministers: 'Go with this man.' But at that, none of the men were willing to board the ships.

49.

49.

Tadā sīho vicintetvā, sayaṃ hutvā tirohito;

Attano parihāraṃ so, rājalakkhaṇasammataṃ.

Then the Lion, having reflected, made himself inconspicuous; his own royal insignia, which are regarded as the marks of a king,

50.

50.

Sabbaṃ [M 0.0295] tasseva datvāna, alaṅkārampi attano;

Āropetvāna taṃ nāvaṃ, gaccha ṭhatvāna sāgare.

he gave entirely to him, even his own ornaments. Having made him board the ship, he stood by the ocean and said, 'Go!'

51.

51.

Imaṃ bheriṃca vādehi, koṭṭhanāmanti yojayī;

So’pi sabbaṃ tathākāsi, rājāno agamā iti.

He also instructed: 'Beat this drum named Koṭṭha.' He did all this accordingly, so that it was thought, 'The king is departing.'

52.

52.

Āruhiṃsu janā nāvaṃ, ekaṃ katvā narādhipaṃ;

So taṃ senaṅgamādāya, māṇo gantuṃ samārabhi.

The people boarded the ship, making the ruler their one leader. Then Māṇa, taking that army, began to go.

53.

53.

Kevalo’pi samuddo so, ahobhi nagarūpamo;

Atha so paṭṭanaṃ patvā, otaritvā savāhano.

That entire ocean became like a city. Then, having reached a port, he disembarked with his retinue.

54.

54.

Vissāmetvā balaṃ tattha, vasaṃ katipaye dine;

Uttaraṃ desamādāya, katvā hatthagataṃ janaṃ.

Having rested his army there and stayed for a few days, he took the northern region, bringing its people under his control.

55.

55.

Akkhobbhiya mahāseno, nagaraṃ gantumārabhi;

Potthakuṭṭhopi taṃ sutvā, paccuggañchi mahābalo.

With an unshakable, great army, he set out for the city. Potthakuṭṭha, hearing of this, marched out with his mighty force.

56.

56.

Saṃgacchiṃsu ubho senā, bhinnavelā’va sāgarā;

Māṇavammo tato hatthi-māruyha gahitāyudho.

The two armies clashed like oceans with broken shores; then Māṇavamma, with weapon in hand, mounted his elephant.

57.

57.

Potthakuṭṭhañca rājānaṃ, dvedhā katvā palāpayi;

Hatthadāṭhaṃ palāyantaṃ, disvā janapadā narā.

He routed King Potthakuṭṭha and made him flee. Seeing Hatthadāṭha fleeing, the people of the countryside,

58.

58.

Sīsamassa gahetvāna, māṇavammassa dassayuṃ;

Potthakuṭṭhopalāyitvā, merukandaramāgami.

seized his head and showed it to Māṇavamma. Potthakuṭṭha, having fled, reached a cave on Mount Meru.

59.

59.

Tato taṃ sāmiko disvā, sahāyo me ayaṃciraṃ;

Tasmā na sakkā caḍḍetuṃ, āpade saraṇāgataṃ.

Then his master, seeing him, thought: 'This has long been my companion; therefore, it is not possible to abandon one who has come for refuge in distress.'

60.

60.

Sāmino ca sahāyassa, niddosohaṃ kathaṃ bhave;

Iti cintiya pūvaṃ so, savisaṃ khādiyā’mari.

'How can I be blameless with respect to my master and companion?' Thinking thus, he ate a poisoned cake and died.

61.

61.

Kuṭṭhakopi ca teneva, khāditvā pūvakaṃ mato;

Māṇavammassa tassevaṃ, dīpo āsi akaṇṭako.

Kuṭṭhaka also died by eating that same cake; thus the island became free of thorns for Māṇavamma.

62.

62.

Māṇavammo tato dīpe, chattaṃ ussāpayi tadā;

Vārento viya teneva, dukkhaṃ dīpe janassa so.

Then Māṇavamma raised his parasol over the island, as if by that very act he were warding off the suffering of the people of the island.

63.

63.

Puññakammāni so’kāsi, anagghāni bahūni ca;

Samattho kohi taṃ sabbaṃ, vattuṃ paṭipadaṃ naro.

He performed many priceless meritorious deeds; what man is capable of recounting them all in detail?

64.

64.

Kappagāmavhayañceva, tathā sepaṇṇināmakaṃ;

Padhānarakkhe ca siriṃ, sirīsaṅghādi bodhike.

He built the monastery called Kappagāma, and likewise the one named Sepaṇṇi, and at Padhānarakkha the Siri monastery, and the Sirisaṅghabodhi monastery.

65.

65.

Pāsādaṃ [M 0.0296] sova kāresi, pasādāvahamuttamo;

Chādesi lohapāsādaṃ, thūpārāmagharaṃ tathā.

He had a beautiful and inspiring palace built, a most excellent abode; he roofed the Lohapāsāda, and likewise the shrine-house of the Thūpārāma.

66.

66.

Thūpārāme ca pāsādaṃ katvā’dā paṃsukūlinaṃ;

Jiṇṇakaṃ paṭisaṅkhāsi chattaṃ cetiyamuddhani;

Bahavo jiṇṇakāvāse tattheva paṭisaṅkhari.

At the Thūpārāma, he built a residence and gave it to the rag-robed monks; he repaired the old parasol on the summit of the cetiya, and also repaired many old residences there.

[Ettha māṇavammassa rajjakathāya ūnatā dissati. Ito paṭṭhāya aggabodhissa rajjapaṭibaddhā kathā vira khāyati.]

[Here, the account of Māṇavamma's reign appears deficient. From this point onward, the story connected to Aggabodhi's reign becomes clear.]

Chacattālīsatima pariccheda

The Forty-Sixth Chapter

1.

1.

…Vāsaṃ-katvā sulabhapaccayaṃ;

Dāsi dhammarucinaṃ so, rājinī dīpakampi ca.

…having established a residence with easily obtainable requisites, he gave it to those who delight in the Dhamma, and also to the queen and Dīpaka.

2.

2.

Kāretvāna paricchedaṃ, mahānettādi pādikaṃ;

Tesameva adā koḷu-vāte so devatissakaṃ.

Having had a boundary demarcated, beginning with the great leaders, he gave Devatissaka at Koḷuvāta to those same monks.

3.

3.

Vahatthale ca so katvā, kadambagonanāmakaṃ;

Devapāḷimhi katvāna, gīrivhanagaraṃ tathā.

And at Vahatthala he built the one named Kadambagona; at Devapāḷi he likewise built the Girinagara.

4.

4.

Katvā antarasobbhamhi, devanāmaṃ vihārakaṃ;

Rājamātikamārāmaṃ, katvā’dā paṃsukūlinaṃ.

Having built the Devanāma monastery at Antarasobbha, and having built the Rājamātikārāma, he gave it to the rag-robed monks.

5.

5.

Gokaṇṇakavihāre’kā, padhānagharameva ca;

Jiṇṇagehañca kāresi, vaḍḍhamānakabodhiyā.

At the Gokaṇṇaka monastery, he built a meditation hall; and he had an old house built for the growing Bodhi tree.

6.

6.

Saṅghamittavhaye ceva, aññattha ca mahāyaso;

Tattha tattha vihāresu, navakammamakārayi.

In the monastery called Saṅghamitta and elsewhere, that one of great fame had renovation work done in various monasteries.

7.

7.

Chabbīsati sahassāni, suvaṇṇānaṃ samappiya;

Jiṇṇāni paṭisaṅkhāsi, rājā cetiyapabbate.

Having offered twenty-six thousand gold pieces, the king renovated the dilapidated buildings at Cetiyapabbata.

8.

8.

Tālavatthuvihārañca, kāretvā paṇṇabhattakaṃ;

Vihārassa mahāsena-narindavhassa dāpayi.

Having had the Tālavatthu monastery built, he established a ticket-meal offering for the monastery named after Mahāsena, the king of men.

9.

9.

Goṇḍigāmikavāpiñca, chinnaṃ bandhi yathā purā;

Dānabhaṇḍañca so sabbaṃ, sabbesaṃ dāsi pāṇinaṃ.

He repaired the breached Goṇḍigāmika tank as it was before; and he gave all items of donation to all living beings.

10.

10.

Uposathaṃ [M 0.0297] upavasati, saddhiṃ dīpajanehi so;

Dhammañca tesaṃ deseti, dātuṃ lokuttaraṃ sukhaṃ.

He observed the Uposatha together with the people of the island; and he taught them the Dhamma in order to bestow supramundane happiness.

11.

11.

Kammaṃ sovaggiyaṃ tassa, rajje sabbo samācari;

Yaṃ karoti mahīpālo, taṃ tassa kurute jano.

His deeds were conducive to heaven; everyone in the kingdom conducted themselves accordingly. Whatever the ruler does, that the people also do.

12.

12.

Tasmā rājā mahāpañño, dhammameva samācare;

So nivutthanivutthamhi, ṭhāne hoti mahāyaso.

Therefore, a king of great wisdom should practice only the Dhamma; established in each successive state, he becomes greatly renowned.

13.

13.

Sampattaparivāro ca, ante gacchati nibbutiṃ;

Attatthañca paratthañca, tasmā passeyya buddhimā.

Endowed with prosperity and a retinue, in the end he attains cessation. Therefore, a wise person should consider both his own welfare and the welfare of others.

14.

14.

Attanā yadi ekena, vinitena mahājanā;

Vinayaṃ yanti sabbepi, kotaṃ nāseyya paṇḍito.

If by one person alone being disciplined, the great populace—all of them—attains discipline, what wise person would destroy that?

15.

15.

Payogo yo hi sattānaṃ, lohadvaya hitāvaho;

So tena akato natthi, rattandivamatandinā.

Indeed, whatever effort for the welfare of beings brings benefit in both worlds, none was left undone by him, who was tireless day and night.

16.

16.

Attano so nivatthāni, vatthāni sukhumāni ca;

Paṃsūkūlikabhikkhūnaṃ, cīvaratthāya dāpayi.

He had his own worn garments, as well as fine and delicate clothes, given to the rag-robe-wearing monks for the purpose of making robes.

17.

17.

Aṭṭhānaviniyogopi, saṅgaho vā virūpako;

Sāvajjo paribhogo vā, tassa nāhosi sabbaso.

Improper application, or unsuitable patronage, or the use of what is blameworthy—none of these were found with him at all.

18.

18.

Ye ye sattā yadā hārā, tesaṃ taṃ taṃ sadāpayi;

Ye yena sukhī honti, te te tena sukhāpayī.

Whatever beings required whatever sustenance, he always had that provided for them. By whatever means they became happy, by that very means he made them happy.

19.

19.

Evaṃ puññāni katvāna, chabbassāni narādhipo;

Agamā devarājassa, santikaṃ santiyāvaho.

Having thus performed meritorious deeds for six years, the lord of men, the bringer of peace, went to the presence of the king of the devas.

20.

20.

Atha tassa nujo rājā, kassapo hoti khattiyo;

Samattho rajjabhārassa, vahituṃ pubbavuttino.

Then his younger brother, the khattiya Kassapa, became king, capable of bearing the burden of kingship as practiced before.

21.

21.

Pitā viya niyaṃ puttaṃ, so saṅgaṇhi mahājanaṃ;

Dānena peyyavajjena, atthassa cariyāya ca.

Like a father his own son, he cherished the great populace with gifts, kind speech, and beneficial conduct.

22.

22.

Ṭhānantarañca dāpesi, tassa tassa yathārahaṃ;

Sayaṃ bhuñjittha bhogepi, sabbadukkhavivajjito.

He had positions assigned to each according to their merit; he himself also enjoyed wealth, being free from all suffering.

23.

23.

Gīhinañceva bhikkhūnaṃ, brahmaṇānañca khattiyo;

Vattāpayi sakāvāre, māghātañceva kārayi.

The khattiya caused householders, monks, and brahmins to perform their respective duties, and he had a proclamation of non-killing made.

24.

24.

Macchatitthe duve ceva, āvāsaṃ heḷigāmakaṃ;

Vaṇijjagāmamārāmaṃ, kassapādīgiriṃ tathā.

He built two monasteries at Macchatittha, the Heḷigāmaka residence, the Vaṇijjagāma monastery, and likewise Kassapādigiri.

25.

25.

Tathā [M 0.0298] ambatanavhañca, padhānaghara muttamaṃ; Bhogagāmañca…

Likewise also the Ambatanavha, the excellent meditation hall, and Bhogagāma…

[Etthakassapassa rajjapaṭibaddhāya kathāya ūnatā dissati.]

Here a deficiency is seen in the story connected with the reign of Kassapa.

26.

26.

Tesaṃ sabbakaniṭṭhopi, mahindo nāma khattiyo;

Sampattarajjo nāhosi, rājā rajja dhurandharo.

Their youngest of all, the khattiya named Mahinda, did not attain the kingship, though he was a ruler and a bearer of the kingdom's burden.

27.

27.

Tassapi kira nilavho, sahāyo cīrasatthuto;

Mato pubbeva tasmā, so saranto taṃ na icchitaṃ.

Indeed, his long-acquainted friend named Nila had died previously; therefore, remembering him, he did not desire it.

28.

28.

Ahorajjampi dīpamhi, na maññittha sukhāvahaṃ;

Abhāvena sahāyassa, sahāyā’tīva dullabhā.

He did not consider kingship on the island, even for a single day, to be conducive to happiness, due to the absence of his companion—for companions are exceedingly hard to find.

29.

29.

Teneva vuttaṃ muninā, dhammā yekeci lokiyā;

Tathā lokuttarā ceva, dhammā nibbānagāmino.

For that very reason it was said by the Sage: 'Whatever worldly states there are, and likewise the supramundane states, the states that lead to Nibbāna—

30.

30.

Kalyāṇamittaṃ āgamma, sabbe te honti pāṇinaṃ;

Tasmā kalyāṇamittesu, kattabbo’ti sadā daro.

—all these come to be for living beings by relying on a spiritual friend. Therefore, reverence for spiritual friends should always be shown.'

31.

31.

Ādipādova so tasmā, hutvā rajjaṃ vicārayi;

Pāletuṃyeva dīpamhi, jivanto viya pāṇino.

Therefore, having become the Ādipāda, he administered the kingdom, protecting the living beings on the island as if they were his own life.

32.

32.

Kassapassa sabhātussa, puttaṃ so aggabodhikaṃ;

Ṭhapetvā oparajjamhi, datvā bhogamanappakaṃ.

He established Aggabodhi, the son of his own brother Kassapa, in the position of sub-king, having given him abundant wealth.

33.

33.

Desaṃ datvāna pācinaṃ, vasituṃ tattha pesiya;

Desaṃ dakkhiṇamādāsi, rāja puttassa attano.

Having given the eastern region, he sent him there to dwell; he gave the southern region to his own royal son.

34.

34.

Mahāpāḷimhi dānañca, dāpesi dasavāhaṇaṃ;

Sabbe bhoge same’kāsi, yācanānaṃ saha’ttanā.

At the Mahāpāḷi alms hall he had alms consisting of ten cartloads given; he made all his possessions common to supplicants and to himself.

35.

35.

Adatvā yācakānaṃ so, nu kiñci paribhuñjati;

Bhuttaṃ vā satiyā deti, dvi guṇaṃ attabhuttato.

He would enjoy nothing without first giving to supplicants; or, if he had already eaten, he would mindfully give double of what he himself had consumed.

36.

36.

Sakanāmaṃ sakāresi, bhikkhunī na mupassayaṃ;

Pādānagaragallañca, ārāma mariyādakaṃ.

He had a nunnery built bearing his own name, and had the boundary of the Pādānagaragalla monastery established.

37.

37.

Mahindataṭamārāmaṃ, sampatta catupaccayaṃ;

Aññampi bahudhā kāsi, puññaṃ puññaguṇerato.

He established the Mahindataṭa monastery, complete with the four requisites; delighting in the quality of merit, he also performed many other kinds of meritorious deeds.

38.

38.

Tiṇī vassāni kāretvā, rajjameva mahāmati;

Gavesanto sahāyaṃ’va, devalokamupāgami.

Having administered the kingdom for three years, the one of great wisdom went to the world of the devas, as if seeking his companion.

39.

39.

Vasanto [M 0.0299] dakkhiṇe dese, aggabodhi kumārako;

Kenāpi karaṇīyena, nagaraṃ āgato ahu.

While dwelling in the southern region, Prince Aggabodhi came to the capital city on some business.

40.

40.

Tasmiṃ tattha vasantamhi, ādipādo mahindako;

Mato āsi tato tassa, rajjaṃ hatthagataṃ ahu.

While he was residing there, the regent Mahinda died; thereupon the kingdom came into his hands.

41.

41.

So taṃ hatthagataṃ katvā, saṇṭhapetvāna sāsanaṃ;

Pācina desapatino, aggabodhissa pesayi.

Having taken control and stabilized the Dispensation, he sent word to Aggabodhi, the ruler of the eastern country.

42.

42.

Sa āgantvā ahu rājā, silāmeghoti saññito;

Oparajje kumārañca, abhisiñcittha bhūpati.

He came and became king, known as Silāmegha. The new lord of the land then consecrated that prince as sub-king.

43.

43.

So rājā naṃ niyojetvā, cintā bhāraṃ vimuñciya;

Bhoge bhuñjatha tumheti, sayaṃ rajjaṃ vicārayi.

That king appointed him and, released from the burden of care, said: 'You all may enjoy the revenues.' He himself administered the kingdom.

44.

44.

Yathāyogaṃ janassesa-kāsi niggahasaṃgahe;

Dese ubbinayaṃ sabbaṃ, maggaṃ pāpesi cakkhumā.

As was proper, he dispensed both punishment and favor to the people. The one with vision eliminated all indiscipline in the country and set it on the right path.

45.

45.

Evaṃ tesu vasantesu, otāraṃ pāpakammino;

Na labhantā vicintesuṃ, bhinditabbā ime iti.

While they were living thus in harmony, evil-doers, finding no opportunity, reflected thus: 'These two must be set against each other.'

46.

46.

Rājānamupasaṅkamma, avocuṃ pisunaṃ raho;

Tuvaṃ rājāsi nāmena, rājā añño sabhāvaho.

Approaching the king in secret, they spoke slanderously, saying: 'You are king only in name; another is the king in substance.'

47.

47.

Uparājā ayaṃ rajjaṃ, gaṇhissati mahājanaṃ;

Saṅgayha na cireneva, hoti rājā na saṃsayo.

'This sub-king, having won over the great populace, will seize the kingdom. Before long, without a doubt, he will be king.'

48.

48.

Taṃ sutvāna mahīpālo, paribhijji kumārake;

Kumāropi vidhitvā taṃ, coro hutvāna rājindo.

Hearing this, the lord of the earth turned against the prince. The prince, understanding this, became an outlaw, O king of men.

49.

49.

Palāyitvā sakaṃ desaṃ, saṅgaṇhitvā tahiṃ jane;

Mahantaṃ balamādāya, kātuṃ saṅgāma mārabhi.

Fleeing to his own region and gathering the people there, he raised a great army and began to make war.

50.

50.

Kadalyādinivātamhi, saṅgāmo bhiṃsano ahu;

Gato tattha parājitvā, kumāro malayaṃ vaso.

A fearsome battle took place at Kadalī-ādi-nivāta. Having been defeated there, the prince went to Malaya and dwelt there.

51.

51.

Tato rājā kataññū so, upakāraṃ sabhātuno;

Cintetvā rajjadānādiṃ, paridevittha pākaṭaṃ.

Then that grateful king, reflecting on the help of his kinsman—the gift of the kingdom and so on—lamented openly.

52.

52.

Kumāropi ca taṃ sutvā, ahosi muducittako;

Evaṃ te aññamaññassa, siniddhantaṃ pakāsayuṃ.

And the prince, upon hearing this, became softened in heart. Thus they revealed their affection for one another.

53.

53.

Rājā gantvā sayaṃyeva, malayaṃ ekako vaṃso;

Kumāraṃ taṃ samādāya, āgamittha sakaṃ puraṃ.

The king, the scion of his dynasty, went himself to Malaya alone. Taking that prince with him, he returned to his own city.

54.

54.

Hoti [M 0.0300] nissaṃsayaṃ [evaṃpi citto] atīva so;

Vivāhaṃ tena kāresi, dhītaraṃ saṅghanāmikaṃ.

Without doubt the king was very pleased, and he arranged for the prince to marry his own daughter, who was named Saṅghā.

55.

55.

Tāya saddhiṃ vasanto so, vissattho tena rājinā;

Pahāraṃ tāya pādāsi, duṭṭho dosamhi kismiṃci.

While living with her and trusted by the king, the prince became angered over some fault and struck her a blow.

56.

56.

Pitaraṃ sā upāgamma, karuṇaṃ roditampati;

Akāraṇe maṃ māreti, dinno vo sāmiko iti.

She went to her father and wept piteously, saying: 'He is killing me without cause, this husband that you gave me!'

57.

57.

Sopi taṃ sutamatteva, dukkataṃ vata me iti;

Pabbājesi lahuṃ gantvā, bhikkhūnī na mupassayaṃ.

As soon as he heard this, he thought, 'Alas, what a wrong I have done!' Going quickly, he had her ordained in a nunnery.

58.

58.

Aggabodhisanāmotha, tassā mātula puttako;

Sucireneva kālena, tassaṃ sā rattamānaso.

Now there was one named Aggabodhi, who was her maternal uncle's son. Before long, his mind became inflamed with passion for her.

59.

59.

Kālo’yanti viditvāna, tamādāya palāyituṃ;

Aññato taṃ gahetvāna, gato ekova rohaṇaṃ.

Recognizing that the time was right to take her and flee, he abducted her from a certain place and went alone to Rohaṇa.

60.

60.

Aggabodhiṃ narindo so, aggabodhi namādiya;

Aggabodhiṃ nihantuṃ taṃ, rohaṇaṃ tamupāvīsi.

That king, Aggabodhi, taking the other Aggabodhi with him, entered Rohaṇa in order to slay that Aggabodhi.

61.

61.

Aggabodhi nisedhetvā, aggabodhiṃ sabhātaraṃ;

Apare pabbate hantu-maggabodhiṃ sayaṃ gato.

Aggabodhi, having checked the other Aggabodhi and his kinsmen, himself went to another mountain to slay that Aggabodhi.

62.

62.

Kasiṇaṃ rohaṇaṃ hattha-gataṃ katvā mahā balo;

Yujjhitvā tena taṃ gaṇhi, bhariyaṃ saṅghamattano.

The one of great strength, having brought the whole of Rohaṇa under his control, fought with his rival and took back his own wife, Saṅghā.

63.

63.

Tato paṭṭhāya sukhitā, samaggā te tayo janā;

Vissaṭṭhā aññamaññesu, vihariṃsu yathāruciṃ.

From that time onwards, those three people lived happily and in harmony. Trusting one another, they dwelt together as they pleased.

64.

64.

Vāpāraniṃ akārāmaṃ, tathā māṇaggabodhikaṃ;

Sabhattuddesabhogañca, vihāre atiyuttare.

He made the Vāpāraṇi cistern, the Māṇaggabodhi Park, and the Sabhattuddesabhoga, and gave revenues to most excellent vihāras.

65.

65.

Hatthi kucchivihāre ca, vihāre puna piṭṭhike;

Mahādīpariveṇe ca, pāsāde vāhadīpake.

He also performed works at the Hatthikucchi-vihāra, the Piṭṭhika-vihāra, the Mahādīpa-pariveṇa, and the Vāhadīpaka palace.

66.

66.

Thūpārāmamhi gehassa, dvāre ca parijiṇṇake;

Kāsi pākatikaṃ tattha, thambhe ca parivattayi.

He restored the dilapidated gate of the house at the Thūpārāma and replaced the pillars.

67.

67.

Evaṃ katvāna puññāni, puññāni ca yathābalaṃ;

Cattālīsatime vasse, yathākamma mupāgami.

Having thus performed meritorious deeds according to his ability, in his fortieth year he passed away in accordance with his kamma.

68.

68.

Athoparājā rājā’si, aggabodhi sirīdharo;

Tanayo so mahindassa, ādipādassa dhīmato.

Then the sub-king, Aggabodhi the glorious, became king. He was the son of the wise Ādipāda Mahinda.

69.

69.

Sāsanampi [M 0.0301] ca lokañca, saṅgaṇittha yathārahaṃ;

Oparajje’bhisiñcattha, mahindaṃ puttamattano.

He patronized both the Dispensation and the world as was proper. He had his own son Mahinda consecrated in the office of sub-king.

70.

70.

Mahābodhissa kāresi, gharaṃ jiṇṇaṃ navaṃ thiraṃ;

Ārāme dve ca kāresi, kaḷandaṃ mallavātakaṃ.

He had the dilapidated house for the Great Bodhi Tree made new and firm. He also had two monasteries built, the Kaḷanda and the Mallavātaka.

71.

71.

Dhammakammehi sakkaccaṃ, sodhesi jinasāsanaṃ;

Vinicchananto dhammena, chindi kūṭaṭṭakārake.

He carefully purified the Conqueror's Dispensation with acts of Dhamma. Judging in accordance with the Dhamma, he cut off those who brought false charges.

72.

72.

Bhesajjañca gilānānaṃ, maṅgalaṃ cāvamaṅgalaṃ;
