26.

Ākaḍḍhitvāna sayanaṃ, samāropiya pemato;

Āliṅgiṃ supinamhīti, devī cāpi tamabravī.

‘Having drawn the bed near, having lifted me up with affection, it embraced me in the dream.’ Thus also the queen spoke to him.

27.

27.

Ubho te aññamaññassa, diṭṭhamevaṃ pakāsiya;

Uṭṭhāpesuṃ pahaṭṭhāva, vītaniddāruṇaṃ tadā.

Both of them, having thus revealed their visions to each other, then arose, joyful and free from sleepiness at dawn.

28.

28.

Tato pāto upaṭṭhātu, mupayātaṃ purohitaṃ;

Nemittake ca pucchiṃsu, sunitvā te pamoditā.

Then, at dawn, they questioned the chaplain who had come to attend, and the soothsayers. Having heard their words, they rejoiced.

29.

29.

Na cirasseva puttassa, dhaññalakkhaṇasālino;

Uppattiyā avassaṃ’va, bhavaṃtabbanti kittayuṃ.

‘Before long, there will certainly be the birth of a son endowed with auspicious marks,’ so they proclaimed.

30.

30.

Taṃ suṇitvā amaccā ca, tathā nagaravāsino;

Avindiṃsu janindo ca, sabbepīti mahussavaṃ.

Having heard that, the ministers, and likewise the city dwellers, and the lord of the people—all indeed experienced great festivity.

31.

31.

Tato paṭṭhāya sotthānaṃ, patthayaṃ patthivobhusaṃ;

Bhikkhusaṅghena bahuso, bhaṇāpesi parittakaṃ.

From that time onward, the king, greatly desiring their well-being, repeatedly had protective chants recited by the community of monks.

32.

32.

Maṇimuttādikaṃ cittaṃ, mahagghamanuvāsaraṃ;

Pariccaji dānamukhe, yācakānamanekaso.

Day by day, he bestowed various gems, pearls, and so forth of great value as gifts upon many beggars.

33.

33.

Purohitādivippehi, vedavedaṅgaviññūhi;

Vattāpesi ca homādi-vidhānaṃ sotthi sammataṃ.

He also had rites such as the homa sacrifice, considered conducive to well-being, performed by the chief priest and other brahmins skilled in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.

34.

34.

Suvinaṭṭhe vihāre ca, dhātugabbhe ca vāpiyo;

Jiṇṇā ca paṭisaṅkhattuṃ, yojayī rājakappike.

He employed royal artisans to repair the greatly dilapidated monasteries, relic chambers, and reservoirs.

35.

35.

Dinaṃ nayante kalyāṇa-kammene’vaṃ narissare;

Na ciraṃ saṇṭhahi gabbha-varo kucchimhi deviyā.

While the lord of men was thus passing his days with meritorious deeds, before long an excellent embryo was established in the queen's womb.

36.

36.

Tatovagamma taṃ haṭṭha-pahaṭṭho so narissaro;

Mahantaṃ deviyā gabbha-parihāramadāpayi.

Then, having understood that, that lord of men, joyful and delighted, caused great care to be given for the queen's pregnancy.

37.

37.

Paripakkagabbhā devī, kamena janayīsukaṃ;

Samaye bhaddanakkhatta-muhuttenabhilakkhite.

The queen, her embryo being fully developed, in due course gave birth with ease at a time marked by an auspicious constellation and moment.

38.

38.

Suppasannā asesā ca, disāyo taṃkhaṇe ahu;

Samīraṇe ca vāsiṃsu, sugandhimudusītalā.

At that moment, all the directions became perfectly serene, and fragrant, soft, and cool breezes blew.

39.

39.

Dantīnaṃ [M 0.0378] koñcanādena, hayānaṃ hesitena ca;

Rājaṅgaṇaṃ tadājātaṃ, mahākolāhalā kūlaṃ.

With the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses, the royal courtyard then became filled with a great uproar.

40.

40.

Accherātisaye evaṃ, pātubhūte anekadhā;

Disvā taṃ vimhayappatto, māṇabharaṇabhūpati.

When such extraordinary and wondrous events had thus manifested in many ways, King Mānabharaṇa, seeing this, was struck with amazement.

41.

41.

Sutvā nijassa puttassa, tadā sañjātasāsanaṃ;

Amatenābhisittova, pītipuṇṇamanoratho.

Then, having heard the news of his own son's birth, he was as if anointed with ambrosia, his heart filled with joy.

42.

42.

Mocāpetvā tadā kārā-ghare baddhe bahūjane;

Dānaṃ uḷāraṃ samaṇa-brāhmaṇānaṃ padāpayi.

Then, having had the many people bound in prison released, he had generous gifts given to ascetics and brahmins.

43.

43.

Amaccapamukhā cāpi, janāpuranivāsino;

Kadalītoraṇādīhi, rājadhānī manekadhā.

The ministers, chiefs, and the city-dwelling people decorated the capital in many ways with banana-plant arches and the like.

44.

44.

Alaṅkaritvā sakalaṃ, sumaṇḍitapasādhitā;

Chaṇaṃ mahantaṃ vattesuṃ, katipāhaṃ manoramaṃ.

Having adorned the entire city, they, being well-decorated and attired themselves, held a great and delightful festival for several days.

45.

45.

Vede vuttavidhānena, jātakammādikaṃ vidhiṃ;

Sabbaṃ samāpayitvāna, kumārassā’vanīpati.

The lord of the earth, having had all the rites for the prince, such as the birth ceremony, completed according to the procedure stated in the Vedas,

46.

46.

Purohitādayo vippe, tato lakkhaṇapāṭhake;

Āṇāpetvāna sakkāra-sammānavidhipubbakaṃ.

then commanded the chief priest and other brahmins, those skilled in reading marks, after first performing rites of honor and respect.

47.

47.

Niyojesi kumārassa, lakkhaṇānaṃ paṭiggahe;

Sādhakaṃ sakalaṃ tassa, yatthapādādilakkhaṇaṃ.

He appointed them to the task of examining the prince's marks, whereby all his characteristics, beginning with those on his feet, were confirmed as auspicious.

48.

48.

Upadhāriya mahāmacca-gaṇamajjhagatassa te;

Rājino deviyā cāpi, pakāsesuṃ pamoditā.

Having ascertained this, they joyfully proclaimed their findings to the king, who was in the midst of the great assembly of ministers, and also to the queen.

49.

49.

Laṅkādīpaṃ ṭhapetvāna, jambudīpatalampi ca;

Ekacchattaṅkitaṃ katvā-nubhottuṃ nipuṇo iti.

‘He is able to bring the entire surface of Jambudīpa, let alone the island of Laṅkā, under the authority of a single parasol and to rule over it.’

50.

50.

Te santappiya bhogehi, bhiyyo pucchittha sādaraṃ;

Sandissamānaṃ yaṃkiñci, ariṭṭhaṃ atthi natthī’ti.

Having satisfied them with riches, he asked further with respect: ‘Is there any inauspicious sign to be seen, or is there not?’

51.

51.

Dīghāyuko kumāro’yaṃ, kiñci paññāyate vata;

Janakāriṭṭhayogo’ti, te mahīpatino’bravuṃ.

‘This prince is long-lived, yet something is indeed discerned: an astrological conjunction portending misfortune for his father,’ they told the lord of the earth.

52.

52.

Tassārijanasammaddi-patāpabhujayo gato;

So parakkamabāhū’ti, anvatthanāmamaggahī.

His majestic arms were renowned for crushing the enemy host; therefore, he received the fitting name ‘Parakkamabāhu,’ meaning ‘He of the Mighty Arm.’

53.

53.

Kaṇṇave dhamahañceva, annupāsanamaṅgalaṃ;

Kārāpiya vidhānaññū, yathāvidhimasesato.

Knowing the proper procedure, he had the ear-piercing ceremony and the first rice-feeding ceremony performed in their entirety and according to rule.

54.

54.

Rañño [M 0.0379] vikkamabāhussa, saputtuppattisāsanaṃ;

Vattuṃ sadūte pesesi, pulatthinagaraṃ tadā.

Then he sent his messengers to the city of Pulatthinagara to announce to King Vikkamabāhu the news of his son's birth.

55.

55.

Tehiso bhāgineyyassa, mahābhāgattanampi ca;

Janakāriṭṭhayogañca, sutvā vikkamabāhuso.

Having heard from them of his nephew's great good fortune and also of the astrological conjunction portending misfortune for the father, that Vikkamabāhu...

56.

56.

Dhaññaṃ vijayarājādi-rājamālāya nāyakaṃ;

Maṇiṃva bhāsuraṃ mayhaṃ, bhāgineyyaṃ janesiso.

‘Fortunate, a leader in the royal lineage beginning with King Vijaya, radiant like a gem, is my nephew, the lord of people.’

57.

57.

Hāni yākācisatataṃ, yathā tassa na hessati;

Tathā mamantikeyeva, kumāro ettha vaḍḍhataṃ.

‘So that no harm whatsoever may ever befall him, may the prince grow up right here in my presence.’

58.

58.

Aladdhaṃ labhituṃ lābhaṃ, laddhañca parirakkhituṃ;

Sabbathā na samatthoyaṃ, putto gajabāhu mama.

‘To gain the gain not gained, and to protect what has been gained, in every way my son Gajabāhu is not capable.’

59.

59.

Sūrabhāvādiyutto’pi, mahindavhaparosuto;

Nihīno mātugottena, na rajjassa raho mama.

‘Though the other son, named Mahinda, is endowed with bravery and other such qualities, he is of inferior maternal lineage and not worthy of my kingdom.’

60.

60.

Ṭhitassa vikkajātena, nekaso sañcitena me;

Rajjassa bhāgineyyo’va, kāmaṃ bhāgī bhavissati.

‘Of the kingdom, established and amassed by me in many ways through valor, my nephew indeed shall surely become the heir.’

61.

61.

Itipesesi dūte so, ānetuṃ taṃ kumārakaṃ;

Kumārā bharaṇaṃ datvā, sesaṃ sārañcupāyanaṃ.

Thus he sent messengers to bring that young prince, having given them ornaments for the prince and other valuable gifts as tribute.

62.

62.

Sabbaṃ dūtamukhā sutvā, vīrabāhu mahīpati;

Tassetaṃ vacanaṃ yuttaṃ, vuttaṃ mehita buddhiyā.

Having heard all from the mouth of the messenger, the king Vīrabāhu thought: ‘These words of his are fitting, spoken with a mind concerned for my welfare.’

63.

63.

Tathāpi ca nijāriṭṭha-paṭikāratthamīdisaṃ;

Orasaṃ puttaratanaṃ, pesetuṃ nā’nurūpakaṃ.

‘Nevertheless, even for the sake of remedying his own misfortune, it is not fitting to send away one's own precious son.’

64.

64.

Kiñca tattha kumāramhi, nīte vikkama bāhuno;

Pakkho laddhamahāvāha-balo viya hutāsano.

‘Moreover, when the prince is brought there, the faction of Vikkamabāhu will be like a fire that has gained the power of a great wind.’

65.

65.

Accunnatena mahatā, tejasā sañjalissati;

Hānireva vatamhākaṃ, mahatī hessate bhusaṃ.

‘With exceedingly great and lofty power, it will blaze forth; indeed, our decline will be exceedingly great.’

66.

66.

Iti hatthe gatānaṃ so, dūtānaṃ thanayaṃ sakaṃ;

Apesetvā visajjesi, pasādiya manena so.

Thus, not sending his own son, he pleased the messengers who had come to him with his words and dismissed them.

67.

67.

Saputtadārehi [M 0.0380] samaggavāsaṃ,

Narādinātho nivasaṃ tahiṃso;

Tibbena phuṭṭho mahatāgadena,

Rajjena saddhiṃ vijahittha desaṃ.

That lord of men, living there in harmony with his sons and wives, was afflicted by a severe and great disease, and gave up his life along with his kingdom.

Sujanappasādasaṃve gatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of the virtuous,

Kumārodayo nāma

Named “The Rise of the Prince”

Saṭṭhimo paricchedo.

The Sixtieth Chapter.

Ekasaṭṭhima pariccheda

The Sixty-First Chapter

Saṅkhatthalipurābhigamano

The Journey to Saṅkhatthalipura

1.

1.

Sutvā dve bhātaro aññe, jeṭṭhasso paratiṃsadā;

Khippaṃ saraṭṭhā āgamma, kāresuṃ antimaṃ vidhiṃ.

Hearing of the death of the eldest, the two other brothers quickly came from their own countries and performed the final rites.

2.

2.

Atha kittisirimegho, raṭṭhaṃ jeṭṭhassa bhātuno;

Attādhīnaṃ karitvāna, āmantiya kaṇiṭṭhakaṃ.

Then Kittisirimegha, having brought the kingdom of his elder brother under his own authority, addressed the younger brother.

3.

3.

Datvā raṭṭhadvayaṃ aññaṃ, vatthuṃ tattheva ādisi;

So’pi jeṭṭhassa bhātussa, vacanaṃ sampaṭicchiya.

Having given him the two other kingdoms, he ordered him to dwell there. He, in turn, accepted the word of his elder brother.

4.

4.

Samādāya kumārañca, deviñca ratanāvaliṃ;

Dhītaro dve ca gantāna, mahā nāmahulaṃ puraṃ.

Taking the prince, Queen Ratnāvalī, and the two daughters, he went to the great city of Mahānāgahula.

5.

5.

Samaggā nivasaṃ tattha, kumārassa sikhāmahaṃ;

Kāretvā parihārena, vaḍḍhesi mahatā sadā.

Living there in harmony, he had the tonsure ceremony for the prince performed and always raised him with great care.

6.

6.

Tato so deviyā jeṭṭhaṃ-dhītaraṃ mittanāmikaṃ;

Dātukāmo saputtassa, sahāmaccehi mantayi.

Then, wishing to give the queen’s eldest daughter, named Mittā, to his own son, he consulted with his ministers.

7.

7.

Kāliṅganvayasambhūtā, pāyenakhalu bhūmipā;

Sāmibhāvaṃ gatā asmiṃ, laṅkādīpamhī bhūyaso.

‘Kings born of the Kāliṅga lineage have, for the most part, indeed attained sovereignty in this island of Laṅkā.’

8.

8.

Kāliṅgagotta sambhūta, gajabāhussa dātave;

Gūḷarūpena devī’yaṃ, yadi peseyya dhītaraṃ.

‘If this queen were to send her daughter secretly, to be given to Gajabāhu, who is born of the Kāliṅga clan,’

9.

9.

Bhiyyo [M 0.0381] vivāhasambaddho, balavā so bhavissati;

Mayhaṃ eso nirālambo, putto hehīti sabbathā.

‘Being further connected by marriage, he will become powerful, and this son of mine will be utterly without support.’

10.

10.

Tasmā me sunūno esā, dātuṃ yuttā kumārikā;

Evaṃ sati vatamhākaṃ, vaḍḍhiye’va siyā “iti”.

‘Therefore, it is fitting that this maiden be given to my son. This being so, our prosperity will indeed increase.’”

11.

11.

Devīpi sutvā taṃ sabba-mādiccanvaya maṇḍanā;

Sabbathā tamanicchanti, idamāha mahīpatiṃ.

The queen, an ornament of the solar lineage, having heard all this and in no way desiring it, spoke thus to the king:

12.

12.

Ghātetvā sakale yakkhe, kumāro vijayavhayo;

Laṃkādīpamimaṃ’kāsi, manussāvāsakaṃ sadā.

‘Having slain all the yakkhas, the prince named Vijaya made this island of Laṅkā a permanent dwelling for humans.’

13.

13.

Tato pabhuti amhākaṃ, ghaṭesuṃ vijayanvayaṃ;

Kāliṅgavaṃsajeheva, sambandhaṃ katva pubbakaṃ.

‘From that time onwards, our ancestors established the Vijayan lineage by forming connections only with those born of the Kāliṅga lineage.’

14.

14.

Aññabhūpāla sambandho, sutapubbo pinatthino;

Somavaṃsa samumbhūte, ṭhapetvā dharaṇissare.

A connection with other kings, heard of in the past, is not desired, excepting the lord of the earth born in the Somavaṃsa lineage.

15.

15.

Tuyhaṃ jātoti amhākaṃ, sambandho so kathaṃ siyā;

Ariyanvaya sambhūta, kumārena sahāmunā.

Since he is born of you, how could that connection of ours be with this prince, who is born in the noble lineage?

16.

16.

Evaṃ so deviyā tāya, nekaso vārayantiyā;

Pasayhasaka putthassa, taṃ kumārimadāpayi.

Thus, though that queen repeatedly tried to dissuade him, he forcibly gave that maiden to his own son.

17.

17.

So anekaguṇodāra- bhariyānugato tato;

Rañjayanto jane sabbe, janakasantike vasi.

Then, accompanied by his wife, who was endowed with many excellent qualities, delighting all the people, he dwelt near his father.

18.

18.

Ekavīsatiṃ vassāni, rajjaṃ vikkama bāhuso;

Anubhotvā yathākammaṃ, kāyabhedā gato paraṃ.

That Vikkamabāhu, having enjoyed the kingship for twenty-one years, passed on to the next world upon the dissolution of the body, in accordance with his kamma.

19.

19.

Tato gajabhujo ṭhitaṃ, sampannabalavāhanaṃ;

Rajjaṃ hatthagataṃ katvā, pulattinagare vasī.

Then Gajabāhu, having taken into his possession the kingdom, which was established and endowed with forces and transport, dwelt in the city of Pulatthi.

20.

20.

Tato kittisirīmegha, sirīvallabha bhūmipā;

Vuttanta metaṃ viññāya, evaṃ samanucintayuṃ.

Then Kittisirimegha and Sirivallabha, the lords of the earth, having learned of this matter, contemplated thus.

21.

21.

Tassa vikkama bāhussa, vuddhabhāvena nekadhā;

Mūlarajjādhipaccaṃ taṃ, ammaṃ nindākaraṃ na hi.

Indeed, that sovereignty over the ancestral kingdom of Vikkamabāhu, who is now old in many ways, is not blameworthy.

22.

22.

Tadatthajassa bālassa, mūlarajjaṃ pasāsano;

Upekkhaṇaṃ panamhākaṃ, nevānucchavikaṃ vata.

But for us to be indifferent while that self-interested fool governs the ancestral kingdom is truly not fitting.

23.

23.

Te soyāva sarajjamhi, baddhamūlo bhavissati;

Pasayha tāva taṃ rajjaṃ, vaṭṭati gaṇhituṃ iti.

Before he becomes firmly rooted in his own kingdom, it is fitting to seize that kingdom by force.

24.

24.

Velakkāra [M 0.0382] balaṃ sabbaṃ, bhindiṃsu dhana dānato;

Ṭhapetvā sevake keci, tassabbhantarike tadā.

By giving wealth, they caused the entire Velakkāra army to defect, excepting only a few attendants who were in his inner circle at that time.

25.

25.

Gajabāhu mahīpāle, virattā raṭṭhavāsino;

Ubhinnaṃ rājūnaṃ dūte, pesayuṃ nekaso tato.

The inhabitants of the country, being disaffected with King Gajabāhu, then repeatedly sent messengers to both kings.

26.

26.

Rajjaṃ sādhetvā dassāma, ekībhūtā mayaṃ pana;

Upatthambhakabhāvo’va, kātabbo kevalaṃ iti.

“We, having become united, will secure the kingdom and deliver it; on your part, only the role of a supporter is to be undertaken.”

27.

27.

Tato dve bhātukā senaṃ, sakaṃ sannayha vegasā;

Ubhato mukhato tassa, raṭṭhamajjhamupāgamuṃ.

Then the two brothers, swiftly mustering their own armies, approached the middle of his kingdom from both sides.

28.

28.

Pahiṇiṃsu ca te dūte, tato gajabohuvhayo;

Bhūmipālo nijāmacce, sannipātiya mantayi.

And they sent messengers. Then the king named Gajabāhu, having assembled his own ministers, took counsel with them.

29.

29.

Veḷakkārabalaṃ sabba-mujupaccattikaṃ ahu;

Rājāno dve ca no raṭṭhaṃ, saṅgāmatthamupāgatā.

The entire Velakkāra army has become directly hostile, and two kings have come to our kingdom for the sake of battle.

30.

30.

Paṭhamaṃ tesu pakkhassa, ekassa balino bhusaṃ;

Mukhabhaṅge kate khippaṃ, tato aññe susādhiyā.

First, if the front of one of the exceedingly strong sides is quickly broken, then the others will be easy to conquer.

31.

31.

Iti nicchiya senaṅgaṃ, sabbamādāya attano;

Sirivallabharājābhi-mukhaṃ yuddhā’yupāgami.

Thus having decided, taking all his own forces, he advanced towards King Sirivallabha for battle.

32.

32.

Sirivallabharājāpi, saṅgāma mahibhiṃsanaṃ;

Pāto paṭṭhāya sāyanha-kālaṃ yāva pavattayaṃ.

King Sirivallabha also waged a very terrible battle, continuing from dawn until the time of evening.

33.

33.

Asakkuṇanto’bhibhavaṃ, vidhātuṃ tassa kañcipi;

Tatova so nivattitvā, sakaṃ raṭṭhaṃ gato lahuṃ.

Unable to inflict any defeat upon him, he then turned back and swiftly went to his own country.

34.

34.

Gajabāhussagokaṇṇa-sacivena parājito;

Agā raṭṭhaṃ sakaṃ kitti-sirimegho’pi bhūpati.

Defeated by Gajabāhu's minister Gokaṇṇa, King Kittisirimegha also went to his own country.

35.

35.

Gajabāhunarindopi, saṅgāme tamhi kiñcipi;

Parihānimasampatto, punā’gamma purantikaṃ.

King Gajabāhu too, having suffered no loss whatsoever in that battle, came again to the vicinity of his city.

36.

36.

Balanāthe viniggayha, sāparādhe bahū balī;

Raṭṭhaṃ vūpasametvāna, pāvekkhi nagaraṃ sakaṃ.

The powerful one, having subdued the many guilty army commanders, pacified the kingdom and entered his own city.

37.

37.

Raṭṭhe sake sakeyeva, tato pabhūti bhūmipā;

Aññoññamitte sambandhaṃ, vidhāya vihariṃsu te.

From then on, those kings dwelt each in his own country, having established a bond of mutual friendship.

38.

38.

Tato parakkamabhujo, dharaṇī pālanandano;

Medhāvīnekasippesu, sikkhamāno susādhukaṃ.

Then Parakkamabhuja, son of the protector of the earth, being wise and training very well in the various arts,

39.

39.

Vicārakkhamapaññattā[M 0.0383], kiccā kiccesu nekaso;

Accuḷārāsayattā ca, mahābhāgattanena ca.

Because of his discerning wisdom in what should and should not be done in many instances, and because of his very noble disposition, and because of his great good fortune,

40.

40.

Attano mātubhaginī, sahavāsa sukhamhi ca;

Alaggamānasoneka, balākīḷārasesu ca.

His mind was unattached to the pleasure of dwelling with his mother's sister and to the various delights of childish sports and games.

41.

41.

Sūrabhāvādisaṃyuttā, rājaputtā tu mādisā;

Paccante īdise dese, kathaṃ nāma vasissare.

Princes like me, endowed with courage and other such qualities, how indeed could they live in such a remote country?

42.

42.

Jātadesañca me dāni, yuvarājapabhogiyaṃ;

Gamissāmīti niggañchi, tamhā parijanatthito.

‘Now I will go to my birthplace, which is fit for a crown prince's enjoyment,’ thus thinking, he departed from there, unattended by his retinue.

43.

43.

Kamena santikaṃ saṅkha-nāyakatthalisaññino;

Gāmassāgā ahiṃ kitti-sirimegho nisamma taṃ.

King Kittisirimegha, having heard that, went in due course to the vicinity of the village known as the Place of the General Saṅkha.

44.

44.

Abhāvā rajja dāyāda-samānassa’trajassa me;

Ekākī’hanti yo citta-santāpo santataṃ gato.

Due to the absence of a son, a royal heir equal to myself, the mental anguish, 'I am alone,' constantly arose.

45.

45.

Jeṭṭhaṃva bhātaraṃ mayhaṃ, taṃ dehapaṭibimbakaṃ;

Daṭṭhuṃ me sattataṃ puññaṃ, mahantamuditaṃtica.

To see him, who is like an elder brother to me, a reflection of my own body, would constantly be for me a source of merit and great joy.

46.

46.

Pāmujjavegavasago, nagaraṃ taṃ manoharaṃ;

Alaṅkārā payitvāna, toraṇādīhi nekadhā.

Overwhelmed by a rush of joy, he caused that charming city to be adorned in many ways with gateways and so on.

47.

47.

Gantvā paṭipathaṃyeva, baloghaparivārito;

Narindo tithinakkhatta-visese subhasammate.

The king, surrounded by a host of troops, having gone forth to meet him, on a special lunar day and constellation deemed auspicious,

48.

48.

Anaññasādhāraṇataṃ, sampattehi guṇehi ca;

Lakkhaṇehi ca sabbehi, kalyāṇeyi susaṃyutaṃ.

endowed with qualities not common to others, and well-possessed of all auspicious and excellent marks.

49.

49.

Disvā kumāraṃ santuṭṭho, āliṅgitvāna pemato;

Ure katvāna cumbitvā, matthakamhi punappunaṃ.

Seeing the prince, delighted, he embraced him out of affection; holding him to his chest, he kissed him again and again on the head.

50.

50.

Janassa balato tassa, passato locanehi so;

Santosa assudhārāyo, vassāpento nirantaraṃ.

While the people watched, he, from the strength of his joy, continuously shed streams of tears.

51.

51.

Manuññameka māruyha, vāhanaṃ saha sūnunā;

Bherini dena pūrento, disā dasa samantato.

Having mounted a single charming vehicle with his son, he filled the ten directions all around with the sound of drums.

52.

52.

Pavisitvā puraṃ tattha, alaṅkāre manorame;

Dassayanto saputtassa, pāvisi rājamandiraṃ.

Having entered the city there, which was delightful with its adornments, and showing it to his son, he entered the royal palace.

53.

53.

Laddhā [M 0.0384] tato kañcukī-supakāra,

Vagādineke paricārake so;

Nānāguṇā rādhitamānasassa,

Vasīsakāse pituno sukhena.

Having obtained from him many attendants, such as chamberlains and cooks, he, whose mind was delighted by their diverse qualities, lived happily in the presence of his father.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people.

Saṅkhatthalipurābhigamano nāma

Named 'The Arrival at Saṅkhatthalipura'.

Ekasaṭṭhimo paricchedo.

The Sixty-first Chapter.

Dvisaṭṭhimapariccheda

The Sixty-second Chapter.

Paramaṇḍalābhigamano

The Arrival in the Other Regions.

1.

1.

Attanābhimatassā’su, jātadesassa pattiyā;

Sampuṇṇamanasaṅkappo, dussaṅkapavivajjito.

Through the swift attainment of his desired birthplace, his mental resolve was fulfilled, and he was devoid of evil intentions.

2.

2.

Vajirūpamorupaññā, balena gurusantike;

Lahuṃ bahuñca gaṇhanto, sippajātamaneka kaṃ.

With great, diamond-like wisdom and with strength, in the presence of his teacher, he swiftly grasped much concerning many kinds of crafts:

3.

3.

Jināgamesu nekesu, koṭillā dīsu nītisu;

Saddasatthe ca kāveyye, sanighaṇḍuka keṭubhe.

in many teachings of the Conqueror, in political sciences such as that of Kauṭilya, in grammar and poetry, with lexicography and rhetoric;

4.

4.

Naccagītesu satthesu, hatthisippādikesu ca;

Dhanu khaggādinekesu, satthesu ca visesato.

in dance, song, and instrumental music, in crafts such as elephant training, and especially in many weapons such as the bow and the sword.

5.

5.

Pārappatto vinītatto, pitu rañño samācari;

Adhippāyānukulaṃ’va, sadā bhattipurassaro.

Having become accomplished and self-disciplined, he always acted in accordance with the intention of the king his father, with devotion at the forefront.

6.

6.

Tadā sadā darācāra-guṇārādhitamānaso;

Piyena viya mittena, tena saddhiṃ mahīpati.

Then the lord of the earth, whose mind was always delighted by the quality of his son's conduct, was with him as with a dear friend.

7.

7.

Uyyānajalakīḷādi-sukhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ;

Anubhotvā sadesasmiṃ, sañcaranto tahiṃ tahiṃ.

Experiencing the various pleasures of gardens, water sports, and so on in their own country, they wandered here and there.

8.

8.

Ekadāsaṅkhasenādhi-patinā daḷhabhattinā;

Saraṭṭhasīmā rakkhāya, yo jitena balīyasā.

Once, Saṅkha, the commander of the army, a steadfast devotee, had been appointed by his powerful lord for the protection of the Saraṭṭha border.

9.

9.

Ajjhāvutthassa [M 0.0385] ca balattha-linamassa ca santikaṃ;

Gāmasā’gañchi sutvāna, tamatthaṃ dhajinīpati.

The king, having heard of that matter, went to the village and into the presence of him who dwelt there, strong and diligent.

10.

10.

Gāmaṃ taṃ sādhukaṃ sajju, sajjāpetvā saputtakaṃ;

Paccuggantvā mahīpālaṃ, paṇamitvā ṭhito tadā.

With his son, having caused that village to be well and quickly prepared, he went out to meet the king, and having bowed down, he then stood there.

11.

11.

Pitā putto ubho tassa, sambhāsiya piyaṃ vaco;

Nekadhā’rādhitā tena, taṃ gāmaṃ samupāgaguṃ.

The father and son, both of them, having spoken pleasant words to him, and being pleased by him in many ways, arrived at that village.

12.

12.

Tahiṃ katici bhūpālo, vāsare vītināmiya;

Senāpatiṃ samāhūya, idaṃ vacanaṃ mabravi.

There, the king, having spent a few days, summoned the commander-in-chief and spoke these words:

13.

13.

Putto me dānivayasi, ṭhito’ panayanārahe;

Tassopanayanaṃ kātuṃ, mahopakaraṇaṃ lahuṃ.

"My son is now of an age suitable for the initiation ceremony. To perform his initiation, great preparations must be made quickly."

14.

14.

Sajjetabbanti taṃ sutvā, sopi senādhināyako;

Sabbupakaraṇaṃ khippaṃ, maṅgalatthaṃ susajjayi.

Hearing that it should be arranged, that commander-in-chief also quickly and well prepared all the requisites for the auspicious ceremony.

15.

15.

Sugandha dīpapupphādi-vatthūhi divasattayaṃ;

Pubbakāraṃ karitvāna, mahantaṃ ratanattaye.

For three days, with offerings such as perfumes, lamps, flowers, and cloths, he made a great preliminary act of reverence to the Triple Gem.

16.

16.

Vedikācāradakkhehi, dvijehi puthuvīpati;

Sampabhāvānu rūpaṃva, maṅgalaṃ taṃ samāpiya.

With Brahmins skilled in Vedic rites, the king completed that auspicious ceremony, befitting his majesty.

17.

17.

Parakkamakumārena, tena saddhiṃ samārabhi;

Vasantakīḷaṃ mahatiṃ, sāmacco kīḷituṃ tadā.

Then, together with Prince Parakkama, he and his ministers began to engage in the great spring festival at that time.

18.

18.

Rājā kitti sirīmegho-rohaṇe vasato tadā;

Sirīvallabhanāmassa, sabhātu maraṇampi ca.

At that time, while King Kittisirimegha was residing in Rohaṇa, (he heard of) the death of his own brother, Sirīvallabha.

19.

19.

Māṇabharaṇanāmassa, rajjalābhañca deviyā;

Mittāya paṭilābhañca, sirīvallabhasūnu no.

And of the gaining of the kingdom by Māṇābharaṇa and the queen, and the obtaining of Mittā by the son of Sirīvallabha.

20.

20.

Rohaṇāgatadūtehi, suṇitvā sakabhātuno;

Kālakriyāya sañjāta-sokavegaṃ sudussahaṃ.

Hearing from the messengers who had come from Rohaṇa of his own brother's death, he was overcome by an unbearable surge of grief.

21.

21.

Mittāyatanayuppatti pavattiṃ savaṇena taṃ;

Vineyya virato tamhā, vasantasamayussavā.

Hearing the account of the birth of a son to Mittā, he thereby dispelled his grief and abstained from the spring festival.

22.

22.

Nivattetvāna tattheva, senāniṃ saṅkhanāmakaṃ;

Puttena saha so saṅkha-tthali nāmaṃ puraṃ gami.

Having turned back right there and dismissed the general named Saṅkha, he, together with his son, went to the city named Saṅkhaṭṭhalī.

23.

23.

Parakkamakumārena, tena saddhiṃ tahiṃ sukhaṃ;

Vasato tassa bhūpassa, vassamekamatikkami.

As that king was living there happily with Prince Parakkama, one year passed.

24.

24.

Māṇābharaṇabhūpassa[M 0.0386], devī cāpi pabhāvatī;

Labhittha dutiyā kitti-sirī meghavhayaṃ sutaṃ.

And Pabhāvatī, the queen of King Māṇābharaṇa, obtained a second son named Kittisirimegha.

25.

25.

Suṇitvā tañca so amhaṃ, vaṃso jāto mahā”iti;

Ahu kittisirīmegho, tadā attamano bhusaṃ.

Hearing this, King Kittisirimegha was then greatly delighted, thinking, 'Our lineage has become great!'

26.

26.

Laṃkādīpopabhogeka-hetunā mahatā satā;

Asādhāraṇabhūbhena, codito puññakammunā.

That extraordinary ruler, a great being, was urged on by his meritorious deeds, which had as their sole cause the enjoyment of the island of Laṅkā.

27.

27.

Kumāro so’tha pitarā, piyamitte viyattani;

Kariyamānaṃ sasnehaṃ, mahantaṃ co’palālanaṃ.

Then, the great and affectionate indulgence being shown by his father to that prince, who was like a dear friend and wise,

28.

28.

Sacivānamanekesaṃ, bhayabhattī purassaraṃ;

Kriyamānamupaṭṭhānaṃ, na maññanto tiṇāyapi.

And the service rendered by many ministers with fear and devotion foremost, he regarded not even as a blade of grass.

29.

29.

Laṃkādīpamimaṃ sabba mekacchatto pasobhitaṃ;

Khippaṃ kāretukāmo so, sayaṃ iti vicintayi.

Desiring to swiftly make this entire island of Laṅkā resplendent under a single parasol, he himself thought thus:

30.

30.

Kesa akkhaka gīvaṭṭhi-dāṭhā pattāna meva ca;

Padacetya mahābodhi-sākhānañcāpi satthuno.

The hair, collarbone, neck-bone, tooth, and bowl relics of the Teacher, and also the footprint shrine and the branches of the great Bodhi tree—

31.

31.

Caturāsītisahassānaṃ, dhammakkhandhāna meva ca;

Sammāsambuddhakappānaṃ, ādhārattā ca niccaso.

And of the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma, and because of being the constant support of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones,

32.

32.

Ākarattā ca nekesaṃ, maṇimuttādivatthūnaṃ;

Sammatopi visiṭṭhoti, dīponāti mahā ayaṃ.

And because it is a mine of many gems, pearls, and other valuables, this great island is considered most excellent.

33.

33.

Tayo me pitaro bhūpā, mātulopi ca sabbathā;

Ekacchattena vattetu, masamatthā vibhajji’maṃ.

My three fathers, who were kings, and my maternal uncle as well, were altogether unable to rule under a single parasol and divided this land.

34.

34.

Bhuñjantā ettakeneva, katakiccā mayaṃ iti;

Maññantā vigatacchandā’bhisekamhi kulocite.

Enjoying just this much, thinking, 'We have done our duty,' they lost their desire for the consecration befitting the lineage.

35.

35.

Raṭṭhesake sakeyeva, isseraṃ sampavattayuṃ;

Kasikammādikaṃ gāma-bhojakā viya nissitā.

In their own respective kingdoms they exercised their authority, dependent, like village headmen, on agriculture and the like.

36.

36.

Tesu kittisiri meghaṃ, petteyyaṃ me ṭhapetva te;

Agamaṃsu yathākammaṃ, sesā bhūpatayo tayo.

Among them, having established my paternal uncle Kittisirimegha, the other three kings have departed according to their kamma.

37.

37.

Maccānaṃ paramaṃ āyu, vate’dāni parittakaṃ;

Bālāyuvāno vuddhā ca, ime sattā’nupubbaso.

The maximum lifespan of mortals, alas, is now but short; these beings—the young, the middle-aged, and the old—pass away in succession.

38.

38.

Pāpuṇissanti maraṇa-mīti’yaṃ niyamopi ca;

Na heva asmiṃ lokasmiṃ, saṃvijjati kadācipi.

They will meet death—this too is a fixed rule; for in this world, nothing exists forever.

39.

39.

Tasmā [M 0.0387] sarīrake asmiṃ, bhaṅgure sāravajjite;

Hīḷite sāradassīhi, apekkhaṃ hitvā sabbathā.

Therefore, having completely abandoned attachment to this body—which is fragile, devoid of essence, and despised by the discerning—

40.

40.

Pihaniye yasodehe, ciraṭṭhāyimhi sabbadā;

Amhādisehi kattabbo, rājaputtehi ādaro.

Reverence should always be shown by princes like us for the desirable, ever-enduring body of fame.

41.

41.

Ummaggajātakādīsu, cārittañcāpi bhūmisu;

Vihitaṃ bodhisattena, vīrabhāvādinissitaṃ.

In the Ummaggajātaka and other such accounts, the conduct established by the Bodhisatta, founded on heroism and other such qualities,

42.

42.

Rāmāyaṇabhāratādi-lokiyāsu kathāsupi;

Rāmassa vikkamañceva, tassa rāvaṇaghātino.

And also in worldly stories such as the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, the prowess of Rāma, the slayer of Rāvaṇa,

43.

43.

Duyodhanādirājāno, hantvāyuddhe pavattitaṃ;

Vikkamāti sayañceva, pañcannaṃ paṇḍusūnūnaṃ.

And the very prowess of the five sons of Paṇḍu, displayed in the battle where they slew Duryodhana and other kings,

44.

44.

Itihāsakathāyañca, devāsuraraṇe purā;

Dussantādimahīpehi, katañca caritabbhūtaṃ.

And in the historical accounts, the wonderful deeds performed by great kings such as Dushyanta in the ancient war between the gods and asuras,

45.

45.

Ummūlitavato tassa, nandavaṃsanarissare;

Cārakkadvijaseṭṭhassa, sutvā buddhibalampi ca.

Having heard also of the power of the wisdom of that foremost brahmin Cāṇakka, who had uprooted the lords of men of the Nanda lineage.

46.

46.

Sabbā netāni lokamhi, yāvajjadivasā bhuvi;

Tesaṃ asannidhānepi, suppasiddhiṃ gatāni hi.

All these in the world, for as long as days endure on earth, have indeed attained great renown, even in their absence.

47.

47.

Suladdhaṃ jīvitaṃ tesaṃ, asādhāraṇamīdisaṃ;

Caritātisayaṃ kattuṃ, samatthā honti ye bhuvi.

Well-gained is the life of those, so extraordinary, who are capable of performing exceedingly excellent conduct on earth.

48.

48.

Jāyitvā khattavaṃsamhi, khattavīravarodhitaṃ;

Yadihaṃ na karissāmi, moghā me jāti hessati.

Born into the warrior lineage, distinguished by the best of warriors, if I do not act now, my birth will be in vain.

49.

49.

Tesamabbhadhikā kāla-sampadāyeva kevalaṃ;

Mayā te adhikā kintu, paññādīhīti cintiya.

Theirs was simply a greater fortune of time; but I surpass them in wisdom and so forth—so he reflected.

50.

50.

Piturājā ca me’dāni, pacchime vayasiṭṭhito;

Yadidaṃ pettikaṃ rajjaṃ, mama hatthagatabbhave.

Now my father, the king, is in his final years; this paternal kingdom should come into my hands.

51.

51.

Rājalakkhiva so peta-cetaso me pamādato;

Yathicchitañce na bhave, mahatī jāni me bhusaṃ.

If, due to my negligence, this royal fortune is not as I wish, it will be a great loss to me, whose mind is like that of a departed one.

52.

52.

Ettheva nivasanto’haṃ, carāpiya sake vare;

Paramaṇḍalavuttantaṃ, jāneyyaṃ yadi tattano.

Dwelling right here, and even while moving about in my own excellent domain, how could I know the true state of affairs in other kingdoms?

53.

53.

Randhaṃ paccatthikānantu, pakāsetuṃ rathātathaṃ;

Adhippāyānurūpaṃ me, samatthā vā na vācarā.

Are my spies capable or not of truly revealing the weaknesses of the enemy, in accordance with my intention?

54.

54.

Ye [M 0.0388] keci’dha janā santi, sabbe te mama sammukhā;

Balīyattaṃ’va sattūnaṃ, kathayanti anekaso.

Whatever people are here, all of them, in my presence, repeatedly speak only of the enemy's strength.

55.

55.

Paccekaraṭṭhasāmīhi, pitubhūpehi tihipi;

Ekībhūya karitvāna, sattakkhattuṃ mahāhavaṃ.

With the rulers of each kingdom and with three paternal kings, having united, they waged a great battle seven times.

56.

56.

Sādhetuṃ dukkaraṃ raṭṭhaṃ, bhavate kākinā kathaṃ;

Sisunā gaṇhituṃ sakkā, khuddarajjo pabhoginā.

A kingdom is difficult to conquer; how can it be done by you, who are like a crow? A small kingdom can be seized by a child, an enjoyer.

57.

57.

Sukaraṃ mūlabhūtassa, tassa rajjassa sādhanaṃ;

Iti duccintaṃtaṃ tuyhaṃ, dūre tabbamidaṃ”iti.

The conquest of that well-established kingdom is easy. Thus, this evil thought of yours should be kept far away.

58.

58.

Kaṇṇe tatthasalākāyo, pavesentā’va nekaso;

Mahantattaṃ kathente’vaṃ, bahudhā paramaṇḍale.

As if repeatedly inserting heated rods into the ear, thus they speak in many ways of the greatness of the other kingdom.

59.

59.

Ajānanaṃ yathābhūtaṃ, vadantānaṃ kubuddhinaṃ;

Sabbametaṃ vaco jātu, saddhātabbaṃ siyā na hi.

All this speech of those of poor intellect, who speak without knowing the truth as it is, should never be believed.

60.

60.

Lesenekena gantvāna, khippaṃ’va paramaṇḍalaṃ;

Sarūpaṃ tattha ussāmi, ahameveti cintayi.

Having gone quickly to the other kingdom by some pretext, I myself will ascertain the true situation there, so he thought.

61.

61.

Yadi me pītubhūpālo, viññāyetaṃ vitakkitaṃ;

Abhijātassa puttassa, vaṃsajotikarassa me.

If my father-king were to know this thought of me, his noble-born son who illuminates the lineage—

62.

62.

Gatassa satthu visaya-manatthopi siyā iti;

Anukampādhiyā mayhaṃ, gamanaṃ vārayissati.

Thinking, 'There might be misfortune for me, having gone into enemy territory,' he, out of great compassion for me, will prevent my departure.

63.

63.

Manorathassa saṃsiddhi, sabbathā mena hessati;

Tasmā niguḷarūpena, gamanaṃ bhaddakaṃ iti.

The fulfillment of my wish will in no way come to be; therefore, it is good to go in a concealed form.

64.

64.

Laddhāna rattiyama thekadinaṃ khaṇaññū,

So tādisaṃ khaṇamakhīṇatarorūpāyo;

Jānāti no sakapitāgamanaṃ tathātaṃ,

Gehā’bhinikkhamitathā caturo kumāro.

The knower of the opportune moment, having obtained a single night and day, and possessing great and unfailing means for such a moment, knowing that his father's return was not imminent, thus the clever prince departed from his home.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the purpose of the faith and spiritual urgency of good people.

Paramaṇḍalābhigamano nāma

The Chapter named The Journey to the Other Kingdom.

Dvisaṭṭhimo paricchedo.

The Sixty-second Chapter.

Tisaṭṭhima pariccheda

The Sixty-third Chapter.

Senāpativadho

The Slaying of the General.

1.

1.

Nijāyudhadutiyassa[M 0.0389], nikkhamantassa tassa hi;

Taṃ khaṇaṃ purato ko’pi, saṅkhasaddo samuggato.

Indeed, at the moment he was setting out, accompanied by his own weapon, a certain conch sound arose before him.

2.

2.

Tato nekanimittaññū, kumāro taṃ suṇi tva so;

Nipphajjissati saṅkappo, khippaṃ yeveti modavā.

Then that prince, a knower of many omens, having heard that, rejoiced, thinking, 'My resolve will be fulfilled quickly indeed.'

3.

3.

Tattha tattha niyuttānaṃ, rakkhakānamajānataṃ;

Nikkhamitvā purāvīta-bhayo sīhaparakkamo.

While the guardians appointed here and there were unaware, the fearless one with the prowess of a lion departed from the city.

4.

4.

Vegena maggaṃ gantvāna, pañcagāvutamattakaṃ;

Badalatthalagāmassa, padesenāti dūrake.

Having gone swiftly along the road for about five gāvutas, he came to a place at a distance from the region of the village of Badalatthalā.

5.

5.

Gāma mekamupāgañci, piliṃ vatthūti saññitaṃ;

Janānaṃ sannipātāya, nijānaṃ so katāvadhi.

He approached a certain village named Pili Vatthu; he made it a rendezvous point for the gathering of his own people.

6.

6.

Nijāgamanato pubbaṃ, paṭimagge nisīdituṃ;

Paṭiladdhaniyogānaṃ, yeci devāgate tadā.

Before his own arrival, those who had received their orders and who had arrived there then were to be seated along the path.

7.

7.

Tahiṃ ṭhite so passitvā, ettakā kinnu āgatā;

Iti pucchi kumārotha, tepi taṃ ida mabravuṃ.

Seeing them standing there, the prince then asked, 'How many indeed have come?' They, in turn, replied to him thus:

8.

8.

Lokappavattiṃ sakalaṃ, jānantenāpi sāminā;

Kimeva muccate maccu-bhayaṃ kesaṃ na vijjati.

Even though the Lord knows the entire course of the world, how can one be freed from the fear of death? For whom does it not exist?

9.

9.

Bālātānugato sāmi, ṭhito vayasi īdise;

Ajjāpi hi mukhe tuyhaṃ, khīragandho pavāyati.

Master, you still follow childish ways, standing at such an age; even now, the scent of milk wafts from your mouth.

10.

10.

Na hevatthi visuṃ vitta-jātaṃ saṅgahitaṃ tava;

Tadaññā copakaraṇa-sāmaggī neva vijjate.

There is no wealth separately amassed by you; nor is there any other collection of equipment.

11.

11.

Ciramparicitattehi, daḷhaṃ sāruḷabhattihi;

Vinā’mhehi visuṃ kevā’nugantāro janātuvaṃ.

Long familiar with you, with firm and ardent devotion, without us, what other people would follow you?

12.

12.

Kiñcāgatānamamhākaṃ, pitā tuyhaṃ narissaro;

Kāressati idaṃ nāma, sabbathā neva ñāyate.

Even though we have come, it is not known at all what your father, the lord of men, will cause to be done to us.

13.

13.

Amhākamantarāmagge[M 0.0390], saṅkho nāma camūpati;

Mahabbalo mahāvīro, rajjasīmaṃ tamāvasaṃ.

On our path, in between, is a general named Saṅkha, of great strength and a great hero, who dwells at the kingdom’s border.

14.

14.

Paccatthite ṭhapetvaññe, ete katipayā mayaṃ;

Aññamaññamhi niyata-māsaṅkī hadayā bhusaṃ.

Setting aside other opponents, we are but a few, with hearts greatly suspicious of one another.

15.

15.

Aruṇuggamavelā ca, samāsannatarādhunā;

Iti bhītiṃ pakāsesuṃ, paccekaṃ hadayassitaṃ.

The time of dawn’s rising is now very near; thus they voiced the fear dwelling in each of their hearts.

16.

16.

Nisamma tesaṃ vacanaṃ, vidhāya madhuraṃ sitaṃ;

Vītasaṅko kumāro so, mukhāne’saṃ vilokiya.

Having heard their words and made a sweet smile, that fearless prince looked upon their faces.

17.

17.

Caritvāpi mayā saddhi-mete’ho kālamettakaṃ;

Na jāniṃsu mamaṃ sabbe, yesañhi bhayamidisaṃ.

Alas, even after journeying with me for all this time, all those for whom such fear has arisen have not known me.

18.

18.

Iti vatvā bhayaṃ tesaṃ, vinodetu mupaṭṭhitaṃ;

Sīhanādaṃ tadā’kāsi, mahantaṃ sīhavikkamo.

Having spoken thus to dispel their arisen fear, he who had the prowess of a lion then uttered a great lion's roar.

19.

19.

Tiṭṭhantu mānusā sabbe, mayi hatthagatāyudhe;

Sakko devānamindopi, kupito kiṃ karissati.

Let all men stand aside while I have a weapon in hand; even Sakka, the lord of devas, enraged—what could he do?

20.

20.

Bāloti maṃ cintaya taṃ, jātā vo kumatīdisī;

Parikkhīyati te jāṇā, navayo’ti na kiṃ sutaṃ.

Thinking me a child, such a wrong thought has arisen in you. Your knowledge is found wanting; have you not heard that it is not a matter of age?

21.

21.

Ajjeva kātumekena, kammunā cintitena me;

Sadesapara desaṭṭhā, bhayabhattī yathāmayi.

This very day, by a single deed I have conceived, I will make it so that those in my own land and in foreign lands hold me in fear and devotion.

22.

22.

Karissanti yathā vedaṃ, bhayaṃ tumhe jahissatha;

Tathā rattiyametāya, vibhātāmaya khaṇena me.

When they do so, you shall abandon fear. Thus, in a moment, as this night dawns, it will be accomplished by me.

23.

23.

Unnate dassayissāmi, buddhi sāhasavikkame;

Anudhāvati maṃ tāta, setehi yadi vo bhayaṃ.

I will display my eminence in wisdom, courage, and prowess. If you are afraid, dear friends, follow me.

24.

24.

Purato hotha tumhehi, vatvā te gahitāyudho;

Sāhasekaraso vīro, tamhā nikkhamma gāmato.

Having said to them, 'You go ahead,' the hero, whose sole delight was in courage, took up his weapon and departed from that village.

25.

25.

Udayā’calasīsaṭṭhaṃ, jetumādiccamaṇḍalaṃ;

Aparaṃ ravi bimbaṃva, pacchimā sā mukhoditaṃ.

Like another sun's disk risen from the western direction to conquer the sun's orb standing on the peak of the Udaya mountain.

26.

26.

Tejasā pasarantena, janānaṃ pavikāsayaṃ;

Netambujavanaṃ pāto, badalatthalimāgami.

With his spreading radiance, causing the lotus-grove of the people's eyes to bloom as if at dawn, he arrived at the banyan terrace.

27.

27.

Jaghasaṅkhassarenā’tha, senā nātho pabujjhiya;

Sañjātasambhamo ñatvā, rājaputtamupāgataṃ.

Then, at the sound of the waking-conch, the lord of the army awoke; and knowing that the prince had arrived, he became agitated.

28.

28.

Saddhiṃ [M 0.0391] balena mahatā, padhuggammakatādaro;

Paṇāmamucitaṃ kattu-mānato vasudhātale.

With a great force, having gone forth and shown respect, he paid due homage, prostrating himself on the ground.

29.

29.

Amhākamesajīvanto, kiṃ nāmatthaṃ karissati;

Māretabbo’dhuneveti, passante samukhaṃ bhaṭe.

'Living while being supported by us, what benefit will he do? He must be killed right now!'—thus spoke the soldiers, seeing him face to face.

30.

30.

Nevā’diṭṭhāparādhassa, maraṇaṃ puriso citaṃ;

Vadho virodhe sakkā’ti, iṅgitena nivāriya.

'Death is not fitting for a person whose offense has not been seen; killing is permissible only in conflict'—thus he restrained them with a gesture.

31.

31.

Senāpatissa so hatthaṃ, gahetvā sīhasannibho;

Bhāsanto madhuraṃ vācaṃ, tassevā’gañchi mandiraṃ.

He, resembling a lion, took the hand of the commander; and speaking sweet words, he went to the commander's own mansion.

32.

32.

Athassa gamanaṃ rañño, bhavitabbamajānatā;

Sarūpaṃ yāva jānāmi, tāvassete sahāgatā.

Then the commander, not knowing what was to come of the prince's journey, thought: 'Until I know his true nature, these men who came with him shall stay.'

33.

33.

Yathā na sahitā honti, ṭhapetabbā visuṃ visuṃ;

Kumāro’va mamāgāre, vasatū’ti vicintiya.

Thinking, 'So that they are not united, they must be kept apart from each other; and let the prince himself dwell in my house.'

34.

34.

Tathā senāpati katvā, vañcetuṃ taṃ mahāmatiṃ;

Dassetvā’ti thīsakkāraṃ, rañño dūte sa pesayi.

Having done so, the commander, in order to deceive that wise prince, showed him great hospitality and sent messengers to the king.

35.

35.

Kumāro’tha viditvāna, tena taṃ vañcanaṃ kataṃ;

Kattabbametthā’katvāha, mudāsīno bhave yadi.

Then the prince, understanding the deception wrought by him, thought: 'If I remain indifferent, not doing what must be done here...'

36.

36.

Icchitatthassa nipphatti, na me jātu bhavissati;

Ayaṃ tāvā’dhunāvassaṃ, māretabboti cintiya.

'...the fulfillment of my desired goal will never come to be. This one must certainly be killed right now!'—thus he thought.

37.

37.

Sahāgataṃ payojetvā, ghātāpayi camūpatiṃ;

Hato senādhinātho’ti, mahantaṃ khubhitaṃ ahu.

Having employed an accomplice, he had the army chief slain; 'The army chief is slain!'—great was the commotion that arose.

38.

38.

Senānāthabhaṭo eko, sutvā senāpatiṃ hataṃ;

Māraṇaṃ sāmino mayhaṃ, kiṃ nimittamīti bravi.

A certain soldier of the army chief, hearing that the commander was slain, said: 'What is the reason for the killing of my lord?'

39.

39.

Nettiṃ sapāṇī sahasā, kumāraṃ ṭhitamekakaṃ;

Abhidāvi sasāmissa, paricattattajīvino.

With a net in hand, he swiftly rushed towards the prince who was standing alone, having given up his own life for his master.

40.

40.

Kumārassa mukhaṃ disvā, vedhamāno bhayena so;

Pure ṭhātumasakkonto, pādamūle tato sayi.

Seeing the prince's face, he, trembling with fear and unable to stand before him, then lay down at his feet.

41.

41.

Gaṇhathe’tantivacanā-kumārassa [M 0.0392] puretaraṃ;

Tasseveko sahacaro, bhaṭametaṃ vighātayi.

Even before the prince's words, 'Seize him!', a certain companion of his struck down this soldier.

42.

42.

Niyogaṃ me vinā tena, kataṃ kammaṃ na yujjati;

Iti daṇḍanametassa, kārāpesiyathocitaṃ.

'An act done by him without my command is not proper.' Thus, he had this one punished as was fitting.

43.

43.

Atha taṃ kālayambhūta-saṅkhobhamatibhiṃsanaṃ;

Bhamukkhipanamattena, rājaputto samaṃ nayi.

Then that very fierce commotion that had arisen at that time, the prince subdued with the mere raising of his brow.

44.

44.

Vīro yasodharadhano dhitimā kumāro;

Vīropakāracaturo varakittisāro;

Senindasañcitamanappadhanaṃ bhaṭānaṃ;

Sabbaṃ visajjayi yathāruciyā gahetuṃ.

The heroic prince, rich in fame and steadfast, a hero skilled in benefiting others, of excellent and essential renown, distributed all the abundant wealth amassed by the lord of armies, for the soldiers to take according to their liking.

Sujanappasādasaṃvegatthāya kate mahāvaṃse

In the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the serene joy and spiritual urgency of good people.

Senāpativadho nāma

The Slaying of the Commander

Tisaṭṭhimo paricchedo.

The Sixty-third Chapter.
